News.title: Shocking moment wrong-way driver crashes into woman, 75, at 69mph – slamming car back 23 metres & killing her
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment a car slams into another vehicle while heading the wrong way down a road, killing the 75-year-old driver.

Horrifying CCTV footage shows a silver Vauxhall Astra mounting a pavement just minutes before the fatal collision in Borrowash, Derbyshire on April 10.



It is then seen ploughing into an oncoming blue Honda at speed, with the force of the crash lifting the back of the Honda off the ground.

The Honda’s bonnet crumples instantly as it is pushed 23 metres back from the point of impact.



Both vehicles then collided with another car on Nottingham Road.

Scott Bradley, who was driving the Vauxhall, was arrested at the scene and replied no comment to all questions.





Victim Kathleen O’Neill suffered serious injuries and was taken to hospital, but tragically died two weeks later on April 23.

Investigations found Bradley’s car had been travelling at around 69mph in a 30mph zone at the time of impact.

Two people who had been with Bradley the night before the horror crash said he he had been drinking and taking cocaine during the night and into the following morning.

A female passenger who was in the Vauxhall at the time of the collision claimed she had begged Bradley to slow down but this had only made him accelerate.

She added that a friend had taken the keys from him and driven the car, as he didn’t think he was fit to drive.



But Bradley, 45, had later retrieved these from him and driven off.

Examinations of the Vauxhall showed the speedometer’s last recorded speed at 73mph.

Bradley, from Draycott, was later charged with causing death by dangerous driving.

He admitted the offence and was jailed for 10 years and 6 months on September 21.

He was also banned from driving for a total of 14 years and 3 months and must take an extended re-test before he can drive again.



Detective Constable Rich Howiss, who led the investigation, said: “It is clear from the CCTV and the witness accounts that Bradley was not fit to drive on this day and that he shouldn’t have been behind the wheel.

“He mounted pavements, crashed into street furniture and then eventually crashed straight into Kathleen’s car as she approached him from the opposite direction.

“She had no opportunity to react, or take evasive action as Bradley’s car hit her at speed and pushed her a considerable distance down the road.”

He said that Kathleen’s family had endured an “agonising” two weeks at the hospital, but that she sadly succumbed to her injuries.

He added: “Bradley did manage to survive his injuries but in police interview refused to answer any questions or give his own account. I am glad therefore that he has finally accepted responsibility for his actions by pleading guilty.



“He is now rightly serving a prison sentence and I hope this sentence brings some small form of comfort for Kathleen’s family.

“I’d also like to hope that this shows the very real consequences of dangerous driving, and driving while under the influence.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The risks are real – and you could be responsible for taking someone’s life.

“Please stick to the rules of the road and think about others as well as yourself.”

News.title: Man, 52, found unconscious in the street dies after ‘assault’ during early hours as cops launch murder probe
News.content:
'MURDER' PROBE Man, 52, found unconscious in the street dies after ‘assault’ during early hours as cops launch murder probe







Next

A MURDER investigation has been launched after a man found unconscious in the street later died.

A 52-year-old man was found in Rochdale, Greater Manchester, in the early hours of Saturday morning.

He was rushed to hospital but later died.

Two men have been arrested in connection with the incident.





Greater Manchester Police said: “At around 1.30am, officers responded to reports of an assault on South Parade in Rochdale, where a man, aged 52, was found unconscious.

“He was taken to hospital for treatment but, despite the best efforts of emergency services, he sadly died.

“Two men have been arrested in connection with the incident and remain in custody for questioning.

“Detectives from our Major Incident Team are now leading the investigation and are appealing for anyone who witnessed the incident, has information about what happened, or has relevant CCTV, mobile phone or dashcam footage to come forward.”

Detective Chief Inspector Claire Brennan from the Major Incident Team said: “This is a heart-breaking incident in which a man has tragically lost his life.

“Our thoughts are first and foremost with his family and loved ones who are being supported by specially trained officers at this incredibly difficult time.

“We understand an incident of this nature will also cause concern within the local community.

“I want to reassure people that we have a dedicated team of detectives working to establish the full circumstances surrounding this incident and understand exactly what happened in the moments leading up to it.



“Two men have been arrested in connection with the incident and our enquiries remain ongoing.

“We are now appealing directly to anyone who was in the South Parade area in the early hours of this morning and may have witnessed the incident, or seen anything suspicious before or afterwards, to please speak to us.

“We are particularly keen to hear from anyone who may have CCTV, doorbell, dashcam or mobile phone footage from the area as it could provide vital information to assist our investigation.

“If you have any information, no matter how insignificant you think it may be, please come forward and speak to our officers on 101 or LiveChat quoting log 250 of 26/09/2026”

“Alternatively contact independent charity Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.”

News.title: Frat leaders arrested after dozens of half-naked teens found injured & smeared in condiments in basement
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FRAT BUST Frat leaders arrested after dozens of half-naked teens found injured & smeared in condiments in basement







Next

A GROUP of frat leaders have been arrested after dozens of half-naked teenagers were found injured and smeared in condiments in a basement.

Fraternity president Brayden Klein and vice president Samuel Vane, both 20, were cuffed on suspicion of misdemeanour hazing and disorderly conduct.

Wisconsin police discovered the troubling scene at the Alpha Epsilon Pi fraternity house while following up an anonymous tip.

They found around 30 partially-clothed teen pledges covered in sauces and huddled in a sweltering basement.





The property, near the University of Wisconsin in Madison, was searched at around 8.20pm on Wednesday.

Some of the men had “visible injuries consistent with being physically assaulted”, the police report said.

Others were covered in food, condiments and other liquids, cops claimed.

The room was extremely stuffy and overheated, as the heating was set to 27C, authorities added.

Everyone inside the home was taken outside by police.

The pledges – most of whom were just 18 years old – were checked for ID and injuries.

Local police said the frat was “unrecognised and unaccredited”.

It was “terminated” by the university more than a decade ago, cops explained.



The uni said it was “fully committed to preventing and addressing hazing and takes all incidents involving our community seriously”.

They warned: “Any student determined to be in violation of law, regulation, or university policy may be subject to sanctions according to Wis. Admin. Code Chapter UWS 17.

“These sanctions may include a written reprimand, disciplinary probation, disciplinary suspension, termination, or educational sanctions.”

The uni highlighted Alpha Epsilon Pi was banned from their campus.

But they added it is still a nationally recognised fraternity and therefore is legally allowed to operate as a chapter unaffiliated with the school.

News.title: Jay Slater’s mum reveals fateful moment she ‘still feels guilty about’ & addresses riddle about why he never turned back
News.content:
Next

JAY Slater’s devastated mum has revealed the fateful decision she still feels guilty about as she retraced her son’s final steps in Tenerife.

Debbie Duncan, 57, said she is haunted by why she did not call the 19-year-old after seeing a Snapchat he posted from an Airbnb less than two hours before he vanished.



Jay disappeared in the rugged mountains of northern Tenerife after leaving the remote property following a night out at the NRG music festival.

His disappearance triggered a massive 29-day hunt before his body was discovered at the bottom of an 82ft-deep ravine.



In a new Channel 5 documentary, Debbie reveals she is desperate to understand why Jay couldn’t turn back on to the road after telling pal Lucy in their first call that he felt “frightened”.

Recalling the last Snapchat she saw that morning, Debbie said: “I think, ‘Why did you not ring me?’

“But then I also think, ‘Why did I not ring him when I saw his Snapchat that morning?’

“Nobody knew what was going to happen. I need to stop feeling guilty about that. It’s really hard.”

Jay had left the Casa Abuela Tina Airbnb in Masca at around 8am before apparently attempting to make his way back towards Los Cristianos.

At 8.13am, the apprentice bricklayer shared his location with pals on WhatsApp – later allowing forensic experts to pinpoint where he had been.



But his increasingly desperate calls to pal Lucy Law painted a chilling picture of the trouble he was in.

When Lucy called him at 8.32am, Jay said he was thirsty and “frightened”.

His final communication came at 8.50am when he told her he was in the “middle of nowhere” and “all I can see are mountains”.



His phone died just two minutes later.

One question has tortured Debbie ever since – why her terrified son did not turn around and retrace his steps back towards the road.

She returned to the treacherous landscape with her brother Glen Duncan for the documentary Cause Of Death to follow the route Jay is believed to have taken.

And after finally seeing the unforgiving terrain for herself, Debbie said she understood how her son could have become trapped in the wilderness.

She said: “We thought, how was it possible to get to a place where he said to Lucy, ‘I’m lost, all I can see is mountains’? He must have been so scared, thinking, I can’t turn back.



“And when you look at it, you just know why. The closure I’ve got is from the walk, knowing where he set off from, how he has seen the ocean and gone down, and where he got to before he died.



“Seeing all that now, I understand it better. That’s what closure has given me.”

The emotional journey came after Debbie finally received the delayed Spanish post-mortem report into Jay’s death this summer.

It confirmed the teenager was killed by the catastrophic injuries he suffered in the fall.

Debbie had spent two years tormented by fears that her “beautiful boy” could have lain injured and suffering on the mountainside.

But pathologist Dr Richard Shepherd, who conducted the Home Office post-mortem, was able to give her a crucial answer.



He told The Sun: “The main question Debbie had was, ‘Did he feel anything?’

“She wanted to know how his injuries would have affected him.

“I was able to tell her that yes, it was an awful injury, and yes, it killed him.

“But the head injury was so severe that it probably would have killed him immediately. It was the end – there was no pain and suffering.

“He wasn’t injured on the hillside dying slowly, and that was important for her to understand.”



Jay’s disappearance had sparked a frenzy of wild conspiracy theories online, with TikTok sleuths flooding social media with claims about what had happened to him.

The Spanish post-mortem revealed police had even sent his voice box for further examination amid fears he may have been strangled.

But a second post-mortem found no evidence of strangulation or any other deliberate harm.

Dr Shepherd said neither examination suggested anything other than Jay becoming confused and disorientated before suffering a tragic fall.

For Debbie, physically walking through the brutal landscape finally helped make sense of a question she had carried for two years.



Laying flowers near the spot where her son left the road, the grieving mum broke down as she imagined what Jay would tell her now.

She said: “I know he’d be so sorry for the mistakes he made.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“He’d be saying, ‘I’m so sorry, Mum.’”

News.title: Viral TikTok baker with over 1million followers arrested on suspicion of fraud after customer complaints
News.content:
PIECE OUT Viral TikTok baker with over 1million followers arrested on suspicion of fraud after customer complaints







Next

A VIRAL TikTok baker with over 1million followers has been arrested on suspicion of fraud after a string of customer complaints.

Terry Pegler, known as Terry Bakes on social media was taken into custody yesterday on suspicion of fraud by false representation.



The 39-year-old, from Easton, Norwich, said the arrest has left his “family going through hell.”

Neighbours reported seeing several police cars outside his four-bedroom detached home early yesterday morning.



Cops also took Pegler’s wife, Nikita, into custody when they arrested the social media star.

Both have since been bailed while police continue to investigate the couple.



Pegler took to social media after his arrest to tell his customers he would not complete his backlog of orders.

People were told to seek chargebacks from their banks as Pegler said he couldn’t issue refunds.

Trading Standards said it was reviewing complaints it had received about the baker, who used to run a business called Bake Away.

In a social media video, Pegler said he would use money he earned on TikTok to tackle his backlog of orders.



He said: “On the fifteenth of each month, I get paid on TikTok. Every penny I earn, through the views I get on TikTok I will put towards sending your boxes out.”

Pegler posted several videos after the announcement, including one where he was baking his “last drip cake” as well as a “viral millionaires bolognaise”.

A police spokesperson said: “A man aged in his 30s and a woman aged in her 40s arrested yesterday, on September 24, on suspicion of fraud by false representation have been released on bail until 16 December while inquiries continue.”

News.title: Married men sneak off on their lunch breaks & hire me for a hotel ‘quickie’ but it’s not cheating… rise of alt ‘escorts’
News.content:
Next

A LONELY husband opens the hotel room door to a glamorous young woman – and for as little as £70 she’ll keep him busy on his lunch break.

The busty brunette is 5’11” and sets his heart pounding as she ushers him onto the bed.



But it’s not sex she is offering. Clients of the new wave of alternative escorts can cuddle up to some of the most beautiful women in the world – but nothing more.

The idea of a professional cuddle service is born from touch therapy, which can help build confidence and reduce stress.

However, sites like CuddleComfort.com – where cuddlers and clients create profiles with photos, interact and leave reviews – give it the feel of something closer to OnlyFans or even AdultWork.



With many sessions taking place in hotel rooms and a growing focus on cuddlers’ looks and sex appeal, it can appear to blur the line between companionship and something more sexual.

Visitors to the Cuddle Comfort website must sign a waiver agreeing not to make “sexual advances” towards the “pros” before meeting them.

The rules also stipulate that both parties must remain clothed during sessions.

However, that isn’t always the case, with cuddlers and clients both reporting boundaries being pushed.

Luana, 24, from London, is one of scores of glam Brits moonlighting as a professional cuddler, offering men the chance to tuck up in bed for a warm embrace.



Luana goes by the username HeartToHeal and is rated at five stars.

Her bio says she’s 5ft 11in and fit and says: “I’m in a serious relationship and do not appreciate any type of sexual requests.”

But despite her clear warning, it hasn’t always been respected.



Luana, who has been a professional cuddler since 2022, told The Sun: “People push boundaries very often sadly – that’s why I have to be quite strict about it, no exceptions.”

She keeps herself safe by telling loved ones whenever she’s meeting a client – and often doubles up with another cuddler for an extra fee and extra protection.

Luana said her first ever experience was “actually quite bad” and said the man wanted to roleplay 50 Shades of Grey.

The glamourous brunette says: “He asked me for extras and just kept being inappropriate throughout the session.

“He was rubbing on me constantly in a very sexual manner.



“I don’t think I was as strict back then as I should’ve been. I should have kicked him out. He was looking for pleasure not therapy.”

Luana prefers to meet her clients at home – but many others use hotels.

The parallels with the sex industry run deeper, however, with clients using hotel day-booking apps for sessions.



One professional cuddler wrote on the Cuddle Comfort forum of such apps: “They don’t ask for credit card as they allow cash payments… It’s known to be discreet.”

Delving into the forums, both cuddlers and clients talk about a “dark side” to the industry, with little to protect them if things go wrong.

One customer even said he had to bail out of a session because the cuddler failed to respect his boundaries, adding: “Just wanna keep everyone safe.”

Writing in The Baffler, a former Cuddle Comfort cuddler said: “The value the service cuddle sites offered and their niche in the market depended on successfully maintaining the distinction between sex work and cuddling – as did the sites’ legality.”

She said there were plenty of rules, and a signed agreement, but the prospect of ensuring they were all followed was “daunting”.



She added that “boundary-pushing proved to be the standard among paid Cuddle Comfort users rather than an exception”.

Luana, who found out about “professional cuddling” through TikTok, makes between £300 and £600 a week through the website, arranging at least three cuddles a week.

She says: “⁠I started doing it for the money and of course that’s the main part of it.”

But while Luana and other cuddlers have to be on their guard, and there are some unpleasant clients, there are others where she can see they benefit from the therapy.

She explains: “⁠People feel lonely, anxious, exhausted or disconnected from themselves or others so this is a way to feel valued, cared for and forget about the real world and its struggles for a bit.



“Cuddling is a more efficient form of therapy because it mixes talking and touching in one. It should be more widespread.”

The Sun has approached Cuddle Comfort for comment.

News.title: Smiling Burnham arrives for his 1st Labour conference & promises ‘new direction’ for UK after ruling out early election
News.content:
NO BURN Smiling Burnham arrives for his 1st Labour conference & promises ‘new direction’ for UK after ruling out early election







Next

SMILING Andy Burnham has arrived for his first Labour conference as he promised a “new direction” for the UK – after ruling out an early election.

The Prime Minister – who also had his inaugural trip to the United Nations this week – today vowed to set out how he will deliver “good growth in every postcode, hope in every heart”.



Speaking on Saturday afternoon outside the Liverpool Experience Campus after posing for selfies with supporters, Mr Burnham said: “We’re going to make this a really important week where we set out a new direction for the country.

“We’ve had a decade since Brexit and it’s been a decade of too much drift, too much division, and we need to draw a line on that.”





He said his vision would leave “people able to have hope again that things will improve, that life will get better – and it will”.

It comes after the PM said yesterday he is determined not to put the voting public through the division of an early poll.

He can wait until the summer of 2029 before deciding to hold an election.

His remarks came as a mega-poll this week revealed Labour would lose their majority and be left with only 241 seats – short of the 326 seats needed.



When asked whether he was tempted to hold an early poll, he told BBC West: “Not particularly. No, I’m not.

“And I see all the speculation and it just races ahead. And, you know, the media love to do that. No, no election any time soon.”

During his inaugural trip to the UN, Mr Burnham avoided being chewed up and spat out by Donald Trump – something banked as a win by No10.



While Trump’s mauling of the “ridiculous” Chagos deal grabbed the headlines, Burnham’s team played up the firm defence of the Falkland Islands he gave behind closed doors.

The White House was left in no doubt about Britain’s unwavering position on the islands, sources say.

But senior insiders also say the President subjected Burnham to his usual shellacking over illegal immigration.

They say that Trump’s blistering criticism of countries failing to tackle migration during his main speech was primarily directed at Britain.

So while Burnham survived this time – he is after all only weeks into the job – failing to deliver could see the relationship sour.



Ahead of the conference, several Labour figures have acknowledged Burnham’s leadership has reinvigorated Labour following Sir Keir Starmer’s time in No 10.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell told the Guardian said the Government under Sir Keir had “lost sight of some of the politics and the purpose”.

Speaking to the BBC on Saturday, Lisa Nandy said: “I think the reason, frankly, that we had a change of leadership at the start of this year is because we all felt that people need to feel the change in their lives that we promised in 2024 much more quickly.”

Labour chair Bridget Phillipson would not be drawn when asked if Sir Keir’s two years of leadership had been a wasted opportunity for the party.

Instead, she told PA: “I’ll be forever grateful to Keir for taking us to one of the best election results in our history, and over the last two years we’ve made huge strides forward, whether it’s on better rights at work, on giving more protections for renters, and on tackling child poverty, and we are on course to lift the biggest number of children out of poverty in any parliament.



“That is extraordinary in terms of the scale and depth of the achievement. But there is more to do, and we know that the public are impatient for change, want to see it, and they want to feel it.

“That’s why Andy Burnham this week will be setting out how we step up that change, how we demonstrate that people can feel better off, can see that sense of change within their communities.

“But Andy Burnham builds on two years of a fantastic Labour Government, but with more to come.”

The Prime Minister faces unrest among senior Labour figures as the party heads into his first conference in power.

Peter Kyle – who served as Sir Keir’s business secretary – warned that Mr Burnham was not doing enough to boost economic growth.



Mr Kyle insisted he was not making a criticism of Mr Burnham, as he told the BBC the Government needed to make more short-term decisions to boost growth, like slowing the rollout of new workers’ rights.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Communities Secretary Angela Rayner meanwhile used a pre-conference interview with the Times to hit out at plans by her Cabinet colleague Shabana Mahmood which would lengthen foreign social care workers’ path to claiming permanent settlement.

The plans are also opposed by other figures across Labour, and could be the source of a row at the party conference.

News.title: Moment rapist says ‘if you can’t look after your kids don’t have them’ as cops quiz grooming gang
News.content:
Next

THIS is the chilling moment a grooming gang rapist blames his victim’s parents telling cops “if you can’t look after your kids don’t have them”.

Five people have been sentenced to more than 80 years in prison after they were convicted of multiple child sexual exploitation offences across Denbigshire, North Wales.



The four Asian men and a British-born woman were convicted of their roles in the sexual exploitation of the girls then aged between 14 and 16.

The vulnerable girls were targeted after being spotted out walking alone at night in a seaside town, pressured into providing sexual services in exchange for cannabis and cocaine.





Mustafa Iqbal, 43, Ziaullah Badsha, 25, Mohamed Arshad, 36, and Jaswinder Singh, 65, faced 28 charges including trafficking for sexual exploitation, rape, supplying drugs and sexual assaults.

And as Badshah was quizzed by cops, he told them: “If you can’t look after your kids, don’t have them.”



Sarah Gray, 53, was was also found guilty of perverting the course of justice, assisting an offender, conspiracy to supply cocaine and cannabis, with a judge telling her she had “sold her soul” to the gang.

Caernarfon Crown Court heard how two girls – aged 14 and 15 – were spotted walking late one night in Rhyl, having smoked drugs in March 2022.

They were then spotted by Iqbal, a drug dealer and takeaway driver, who was riding an e-scooter and invited them to his home, reports Metro.

He then invited Arshad and Badshah to join them as they gave the teens drugs and alcohol and played “spin the bottle”.

The court heard sex happened in cars, residential addresses and at business premises.



Iqbal also treated a third girl, aged 16, who was a crack cocaine addict, as a “sex slave” and handcuffed her to carry out a brutal rape.

And he was nearly caught having sex with the teen at his home by his own children, the court was told.

Judge Mills told him: “You have raped two girls, one of whom you raped on multiple occasions, including the final brutal rape, during which you handcuffed her and used other significant force, as well.

“You did everything you possibly could to damage that girl. You treated her simply as a sexual object in an extremely controlling way, and you raped her, in my judgement, on many occasions.

“I have no doubt you are a dangerous offender.”



CHILLING CASE Five people were sentenced to a combined 80 years in prison following a three-month trial at Caernarfon Crown Court. Mustafa Iqbal, 43, of Trellewelyn Road, Rhyl, was convicted of: Four counts of rape

Three counts of conspiracy to require a person to perform compulsory labour

Three counts of sexual assault

Three counts of causing a person to engage in sexual activity without consent

Two counts of conspiracy to traffic

Conspiracy to supply cannabis to another

Conspiracy to supply cocaine to another

Supplying cannabis to another

Arranging or facilitating the travel of another person with a view to exploitation

Breaching a slavery/trafficking risk order Mohamed Usman Arshad, 36, of Clifton Grove, Rhyl, was convicted of: Three counts of rape

Two counts of conspiracy to traffic

Two counts of conspiracy to require a person to perform compulsory labour

Supplying cannabis to another Ziaullah Badshah, 25, of Brighton Road, Rhyl, was convicted of: Two counts of rape

Two counts of conspiracy to traffic

Two counts of conspiracy to require a person to perform compulsory labour

Supplying cannabis to another Jaswinder Singh, 61, of River Street, Rhyl, was convicted of: Two counts of conspiracy to traffic

One count of supplying cannabis to another Sarah Gray, 53, of Llanasa Road, Gronant, was convicted of: Perverting the course of justice

Assisting an offender

Conspiracy to supply cocaine to another

Conspiracy to supply cannabis to another

It was also heard how Singh had arranged to take one of the girls to London.

He told the girl that she should pretend to his sister that she was his 22-year-old carer to avoid her concluding that he was part of an “Asian grooming gang.”

The police were contacted after a friend of the girl became concerned and the four men were arrested.

A three-month trial at Caernarfon Crown Court heard evidence of rape, sexual assault, child sexual exploitation, modern day slavery offences, drug supply, and attempts to obstruct justice.

All offences were reviewed by North Wales Police detectives as part of linked investigations named Operation Embank and Operation Zirconium, which targeted those involved in child sexual exploitation and human trafficking.



Iqbal was jailed for 30 years and given a five year extended licence period while Arshad was jailed for 19 years.

Badshah was sentenced to 17 years while Singh and Gray were jailed for eight years each.

Senior Investigating Officer, DCI Richard Sidney said: “The conclusion of this case marks an important moment for the three victims, who have had to live with the consequences of what happened to them for a considerable period of time and continue to do so.

“The sentences imposed today reflect the gravity of the group’s offending and the very serious nature of the crimes committed against these young women.

“These investigations were complex and involved extensive work to understand what had happened, gather evidence, and ensure those responsible were brought before the court.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“I recognise that the criminal justice process can be incredibly difficult for victims of sexual exploitation, particularly when they are required to revisit traumatic experiences. The courage shown by the victims throughout these investigations and the trial that followed has been remarkable.

“I hope that today’s outcome provides them with some sense of justice and allows them to look towards the future with greater confidence.”

News.title: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years
News.content:
Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.

The government had hoped the new runway at the UK's busiest airport, estimated to cost Â£49bn, would open by 2035.

But Heathrow sees this deadline as increasingly difficult to deliver without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said on Saturday that it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade".

The Department for Transport (DfT) said the project's timeline had "always been ambitious" and that it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter.

The airport said its "core scenario" had always been to open a new runway within a decade of securing planning permission.

It said it was encouraged by the chancellor's efforts to streamline infrastructure and remove policy and regulatory bottlenecks, and promised to continue to work with ministers, airlines and stakeholders to "progress the planning application with pace".

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government's support for the project in January 2025, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was previously critical - said he was "open-minded" about the scheme when he came to office.

Despite attracting wide opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups from neighbouring areas, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the economy.

The expansion would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway.

The number of flights from the airport, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average.

London Mayor Sadiq Khan has always opposed the project, warning of the impact on noise, air pollution and climate change.

A consultation on the expansion was published in June this year. Once finalised, it then needs to be put to a parliamentary vote, which could reportedly be delayed until 2027.

News.title: No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains
News.content:
It is impossible to know exactly to what extent City benefited on the field from their rule breaches. And which players they may not have been able to afford if they had adhered to the regulations.

And what about the period between December 2018 and February 2023, when City stand accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations?

Should retrospective action be applied then too? Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City twice during that time, by a single point in both 2019 and 2022. Last year, the German coach joked he would host a party in his garden if his former club were suddenly awarded those titles.

Some will conclude that the rule breaches between 2009 and 2018 helped City to lay the foundations on which Guardiola built on to achieve so much success, culminating in the Treble triumph of 2023.

Does that era come into scope? Where does it end?

For some, the mass reallocation of titles over such a long period would risk making a mockery of Premier League history, jeopardising its reputation and commercial viability. Others would argue that some 17 years after the first alleged breach, and with City accused of distorting the competition over multiple seasons, serious damage has already been done to the league's standing.

And while there is no Premier League precedent, such concerns have not prevented such punishments being applied before in football. Juventus had the Serie A titles they won in 2005 and 2006 revoked as a result of the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal - when five Italians teams were penalised for attempting to influence results by picking certain referees. The first title was left blank by authorities, with the second reallocated to Inter Milan.

There is also a British precedent. Elgin City won the 1992-93 Highland League, but were later stripped of the title after having been found to have fielded ineligible players.

There are examples in other sports too. In 2012, Lance Armstrong was stripped of his seven Tour de France titles by the UCI, cycling's governing body, for doping. And the reallocation of medals has become commonplace in athletics as a result of positive drugs tests that can emerge long after events have taken place.

In cases such as City's, involving financial rule breaches, the argument for such a punishment is more complicated. Many will see it as unfair that players and fans unconnected to any rule breaches should suffer by losing titles.

And with some suggesting that relations between the United Arab Emirates and the UK could be put under serious pressure by this ruling, one can only imagine the diplomatic tensions if past titles were then taken away from the club.

On Friday, former City midfielder Rodri dismissed talk of the club being stripped of some of the titles they won.

"What we did, they cannot take out of us," he added.

"It's something that is not paid by money. It's paid with effort, with the damage, with, you know, being shoulder to shoulder every day.

"I can tell you that everything was deserved, and I'm glad that I could live one of the best eras of English football in here."

Others, however, will insist the rewriting of history is the only way of restoring the competition's official record, and rewarding clubs that competed within the rules.

In terms of retrospective action, the compensation claims for lost earnings that several clubs are known to be considering launching against City are more likely than the stripping of titles.

A lawyer told me: "The question isn't whether the clubs can take legal action... it's: Where does the line of people who have a case actually end?

"The clubs who didn't win/qualify/stay up; the players who didn't get bonuses, contract extensions; the staff who missed out on bonuses; the agents who didn't get their uplift on their player deals...

"It's endless and potentially so destructive to the whole ecosystem."

Whatever happens, more division and disruption seems guaranteed.

News.title: How long can Labour's feel-good factor last?
News.content:
"He just loves being prime minister," a government insider observes.

Andy Burnham might not yet have delivered his all-important conference speech, but he has been preparing for this moment for years.

He'll lap up the inevitable whoops and cheers â not just as Labour's leader, but the kind of leader who chimes with the party's rank and file, who puts social justice at the top of his list, who is not averse to cranking up the greatest hits â whether taking a pop at Mrs Thatcher, privatisation, or the divides between north and south.

Speaking to MPs, ministers and advisers inside the party, there is no doubt whatsoever that Labour is in a much, much happier place than this time last year.

There is a very simple reason, according to one cabinet minister, fans of Sir Keir Starmer, look away now, "people like the new prime minister more than they liked the old one â that's the truth of it".

Another minister tells me: "There is no appetite for destruction â very little naysaying."

But Labour is in a position that's been all too rare for all our political parties in the last few years â there are no whispers about chucking out the leader, no-one stirring revolt.

And even those who don't like the direction of travel are labelling their opinions as a desire to be helpful, they're not trying to criticise the boss.

"The mood's good â everyone is going into conference with their ears open," one MP said, keen to hear more from the prime minister.

The feel-good factor is also driven by the party inching up a little in the polls â one senior figure says: "We're all witnessing the Burnham bounce â whether that's how you feel when you see the polls, or how we all feel when we have meetings together."

News.title: Met to re-examine CCTV from Jill Dando murder case
News.content:
The Met Police has confirmed it will re-examine CCTV footage relating to the unsolved murder of Jill Dando, 27 years ago.

The BBC presenter and journalist was shot dead with a single bullet on her doorstep in Fulham in April 1999. Despite one of the biggest and most high-profile murder investigations in British history, the case remains unsolved.

A Met spokesperson said recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology had "provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station".

The CCTV includes an unidentified man who was seen sprinting near the scene of the shooting, 20 minutes after the event.

The Met said in the 27 years since Dando's death, the investigation had been "subject to numerous reviews", aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.

It warned this latest review was part of "ongoing inquiries and should not be interpreted as a significant line of inquiry nor as a new investigation being opened on this matter".

News.title: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game
News.content:
Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture.

Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the squad before the game.

But he added that a vote among the squad produced a "significant majority" in favour of playing.

As well as the intention to wear black armbands for Sunday's 'away' game against Israel in Debrecen, Courell said the players will make further gestures for the initial game and the return 'home' fixture against Israel next Sunday in Serbia.

The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.

Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace.

"One of their requests is to remove their media obligations for the remainder of this window," Courell said at Saturday's delayed news conference.

"They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict.

"There will be elements of the pre-match ceremony not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland and it is also the intention of the players to make a significant contribution to charitable donation by virtue of both [Israel] match fees and also the fixture against Austria at the Aviva [Stadium in Dublin on Thursday]."

News.title: Watch: Prince Harry says 'kids are happy' in British school after six years in US
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has said it feels "great" to be back in Britain after spending six years living in California.

He told Canadian network CTV: "It's been great. It's been great to be back on British soil. The kids are happy in school and it gives me a chance to be able to really focus on the Invictus Games in Birmingham in July next year."

Prince Harry and Meghan stepped back as senior royals and began a new life in the US in 2020, before returning to live in Britain last month.

It is thought the family are basing themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

The couple's children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, had to be moved to a different school only days after they started over security concerns about the school run.

It is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had raised concerns about the distance and heavy traffic on the route to the school.

Harry and Meghan's return to the UK has been marked by tensions with the Royal Family.

News.title: How the bare nails trend became a class issue
News.content:
And when waves of Vietnamese refugees gave rise to the nail bar in the 1970s, professional manicures were no longer the preserve of the rich.

But, like many luxuries, as they became more popular and more accessible to the masses, the wealthy began pivoting â a textbook example of behaviour known as "counter signalling", Rudolfo says.

"The same way that logo bags are considered gauche or quiet luxury is more aspirational, bare nails are considered the trend now.

"The examples are almost always white women or celebrities... [and] they'll often conflate class and taste with that bareness."

Others point out bare nails often demand their own time-consuming and costly routine.

"The irony in all this is these natural nails are not natural either," Shapiro says. "They also require a lot of grooming and sometimes pretty premiere services."

Few would argue there aren't valid feminist questions for the beauty industry to answer, around unrealistic standards for example, but the largely female-run nail sector also feels empowering for many women.

"I feel like nail care has very much had a 'for women, by women' sort of ethos around it," Shapiro says. "The first salon opened in New York City was owned by a woman, and she was a remarkably independent one... a lot of the first entrepreneurs offering product lines, opening salons were women."

Hampton admits she's saddened by the way trends have been â and continue to be - weaponised.

"We're taking the fun out of nails... Anyone should be able to wear what they like - nail polish or bare nails," she says. "Why is there an argument? Why is there beef?"

Scanlon too is a little baffled.

"For me, it's like, just stop judging ourselves and everybody else," she says. "Some people like to have the nails done, some people don't.

"I suppose the question that I was posing was, is it doing anything for you?

"The truth of it is: it's not that deep."

News.title: Your child has left home. Here's why it's time to stop checking up on them
News.content:
"Sometimes parents send their child to university and they're not even worried, but then these group chats create a worry that something might be wrong," says Rayyah Uddin, 20, a third-year student at the University of Nottingham.

She knows of WhatsApp group chats being set up by parents of first-year students at her university and has also seen parents use TikTok to share their worries about their child not making friends, and asking other parents for their help.

"These are issues the students should really be figuring out for themselves, and it is better if parents try and talk to their child rather than immediately jump to other parents," she says.

Not hearing from your child all the time isn't necessarily a cause for concern - "they might just be having a really good time and are getting absorbed into university life," Rayyah adds.

Parent social media groups can be useful, according to psychologist Charlotte Armitage, but not when they are used to share private difficulties, track movements or ask questions that the student is capable of asking themselves.

"Constant checking, tracking or intervening may soothe the parent in the short term, but it can inadvertently communicate to the young adult: 'I am not sure you can cope without me.'"

"Of course, where there is a credible safeguarding concern, a significant change in behaviour, or a known risk to their wellbeing, parents should act."

News.title: Man City chairman confident club will prove innocence
News.content:
Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak says he is still confident of proving the club's innocence after they were found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.

City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centring around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations.

On Friday, it was announced City had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them and Al Mubarak has responded with a letter to fans on the club's website.

"Following Friday's media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I," Al Mubarak said.

"Here's what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began.

"There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position.

"But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."

Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told City will appeal.

Sanctions on the club are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine.

Al Mubarak, who was appointed as City's chairman after their 2008 takeover, also said his club was being "undermined".

"While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed," he added.

"There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity."

News.title: Rayner criticises visa rule proposals ahead of Labour conference
News.content:
Before he became prime minister, Burnham said he "understood" where Rayner was coming from on her criticisms of the migrant visa changes, telling reporters in June that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".

Rayner's call for a change of approach has been echoed by York Central Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who also wants a rethink from the home secretary.

She told the Today programme that "technically and morally" what is being proposed represented "the wrong set of values" and would affect "people who have come [to Britain] to serve faithfully and are then told that they have to wait another 10 years" to secure British citizenship.

In recent weeks, trade unions have put pressure on the government to soften its proposals, and a letter to Mahmood jointly signed by dozens of Labour MPs at the start of the year described the plans as "un-British".

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for culture, media and sport, rejected the "un-British" description of the plans.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I don't think they are un-British because I don't think that we have ever had an automatic right to citizenship for most people who come to the UK from overseas."

Nandy said the home secretary was trying to balance respect for people "regardless of who they or where they stand" with the need for "an immigration system that people have confidence in".

Asked if Labour could change its mind on the proposals, she told Today: "We always reserve the right to change our minds but we also will reserve the right to stick to our plans if we think we are getting them right".

The culture secretary said the government will not "change the rules of the game" in a way that unfairly disadvantages migrants who have contributed to the UK.

She said it would "strike the right balance" between treating people "fairly and decently as human beings but making sure there is an asylum and immigration system people can have confidence in."

Nandy's comments are a hint the government is reconsidering. She could have given a full-throated defence of the principle of backdating the changes so they apply to those foreign workers already here.

But she did not. Instead she emphasised the principle of those "contributing" to the UK and treating them fairly.

But if the government does reverse course on applying these changes to those arriving from 2021, the large numbers who came to the UK after that date have a quicker and easier route to settlement. That is a dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK that those parties will be keen to highlight.

The home secretary faced questions about the changes during an appearance at the Home Affairs Committee earlier this month.

Mahmood said she was "very aware that a large group of people who arrived in 2022, absent any change, would qualify in February 2027" for permanent settlement.

She added: "Later this year we will set out the new policy on settlement... as well as any transitional arrangements we might decide to implement."

News.title: E-motorbikes seized by police sold on at auction, BBC finds
News.content:
Electric motorbikes seized by police forces in the UK are being sold on at auction, despite some fears they could end up back in the hands of criminals, the BBC can reveal.

Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally, or used in a crime - most are later destroyed, but a BBC investigation has found some are sold on to members of the public in online auctions.

Across the UK, police sold 161 e-bikes and e-motorcycles last year and 54 in 2024, although the real number could be higher because not every force responded to the BBC's Freedom of Information request.

Some of the forces said they had now ended the practice, but others defended it as a way of putting "money back into policing".

Six forces responded to say some of the vehicles they had seized had been sold, including large forces such as West Midlands Police and Police Scotland.

The figure includes electrically-assisted pedal cycles, which look similar to bicycles and have a motor that kicks in as a rider pedals, as well as electric motorbikes, which are usually more powerful and are propelled only by their motor.

E-bikes and e-motorcycles have become controversial because some think they are linked to crime and anti-social behaviour.

Recent BBC reporting has highlighted cases across the country of balaclava-clad young men riding illegally on footpaths and intimidating residents.

There have also been a number of pedestrian deaths, including 86-year-old grandmother Gloria Stephenson, who was struck at a zebra crossing in Sunderland last year by an illegal e-motorbike.

News.title: Legal challenge to Drumcree parade decision under way
News.content:
A legal challenge to the Parades Commission's decision to allow the Orange Order to march on the mainly-nationalist Garvaghy Road in Portadown is under way at the High Court in Belfast, where a large crowd has gathered outside.

The commission announced that the parade can proceed on Sunday, for the first time in almost 30 years, with restrictions in place.

Rather than start at 13:00 BST on Sunday as intended, the commission has said the march can depart no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants rather than the 60 the Orange Order requested. No bands or supporters are allowed.

The decision is facing the legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition, which opposes the march.

The coalition has also applied to the Parades Commission for a protest to the walk on Sunday, listing the number of participants at 5,000. A decision is expected on Saturday, according to the commission. , external

News.title: Burnham not doing enough to boost growth, says former business secretary
News.content:
A cabinet minister under Sir Keir Starmer has said Andy Burnham's government is not focused enough on boosting economic growth and needs to act with "more urgency".

Speaking to the BBC two months after being sacked in Burnham's cabinet reshuffle upon entering office, Peter Kyle said he wasn't making a "criticism" but "pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government".

"If the destination means prosperity, it means freedom for people to do new things, and it means security for people and families, then why wouldn't we put our foot down and get there quicker," the former business secretary said.

It comes as Labour prepares to gather in Liverpool for its annual conference.

Burnham will address the conference on Tuesday and has said his speech would leave nobody in any doubt about "what I'm trying to do in this role."

He has previously said his time as Greater Manchester mayor had given him "a clear theory of growth" stressing his belief in the importance of devolving powers to local areas.

Giving regions and nations more control would, he has argued, create the conditions for "good growth in every postcode".

Kyle served as science secretary and later business secretary in the Starmer government, but has now returned to the backbenches as the MP for Hove and Portslade.

In an interview with the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg, he said the government should be willing to take decisions that involve "short-term" pain in order to deliver economic growth, suggesting a delay to expanding workers' rights.

"We might need to look and have honest conversations with unions about how we sequence some of the rights going forward in order to make sure that we get growth into the economy in the shorter term," he said.

The government's Employment Rights Act was passed in December 2025 but some of the changes are not due to come into force until next year.

The former minister also suggested introducing a "tax growth test" which would measure the impact of each tax on the economy and asking government experts to review "obstacles" to growth.

Asked if there was enough focus on growth in the government, Kyle replied: "I don't think there is and that isn't a criticism - it is pointing to the potential that we have as a country and as a government.

"I think we need to up our ambition, I think that we need to act with more urgency when it comes to economic growth."

Chancellor John Healey is due to give his first Budget on 28 October, but faces rising debt costs and warnings of slower economic growth.

According to the Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the UK economy is expected to grow by 1%, slightly less than the 1.1% previously forecast.

Responding to Kyle's comments that the government needed to act with more urgency on economic growth, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy suggested that the prime minister was moving faster than his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I think the the reason, frankly, that we had a change of leadership at the start of this year is because we all felt that people need to feel the change in their lives that we promised in 2024 much more quickly."

She added that she believed Burnham was "impatient for change, and he thinks big about the sort of change that the country needs".

News.title: WW2 sailor and SBS member dies aged 101
News.content:
One of the West of England's last surviving veterans from World War Two has passed away aged 101.

Harry Francis, from South Gloucestershire, joined the Royal Navy in 1942 at 16, having lied about his age to serve.

He went on to join the Royal Marines and became one of the first men to join the Special Boat Service (SBS), carrying out covert operations in Italy, Lebanon and Burma, where he was wounded.

South Gloucestershire Armed Forces Day put out a tribute on social media where organisers said: "His quiet bravery and his remarkable life will not be forgotten."

News.title: Memorial for pupils contaminated with HIV and hepatitis
News.content:
The memorial installed at the college, near Alton, Hampshire, depicts two pupils, one with a sling and and another holding a cane, embracing each other.

Adrian Goodyear, 55, who first attended Treloar's when he was nine, said: "We couldn't believe the place we were looking at. Rolling country hills, swimming pools, canoes, a Jacobian mansion. It was just remarkable at first.

"We left school with death sentences."

Goodyear was infected with hepatitis and HIV while at the school.

"In 1985, a doctor tearfully said that I had two to three years to live," he explained.

"I was told this with five other boys and the doctor went round the room and said: 'You haveâ¦ you haven'tâ¦ you haveâ¦ you haven'tâ¦ you have got HIV'."

He said the memorial was important to keep the scandal "in the public consciousness" and to honour those who died.

He added: "When we were here we made promisesâ¦ they died in front of us, one winter we lost five boys.

"I made promises to them, as did the other lads here today, that we would never give up. We would find out what happened."

If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

News.title: 'Our wedding present left us gutted': Couple join dozens in car seller dispute
News.content:
Newlyweds Amber and Nathan Cooper spent all their wedding present money on a Â£7,000 Citroen C4 to take them on their dream honeymoon.

But as they made their way to Cornwall in August 2025, it lost power and began to roll backwards leaving them stranded on the A30, near the Jamaica Inn in Bodmin Moor, they told the BBC.

When they returned it to Trade Centre UK two weeks later, they discovered it needed a new engine, clutch and gearbox.

But a year on, they are still fighting for an apology and their money back.

More than 70,000 utility customers have been left without electricity across the northeastern U.S. as a nor’easter takes aim at the coast, bringing dangerous conditions throughout the weekend.

With tens of millions of people located in the storm's path, powerful winds and torrential rain are already lashing the region as residents prepare for further impacts. Severe coastal flooding is anticipated, particularly along New Jersey and Delaware shorelines, according to the National Weather Service.

Meteorologists warn that gale winds could down trees while heavy rain threatens to leave roadways underwater for extended periods.

"This storm is expected to bring major coastal flooding to the Mid-Atlantic Coast over multiple high tide cycles through the weekend," the weather service said Saturday.

"Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses."

open image in gallery Waves pound the coast as the tide comes in during a Nor'Easter storm in Scituate, Massachusetts on September 26, 2026 ( AFP via Getty Images )

open image in gallery Water inundating homes during the nor'easter in Point Pleasant, New Jersey ( Getty Images )

In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water with rippling surface waves swept through streets, flooding a number of homes. Roughly 34 miles (54.7 kilometers) up the coast in the borough of Manasquan, where roads were also submerging, Mayor Mike Mangan stated he anticipated "a lot of water in the streets for a long time." Voluntary evacuations had been declared earlier for low-lying sections.

The weather prompted concert cancellations alongside dozens of grounded flights at airports in Boston, Nantucket, and Martha’s Vineyard across Friday and Saturday. Several airlines agreed to waive change or cancellation fees on various East Coast flights through the weekend.

New Jersey communities prepare for major flooding

Brian Kelly, the mayor of the tiny New Jersey beach community Sea Bright, said the borough is bracing for winds up to 50 mph (80 kph) and flooding that could reach up to 6 feet (1.8 meters) on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start Saturday and worsen by midday.

“It’s going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event,” Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the Northeast. “I hope I’m wrong, but that’s my gut feeling.”

Kelly hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees.

Damaging winds threaten coastal New England

Peak wind gusts could approach 60 to 65 mph (97 to 105 kph) on Cape Cod, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50 to 55 mph (80 to 89 kph) around Boston and 35 to 40 mph (56 to 64 kph) farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with NWS in Norton, Massachusetts.

“It’s definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you’re likely to see,” Belk said.

open image in gallery A car submerged in water on a flooded road in Point Pleasant ( Getty Images )

open image in gallery People walk along Nantasket Beach as a woman takes photos of high surf on September 26, 2026 in Hull, Massachusetts ( Getty Images )

Belk said nor'easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season is that leaves remain on the trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn can cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said.

Along the Atlantic coasts of New Jersey and Delaware, wind gusts could reach 60 mph (96.6 kph), according to NWS. In southeastern Connecticut and eastern Long Island, New York, gusts could get almost as high, potentially downing tree limbs and power lines.

Storm disrupts concerts, baseball and flights

Air travel was also being disrupted, with Boston particularly hard hit. Flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 39 cancellations at Boston Logan International Airport between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. Saturday, compared with 22 at New York’s John F. Kennedy International Airport. Another 12 flights were delayed at Logan.

Meanwhile, the Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm.

The public ferry service connecting Cape Cod with the islands of Nantucket and Martha’s Vineyard was experiencing widespread cancellations Friday due to strong winds and choppy water.

In Rhode Island, ferries were also canceled for Block Island. The disrupted ferry service was expected to also spill into Saturday.

open image in gallery People walk through water on a flooded road during a nor'easter storm where a voluntary evacuation has been issued in Point Pleasant, New Jersey ( Getty Images )

open image in gallery Cars drive through a flooded road in Point Pleasant ( Getty Images )

For people who regularly travel to and from the islands, the possibility of getting stuck on one side or the other is “part of life,” said Sean Driscoll, a spokesperson for the Woods Hole, Martha’s Vineyard and Nantucket Steamship Authority. Most people have backup plans in place for when boats are canceled.

“It’s a nuisance, but you know, we know what to do with this kind of stuff at this point,” he said. “This is not out of the realm of ordinary.”

Ashley Destino of Gloucester, a coastal city in northern Massachusetts, enjoyed a stroll along the beach with her two young children before preparing to hunker down at home during the storm.

“We came to the beach on Friday afternoon because we knew we were going to be inside all weekend,” said Destino, who has Legos and arts and crafts activities prepared to entertain her two children, ages 7 and 4.

She also prepared by securing her boat with additional lines, and her husband pulled out a generator in case the electricity goes out.

A new era for Scotland has arrived as Sebastien Pocognoli takes charge of his first match, against Slovenia in the Nations League.

The 39-year-old Belgian was something of a surprise replacement for Steve Clarke, who resigned after seven years at the helm following the Tartan Army’s limp group-stage exit from the World Cup this summer.

Pocognoli is expected to shake things up as Scotland try to move away from the conservative team selections and style of play that defined the Clarke era and he’s selected a new-look squad for this first international break, which has games against Slovenia, Switzerland and North Macedonia. His first starting XI sees debuts for Swansea defender Stephen Welsh and Sevilla striker Robbie Ure, while Hull City striker Oli McBurnie will make his first appearance since 2021.

The Scots have returned to League B of the Nations League and a clash with Slovenia at Stadion Stozice in Ljubljana will provide an intriguing first test for Pocognoli as he begins the build-up to Euro 2028, where Scotland will be co-hosts.

A day after his boss met with President Donald Trump in Washington, China's vice president unfurled the nation's familiar list of global talking points, emphasizing development, issuing mild statements about the U.S. war with Iran, artificial intelligence and protectionism, and making no direct mention of Taiwan.

Han Zheng's speech to the U.N. General Assembly landed somewhat anticlimactically after Chinese President Xi Jinping met Trump for a state dinner and a visit to the National Archives. Most noteworthy about the address was the presence of Han himself: China has often used high-profile public events to position its rising leaders on the global stage.

“China has created two miracles at home, namely fast economic roles and long-term social stability,” Han said.

The closest he came to a pointed statement was when he mentioned protectionism. China and the United States have been engaged in a tariff spat for more than a year, though that has ebbed as the Trump administration delayed implementations, court battles played out and Trump seemed to soften his approach to Xi.

“Both history and reality prove that countries can hardly achieve development without an open and cooperative international environment," Han said. "Protectionism produces no winners.”

The lack of direct mention of Taiwan, something that often comes up in China’s U.N. speeches, was noteworthy, particularly given tensions between Washington and Beijing about the self-governing island's fate and defense. Beijing considers Taiwan a part of China.

Development positioned as the most important principle

Typically for China, Han put development at the top of the global agenda, saying much of the world order should be built around it to raise living standards everywhere. He also repeated a familiar refrain of the Chinese government: that development helps create peace.

China's signature initiative of the past decade, known as “Belt and Road,” is an effort to foster development in nations across the world — and, in the process, increase China's influence and soft power. Han said China has worked with three-quarters of the nations through Belt and Road projects.

China has long touted multilateralism as a cornerstone of a stable world, though it hasn't always followed that path in its own relations. The nation's constant refrain — stay out of our internal affairs — reflects its history of trying to secure the edges of the country that are distant from Beijing. That's a longstanding philosophy that dates to the construction of the Great Wall hundreds of years ago and continues today in the pressure points of Xinjiang and Tibet in its far west and Taiwan and Hong Kong off its east coast.

That refrain was reflected in Han's speech Saturday.

“Multilateralism is a choice made by humanity after going through scourges," he said. “We should settle the differences and disputes through dialogue and consultation, and oppose unilateral military actions that violate the U.N. charter and circumvent Security Council authorization.”

In terms of Iran, where the U.S. and Israel have been waging war since early this year, Han had this to say: “China holds that the sovereignty and security of countries in the Middle East, including the Gulf, should be respected.”

“We should safeguard the postwar international order," he said, but — in a statement that could be considered contradictory — he said the world should “reject the Cold War mindset and block confrontation.”

Han also spoke about empowering the Global South, a term used for emerging and economically struggling nations — many of which sit below the equator. Some larger nations have positioned themselves in recent years as leaders of the Global South, including China and India.

Han's presence has meaning, but perhaps not a lot of it

Given Xi's presence in the United States this week, many on-air pundits spent time ruminating about why he wasn't speaking at the U.N. It's not that unusual, though — particularly since Xi, in the grand scheme of things, had bigger fish to fry in Washington.

Wang Zichen, deputy secretary-general of the Beijing-based think tank Center for China and Globalization, said there has never been “a convention” requiring the Chinese president to attend the U.N. General Assembly. Xi’s predecessors, including Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, attended major U.N. meetings only selectively, and Xi himself last addressed the body virtually during the pandemic in 2021.

Last year, Premier Li Qiang represented China. Senior diplomat Wang Yi has also spoken several time in recent years in various capacities; he was accompanying Xi this year on the Washington trip. And Han spoke in 2023.

“Both the premier and the vice president are sufficiently senior representatives that I would be cautious about interpreting the choice between them as a diplomatic signal in itself,” Wang Zichen said.

He added that China portrays the U.N. as an important global institution, so “it would be difficult to argue from the level of representation alone that China is becoming less interested in the U.N.”

Unlike Li's 2025 speech, which ventured into some personal observations about arriving in New York, Han played it straight. The closest he came to being flowery was in the context of multilateralism, and he quickly pivoted back to diplomatic language.

“Diversity has created splendor in the world,” he said. “Condescension and the self-centered mindset have no place in the interactions among different cultures. Promoting mutual trust, mutual respect, solidarity and harmonious coexistence is the right approach to take.”

___

Associated Press writer E. Eduardo Castillo in Beijing contributed to this report.

George Russell re-entered the world championship conversation by holding off Max Verstappen to win Saturday’s nail-biting Azerbaijan Grand Prix by just one tenth of a second – as title rival Kimi Antonelli finished fifth.

Russell all but raised the white flag after the last round in Madrid where Antonelli claimed his eighth victory of the year to extend his title advantage to 81 points.

But the British driver has been in inspired form on the streets of Baku, charging to pole position before navigating his way through two safety car periods, and Verstappen’s late advances, to take his third win of the campaign and his first since the Austrian Grand Prix, 90 days ago.

Russell trims Antonelli’s title lead to 66 points with 208 still to play for across the scheduled remaining eight rounds. It was damage limitation for Antonelli after his qualifying crash left him 16th on the grid. Antonelli was in the points by the 16th lap and a safety car, deployed on the 31st lap after Alex Albon crashed out, fortuitously propelled him onto the back of the leading drivers.

South African police said Saturday that another woman’s body had been found near Johannesburg, bringing to 10 the number of victims in a series of killings under investigation.

Police began investigating after the bodies of three women were found in July and August within about 7 kilometers (4.3 miles) of one another in the Ekurhuleni municipality, east of Johannesburg.

The discovery of six bodies in Ekurhuleni over 10 days earlier this month raised fears that a serial killer or killers were responsible.

Two women were arrested and charged last week with murder in relation to the ninth body, discovered on Sept. 17. The victim had been stabbed and had her throat cut, police said. Police did not link the two women charged to any of the other killings.

Provincial police commissioner Lt. Gen. Tommy Mthombeni told state broadcaster SABC on Saturday that investigators believed the ninth killing was an isolated case but could not rule out the possibility that some of the other cases were linked.

Police have identified similarities in some of the killings but said they had not found conclusive evidence that the same person or people were responsible.

All nine of the bodies discovered before Saturday were those of women in their 20s or 30s, according to police. Several were naked or partially clothed and left in open areas near main roads. Officers from the Investigative Psychology Unit, which specializes in complex or serial violent crimes, are part of the investigation.

Police released limited details about the 10th body, which was found early Saturday, and did not immediately identify the victim.

“We can only confirm the discovery of the body,” the South African Police Service said in a statement. “Crime scene management and all the necessary role players are currently on the scene.”

South Africa has high rates of violent crime and violence against women. The killings in Ekurhuleni have sparked a national outcry over women's safety.

Manchester City’s chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak has released a statement to supporters concerning the reports that the club will be found guilty of breaching the Premier League’s financial rules.

Man City have been under investigation since 2023 over 115 charges of financial rules breaches and the verdict is expected to find City guilty of 114 of the charges against them.

Reports of the expected verdict started to appear on Friday 25 September though the process is still ongoing and there has been no official word from the Premier League. The investigation and its findings remain legally sensitive as well as private and confidential process.

Nevertheless, speculation over possible punishments for Man City as well as their opportunity to appeal against the verdict have risen over the last 24 hours causing Al Mubarak to respond.

City’s chairman did so in a statement posted to the club’s website which insisted on their innocence and explained that the process still has ‘a long way to run’.

The statement reads: “I have been part of this club for 18 years. I have had the privilege to stand with you in the Etihad, at Wembley, and in Istanbul. This club matters to me, and you have shown and told me – time and time again - how much Manchester City matters to you. This is why I am writing to you today.

“Following Friday’s media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I. Here’s what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began.

“There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position. But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies.

open image in gallery Media reports claim that Manchester City will be found guilty of most of the 115 charges of breaching financial rules ( Reuters )

“I ask you to please carefully read the statement below, which we gave on Friday, and the statement we issued in February 2023 (also below). Every word matters and holds true.

“While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity.

“We have some exciting moments to look forward to after this international break. We travel to Anfield in a fortnight, and then host Paris St Germain in the Champions League back at Etihad Stadium - moments that give us an opportunity to celebrate the strength of the Manchester City family.”

The statement is the second official word from Manchester City since reports of the expected guilty verdict broke with the first also acknowleding that the ‘process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed’.

City also claim that they have ‘diligently respected due process for eight years’ and that they expect the ‘Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence’.

News.title: Man City charges verdict – live: City chairman insists innocence in statement on reports over Premier League charges
