His appointment offers continuity at a time of upheaval in the Liverpool hierarchy with Hughes and Michael Edwards, the former chief executive of football at FSG, leaving this year and the owners in the process of selling a 38% stake in the club to 1892 Holdings for £2bn. The consortium, fronted by Amit Bhatia and including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, has an option for a full takeover should FSG decide to sell up.

View image in fullscreen Jürgen Klopp signs a contract extension in April 2022 with FSG’s Michael Gordon (left) and Julian Ward, then Liverpool’s assistant sporting director. Photograph: Andrew Powell/Liverpool FC/Getty Images

The 45-year-old Ward replaced Edwards as sporting director in 2022, but told FSG he wished to step away for personal reasons a few months into the role. Luis Díaz, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Darwin Núñez were signed during his first spell although the manager at the time, Jürgen Klopp, had a greater say on transfers after Edwards left.

Ward remained highly regarded by FSG, however, and Gordon, who had resumed the day-to-day running of Liverpool after Hughes’s departure, considers his extensive knowledge of the club and of squad planning as invaluable. As FSG’s technical director, Ward had oversight of the global talent strategy that has led Liverpool to sign several highly rated young prospects this year.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Liverpool’s new sporting director will lead the club’s football operation alongside the assistant sporting director, David Woodfine, the chief scout, Barry Hunter, FSG’s director of football development, Pedro Marques, and Andoni Iraola’s senior leadership team.

Sports.title: ‘Island girl’ Malard aims to become a legend with Bompastor at Chelsea
Sports.content:
It is rare to see Melvine Malard without a grin and she has a mountain of reasons to keep it that way. A wedding in June, a big-money move to Chelsea, a Ballon d’Or nomination and a first taste of a London derby against Arsenal at Stamford Bridge on Sunday. The France forward is loving life and the personality behind the smile that instantly connects her to teammates is infectious.

“Goals,” says Malard, with a laugh, when asked what keeps her happy. “Seriously though, it’s seeing the kids, the families, my family, in the stands. It is crazy. I love my life, I love my job, I’m happy with my wife and everything is good. I smile because of those things, because I’m happy.”

You cannot help but feel the childlike wonder emanating from the 26-year-old at football being her job and this being her life. The little girl who started playing later than most, at six or seven, after she had tried “every other sport”, retains the deep appreciation for the joy it has brought her.

The love of the game was instant, “partly because it’s a team sport and I loved that you get to enjoy it with everyone in your team. Then I also found I felt strong and free when I play football.

“I have to play with a lot of energy and a lot of smiles. It’s also important that the fans get to know me and get to enjoy the football with me.”

0:46 Chelsea’s Melvine Malard: ‘Football is the last sport I tried’ – video

Malard grew up on Réunion, a small island east of Madagascar that has a population of less than one million, was formerly a French colony and is now an overseas department of France. “It’s a little island with a lot of people smiling, good life and good food,” she says. Girls did not really play football, but Malard paved the way: “I’m very proud of that.”

At 14, she caught the eye of Sonia Bompastor at an under-15s match at France’s national football centre in Clairefontaine. The Chelsea manager was in charge of Lyon’s academy at the time.

Bompastor persuaded Malard’s mother to allow her daughter to move more than 5,600 miles, though home is far from forgotten. “Everywhere I go and wherever I think about where I’m from, I want to show where I’m from and I want to give back and just make everyone proud of me.”

Signing for Chelsea from Manchester United this summer reunited her with the manager who plucked her from her island life and gave her the chance to pursue her dream at one of the biggest clubs in Europe. “I will never forget Manchester United,” Malard says. “They helped me make a change in my life when I really needed change.”

She has a lot of love for many people at the club. However, she wanted to be somewhere that matched her ambitions. She loves life, but life is short.

View image in fullscreen Melvine Malard celebrated with a Réunion flag after helping Manchester United win the FA Cup in 2024. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

It was frustrating for her that things did not kick on after Manchester United’s FA Cup win in 2024, with a lack of club support for the women’s side widely reported, Malard says: “It’s for that reason that I’m here. I don’t want to lose any time in my career. Football moves quickly and sometimes you need to make the choice that is best for your career. Coming here was a good choice.

“At Chelsea, there are clear ambitions: to win the game, win the trophies and raise the level higher. That is where I need to be.”

Bompastor’s pursuit was a real vote of confidence in her as a player and person. “She knows my qualities, my energy, my personality and she knows what I need to learn and where I need to progress,” Malard says.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Bompastor wields influence. “It’s not just about Sonia as a manager,” Malard says. “Sonia is also a legendary player, [her assistant and partner] Camille Abily also. They played football, they know football, and when they speak with me I can’t say anything because they know more than me. That can help you progress a lot. They set the level you know you need to be at to become a legend.”

The Champions League is the way she believes she can do that: “I want to write my name on a new page, but not any page, a page you remember. The way to do that with Chelsea is to win something the club has never won..”

She came off the bench in the 5-2 home win over Real Sociedad in qualifying, making the difference with the score at 2-2 by scoring the first of her two goals 12 minutes later.

View image in fullscreen Malard scored on her WSL and Champions League debuts for Chelsea. Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian

“It felt good, very good,” she says. “I think it’s because of my personality too. I’m not a player that is difficult to play when things aren’t going to plan. I’m the player that puts energy into every area on and off the pitch. The girls know that about me already, they know where I want to go.”

A frustrating couple of weeks out with injury followed, but she scored in Chelsea’s 2-0 win over Birmingham and featured in the 1-0 win over Austria Vienna on Wednesday.

Sitting by the Shed End sign in the royal blue Stamford Bridge seats, Malard is excited at the prospect of facing Arsenal here. “All players want to play this game,” she says, the smile still there, but with an edge this time. “You train hard for these games against big teams in big stadiums with lots of fans waiting for you to play and score. I can’t wait.

“When I look at the little girl from that island today playing for Chelsea and nominated for the Ballon d’Or, it’s a lot for me to take in and a lot for my family,” she says. “It gives me the motivation to continue this way and I’m very proud of myself.”

Sports.title: Manchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated?
Sports.content:
What happens next?

Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of the 134 disciplinary charges brought against them by the Premier League.

In keeping with the history of this explosive case which has been conducted exclusively in private and with every party sworn to secrecy, there is a lot we don’t know. We do not even have an official confirmation that the three-person judicial panel has reached a verdict on the case. All of football is acting as if they have, however, and that reports of a big win for the Premier League are correct.

If these assumptions are correct, and neither party have formally denied them at least, then the immediate thing to watch out for is news of an appeal. Under Premier League rules, City would have 14 days from the announcement of the verdict to submit an appeal and the process that follows should be completed in less than 12 weeks from then. Once the appeal has been heard – which should happen in one block of no more than five days – and a verdict reached, the appeal panel are also expected to publish written reasons behind their decisions. We should also see the written reasons from the original judicial panel too, but the unique scale of this case has meant that normal procedures have not always been followed, and the date of publication for these reasons remains unknown.

If City do appeal, what happens?

The club would be submitting an appeal based solely on the decision and not any resulting punishment, which is yet to be determined. In hoping to make the case that the judicial panel were wrong in their observations, City would be allowed to submit new evidence, providing it had not been previously available to them, and make new oral presentations. Once the hearing is concluded, a verdict would be expected in 30 days.

If an appeal fails, what then?

According to Premier League rule W.97, “the decision of an Appeal Board shall be final”, but even this is subject to one final route, that of arbitration. This would again mean appearing in front of another panel of eminent legal figures, but the criteria for any hearing would be a lot stricter and successful arbitration only possible in the main if the judicial panel or appeal board was found to have abused the legal process. City have recently been through the arbitration process with the Premier League over its rules related to associated party transactions and, after an initial verdict challenged two applications of the rules but otherwise found them to be sound, City and the Premier League reached a settlement which stopped the case from going to court.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

When and how would City be punished?

If City managed to overturn the verdict, there would of course be no sanction. If City’s appeals failed, there are a number of measures available to the panel. They start at fines and end at complete expulsion from the league, with a variety of sporting sanctions including point deductions falling in-between. Given the magnitude of the verdict, City can expect to receive a punishment at the sharper end of the scale should their appeal not prove successful.

Could relegation be the end of it?

It seems unlikely. Premier League clubs and those who have been relegated from the division are understood to have been assessing any potential financial losses they may have incurred during the period City were winning and, appeal pending, breaking the rules. A wave of lawsuits is likely to follow, with Manchester United, for example, having finished second behind City in 2017-18 and potentially denied a record-breaking 21st league title in the process. It is possible that clubs who were relegated could argue that they were sent down because of points denied them by a City side subsequently found to have cheated. Premier League clubs reportedly lost their appetite for legal action after an estimated £50m cost to the competition last season, but if the verdict against City revealed this week is ultimately upheld, a new wave of lawsuits will surely follow.

Sports.title: How do England beat Spain, or even score against them? The data suggests crosses
Sports.content:
England are about to face the hardest challenge in international football, maybe at any level of the game. They are going to try to score against Spain. Spain conceded one goal in eight games on the way to winning the World Cup while allowing their opponents 2.37 expected goals, a mere 0.30 per 90 minutes played.

Thomas Tuchel has said he hoped his side “became for 10 minutes more like Spain” to comfortably dominate possession when the heat was on. A fine aspiration for those situations, but it is not an approach that will help England unlock the Spain backline. The pass masters cannot be toppled that way. The solution may lie elsewhere within the same Tuchel press conference.

Tuchel spoke of how English fans and players prefer chaos. “There is no heritage of: ‘Oh, let’s control around the middle line. Let’s do a deep buildup and then bring them out’,” he said. “It’s just like: ‘Come on. Let’s kick the ball into the opponent’s box and fight with them’.”

And this is how England can beat Spain. Granted, it requires a little more nuance than Tuchel’s simple summation. But not much. The two defeats Spain have suffered in the Luis de la Fuente era help prove the point. Both occurred in the UK.

The first was in Euros qualifying at Hampden Park in March 2023, with Scott McTominay scoring both goals in a 2-0 win for Scotland. “For me, this is not football,” Rodri said after enduring the home side’s combative, time-wasting approach. No, pal, and that is why it worked. Nobody can out-football Spain; alternate methods are required to win. McTominay’s second came after he crashed into the penalty area to fire home after David García failed to clear a Kieran Tierney cross.

View image in fullscreen Spain’s only loss in a competitive game under Luis de la Fuente came thanks to two goals from Scott McTominay. Photograph: Robert Perry/EPA

When Colombia beat Spain 1-0 in a friendly at the London Stadium 12 months later, it was again a delivery from the left flank that did the damage. And again, there was a Premier League past-and-present vibe with Luis Díaz crossing for Daniel Muñoz to score.

These moments carry positive confirmation bias as they occurred in losses for Spain. They look important because they were. While no side beat them this summer, teams relied on crossing to fashion even vaguely decent opportunities.

The stats for the chances they allowed highlight this superbly. The average value of a shot is 0.1 xG. It can vary slightly from season to season or between competitions, but as a rule of thumb it works. In 750 minutes this summer, Spain conceded six chances Opta deemed to be of greater value. Lowering the bar to 0.07 xG still only finds 10 shots that were worth more. The eight teams Spain faced had to work for a collective average of 75 minutes for an opportunity that had a better than one-in-14 likelihood of becoming a goal. It was very hard graft.

It is remarkable that the highest value shot they allowed in the tournament occurred in the 121st minute of the final. A match Spain utterly dominated from start to finish might have gone to penalties had Giuliano Simeone fired under the crossbar rather than over it. The move for his chance originated from a corner, as did the cross that presented Cape Verde’s Diney with a 91st-minute opportunity to produce a titanic upset in Spain’s first game.

Charles De Ketelaere’s goal for Belgium, the only one Spain conceded, was set up by a Timothy Castagne cross. It was one of the four Opta-defined big chances Spain allowed at the World Cup; all of them headers, all set up via deliveries from wide areas.

Cristiano Ronaldo had a relatively high value effort in the last-16 Iberian derby after a cross to the back post had been headed back towards him in the six-yard box. It was a better chance than any France produced in the semi-final. Their highest value attempt was rated at 0.06 xG. It came from a corner.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There seems little other way to produce even a shot against Spain. Cape Verde, Saudi Arabia and Uruguay all tried to score from within their own halves, so starved were they of goalscoring opportunities.

Crosses seem to work though, at least relatively speaking, perhaps because Spain’s key defensive players are unaccustomed to facing them too often. Pau Cubarsí’s Barcelona conceded the second-fewest crosses per game of the 96 clubs in Europe’s big five leagues last season. Athletic Bilbao, featuring the other two-thirds of Spain’s first-choice combination of goalkeeper and centre-backs (Unai Simón and Aymeric Laporte), were joint-ninth.

Cubarsí and Laporte each contested fewer than four aerial duels per 90 minutes; many centre-backs in the Premier League won, let alone contested, more than that. Balls in the air are a much bigger part of the game in England, where ‘they kick the ball into the opponent’s box and fight with them’, to re-quote Tuchel.

In an age of tactical sophistication, crossing is deemed too inefficient. It is very old-school, leaning heavily on English football stereotypes. But we are not plotting out the development programme at St George’s Park for the future of the game, we are trying to see how England can score in one match against the meanest defence in international football.

If Trent Alexander-Arnold is keen to get back into Tuchel’s good books, delivering a t cross on to the head of Harry Kane against Spain would be a strong starting point. There may be no other way for him or England to prosper against the world champions.

Sports.title: Lamine Yamal: ‘Football is mechanised but players like me have that special spark’
Sports.content:
Like the kid he is, Lamine Yamal just wanted to keep playing. This wasn’t Plaça Joan XXIII, wasn’t El Parque de Rocafonda either; it wasn’t the Mataró neighbourhood where it all began, but it might have been. “We’re in a World Cup final and I wanted to carry on,” he says, and there’s the smile again, the braces. Really? “Yes”. No nerves? “No. I never thought: ‘Just blow the whistle’. I was enjoying it.” No fear, just fun: 19 July, New Jersey and he knew: this 19-year-old who had happily been asleep on the bus to the biggest match of his life.

And now he sits in a first-floor office in Las Rozas, surrounded by tactics boards and stats sheets. There’s a Spain keyring hanging from the door and a second star on his shirt. In the corridor, crates loaded for London. Son of Mounir and Sheila, named after the family friends who helped them, “touched by God’s wand” in the words of the coach whose office is next door, there’s something about Lamine Yamal. He turned 17 the day before the final of Euro 2024, a schoolboy sitting exams, and 19 the day before the semi-final of the World Cup. Asked what he wanted, he said a trip to New York, so there he was, about to be a champion again.

The way Lamine Yamal tells it, Spain knew they were world champions before they had scored, in the moment Enzo Fernández was sent off. It was the third minute of second-half stoppage time, still 0-0, but now, he says: “We knew it was impossible they would score, and with the ball against 10, very difficult for us not to.” The surprise was that they hadn’t already, but on 106 minutes the ball came to his feet. He had been thinking about this moment for some time.

The battle with the one, two, three players facing you is “very psychological”, Lamine Yamal says. “A full-back will have a coach who says: ‘OK, Lamine: what he does is …’ I think of him as a robot, trying to stop me. Robots can be almost perfect but a human will have something a robot doesn’t. Football is mechanised but there are players like me, Pedri, many others, who have that special spark. There’s a typical Neymar move when he stops, fakes, goes the other way: I watched so many videos of him. I try to play with opponents, ensure they can’t mechanise me, don’t know where I’m going.”

View image in fullscreen Lamine Yamal with the World Cup after Spain beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time. Photograph: Alex Livesey/Danehouse/Getty Images

“I remember three plays in minutes 60, 70, 80 or thereabouts, when I took on the full-back. Every time, [Alexis] Mac Allister came over. If I had really wanted to go at the full-back, I would have gone at him fast; instead this time I went slower, carrying the ball, so that Mac Allister had time to get to me, Pedro [Porro] could arrive behind me and I could play it back.” A little space made, from Porro’s cross Nico Williams headed back and Ferran Torres, who had struggled throughout the tournament, scored the goal.

“We knew Ferran needed it,” Lamine Yamal says, then laughs: “Well, everyone needs a goal in a World Cup final. If Unai Simón had scored, great. When it goes in, it’s spectacular, you feel you’re champions. You can’t explain the emotion. All I wanted was to keep playing. I never thought: ‘They might equalise’. There was a small push, a chance [Pau] Cubarsí cleared, but I was enjoying it.”

The mini trophy is at Lamine Yamal’s mum’s house; he gave the Lego trophy to his dad but his little brother, Keyne, broke it. At the final whistle, he embraced Lionel Messi. “I said thank you for everything you gave football. I don’t do things to look nice for the photo; that came from inside,” Lamine Yamal says, but the symbolism was powerful, like a rite of passage, a passing of the torch. Lamine, 19, hugging Messi, 39, who had bathed him when he was a baby, as if it was a baptism, the creation. As if he had made this happen.

Lamine Yamal talks to the Guardian’s Sid Lowe about his iconic photos with Lionel Messi

Almost absurd in its perfection, utterly implausible, the bathtub origin story poses so many questions, but here’s one that baffles: why on earth did your dad not produce that picture for 17 years? “Because I told him not to,” Lamine Yamal says. “He put it on Facebook once and I told him to take it down. Comparisons were too easy, that was all people would talk about. I wanted to be Lamine; I didn’t want to be Messi. I just wanted to get where I could get. I asked him to wait. When I’m Lamine, do what you want.”

Oh, he’s Lamine all right, and where he has got to no one has. A global social phenomenon, his image was everywhere at the World Cup, whole stadiums waiting on him, the comparisons he tried to avoid inevitable. And, amazingly, in his favour. No one had ever won a Euros and a World Cup younger, at 19 years and six days. Messi was 35 when he won the World Cup; Diego Maradona was 25; Cristiano Ronaldo never has. Who knows what he could achieve? Spain’s candidate for the Ballon d’Or (even if Kylian Mbappé has support in Madrid), he would be the youngest winner, ever.

Nor is it just about the titles. It is about the play and the personality, something different, an appeal, apparent even in this office. And something deeper, too. Luis de la Fuente likened Lamine Yamal to Salvador Dalí and Michelangelo, a genius. He knows that himself and doesn’t mind saying so. Doesn’t mind saying that, yes, he should be named the world’s best footballer. Because, well, he is. Even at 19, which may in fact be what goes against him.

View image in fullscreen Lamine Yamal: ‘There are times I enjoy the pressure. I enjoy going on to the pitch, when a lot is expected.’ Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“Being completely honest, it’s not just this year I’ve been at a Ballon d’Or [winning] level, but longer. Everyone knows that; they know I am differential,” he says. “I think people think: ‘Lamine is 19, he’ll win it at some point, so let’s say someone else …’ I just have to win, win, win, and there will be a time when there’s no debate. There will be people who love me, people who say: ‘What a pain in the arse he is’, and that’s fine.”

“After the final, my family were so happy,” Lamine Yamal continues, laughing once again. “The problem with that is they don’t know what it is to lose. I go to the Euros, I win it. I go to the World Cup, I win it. It seems easy. There was a moment I thought: ‘When I don’t win they’re going to think I’m terrible.’ I told them: ‘Calm down, there will be plenty more World Cups.’ I have to play more and win more.

“At the Euros I didn’t even know who I was, where I was, the significance of it all. I could sit an exam and the next day play France because I wasn’t really conscious of the difference. I won it and said: ‘Well, that’s good, but a World Cup is better, no?’ Now I know what a Euros means. I know what a World Cup is, although I think you truly realise when you go to the next one and lose. There’s a lot still to do. Why not be the best national team in history? The best Barcelona? And if there’s anyone in the world who doesn’t ‘rest’ on success, who doesn’t have normal standards, it’s me.” No pressure, kid.

Lamine Yamal has lived that from the start. He was 13 the first time he felt some sort of fame. One day we will stop talking about his age but stop for a minute and it is still absurd: he went to the Euros at 16, a literal child, and the World Cup at 18 and won both. He has three league titles. The money, the fame, the exposure. It’s remarkable really that, to put it bluntly, he’s not a dickhead. “Well,” he laughs, “it depends how you’re brought up. I will never say: ‘Who are you? I won the World Cup.’ Only stupid people would do that. I know that football is 0.000001% of life.”

And there it is again; the maturity. Here’s a teenager supporting a family, who in his own words was handed “too much responsibility” too soon, who talks eloquently about the demands, exposure and about embracing them. At times he can seem to actually enjoy the attention and the pressure, wilfully adding to it, all a game. He can be accused of talking too much, and can reply: “Well, as long as I am winning … sport is serious but I want a show, some fun.” Remember Adrien Rabiot? He does. “That day you all saw how much I like it,” he says, grinning. At the World Cup his headband read: “Ego Yamal”. There’s a cheek, a mischief; he’s “playing” with us, he admits, with the silliness of it all.

At times, but not all times. He says “a bad game from Lamine equals 400 bad games for anyone else”, that “I’ll produce a nine out of 10 and people will say seven out of 10”. At the World Cup, he visited Nashville: there’s a smile as he recalls the “cowboys, the atmosphere” … and the anonymity. A photo appeared of him at Walmart, a silly thing that mattered. “If we stopped in a gas station, I could get out and grab something,” he says. What he posts, what he says, he controls – which doesn’t mean always getting it right, or being happy. One post last season was entitled “my inner abyss”.

View image in fullscreen Lamine Yamal with his brother Keyne after Spain had beaten England in the Euro 2024 final in Berlin. The winger had just turned 17. Photograph: Stefan Matzke/sampics/Getty Images

Do we know you? “No. Not at all. No one,” he insists. “Only my inner circle know what I think, the way I am. People don’t have a clue – not a clue, Not. A. Clue.” Why? “I grew up in a barrio where the less people know about you, the happier you are, the quieter your life. Obviously I like a footballer’s life, but I would also like to live in peace, a normal life. The nearest I can get is for people to know as little as possible. If I post something, I need to know I can handle what comes. At first it annoyed me to read things because I didn’t understand it. My mum would read something, call me and say: ‘Son, what’s this?!’ That affected me but it doesn’t affect me now.

“There are times I enjoy the pressure. I enjoy going on to the pitch, when a lot is expected. Then there’s a different kind of pressure which is nothing to do with what people say, nothing to do with football; it’s life. I don’t feel pressure in football. I will never lie at home thinking: ‘I played really badly, I didn’t win the Ballon d’Or, we didn’t win the league.’ It’s responsibility: I have my family. I’ve suffered, struggled with them, we’ve been through bad times and now that we’re enjoying life, I have to continue. If I have played football all these years, it’s because I love football but also for them. I know life is much longer. I have to look after my family, my little brother.”

“In football there’s no fear,” he adds. “I saw my mum struggle so that I could play football. I’ve seen my dad go round the streets collecting scrap metal so I could eat. That’s fear. Now if I had a son, I could look after him. If my mum or my dad need anything, I can help. I don’t have that fear now and that’s the only fear I could have in life.”

View image in fullscreen Lamine Yamal in full flight against Argentina in the World Cup final. Photograph: Hannah McKay/Reuters

So, play the game. Your way, as always, made in Rocafonda, the hard barrio whose postcode Lamine Yamal signals with every goal. Besides, he insists, fun is underrated in football. “Barcelona give you good things but you also need something of your own, your roots,” he says. “Barcelona gave me control, understanding, IQ. In the park there’s no IQ: you go at your opponent, then go back again. I have that. If I hadn’t come from where I came from and been at La Masia, I wouldn’t have come out like this.

“The thing is, I love football. I don’t play for money, I play because I love it. Players who obsess over goals or assists don’t enjoy it. I play for the fun: to dribble, to play one touch, two touches, to make a teammate who hasn’t scored score. For the fans’ happiness. To hear the olés. I play for that. I enjoy it. I get home and I say: ‘I’ve had a great time.’ If every player did that, we would enjoy it much more.

“At the World Cup, you heard it, felt it: when I got the ball, they would stand up, one after the other, all along the row. Like they were saying: ‘Let’s see if this guy is what they say he is.’ At the Camp Nou, people know I’m going to go at someone. That feeling, that expectation, is something you can only experience in sport, being a player like me. It’s like there’s something inside that makes you feel more powerful than anyone and I hope it’s there until the day I retire. There’s a surge around you and you feel like Superman, you feel like Spiderman. You feel spectacular.”

Sports.title: Burnham’s booze ruse is a non-starter: just keep doing your drinking in the pub | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
Hi, I’m Andy Burnham and I don’t believe any child should eat gravel for breakfast. That’s why we’ve launched the National No Gravel Breakfast initiative. Hi, I’m Andy Burnham and I think everyone should have access to sitting on a chair no matter if they live in the north or the chair-rich south. Hi, I’m Andy Burnham and I don’t think pensioners should be required to stab themselves in the hand with cocktail sticks. Unless that’s what they want. In which case I will personally do this for them.

Hi, I’m Andy Burnham and I believe in a mother’s love, the laughter of baby horses and beautifully crisp and gooey churros straight from the pan. Unless you don’t want those. In which case I believe you have that choice and I will fight for it. Or not fight for it. Whichever.

In the absence of a manifesto or an actual election campaign, it feels like the best place to experience raw, unfiltered Burnham-ism, to really get a handle on his vision as mid-season firefighting prime minister, is the videos on his LinkedIn page. Which are pretty good and, yeah, he seems nice, and like he generally agrees with me, so that’s fine.

This is not a criticism of Burnham. It seems a pretty clear-sighted strategy on his part, mainly because politics is ridiculous now. Keir Starmer is widely seen as perhaps the worst prime minister of all time, the man who lost control of immigration and did something terrible to the economy. Reality: immigration went down under Starmer. The economy is sluggish but not terrible. Starmer was above all a terrible communicator, choosing to make every public statement in that fussy, nasal upwards-register, like a notably dull and pissy professional angler explaining at great length why your waterproof trousers are inadequate.

View image in fullscreen The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has a pint in a pub, which is a much better place to have a pint than a football stadium. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images

Burnham does seem to have a more state-of-the-art understanding of presentation. Most notably of the fact he must perform two simultaneous roles. First, the public one, which is basically a cover job, a way of stopping people reflexively hating him, as they must now hate all politicians in the end. Meanwhile any actual politics, the usual hard choices and compromises, will have to be Trojan-horsed beneath that. This may seem undesirable, but it’s a choice we have forced on these people, and a method that might actually allow him to at least get something done before he is inevitably chewed up by the rage and stupidity of the digital hive mind.

It is in this context that his comments this week about drinking in the stands at football must be interpreted. By now Burnham’s off-the-cuff response to a question has been sliced and diced and generally dismissed. It is worth adding some further context, pointing out exactly why this is not just a pointless idea but a bad one. But the most interesting part of his most significant engagement so far with football, the great public megaphone, is what it says about Burnham himself.

First up, this is just a dead issue. Burnham was just re-stating a long-held personal opinion, not making policy, or expressing any real intention to do anything. He’s in a period of ambient electioneering. In his mind this is an easy issue, a free hit, like saying yes we must have more chocolate at Christmas. It won’t actually happen. Alcohol has been banned within sight of the pitch since the late 1980s, and with good reason. I love drinking. I’m a fan, a cheerleader, a devotee. I love the softness, the booze-haze, the first three drinks, that delicious transition from sober towards something else that is always the best part, the bit you keep chasing across all the lost drinks that must inevitably follow. But really, come on.

Of all the many problems facing the nation, insufficient access to alcohol really doesn’t seem like a hot-button issue. Currently the average urban centre has 60 booze outlets per square mile. Maybe if you’re spending your days skipping warily between a shotgunned bottle of Oyster Bay in the Nisa local and the five-minute walk up the road to the Meatbag and Carrot, it would genuinely help if you could stagger into Loftus Road for a pint of warm Foster’s on the way. But nobody really needs to be more drunk at football. And if you really must drink, it’s not that hard to smuggle in the gin flask.

View image in fullscreen Fans can drink in their seats in the top two divisions of women’s football, but there is little indication that the men’s professional game will follow suit. Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images

Young people also don’t really drink. And many people who already feel excluded; new fans, women in particular, feel doubly uncomfortable around a pissed-up football crowd. As a final hard pass, within three minutes of re-legalising this, someone somewhere is chucking a pint in the air. No thanks.

The most interesting part of all this is that Burnham chose booze and football as an obviously tribal issue, choosing to introduce the idea of “discrimination”, as though people who want to drink at football are a lobby group, an oppressed section of society, or even any kind of identifiable demographic. Hang on, you can drink at the opera! Well, yes, but you also can’t sing songs at the opera, do the Poznan or call people wankers. Different environments have different rules. And plenty of people at the opera will have hot-footed it there from consuming the Premier League. What was the point again?

If we really are going to make this an-us-and-them issue I can kill it right here on Burnham’s own terms. This is a bad idea because it would help to close down pubs, and shovel money instead into the pockets of clubs owned by hedge funds. You might say buying a couple of pints in sight of a football pitch isn’t going to change pub culture. But that’s not how it works. That minor prohibition has helped create a culture of external football drinking, and this is one of the few physical match-day elements to exist outside football’s corporate force field.

Pubs are great and vital places. I love all of them. Urban pubs with flat felt roofs. Pubs with mock-Tudor cream cheese wall-coverings, unlike any other building known to man. Pubs that sell obscure brands of pub-only crisps. Crucially, pubs still provide a third space, a place where people can meet, where men actually speak. And they thrive around football grounds.

An amazing and deeply cheering fact: there are 174 active pubs within a one-mile radius of St James’ Park. Molineux has 50 pubs, Portman Road 29. Arsenal 33. When Andy Burnham sits down at Everton with Mark Carney and feels annoyed he can’t buy a £9 Peroni, he is also just a 15-minute walk from 23 public bars that survive purely on selling liquid to thirsty people.

All pubs operate on fine margins. Matchdays are their rush hour, guaranteed mega-rounds, a captive footfall. Why would you divert even the tiniest bit of that money to the wildly commodified institutional leisure facility up the road? Also, just to kill this once and for all, you can imagine how awful the fully realised Premier League experience will be? In related football news, it also emerged this week that Manchester United are literally selling off the pitch, just fully giving up on irony and leaning into it. We’ve hollowed this place out, chucked the bentwood chairs on the fire, sold your memories back to you. Yeah we can do a pub. Another round of deliciously fruity Yorke and Cole Witbier sir? Why would you put more money into this, and not into a place with a furry carpet that still performs some kind of authentic social function?

So much for all that. It won’t happen. The police don’t want it. Burnham was just re-sharing a personal opinion. But it does tell you something valuable about his reflexive way of thinking. The idea that this is a vital cultural issue is pure 1980s, from a time when to be interested in football was to be dismissed as a thug, an unwanted emissary of the undeserving working class.

View image in fullscreen Would the prime ministerial joint visit to Hill Dickinson really have been improved by a warm, overpriced pitch-side lager? Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

This is not the case now. Instead, football is the cultural imperialist, out there inflicting itself on everything else, always, always selling. And this is also a first very obvious example of playing to a base that exists most vividly only in his own cultural milieu.

There has been a successful projection of the new prime minister as fresh and novel, a figure from the outside. Which is not bad going for a Blair-era spad who will be 57 in January, the same age as Jacob Rees-Mogg and Woodstock.

But football is always telling you things. The response to that slight false note, a wider head-scratch over what is essentially a non-issue, is useful information. Time for a drink and a rethink.

Sports.title: Defiant Man City insist they are INNOCENT: Chairman breaks his silence with bombshell Premier League verdict leaving club facing threat of relegation
Sports.content:
Defiant Man City insist they are INNOCENT: Chairman breaks his silence with bombshell Premier League verdict leaving club facing threat of relegation

Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak has said the club is confident it will clear its name after being found guilty of financial doping.

The club supremo has warned that while some have been 'quick to reach their own conclusions' after it emerged they had been found guilty on the 'vast majority' of the 115 charges, 'we have faced challenges before and prevailed'.

The Premier League accused the club of widespread financial cheating over an era of sustained success – with an independent panel hearing concluding in 2024.

City are set to appeal the decision but any punishment is now expected to follow, with some fans calling for the club to be stripped of the trophies they won at the time, while relegation and big financial sanctions are also possible.

In a letter to fans, Al Mubarak writes that, despite reporting, the Premier League’s process ‘still has a long way to run’ and adds ‘our confidence in proving the club’s innocence remains as strong as it was when this began’.

While an official statement remains outstanding, it is now known that the competition has scored a huge initial triumph, in a revelation that has sent shockwaves through football and opens the door to a series of punishments including expulsion.

Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak (left) has insisted his club are innocent of the charges they have been found guilty of

However, it is viewed as an inevitability that City will launch an appeal. And, while not referencing the result of a hearing that has been almost two years in the making, Al Mubarak suggested warned that all is not lost.

‘The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the Club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began,’ he wrote.

‘There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position. But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies.

‘While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our Club. We will not give them that opportunity.’

The Premier League are yet to comment. On Friday, a City spokesperson said: ‘The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the Club’s statement of February 2023.

‘The Club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League Board and Executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.'

Relegation could come into play if City are dealt a heavy deduction this season. And that, according to football finance expert Kieran Maguire, is likely.

'There is no doubt a points deduction would be the most likely outcome in the view of many,' Maguire said on TalkTV. 'We have seen them before for Nottingham Forest and Everton for breach of the financial limit rules. So that is feasible.'

The severity of the punishment that could be heading City's way is yet to be determined

It remains unclear what sort of punishment could be handed out, though, and things could yet get worse for the eight-time Premier League champions.

Maguire added: 'If you take a look at the Premier League handbook,' Maguire added, 'it says the recommendations are as broad based as you want them to be. Anything from a fine, to a points deduction, to expulsion from the league.

'Also, it could be that the titles won during that period will be taken away, though you can't retrospectively have the joy that winning a match and title brings from a fans' perspective.'

In that case, a number of clubs could find themselves up on their major honours, with the likes of Manchester United and Liverpool set to benefit if City are stripped of titles.

A number of former United players have taken to social media to suggest they should now have more trophies to their names, while City also won the likes of the League Cup and FA Cup in the period of which they have been charged.

David De Gea, for example, posted on X: 'So…… Let's talk. How many Premier League titles have I won then?'

De Gea played for United from 2011 to 2023, winning the league title in the 2012-13 season.

If City were to hypothetically be stripped of their recent titles, though, he could be quids in.

Former Manchester United players Rio Ferdinand (left) and David De Gea (right) have called for City to be stripped of their titles

Man United finished second in the Premier League in the 2011-12 season – the year De Gea joined the club, were then also runners-up in the 2017-18 campaign, in which De Gea played 37 of the 38 league games, and the 2020-21 season, with the Spaniard featuring in 26 league matches.

Rio Ferdinand was also keen to state his case, posting on X: 'Another Premier League medal to be added to the cabinet.'

Former United manager Jose Mourinho, meanwhile, said in 2024: 'We won the Europa League and finished second in the Premier League. I think we still have a chance to win that league. Maybe they punish Manchester City with points, we win that league. And then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal.'

Some have also likened the situation to that which faced Juventus 20 years ago. In 2006, the Italian giants were relegated, given a 30-point deduction and were stripped of two top-division titles after they were found to have been involved in conduct amounting to sporting fraud.

A can of worms could therefore be opened, and clubs will no doubt be eager to claim what they believe is theirs – whether that be in trophies or money.

Maguire pointed to the fee Everton were ordered to pay Burnley after they were found guilty of breaches in the 2021-22 season, which the Clarets argued helped Everton stay in the Premier League at their expense.

'Then there is a separate issue where clubs who have lost out on titles could put in financial compensation for not getting into Europe,' Maguire added. 'For loss of prize money

'We do have a precedent where Everton were told they had to give Burnley £35million for a single breach in a single season.'

Sports.title: The secrets of Warwickshire's County Championship triumph: How a 'workhorse' newcomer, an Indian spin sensation and a dramatic bowling SOS fired Chris Woakes & Co to glory
Sports.content:
The season was not a month old when the penny dropped that a title challenge could be on.

Nottinghamshire, the county champions, were bolstered by the availability of England duo Ben Duckett and Josh Tongue for the end of April fixture. The ideal calibre of opponent against which to gauge their own credentials.

‘Something that we've spoken about as a team a lot is something you talk about a lot in Test cricket too - about winning windows of matches,’ says Chris Woakes.

‘There was a window on day one at Trent Bridge where we could have easily lost it and all of a sudden we’d have been right on the back foot in the game. But we wrestled some momentum back and put ourselves in a solid position.’

Indeed, with Tongue tearing in from the Radcliffe Road end, Warwickshire were reeling at 179 for six. But thanks to 165 from Ed Barnard along with half centuries from Woakes and Michael Booth, they posted 459. On the third morning, Nottinghamshire followed on.

The game ended in a draw, but it is a match that Warwickshire’s squad cross reference when asked to reflect upon their journey to a ninth County Championship pennant. That particular window had given them a glimpse into what was possible; they knew they had the players to go toe to toe with the best.

Across eight appearances, Woakes has averaged 25 with the bat and 24 with the ball. Solid rather than spectacular, but his mere presence has lifted others.

And it has been heartening to witness him return to the county scene. Twelve months ago, a left shoulder badly dislocated in a Test match against India at The Oval left him ‘worried that I might not play again’.

Warwickshire are winners of the County Championship for the ninth time

Veteran Chris Woakes returned to county cricket to fulfil his father's dream

One of the motivations for extending his career beyond his 217 international caps was to honour his late father Roger, a huge fan of the club. He also wanted ‘to do the badge proud,’ saying: ‘I’ve been a Warwickshire man since the start. I walked through the gates at 11. So it just didn't feel right to finish, really, in the manner that it did with England. Obviously that chapter has been closed, but I always felt like I'd like to leave the game the way I came in, which was obviously through the county grind.’

Walking away from the first-class game as a county champion represents a fitting farewell for one of cricket’s most respected competitors. Woakes will be 38 next season, but he has vowed to keep an open mind, letting the dust settle on this one first before considering becoming a white-ball specialist.

Woakes got his team over the line in what will go down as the pivotal match: the one-wicket nail biter with Sussex at Edgbaston in August, the first of five wins in an unbeaten ‘block’ of six Championship fixtures to finish the season.

In an encounter in which 207 was the highest innings score, Warwickshire needed 47 with three wickets standing, but Woakes kept his nerve with an unbeaten 23.

However, it has been his regular new-ball partner during this period, Ethan Bamber, who has given credence to a couple of cricket’s maxims: the Championship is a marathon not a sprint; and bowlers win you silverware.

At the heart of Warwickshire’s recruitment planning for 2026 was to expand their pool of seam bowlers. They secured their No 1 target in Yorkshire all-rounder Jordan Thompson on a big six-figure salary, lured the much-coveted England Lions player Nathan Gilchrist from Kent and brought back the experienced legs of Keith Barker, a Championship winner with the Bears in 2012, from Hampshire.

Ethan Bamber is the 'workhorse' whose bowling has set the tone for the team

Resources that offered them the opportunity to rotate the attack members, keeping legs fresh. None have featured during a hectic September, though. Thompson has remained on the sidelines, Gilchrist sent on loan to Leicestershire while it has been Barker’s first month of retirement after succumbing to a knee injury.

The Championship’s final stanza represents a punishing schedule of 24 days cricket out of 39, but the indefatigable Bamber has responded in the manner of another workhorse, George Orwell’s Boxer in Animal Farm, who met every demand for increased labour with the pledge: I will work harder.

‘I like to think I'm a good pro and I do the right things, but if I've got up at 8am and had a stretch, Bamber's got up at 7am and run 20km. He is the best pro, you will ever come across in your life, I promise you,’ says team-mate Olly Hannon-Dalby.

‘He's absolutely superb. There's not a stone he doesn't overturn to try to get the best out of himself. And from a physical, mental, tactical, technical point of view, he's outstanding. So there's absolutely no surprise the success he's had this year.

‘I know there's lots of chat about what succeeds at Test level and how fast you need to bowl, but for county cricket Ethan Bamber’s exceptional. He will hammer away for 20 overs a day, never loses any pace and threatens the top of off stump, both inside edge and outside edge.’

Sending down more deliveries than anyone else in the top flight has reaped its rewards for the 27-year-old Bamber. He is the leading wicket-taker across both divisions.

Bamber’s arrival at Edgbaston was triggered by a woeful 2024 season for the club that saw them win just once.

Recognising the need for a strike bowler, they recalled the big impression Bamber had left, taking nine for 91 in Birmingham the previous summer. It was one of the last big cricket decisions made by the former performance director Gavin Larsen.

One of the best of a new regime that has come in for criticism, including the 31% rise in Ashes tickets prices next summer and a poor 2026 season in limited-overs cricket, was a change of captaincy this March.

Barnard didn’t push for the position, but was identified as the right man to lead the team forward by the club’s decision makers: chief executive Stuart Cain, Larsen’s successor James Thomas and Ian Westwood, head the coach. Alex Davies’ resignation was announced on the eve of the season.

Barnard is a quiet, unassuming presence, leading by example on the field.

Some people think he has been too nice at times. One theory was that Thompson was bowling the overs that would ordinarily be supplied by Barnard during periods of the season.

Taking on more responsibility in Thompson’s absence, he took extraordinary match figures of eight for 18 in the crushing innings dispatch of Glamorgan a fortnight ago.

Davies, like Thompson another excellent servant of the domestic game, has also lost his place in Warwickshire’s first-choice XI over recent weeks, but it should be acknowledged that as club captain for three years he was involved in foundational work for this success, including the signing of Beau Webster as one of the club’s overseas players.

Australian Webster proved less effective in his second season with the club, but is a popular character within the group. As is Manav Suthar, the India slow left-armer, Warwickshire secured in June, days before a Test debut that bore seven Afghanistani wickets.

Spin bowler Manav Suthar is highly regarded and viewed as the next big superstar

‘We were all panicking that he might not come over after that, that India would wrap him up in cotton wool, but luckily he did,’ says Hannon-Dalby.

Suthar claimed 11 victims in two mid-season appearances for Warwickshire and returned to Edgbaston once more after taking his Test haul to 23 in three matches during the away series in Sri Lanka.

His new team-mates reckon they have a future world superstar in their midst.

‘He rags it. You often talk about bowlers with regards to their accuracy, but he just spins it a long way. Even in warm-ups, if you watch him, he’s spinning it square,’ says Hannon-Dalby.

‘He's a very cool cat too. Playing Test cricket for India at 23, in the IPL, wearing clobber in the changing room that I could only dream of. Gold chain, never takes his sunglasses off.

‘And he’s totally bought into being here. For example, on the eve of this last match, he was in the nets chatting to all our young academy spinners. Hopefully, there's a relationship with him for many years to come.’

Hannon-Dalby is another of the Bears’ great storylines this summer. Deemed surplus to requirements in April, he was sent on loan to Worcestershire. Serving notice at New Road that he still had life in him at 37, he was recalled by his parent club for first team duty and handed a contract that will see him remain a member of ‘the bad lads’ - the collective term given to the club’s seamers by their exceptional bowling coach Graeme Welch - for three more years.

Like Suthar and Bamber, Hannon-Dalby’s Division One wickets have come at a cost of fewer than 20 apiece.

Along with Sam Hain, the only one of the club’s batsmen to reach the 1,000 run mark in 2026 and contributor of two of their minimalist five hundreds, Woakes and Rob Yates, he was part of the 2021 title-winning squad.

Dramatically sealed on the final evening of the campaign, it was only Warwickshire’s eighth County Championship pennant in a competition that has been in existence since 1890 - a figure that perhaps undersells the size of the club.

‘Warwickshire is one of those clubs where there is arguably a bit more expectation to win things,’ says Will Rhodes, their captain that season and taker of the catch that completed the last-round victory over Somerset.

‘For someone like me who was never going to play international cricket, playing at the top end and winning the County Championship is the pinnacle of a career.

‘It takes a lot of luck, a lot of skill, but a lot of hard graft.’

Words that the winners of Warwickshire’s ninth will no doubt appreciate.

Sports.title: Ireland WILL play Israel: Stars hold FOUR-HOUR crunch talks and stage last-minute vote on controversial game after team-mate refused to take part in Nations League contest - with manager saying 'we're playing against genocide'
Sports.content:
Ireland WILL play Israel: Stars hold FOUR-HOUR crunch talks and stage last-minute vote on controversial game after team-mate refused to take part in Nations League contest - with manager saying 'we're playing against genocide'

Ireland have decided to fulfil their Nations League fixture against Israel after the squad held a dramatic vote on contesting the game on Saturday.

Sunday's match in Debrecen, Hungary, was plunged into chaos after goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu refused to feature amid growing backlash over the conflict in Gaza.

Over 17,000 people have signed a petition calling for the Irish to boycott the game, and tensions mounted when the FAI announced a delay to training and a pre-match press conference as crunch talks were held at the team hotel.

But FAI CEO David Courell told reporters that, following a vote, the players have decided to play Sunday's game.

'I would like to apologise to the media for the delay and interruptions today. It is a challenging time. The squad was in Pristina yesterday. An extensive conversation took place where the consensus from the group was to travel to Hungary. It was a two hour meeting,' he said.

'This morning a player expressed their discomfort to the head coach and indicated their intent to withdraw from the squad. This new variable required time and deliberation for the squad to consider. What preceded was another four hours on conversation, mainly with players but at times with staff and the executive.

'A lot of positions were presented. We were fully respectful of everyone's right to have their opinion on these topics.

'Ultimately, within the last 90 minutes we carried out a squad vote on fulfilling the fixtures. A significant majority [to play] was the result. The association took the decision to fulfill these fixtures.'

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson confirmed that Bazunu will not play in Sunday's fixtures, but the remaining squad will train today.

'This morning was just a change of mind for one of the players,' he said. 'All the rest of the players are training today. The balance changed with this, it's an ongoing discussion. We have not got to a conclusion to this. There will be more discussions tonight and tomorrow. It is a unique situation.'

It was also confirmed that Ireland will not partake in 'elements of the pre-match ceremony' although it remains unclear what that entails.

Hallgrimsson had previously stirred controversy after saying his team are 'playing against genocide' amid Israel's attacks on Palestine, where more than 70,000 people have been killed since the war in Gaza began.

Hallgrimsson's comments sparked an angry backlash from Israeli officials, but there have been growing calls for the game to be scrapped by the Irish public - with a petition attracting over 17,000 signatures.

On Thursday night, Bazunu's team-mate Jason Knight publicly shared his discomfort at the prospect of facing Sunday's opponents.

High drama outside the Irish football team hotel in Debrecen with speculation the players may be about to pull out of their match with Israel tomorrow, a decision the majority of people in Ireland would support. https://t.co/yIuvHE0bwK — Barry Malone (@malonebarry) September 26, 2026

Ireland will play against Israel in Hungary after staging a last-minute vote

The team held crunch talks for four hours after Gavin Bazunu refused to play

'I don't think the game obviously should be going ahead but it is going ahead,' said Knight. 'We'll have a deeper talk about it and what that means, we'll get our thoughts as a group and go from there.

'It is (uncomfortable). There is obviously a lot of talk and rightly so about the scenario we're in, but I thought Dara spoke quite well (on Wednesday).

'It's a bigger spotlight obviously (around the Israel games) and not focused on the football itself. It's very, very unusual and none of us have come into this scenario before so we're learning on the fly as well. So we'll talk as a group and see what is the best foot forward.'

Defender Dara O'Shea, meanwhile, admitted his side are in a 'tough position'.

'As soon as the game was decided by the FAI, the government and Uefa, we were always going to be put in a tough position. We feel exposed, it's come down to us as such at the end,' he said this week. 'We knew that was going to be the case and this was going to come our way. It's a difficult situation but we understand the severity of it too.

'It doesn't really necessarily matter my opinion entirely. It's about the group's decision. We've got to come together as one and navigate that ourselves. This is obviously slightly different.'

Ireland are due to play Israel twice in the Nations League during this international break with both games played at neutral venues. It remains to be seen whether Israel would be awarded the full six points in the events that Ireland boycotts both fixtures.

Hallgrimsson was set to front the media for the first time since telling reporters last weekend: 'We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide. So, we're playing against Israel. We're not playing with Israel.'

The Israeli FA angrily took to social media on Monday to hit back at Hallgrimsson's comments, meanwhile, when he used the word 'genocide' in previewing the upcoming fixtures.

As reports circulated that the Israelis were considering a complaint to UEFA, the Israeli FA posted on X on Monday night: 'We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way,' the post on X stated.

'Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by the Republic of Ireland team coach.

'We're not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we're playing against the coach who embodies them.'

Israel were criticised following their first game of the international break, too, which saw them lose 3-1 against Austria.

Sayed Abu Farchi was sent off in the second-half of his side's defeat, having taken the corner flag out the ground and mimicked a gunshot, though others have suggested he could have been imitating a snooker shot.

Israel's Sayed Abu Farchi was sent off on Thursday after mimicking a gunshot following a goal

Fans were left stunned and judged the move to be in bad taste. Abu Farchi protested with Bulgarian official Georgi Kabakov at the time, insisting he should have stayed on the field.

But he was already on a yellow card, and Kabakov opted to show him a second booking, resulting in his dismissal.

Israel manager Ran Ben-Shimon leapt to the defence of the Colorado Rapids midfielder after the game, insisting the celebration is regularly carried out by Abu Farchi without punishment.

'I've seen it before and everyone can check,' said Ben-Shimon. 'When this young player scores, in the Israeli national team or the MLS or anywhere he plays, he celebrates in the same situation again and again and he never gets a yellow card about it.

'He didn't know about it, this is his way to celebrate every goal he scores. He's a young player, I'm sure this lesson will stay with him a long time, he made a mistake.'

UEFA rules, meanwhile, suggest the referee was right to show a second yellow card.

They say a player must be booked for 'gesturing or acting in a provocative, derisory or inflammatory way'. Removing the corner flag is also yellow card worthy.

Sports.title: George Russell wins Azerbaijan Grand Prix by ONE tenth of a second: Mercedes star back to winning ways - and denies Max Verstappen his first triumph of the season by razor-thin margin
Sports.content:
Only just. By one tenth of a second. Practically a photo-finish. But victory for George Russell at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, achieved in drama with Max Verstappen right alongside him, means the Briton can just glimpse the prize on the horizon – the world title he craves.

Hmm, it still requires binoculars to detect it clearly, but it is no longer out of sight.

After this dramatic win, he remains 66 points behind his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli but this was a rare afternoon of cheer for Russell, with his rival finishing fifth. It means he cut his deficit to the Italian from 81 points, and there are 208 to fight for over eight rounds, including one sprint race.

Russell had not won for three months almost to the day, in Austria, before this and confidence was hissing out of him like a punctured tyre. Antonelli was the coming kid of 20, an unstoppable Exocet, or so it seemed.

But this time the wonderkid was stymied by crashing in qualifying and started 16th. He made good progress up the field and was helped by a couple of safety cars, the first bunching up the field when he was running ninth.

This punctuation in proceedings, brought about by Alex Albon bashing his Williams into the wall at Turn 5 at the mid-point of the race, allowed everyone to stop for fresh rubber. Nobody had pitted by this stage. And now the field was close to him when the green flag was waved after 35 of the 51 laps and the fight restarted.

George Russell claimed his first win in three months as he claimed the Azerbaijan Granx Prix

He beat Max Verstappen by less than a second, denying the Dutchman a first win of the year

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli could only finish fifth, having crashed in qualifying and started 16th

Russell, by the way, had priorly been sailing ahead from pole, the man dominating the race by a distance. His advantage at the time of the safety car’s maiden tour stood in double figures, ten or 11 seconds. Yes, his Mercedes was mighty quick but he was making full use of its potential around Baku’s tight streets.

As for Antonelli's situation. The safety car peeled off and the next moment Franco Colapinto of Alpine came charging into the first corner like a 10-pin bowling ball. Kamikaze stuff. He crashed into his team-mate Pierre Gasly and took him out. Gasly then ricocheted into Lando Norris, a second helpless victim of the madness. The world champion was out of the race and the safety car was recalled.

This incident gave Antonelli – given Gasly retired, too – seventh place. The championship leader later passed Hamilton to claim his finishing place four back from Russell.

It was a decent drive from Antonelli in a fast car well-suited to the track, even if he could not recreate the heroics of his win at Monza earlier in the month when he rose from 19th on the grid.

Russell was too fast for everyone all weekend. Yet having established his huge lead that was eroded by the crashes, he found himself in a battle with Verstappen, who had passed Oscar Piastri for second place after the first safety car.

Ironically, Verstappen had been struggling for speed earlier but was then flying having moved on to soft tyres, just as Russell had, the pair on the same strategy.

The Dutchman, for all his harrying, had to settle for second place, though it looked at the end as if he might just pass Russell as they roared to the line side-by-side. It was touch and go, and one of the closest finishes in modern F1 memory.

Verstappen’s Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar finished third. Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc came fourth, holding off Antonelli’s charge by 0.3sec, with Lewis Hamilton sixth.

Sports.title: World's richest footballer - who is worth THIRTEEN times more than Cristiano Ronaldo - is released by Thai club following academy stints at Chelsea and Leicester City
Sports.content:
The ‘world’s richest footballer’ has been released by Thai League 1 side Ratchaburi F.C. after making just 18 appearances in over three years at the club.

Faiq Bolkiah, 28, is the nephew of Hassanal Bolkiah, the sultan of Brunei and the world’s longest-reigning current monarch. Reports suggest the footballer is worth £16billion.

Having celebrated his Golden Jubilee in October 2017, the sultan is nearing 59 years on the throne, but his globe-trotting nephew has undertaken an unusual footballing pathway.

Born in the United States, Bolkiah was educated at Bradfield College in Berkshire and spent time in the youth setups of Southampton, Chelsea and Leicester City, but didn’t realise any success in England and made no senior appearances.

He eventually made his way to Primeira Liga side CS Marítimo in 2020 but was let go after less than a year and just eight appearances between the youth teams and the B-team.

Bolkiah was the first Bruneian player signed into the Thai division, Thai League 1, when he was picked up by Chonburi F.C. in 2021.

Faiq Boliah - the world's richest footballer - is without a club after being released

Bolkiah is the nephew the sultan of Brunei and has an estimated worth of £16billion

He spent around four-and-a-half years in the league, transferring to Ratchaburi F.C. in June 2023, before being let go by the club this July.

The 28-year-old made just fifty appearances in the Thai first league in almost five years.

Losing your job at 28 would be tough for the average worker, but Faiq Bolkiah can luckily rely on the support cushion provided by his uncle that is reported to be in the range of $30-50 billion.

This figure has led to Bolkiah being dubbed the “richest footballer in the world” despite not being a direct heir to his uncle’s fortune.

Cristiano Ronaldo and Lionel Messi boast fortunes of $1.1 billion and $1.2 billion respectively, according to Forbes.

Hassanal Bolkiah’s fortune has largely been propped up by Brunei’s oil and natural gas reserves and was briefly declared by Forbes to be the richest man in the world in 1997, overtaking, and then being overtaken by, Bill Gates.

The royal family in Brunei controls almost all aspects of the economy, which allowed the sultan and his brother, Faiq Bolkiah’s father, Jefri, to build a car collection reportedly consisting of over seven thousand vehicles at its height.

The $5billion car collection is kept in a compound surrounded by a razor-wire-topped wall and patrolled by armed Gurkhas and German Shepherds.

Sports.title: Liverpool announce Julian Ward as new sporting director to replace Richard Hughes after £240m summer spend
Sports.content:
Liverpool have appointed Julian Ward as their new sporting director to replace Richard Hughes, who left to join Saudi club Al-Hilal. Ward had held the sporting director job at the Premier League club during the 2022-23 season and most recently served as Fenway Sports Group's (FSG) technical director. Hughes's departure had been the latest in a string of high-ranking executives to leave the club in recent months. Michael Edwards had earlier exited as CEO of football for Liverpool owner FSG. The 2026 summer transfer window was Hughes's final at Liverpool, in which the Reds spent around £240million. His contract was set to expire in 2027. 'I'll always follow and support the club with great affection, and I wish everyone involved nothing but success for this season and beyond,' said Hughes in a statement following news of his departure. He signed the likes of Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak in his time at the club, which he joined following the departure of Jurgen Klopp a little over two years ago. Livrpool have appointed Julian Ward (second left) to replace Richard Hughes (second right) as sporting director Ward, meanwhile, signed the likes of Cody Gakpo, Darwin Nunez and Alexis Mac Allister during his first stint at Anfield. 'The knowledge and expertise he brings will only enhance our football operations, while also ensuring Andoni (Iraola) is provided with the support he requires as he continues to make such a positive impression as head coach,' FSG president Mike Gordon said in the club's announcement. Ward added: 'This is an exciting period for Liverpool - on and off the pitch - in which change and opportunity go hand in hand, but at the same time the culture, values and principles that have underpinned the club for so long remain as strong as ever.' Ward initially joined Liverpool in 2012, working in scouting, recruitment and player development strategy. He was promoted to assistant sporting director in 2020 and succeeded Michael Edwards in 2022, but left at the end of the season. He became FSG's technical director in 2024 when Edwards was made their chief executive of football, and will now step into the role vacated by Hughes.
