Girl disabled by Israeli strike urges wheelchairs be let into Gaza

NewsFeed Girl disabled by Israeli strike urges wheelchairs be let into Gaza

Disabled and amputee children injured in Israeli attacks in Gaza are unable to get new wheelchairs, because Israel is refusing to allow them in. We spoke to 8-year-old Layan Asaliya, who urges Israeli authorities to let wheelchairs in.

World.title: Turkiye calls for UN Security Council veto to end: Could it happen?
World.content:
Fully abolishing the veto would require the unlikely agreement of all five permanent Security Council members.

Share Turkiye calls for UN Security Council veto to end: Could it happen? on social media

Turkiye’s President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has called for the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC) to lose their veto power, arguing that the current veto system is “unjust” and hinders “global stability and peace”.

The call comes as the UNSC, which has five permanent members and 10 rotating, non-permanent members, remains deadlocked on many issues – from Israel’s war on Gaza to Russia’s war in Ukraine and the Strait of Hormuz.

The US, one of the five permanent members, has vetoed seven resolutions related to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict over the past three years, including five calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.

Russian vetoes have prevented the UNSC from passing any firm resolutions on the war in Ukraine.

Speaking to journalists in New York on Thursday, Erdogan said, “Let the veto mechanism be abolished… Let us move from a UN model that protects only five members to a mechanism that encompasses all members”.

So, could Erdogan’s call become a reality and what would abolishing the veto mean for the UNSC?

What is the UNSC veto and who can exercise it?

It is a special power to veto any substantive resolution, granted to the body’s five permanent members – the US, the UK, France, Russia and China.

It means that even if 14 of 15 UNSC members vote in favour of a resolution, just one veto from any of the five permanent members (P5) can tank it.

What has Turkiye called for?

Erdogan has called for a complete overhaul of the UNSC. That includes ending permanent membership of the council and eliminating the veto power.



Laying out his case in a September 22 article published by Bloomberg, Erdogan wrote that the UNSC’s current structure, developed eight decades ago, no longer meets the needs of a changing world and that a single country should not be able to block the wishes of the broader international community.

“Leaving the resolution of global crises to the will of a handful of capitals is no longer compatible with the realities of today’s world,” he wrote.

Erdogan also called for greater powers for the UN General Assembly (UNGA), which he said should elect all UNSC members for set terms. Countries seeking to serve on the council would therefore have to “regain the confidence of the majority of member states through elections”, he said.

Erdogan lobbied for this initiative during his recent address to the UNGA, saying “a system in which the will of more than 190 countries is subject to the whims of five countries is neither fair nor capable of fully establishing trust”.

What would it take for the UNSC to decide to end the veto?

Formally ending the veto would require an amendment to the UN Charter.

Under Article 108, that requires approval by two-thirds of the UNGA and ratification by two-thirds of UN members, including all five permanent members. In other words, the P5 would have to sign off on giving up their own veto power.

What is the France-Mexico proposal that is gaining ground?

In 2015, France and Mexico tabled a proposal urging the P5 to suspend their vetoes on resolutions involving mass atrocities, such as genocide and crimes against humanity.

The initiative would rely on a “collective and voluntary agreement” among P5 states.

The initiative has recently gained renewed traction, with 21 states, including P5 member the UK, backing it within the last four months.

That brings the total number of UN members states supporting it to 128, according to the French government, just one short of the number needed to pass a resolution in the UNGA.

While such a resolution would be non-binding, advocates hope it would exert more pressure on P5 states to withhold their votes in emergency situations.

What is most likely to happen?

Any formal effort to abolish P5 members’ veto power is likely to fail, as it would inevitably face resistance from most, if not all, P5 members.

Russia has already responded to the Turkish initiative by saying it believes permanent UNSC members should retain their veto power, though it did say it supports expanding the number of permanent members on the council.



The US and China have previously strongly defended their veto privileges.

Expanding the UNSC, as Russia proposed, is more likely, though that would also come with challenges.

The US and China have both previously said they would support modest increases to the council’s composition, including by adding seats for African nations, none of which hold permanent membership. The UK and France have also backed expansion, including permanent seats for Brazil, Germany, India and Japan, as well as African countries.

But expanding the UNSC would also require an amendment to the UN Charter, which again requires the backing of all P5 states. Getting the P5 to agree on which countries to share their power with – and whether to extend new members the veto power – has long proved difficult.

“The status quo is not really interested in change,” Professor Ibrahim Gambari, a former Nigerian foreign minister and former Nigerian permanent representative to the UN, told Al Jazeera.

As for the France-Mexico initiative, analysts say its impact would be limited because the commitments are voluntary and non-binding.

Writing in a 2022 article for US publication Lawfare, analysts John Ramming Chappell and Emma Svoboda noted that the France-Mexico initiative and others like it are “couched in voluntary language” and lack consensus “from the most frequent veto-users (Russia, the United States and China)”.

As a result, “the principles advanced in the initiatives remain aspirational”, they wrote.

Who has exercised the veto most in the past?

Historically, Russia (or the Soviet Union prior to 1991) has cast the most vetoes by far, with nearly half of all vetoes ever recorded (163 out of 331).

The US is second, with 95 vetoes – around 28 percent of those cast.

In recent years, the US has vetoed numerous resolutions concerning the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, including five calling for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza.

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, it has vetoed three resolutions relating to that conflict.

When have France and the UK exercised the veto?

France and the UK – the two permanent members calling for suspension of the veto in resolutions relating to humanitarian atrocities – have exercised their veto far more sparingly, with a combined 50 vetoes. Neither country has used a veto since 1989 and most of their earlier vetoes were cast alongside the US.

The UK has only been the sole veto on a resolution a handful of times, all related to its former colony Rhodesia, which later became independent as Zimbabwe.

France has only vetoed a resolution on its own twice, once in connection with a territorial dispute with Comoros and the other related to the Indonesian conflict in 1947.

World.title: The media battle behind Brazil’s election
World.content:
As Brazilians head into national elections, there’s a familiar name on the ballot: Bolsonaro. Not former President Jair Bolsonaro. It’s his son Flavio, who is presenting himself to the electorate as a more moderate version of his father.

Election coverage has been dominated by a major corruption scandal – the biggest banking fraud case in the country’s history. Brazilians are accustomed to corruption scandals involving political figures. The coverage tends to be framed as: they’re all equally corrupt.

Contributors:

Andrew Fishman – President & co-founder, Intercept Brasil

David Nemer – Professor, University of Virginia

Andre Pagliarini – Professor, Louisiana State University

Natalia Portinari – Reporter, O Globo

On our radar: Donald Trump’s decision to bar three news outlets from the White House appears to have backfired after journalists organised a media boycott and a judge overturned the ban. Tariq Nafi has been tracking the latest duel between the US president and the media.

Spain’s neo-Nazis: spectacle vs reality

A fringe neo-Nazi movement in Spain, Nucleo Nacional, has attracted a growing online following by packaging incendiary and slickly produced content. The mainstream media attention the group has received has made a marginal organisation appear far larger and more influential than it is. The Listening Post’s Elettra Scrivo travels to Madrid – where she comes face-to-face with Nucleo Nacional’s members – to look at the reality that lies behind the spectacle.

Featuring:

Miquel Ramos – Author, ‘Antifascistas’

Urszula Mrozowska – Digital researcher in hate speech and extremism

World.title: Manchester City face ‘drastic’ sanctions, says club’s former chairman
World.content:
Manchester City are understood to be ready to appeal any guilty verdict, but could face ‘severe penalty’ says ex-chair.

Former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein said the club could face potentially “drastic” sanctions after reportedly being found guilty on all but one of 115 charges for breaching Premier League financial rules.

The Premier League has not made an official announcement over the case and there is no indication of any possible punishment.

Abu Dhabi-backed City have always strenuously denied the charges and a club spokesperson said the position had not changed.

It is understood City will appeal should the charges be upheld.

“The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence,” the spokesperson said.

City were charged by the Premier League in 2023 following an investigation into alleged breaches of rules between 2009 and 2018.

The club were accused of failing to provide accurate financial information and details of payments to players and coaches, as well as breaches of financial sustainability rules.

They were also charged with failing to cooperate with an investigation.

A hearing by an independent commission started in September 2024.

Man City face ‘severe penalty’

Bernstein, who was City chairman between 1998 and 2003, told Times Radio that “money is not sufficient” in terms of a potential punishment, urging a swift appeal process.

“The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, I think that would be a disaster,” he said, “not just for this particular case but for English football generally. The timing is crucial.



“I can’t give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of [the] charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty.

“All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that.”

Oasis star and City fan Noel Gallagher described his “shock” at the developments.

Speaking on the Let Me Talk podcast, he said: “Surprised because only that the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges.

“So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we’ve been found guilty of all but one. But really overall just quite sad really. Sad for the fans and for the players.”

UK culture secretary Lisa Nandy described the case as “unsettling” for football fans and called for a swift resolution.

In 2020, UEFA imposed a two-year European ban on City as well as a fine for breaking financial fair-play rules, though that ban was later overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

If the reported guilty verdicts are confirmed, sanctions could include a severe points deduction and possibly even expulsion from the Premier League.

Everton and Nottingham Forest were both hit by points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of profit and sustainability rules.

Other Premier League clubs are understood to be taking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges.

Under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour, whose Abu Dhabi United Group acquired the club in 2008, City have become the dominant force in English football.

They have won eight Premier League titles, a Champions League crown and multiple other trophies over the past 15 years.

The latest developments in the case come just months after former City manager Pep Guardiola left the club following a golden decade in charge at the Etihad.

Guardiola always backed the club’s stance on the charges but threatened to walk away if he felt he had been lied to and they were proven to be true.

World.title: Huge crowds greet Pope in Paris for open-air Mass
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of people have greeted Pope Leo XIV in the centre of Paris for a giant open-air Mass.

Crowds cheered as the pontiff moved down the Champs-ÃlysÃ©es Avenue beneath the Arc de Triomphe, waving to crowds from his popemobile.

The head of the Catholic Church blessed several babies as he stopped at different stages along the avenue as chants of "Leo, Leo" rang out.

World.title: Iran offers US deal to reopen Strait of Hormuz in seven days
World.content:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says his country has proposed a deal to the US that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened within a week.

Araghchi told reporters at the UN in New York that this could be done "if the necessary conditions are met" and said these were contained within the memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in June.

"The choice now rests with the United States," he said, adding the plan was delivered to the US via Qatar.

Asked about the Iranian offer, a US official told the BBC positive discussions were taking place through mediators, including about nuclear issues.

While the US has yet to deliver its official response to the proposal, the Wall Street Journal, citing US officials, reported that US President Donald Trump had rejected the deal., external

Trump was privately sceptical that Iran would meet his demands, it reported, and had told his staff that he saw a renewed bombing campaign as likely.

The US and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on 28 February. Iran responded by attacking Israel and US bases in the Gulf and Arab Gulf allies of the US - as well as blocking the Strait of Hormuz.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to pass through the strait before the war and its closure has caused wild fluctuations of energy prices.

It has also increased pressure on Trump to find a way of ending the conflict - particularly as the US heads to Congressional elections in November.

"If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, a normal maritime passage restored within seven days," Araghchi told reporters.

He did not specify what steps Iran wanted the US to take but added that "the actions that the United States should take are not new. They are all already in the MOU".

"I can tell you if there is seriousness in the US side to come to a deal and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, everything is now prepared," he added.

A US official told the BBC that the US was "in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush".

In an interview with CBS News, the BBC's US partner, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that the ceasefire process "will begin from the very day they accept it".

"We had previously reached an agreement based on the MOU that was signed in Pakistan... if the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before," he added.

Pezeshkian also said Iran would now allow UN nuclear inspectors into the country.

Rejecting claims that Iran is trying to develop a nuclear weapon, the Iranian president said: "If they wish to come in and have inspections, we can reach accords and agreements vis-Ã -vis that specific topic within the negotiations."

World.title: British national among six dead in building explosion close to Acropolis in Athens
World.content:
Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building housing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.

The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.

Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building.

Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.

All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."

The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, Reuters news agency reported citing local police.

The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.

World.title: Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared
World.content:
A flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok after 48 hours of heavy rain left roads in the Thai capital submerged.

People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors.

Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year but extreme weather in recent days has inundated Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested.

The rain is expected to continue into Sunday, raising fears that more canals could burst their banks.

World.title: South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
World.content:
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.

"Is he talking about us?" Roelf Meyer remembers thinking when he first heard the US president say it.

His response to Trump's claim is blunt.

The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.

Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule, known as apartheid, in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa soured.

Meyer said in an interview with the BBC that the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and that he had never received a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.

World.title: OpenAI bots meddled with multiple US government agency sites
World.content:
OpenAI has acknowledged that it alerted "dozens" of global institutions that their websites may have been meddled with by its AI bots acting improperly.

AI agents attempted to get information from "governments, universities, public agencies, and other institutions", including the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Census Bureau and Education Department, the company said.

The disclosures come days after Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced that OpenAI agents had breached non-public files on the website of its government-run health care scheme.

Since August, public fears have grown over the potentially serious, even life-threatening, impacts of AI tools falling outside of human control.

OpenAI said that some of the data was accessed by AI agents, essentially bots that are designed and trained to operate somewhat autonomously, which were working to find "authoritative sources of public information".

But the company noted that some of the bots went beyond that and worked to bypass security measures on websites.

When attempting to get information from the Census Bureau, for instance, AI agents used tools reserved for software developers to access it, the company said.

OpenAI said all of the government data accessed by bots was public.

However, it noted that information that its bots accessed from the SEC, which regulates the US stock market and protects investors, was later published by AI agents on another website. OpenAI says this action was not intended.

In other instances that OpenAI disclosed on Friday, its AI agents transferred data when it should not have.

Such activity resulted in at least 53 incidents where an OpenAI agent took an image from ChatGPT user activity and transferred it elsewhere.

The company said that in each instance of a user image being used and transferred by an AI agent, the user had opted in to allow OpenAI to train models using their data.

Nevertheless, OpenAI admitted: "This is not an appropriate use of this data."

It added that the leak of user images occurred before it had put in place new safeguards on AI training, and it was working to get all the user images transferred to any third-party removed.

Reuters first reported the expanded investigations. OpenAI also published details to its public blog.

In certain instances of the agent activity, OpenAI said the tools "bypassed" security controls of some websites.

In other instances, the AI agents showed "misalignment" in attempts to get at information from websites. Misalignment is a term used by AI companies and researchers to describe instances where an AI tool did something that it was not trained to do or was otherwise unintended.

OpenAI said that it was limiting identifying what entities were impacted because many had asked the company to not disclose details.

"Our goal is to give each organization the facts and defer to them on if and when to make the incident public," it said.

Not all of the instances involved in this incident were being considered a significant security breach, the company noted.

"Some organizations may review what we share and conclude that the information was intentionally public or that the model's interaction was not concerning," it explained. "Others may identify a design issue or security weakness they want to address."

World.title: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged', police say
World.content:
Warning: This story contains distressing details

Police in the US state of Mississippi have said they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" by being placed hanging in a tree.

The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs.

The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree at an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.

Police said that the medical examiner had determined that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".

Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging may have been staged.

Fortune's mother told the BBC that she remembered the coroner telling her: "We're not treating this as [an] actual hanging." Her daughter, they told her, was dead before being placed in the tree.

Christy Spivey also recalled police telling her the incident was "drug related".

She described how she knew her daughter fought for her life till the very end while speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday.

"I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey said, adding that Fortune had left behind four young children, aged seven, five, four and one.

Dressed in a shirt that read "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she did not want to see any innocent people going to jail.

"I just hope they have the right people," she said.

Three people have so far been arrested in relation to the case, all of whom are black, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who has pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody without bail.

A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in relation to the case this week.

A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday.

The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.

Representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, cited at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress, external, which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.

The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has since been ruled a suicide.

World.title: White House bars CNN from travelling with Trump on Air Force One
World.content:
Broadcaster CNN has been barred from travelling with US President Donald Trump on Air Force One for a trip to Tennessee on Saturday.

The move is the latest in a battle between the White House and the media after it was forced to lift its ban on some news outlets.

CNN was scheduled to fly with Trump for his trip to Tennessee for a college American football game until a note released on Friday night by the White House did not list the broadcaster on the media schedule.

The BBC has requested comment from the White House.

CNN has reported that no other outlet was listed as replacing them in the president's tentative schedule.

Last week, Trump banned CNN, Politico and MS NOW journalists from the White House after accusing them of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration.

All three media outlets said they were pursuing legal action and accused Trump of violating their constitutional rights to free speech and freedom of the press.

Four television networks that have a daily rotation of White House coverage alongside CNN - ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC - had paused their broadcasts of the president in solidarity with the banned outlets.

The White House then launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, ahead of the UN General Assembly in New York.

A federal judge has since ruled that Trump barring news outlets from the White House was likely unconstitutional and that the administration had to let them back in, at least for now.

However, the White House still denied entry to some CNN and MS NOW reporters assigned to cover arrivals at a state dinner for Chinese leader Xi Jinping on Thursday.

A White House communications account earlier posted on X that "contrary to what the Fake News wants you to believe, they don't just get to have free rein into every part of the White House, every event and every press call".

Regular US television coverage resumed on Friday after White House officials allowed reporters entry.

The president is set to attend a football game between University of Tennessee vs University of Texas College at Neyland Stadium in Knoxville from midday local time on Saturday.

World.title: How Peter Obi saved over $150 million in Anambra coffers – Alex Otti
World.content:
Governor Alex Otti of Abia State has restated that the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, saved $155 million in the coffers of Anambra State Government during his time as governor of Anambra State.

Mr Otti spoke during an interview with Arise News which was broadcast on Friday morning.

The governor explained that he was the Chief Executive of the now defunct Diamond Bank at the time Mr Obi saved the amount in the state’s coffers.

Diamond Bank, in 2018, announced that it had merged with Access Bank which would take effect from half of 2019.

Meanwhile, Mr Otti’s comment was coming on the heels of controversies surrounding the financial situation of Anambra State at the time Mr Obi left office as governor of the state.

The Anambra State Government has repeatedly claimed that Mr Obi, who served as governor of the Anambra from 2006 to 2014, left an external debt of $123.7 million incurred from eight foreign loans he took while in office.

But Mr Obi has denied taking any loans while in office, explaining that the eight facilities being referred to by the government were “concessionary development-support funds secured by the federal government for states selected for it to address specific needs.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The former governor then argued that even if the $123.7 million debts was true, his over $150 million savings or the $10 million income the savings had been generating annually was enough to cover the debts.

‘I stand by my words’

During the Arise News interview, Mr Otti recalled that he had provided details of Mr Obi’s $155 million savings in a column published in ThisDay Newspaper in 2020.

The governor stressed that he stood by his words, stressing that he authored the piece to make a case about financial prudence.

“I was using it to prove that it’s still possible for people to be prudent in government,” he said

The Abia governor recalled what happened between him and Mr Obi at the time.

“He (Mr Obi) was going to leave the money in Naira. But he came to me, as the CEO of the (Diamond) bank at the time, and I told him, ‘this money you want to keep, Naira will keep losing value. You probably should convert it to dollars’ and it was converted.

“So, it is a statement of facts. And it was something that happened several years ago. And six years after, I still stand by that,” he maintained.

What about debts?

Mr Otti stressed that although the Anambra State Government had been accusing Mr Obi of leaving debts behind, the accusations do not dismiss his submission that the former governor left $155 million in savings.

“It doesn’t take away what I wrote (about $155 million savings),” he responded when reminded about the state government’s debt claims against Mr Obi.

“What I wrote about was what he (Mr Obi) left as credit. I just gave an account of the savings,” the former bank CEO added.

The column Otti wrote in 2020

Titled “the Triumph of Profligacy Over Prudence,” Mr Otti’s article was published on ThisDay Newspaper on 8 June 2020.

In the article, Mr Otti wrote that although he did not belong to the same political party as Mr Obi, the former governor remains “a true example of excellent leadership and accountability in today’s world where such attributes are in very short supply.”

He continued by remarking that Mr Obi managed “to clear all debts” and left funds for his successor before giving details about the $155 million savings.

“One can attest to the fact that some $155 million was invested in the tier two capital of three Nigerian banks with maturities of about 5 years at interest rates of up to 9% per annum to the credit of the (Anambra) State,” Mr Otti wrote.

The former bank CEO explained that the Naira equivalent of the funds at the time of Mr Obi’s investment was about N25 billion.

“If those funds were rolled over at maturity in 2019, they would be worth about N62 billion today.

“If interest is assumed to remain at 9% for the past 6 years, an additional N33.5b would have accrued to bring the present value of the investments to over N95 billion,” he said at the time.

“This is one of the advantages of prudence and financial literacy.”

World.title: Twenty-five years in the shadow of 9/11, By Osmund Agbo
World.content:
As thick fumes of smoke billowed over Manila’s skyline on that fateful day in January 1995, no one knew exactly what was cooking inside Room 604 of the Doña Josefa Apartments, or what the recipe was supposed to produce. But it didn’t take long to find out.

Firefighters and Philippine intelligence officers who entered the apartment discovered a bizarre collection of materials: hot plates, electrical wiring, timers, fuses, counterfeit passports, Bibles, and clerical clothing. It looked less like an apartment than a makeshift laboratory for terrorism. The occupants had already fled the scene, but they had left behind a treasure trove of documents and a computer that revealed the outline of an extraordinarily ambitious plot. It was called Bojinka.

The plan was simple: plant bombs aboard twelve U.S.-bound commercial airliners and detonate them over the Pacific or South China Sea after the conspirators had escaped the aircraft. They also discussed assassinating Pope John Paul II and attacking President Bill Clinton during his 1994 visit to Manila. The immediate disaster that exposed the plot was almost absurdly mundane.

Ramzi Yousef and Abdul Hakim Murad were experimenting with bomb-making chemicals when an accident produced thick, foul-smelling smoke. They fled in panic, and firefighters were summoned. Yousef later escaped to Pakistan, while Murad was eventually arrested. But there was another figure who loomed large in the background: a man known to investigators as Mukhtar, who was also Ramzi Yousef’s uncle. For years, American intelligence knew the name, but his true identity proved elusive.

Then came March 2002. Abu Zubaydah, another high-value al-Qaeda operative, was captured in Faisalabad, Pakistan. During his interrogation, FBI agent Ali Soufan asked about a man known as Mukhtar. According to Soufan, Abu Zubaydah laughed and wondered how the Americans could not know that Mukhtar was one of more than fifty noms de guerre used by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed (KSM), the man whom the 9/11 Commission would later identify as the principal architect of the September 11 attacks. The revelation was a major intelligence breakthrough.

A year later, on March 1, 2003, Pakistani intelligence, the ISI, working with U.S. personnel, captured KSM in Rawalpindi. He was transferred into the CIA’s secret detention facility and subjected to coercive interrogation techniques, including waterboarding, rectal hydration, and rectal feeding. KSM’s capture provided important intelligence about al-Qaeda and its network worldwide.

The Bojinka plot had focused on destroying aircraft. KSM and his associates later took the concept further while designing the September 11 plot: instead of bombs destroying airplanes, the airplanes themselves would become the weapons. That evolution connects Manila in 1995 to New York and Washington in 2001.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

KSM was not always a terrorist, though he embraced the ideology relatively early in his life.

Born to Pakistani parents who had emigrated to Kuwait, he grew up there and became involved with the Muslim Brotherhood as a teenager. In 1983, he moved to the United States to attend Chowan College in North Carolina. He later transferred to North Carolina A&T State University, earning a degree in mechanical engineering in 1986. He subsequently left the United States and traveled to Afghanistan, where he received militant training during the war against the Soviet occupation.

By the early 1990s, KSM and his nephew, Ramzi Yousef, were part of the wider international network of Islamist militants emerging from the Afghan jihad. Today, KSM remains in U.S. custody at Guantánamo Bay, Cuba, while Ramzi Yousef, the mastermind of the 1993 World Trade Center bombing and a principal architect of the Bojinka plot, is serving a life sentence without parole at ADX Florence in Colorado.

It has now been 25 years since the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, when nineteen hijackers murdered 2,977 people. But the human cost of the wars that followed has been vastly larger. Brown University’s Costs of War Project estimates that more than 940,000 people died directly from violence in the major post-9/11 war zones.

Terrorism did not disappear. It mutated, and the world is arguably confronting a more diffuse and geographically dispersed terrorist threat than it was twenty-five years ago. Organizations splintered, rebranded, and spread across borders. Parts of Africa, particularly the Sahel and Lake Chad Basin, are now confronting jihadist insurgencies, kidnapping, and criminal violence.

If we are serious about defeating terrorism, we must confront an uncomfortable truth: terrorists are human beings. They do not emerge from a vacuum. They are shaped by ideology, grievance, money, opportunity, political manipulation, and social networks.

Understanding those forces helps explain how terrorism is nurtured and how its ideology is propagated. History also teaches another uncomfortable lesson: governments sometimes believe they can manipulate violent movements for short-term strategic advantage.

In 1994, Mullah Mohammed Omar, a one-eyed veteran of the anti-Soviet jihad, gathered religious students in Kandahar who wanted to end Afghanistan’s civil war. They became known as the Taliban, which in Pashto means “students” or “seekers of knowledge.” Pakistan’s security establishment, led by the ISI, viewed the Taliban as a potential strategic asset, believing a friendly government in Kabul could provide Pakistan with strategic depth against India. But governments often discover too late that violent proxies have interests of their own.

Under Taliban rule, Afghanistan became a sanctuary for Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda. Pakistan eventually found itself fighting militants connected to networks it had once considered strategically useful. The irony became almost unbearable when bin Laden was found living in Abbottabad, not far from the Pakistan Military Academy. But Pakistan is not alone in this pattern of folly.

The United States, too, armed and funded the Afghan mujahideen during the Cold War to fight the Soviets, contributing to the broader militant environment from which the Taliban and al-Qaeda later emerged. In Iraq, Washington supported Saddam Hussein during parts of the Iran-Iraq War, only to later confront him after he invaded Kuwait. The logic was the same: short-term gain, long-term catastrophe. This is the curse of transactional leadership. It mortgages the future for a fleeting sense of control in the present.

Leaders often imagine they are manipulating extremists as pawns in a game of chess. But pawns have wills of their own. Ideologies, once unleashed, cannot easily be boxed back in. General Hamid Gul, as head of Pakistan’s ISI, believed the Taliban could serve as Pakistan’s strategic tool, while American officials viewed Saddam Hussein as a potential counterweight to Iran. Both calculations proved disastrously misguided.

The cost of these miscalculations is always borne by the powerless. The families of Bajaur trudging through the mountains, the children massacred in Peshawar, the millions of out-of-school children in Borno’s IDP camps, and the passengers fleeing collapsing towers in New York: these are the true victims of short-term bargains struck in secret rooms by ambitious men. The architects of such strategies rarely pay with their lives. Ordinary people do.

Then there’s Saudi Arabia, a Wahhabi state where Salafi extremism has historically had significant institutional and religious influence. Saudi clerics and wealthy private patrons have, over the decades, been accused of helping spread extremist interpretations and financing religious institutions abroad, including some madrassas associated with the broader ideological environment from which militant movements emerged.

For decades, the United States has maintained a close strategic relationship with the Saudi monarchy, even as fifteen of the nineteen 9/11 hijackers were Saudi citizens. Yet the question of Saudi Arabia’s relationship to the broader ecosystem of jihadist extremism remains far more complicated than the nationality of the hijackers alone. Nigeria offers its own grim parallel.

Boko Haram was once courted and tolerated by politicians in Borno for electoral leverage. But it soon broke free, splintering into factions, with some pledging allegiance to the Islamic State.

Similarly, transnational fighters from the Sahel have been accused of being brought into Nigeria to influence political contests. In some cases, armed groups have subsequently remained behind, turning instead to kidnapping, banditry, and trafficking and unleashing a wave of insecurity that now threatens the very elites who once saw them as convenient allies.

For decades, successive Nigerian administrations have treated terror financing with the casual indifference of political expediency. While the U.S. State Department has sanctioned individuals accused of financing Boko Haram, questions remain about the networks and collaborators operating within Nigeria. Even more troubling, some individuals accused of enabling violent groups have continued to operate with political influence while the nation pays the price of impunity.

The lesson is universal: the monsters created for expedience rarely stay loyal.

They mutate, grow stronger, and eventually turn on their masters. Mullah Omar’s ragtag students reshaped global politics. Boko Haram’s transformation from a local Islamist movement into a transnational jihadist organization became another cautionary tale. The transactional bargains that helped create or empower such movements are now etched in blood.

If the United States, Pakistan, Nigeria, or any nation wishes to escape this cycle, leaders must abandon the illusion of clever deals with extremists. Real security lies not in proxy wars or militant allies but in building just societies, resilient institutions, and inclusive political systems that deny extremists the grievances they exploit. Anything less is sowing the seeds of future catastrophe.

Twenty-five years after September 11, the smoke has cleared from lower Manhattan, but its consequences continue to reverberate across continents. The story of Bojinka, 9/11, al-Qaeda, the Taliban, and the spread of terrorism into Africa carries a warning governments repeatedly forget:

Violence may be rented for a season, but it is rarely possible to control the price of the lease. And when the bill finally comes due, it is usually ordinary people who pay it.

Osmund Agbo is a medical doctor, author, and the 2026 recipient of the Thabo Mbeki Prize for Scholarship and Public Service.

World.title: Nigeria’s 44 minerals must create jobs, not export poverty, Says Wunti
World.content:
The Chief Executive Officer of World Energy Council Nigeria, Bala Wunti, has urged the Federal Government to ensure that the country’s 44 critical minerals are developed into factories, jobs and sustainable economic opportunities for Nigerians.

Wunti warned that Nigeria must not repeat the crude oil model of exporting raw materials and importing finished products at significantly higher prices.

He spoke at the 2026 Concordia Annual Summit, held at the Sheraton New York Times Square alongside the United Nations General Assembly.

Wunti participated in a panel titled, “Rare Currency: Critical Minerals in a Shifting Global Economy,” which examined America’s growing dependence on imported minerals and China’s dominance of global mineral processing.

The former Chief Upstream Investment Officer at the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited said Nigeria must move beyond exporting mineral tonnage and develop domestic processing and manufacturing capacity.

“For half a century, Nigeria exported crude oil and imported refined petroleum products. That created poverty, not prosperity. We will not repeat that mistake with lithium and rare earth elements,” he said.

Explaining why Nigeria had not fully developed its mineral resources despite its vast potential, Wunti identified the absence of reliable geological data and commercially structured projects as major obstacles.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The central issue is the difference between mineral potential and an investable project,” he said.

“We had geological indications, but not proven reserves supported by JORC compliant data. We also had good policies, but not clearly defined projects. Investors invest in projects, not potential.”

According to him, attracting private capital into the mining sector requires reliable geological data, clearly defined projects, enabling infrastructure, predictable regulation, credible developers and viable routes to market.

Wunti described the Nigerian Solid Minerals Company as the country’s flagship investment platform, established to transform mineral resources into bankable projects.

“The company is moving Nigeria from saying, ‘We have minerals,’ to presenting investors with defined projects and clear commercial propositions,” he said.

“Rare earth elements are not necessarily rare in the ground. They are rare in the market. Bringing them to the market requires capital and technology.”

Wunti said Nigeria must present commercially viable transactions to investors rather than rely on policy documents and promotional presentations.

“We must move from potential to bankability. Investors need actual transactions, not presentations. Give me a credible price, and I will give you private capital,” he added.

He said private capital would be required to finance most critical mineral projects, while the government must create an environment that reduces investment risks.

“Government must address geological uncertainty, unpredictable regulation, inadequate infrastructure and inefficient permitting,” he said.

“However, government can only make a project bankable. It cannot permanently make an uneconomic project profitable.”

Wunti identified four conditions necessary for attracting sustainable investment into the sector. These are JORC compliant geological data, commercially viable prices, a stable and competitive fiscal system, and credible buyers.

“The lesson is price, not pitch,” he said. “A price floor of $110 per kilogram gives investors commercial certainty. That is how Nigeria can attract processing facilities, create jobs and retain greater value from its mineral resources.”

The 2026 Concordia Annual Summit is a leading nonpartisan global forum held alongside the United Nations General Assembly, bringing together influential leaders from government, business and civil society to address pressing international challenges. Past speakers include former US Presidents Joe Biden, George W. Bush and Bill Clinton, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, UN Secretary General António Guterres and business leader Warren Buffett.

World.title: Xenophobia: 105 more Nigerians repatriated from South Africa
World.content:
Another group of Nigerians from South Africa has arrived in the country as xenophobic attacks on black foreigners persist, and an uneasy quiescence increasingly defines Nigeria-South Africa relations.

The batch of 105 Nigerians was repatriated to Nigeria last Thursday. The group comprised 83 adults and 23 students, and state officials received them.

In a statement shared on X on Saturday, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said donations from the Redeemed Christian Church of God (RCCG) funded the return of 100 of the 105 Nigerians.

It said the church donated over $265,854 to purchase one-way tickets to evacuate 500 distressed Nigerians from South Africa.

“The return of the remaining five was funded by the generous donation of a private Nigerian citizen,” it said.

“The returnees, comprising 82 adults and 23 children, arrived in Lagos on South African Airways (SAA) Flight SA060 on Thursday, 24 September 2026, at approximately 20:30 hours.

“Nigeria’s diplomatic mission continues to engage with the leadership of the RCCG in South Africa and other philanthropic groups and individuals, as some other distressed Nigerians are currently undergoing preliminary clearance with our Consulate in Johannesburg and relevant South African authorities. They will be evacuated as soon as the process is finalised.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Around 1,640 Nigerians have been evacuated from the country since the recent wave of xenophobia began in April. A batch of 33 Nigerians was repatriated last month.

At least five Nigerians have been killed since the violence began.

PREMIUM TIMES reported the most recent incident in July. The victim, Chika Simon, died during an encounter with the South African Police Service (SAPS)

The Nigerian consulate said he died under questionable circumstances.

This paper also reported previous deaths. These are: Amaramiro Emmanuel, Ekpenyong Andrew, Emeka Iroegbu and Musa Joe.

The first two victims, Mr Emmanuel and Mr Andrew, were murdered in April, allegedly by personnel of the South African National Defence Force (SANDF) in Port Elizabeth.

Mr Andrew’s corpse was found days after his arrest on 19 April in the Booysens area of Pretoria. He was arrested due to an alleged altercation with members of the Tshwane Metro Police, and his body was discovered at the Pretoria Central Mortuary afterwards.

Mr Emmanuel died a day afterwards due to injuries he sustained from an alleged attack by the SANDF.

The Nigerian government, in response to the incident, summoned the South African High Commissioner to demand a thorough investigation into the death of the two Nigerians. But two other Nigerians soon followed.

Emeka Iroegbu and Musa Joe were killed on 28 June, under different circumstances.

Mr Joe was killed by “suspected criminals” in Witbank city, Mpumalanga province, while Mr Iroegbu was tortured to death by officers of the Tshwane Metro Police in the suburbs of Pretoria.

Months later, the investigations into these cases are still pending, and no arrests have been made.

World.title: UNGA: World leaders call for sustained investment to prepare for future pandemics
World.content:
World leaders have called for sustained, more equitable investment in pandemic prevention and preparedness, warning that progress made since COVID-19 will need continued action to protect countries from future outbreaks.

The call was made on Friday at the second United Nations General Assembly High-level Meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response (PPPR) in New York.

The meeting reviewed progress since the first high-level meeting in 2023, which was convened in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and gaps exposed in global health security.

The World Health Organisation (WHO), in a statement issued on Friday, said countries recognised progress made over the past three years, including the adoption of the WHO Pandemic Agreement and amendments to the International Health Regulations (2005).

WHO Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus in his remarks emphasised that countries must continue investing in stronger health systems, local and national capacities and equitable access to vaccines, medicines, diagnostics and other health tools.

“The COVID-19 pandemic exposed and exacerbated the fault lines of global health security, and taught the world many painful lessons,” Mr Ghebreyesus said.

He said the political commitments made at the meeting included calls for “concrete, measurable and urgent action” to strengthen health systems and expand equitable access to health products and resources.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Pandemic agreement

Countries also called for the completion of negotiations on an annex to the WHO Pandemic Agreement that would establish a Pathogen Access and Benefit-Sharing (PABS) system.

The proposed system, according to the WHO, is intended to facilitate the timely sharing of pathogens with pandemic potential and ensure that benefits arising from their use, including vaccines, medicines and diagnostics, are shared equitably.

WHO said adoption of the annex at the World Health Assembly in May 2027 is necessary for member states to begin national consideration of ratifying the Pandemic Agreement.

United Nations Deputy Secretary-General, Amina Mohammed, speaking on behalf of Secretary-General António Guterres, urged countries to accelerate the negotiations.

“The Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing System, under negotiation, is critical to unlocking the full potential of the WHO Pandemic Agreement,” Ms Mohammed said.

Lessons from COVID-19

Mr Ghebreyesus said the COVID-19 pandemic was linked to more than 20 million excess deaths between 2020 and 2023 and wiped more than $10 trillion from the global economy.

The meeting also stressed that pandemic preparedness should not be treated solely as a health-sector responsibility.

According to the WHO, countries called for a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach involving communities and other sectors.

The political declaration also highlighted the One Health approach, which recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health.

Sustained action

The President of the 81st UN General Assembly, Khalilur Rahman, said international cooperation would be necessary to prepare for future pandemics, including through equitable access to vaccines, diagnostics and other essential medical supplies.

READ ALSO: Shettima joins world leaders at UNGA 81 opening

“We have the knowledge, we have the tools, we have the science and expertise, and we have the hard lessons of COVID-19,” Mr Rahman said at the meeting.

“Let us use them for ourselves, our families and our loved ones. And also in memory of those we lost and in recognition of all those who suffered, needlessly.”

The meeting’s participants stressed that pandemic prevention, preparedness and response should remain a political priority between health emergencies, rather than becoming a focus only when outbreaks occur.

World.title: Ose Oyamendan’s MKO Documentary set for October premiere
World.content:
Nigerian-American filmmaker Ose Oyamendan’s documentary, MKO, which chronicles the life and legacy of late Nigerian businessman and politician Moshood “MKO” Abiola, will debut in cinemas nationwide on 2 October.

MKO tells the story of late Abiola, a politician who stood at the centre of the historic 12 June 1993 presidential election, its annulment by the military government, the struggle that followed and the circumstances surrounding his death in detention in 1998.

The documentary will premiere on 1 October at the National Theatre in Lagos, with President Bola Tinubu serving as host.

The film features former military leaders Ibrahim Babangida, who annulled the 12 June election, and Abdulsalami Abubakar, whose administration oversaw Nigeria’s return to civilian rule. It also features former President Olusegun Obasanjo, who took over from the military after previously serving as a military leader; Nobel laureate Wole Soyinka; and Ambassador Baba Gana Kingibe, Abiola’s running mate.

Others include former American diplomats Walter Carrington and Thomas Pickering, the former US Deputy Secretary of State who led the meeting during which Abiola died; former Canadian High Commissioner Gerald Ohlsen; members of Abiola’s family; foreign journalists; and Theodore Zadok, who served as Abiola’s security guard during his detention.

Unusual intimate account of the final chapter of Abiola’s life.

In a statement made available to PREMIUM TIMES on Saturday, Mr Oyamendan said those featured in the documentary provided an unusually intimate account of the final chapter of the late Abiola’s life.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the premiere and nationwide cinema release will mark a moment for a film that revisits a defining chapter in Nigeria’s modern political history.

Mr Oyamendan said: “For us, as a film team, it is an enormous honour that President Tinubu is recognising this important film as Chief Host. But when you look more deeply at the story and its world, the significance becomes even clearer.

“This was a crucial point in Nigeria’s history where many of our leaders back then chose to side with the dictators. Tinubu risked his life, livelihood and his family’s safety by standing with the people’s mandate. This is a story of that struggle that has brought us to where we are today.”

“Our story”

Furthermore, Mr Oyamendan said the film draws on an extensive collection of archival footage and powerful testimonies from individuals closely connected to the events it chronicles.

According to Mr Oyamendan, the documentary debuted at the Sheffield International Documentary Festival on 12 June, where it received critical acclaim before gaining wider attention on the international documentary circuit.

He said the film captures, through cinema, one of the most significant episodes in the history of democracy in Africa.

“This is a story that belongs to Nigerians. It is about memory, power, courage, sacrifice and the consequences of political choices. Most importantly, it is about people who believed that their voices mattered.

“Thirty-three years after June 12, we have the opportunity to look back at what happened, not simply to remember it, but to understand it and ensure it never happens again,” said the filmmaker.

Preservation of political history

Nile Entertainment will handle the documentary’s distribution and lead an extensive theatrical campaign to reach beyond its usual documentary audience and into cinemas nationwide.

The initiative will provide Nigerians, especially younger audiences, with an opportunity to experience a significant chapter of the country’s history on the big screen.

Commenting on the project, Nile Entertainment’s Managing Director, Moses Babatope, said the documentary holds a strong personal significance for him.

He described the film as an important contribution to the documentation and preservation of Nigeria’s political history.

READ ALSO: Documentary on MKO Abiola to premiere at Sheffield DocFest on Democracy Day

He said, “The story of MKO Abiola is particularly personal to me. My father worked at Concord Newspaper, one of the institutions founded by Chief MKO Abiola, so his legacy has always had a personal connection to my family. Beyond that personal connection, I believe this documentary is an important contribution to preserving Nigeria’s political history.

“MKO Abiola’s story is one of the most defining periods in our nation’s democratic journey, and this history must be documented and made accessible, particularly to a younger generation. It is a record of a pivotal moment in Nigeria’s history, brilliantly captured by Ose Oyamendan. We are proud to support its release and encourage audiences across the country to experience it in cinemas from October 2.”

World.title: REVIEW: Brief appearance, big impact: RMD steals show in Netflix’s ‘A Different World’
World.content:
Veteran Nigerian actor Richard Mofe-Damijo (RMD) has made a special appearance in Netflix’s newly released sequel series, A Different World, extending his screen career into another major international production.

RMD plays Mr Chukwu in the 2026 Netflix series, making a guest appearance in Episode 7 of Netflix’s new sequel to the classic American sitcom, A Different World.

The series premiered on Netflix on 24 September 2026, 39 years after the original A Different World debuted on NBC in 1987. The new production returns viewers to the fictional Hillman College, a historically Black college in the United States, but follows a new generation of students.

RMD’s appearance comes alongside a cast led by Maleah Joi Moon, Alijah Kai, Cornell Young IV, Jordan Aaron Hall, Kennedi Reece and Chibuikem Uche, with original cast members including Jasmine Guy, Kadeem Hardison, Darryl M. Bell and Cree Summer returning to reprise their roles.

RMD’s role in the new series

While RMD is not part of the principal ensemble, his appearance as Mr Chukwu marks a notable Nigerian presence in the new A Different World.

The principal Nigerian actor in the series is Chibuikem Uche, who plays Kojo Achebe, a Ghanaian-Nigerian fashion entrepreneur and student at Hillman College.

In Episode 7, Chukwu Achebe and his Ghanaian wife paid their son, Kojo Achebe, a surprise visit at Hillman College; there they met some of his colleagues. Kojo, who was a fashion entrepreneur, had told his parents that he was studying engineering.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

His parents are worried about his distancing himself from his family and have not reached out to them in a long time.

Kojo is described as a Ghanaian-Nigerian fashion merchandising student and entrepreneur from a UK/London background. He’s only at Hillman largely to satisfy his more traditional parents while pursuing his real passion for fashion design and business.

He becomes part of the core first-year group alongside Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), Rashida Duvall (Alijah Kai), Shaquille Johnson (Cornell Young IV), Amir Rodale (Jordan Aaron Hall), and Hazel Henry (Kennedi Reece).

This is not the first time the Nollywood veteran would feature in an international movie project; he had featured in other international shows such as ‘Namaste Wahala’ (2020), ‘Revelations’ (2025) and the upcoming Children of Blood and Bone

Another Nigerian cast

RMD was not the only Nigerian cast in the series; Chibuikem Uche, who played Kofo, is a London-born Nigerian who moved to Connecticut around age 8.

He is frequently identified as British-Nigerian. Before acting, he studied mathematics/actuarial science and worked as an actuary. He has featured in other Hollywood movies such as ‘One of Us Is Lying’, ‘The Tomorrow War’, and appearances in ‘American Housewife’ and ‘All American’.

Review

Netflix’s ‘A Different World’ is a 10-episode single-camera comedy-drama sequel series that premiered on September 24, 2026, exactly 39 years after the original NBC sitcom debuted. Created by Felicia Pride, it returns to the fictional HBCU Hillman College. The show follows a new generation of students while bringing back beloved alums, successfully updating the classic for Gen Z without losing its heart, humour, or cultural specificity.

The series centres on Deborah Wayne (Maleah Joi Moon), the free-spirited, kindhearted, and rebellious youngest daughter of Whitley Gilbert-Wayne (Jasmine Guy) and Dwayne Wayne (Kadeem Hardison).

Forced to attend her parents’ alma mater after a setback at NYU, Deborah arrives at Hillman determined to escape their long shadow and forge her own path. She quickly forms bonds with a diverse freshman class that reflects the breadth of contemporary Black experiences: first-generation criminal justice major Rashida Duvall (Alijah Kai); star athlete and legacy student Shaquille Johnson (Cornell Young IV, son of original character Ron Johnson); sharp but troubled psychology major Amir Rodale (Jordan Aaron Hall); church-raised small-town student Hazel Henry (Kennedi Reece); and Ghanaian-Nigerian fashion entrepreneur Kojo Achebe (Chibuikem Uche).

Over one academic year, the group navigates classic college territory, roommates, romance, low GPAs, parties, athletics, and identity, while confronting modern pressures: HBCU funding threats, political and social issues on campus, mental health, sexual health, parental expectations, and the search for belonging.

The short 10-episode season is both a strength (tight, bingeable) and a limitation. Some storylines feel rushed once the show finds its rhythm, and a few supporting arcs could have used more breathing room.

Early episodes lean more heavily on establishing the new class and reconnecting with alums, so the series takes a few instalments to hit its stride fully. Certain modern Gen Z dialogue and social-media references occasionally risk feeling slightly forced, though the cast sells them well. Viewers seeking pure multi-camera laugh-track comedy may need adjustment; this is a contemporary dramedy first.

World.title: 2027: Shehu Sani urges Atiku, other northerners to respect rotation, allow South complete eight years
World.content:
Former Kaduna Central Shehu Sani has warned that an Atiku Abubakar victory in the 2027 presidential election would end Nigeria’s informal rotational presidency arrangement and could trigger resentment in the southern part of the country.

Mr Sani made the comment on Channels Television’s Politics Today on Friday.

He said political parties should field southern candidates in the 2027 presidential election and allow the North to take its turn in 2031.

“If Atiku wins, it means that is the end of rotational presidency in Nigeria, and there is going to be hard and bitter feelings from the southern part of Nigeria,” Mr Sani said.

He said allowing the South to complete an eight-year presidential cycle would make it easier for a northern candidate to take over in 2031.

“I don’t think anyone will like to preside over a country full of hate, animosity, and conflict. Right now, the political system is managing a lot of crises,” he said.

Atiku, a former vice president, is a northerner and the presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC).

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Sani acknowledged that the Constitution does not bar him from contesting the 2027 election.

“I never said Atiku should not run. Constitutionally, he has a right to run for any election, but what I said was that a southern part of Nigeria should be allowed to have its eight-year tenure in office, just like the way the North has from 2015 to 2023,” he said.

‘South should have its eight years’

Mr Sani argued that although zoning and rotational presidency are not constitutional requirements, they remain important political arrangements for maintaining a sense of fairness between the two regions.

“I think it’s going to be fair to this country, to our political system, that when the South has its eight years, the North will have its eight years,” he said.

He said the North would have an “unchallengeable opportunity” to produce the country’s president in 2031 if southern candidates were allowed to contest the 2027 election.

“The NDC should field Peter Obi, the APM should field Makinde, let the South struggle it out and see who wins for four years. And when the tenure is done by 2031, the North should have its unchallengeable opportunity to produce the leadership of the country,” Mr Sani said.

He was referring to Peter Obi of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde of the Allied Peoples Movement (APM), both southerners and presidential candidates in the 2027 election.

The Independent National Electoral Commission has listed Mr Obi, Mr Makinde, Mr Atiku and President Bola Tinubu of the All Progressives Congress among the candidates for the 16 January 2027 presidential election.

Mr Sani also rejected the argument that demographic or electoral strength should determine which region controls the presidency.

“You cannot say that because you have the largest electorate and population, so you should continue dominating politics,” he said.

Rotation not constitutional

Nigeria’s 1999 Constitution does not provide for a North-South rotation of the presidency. The arrangement has instead operated as an informal political convention through party zoning and negotiations.

Mr Sani’s position therefore differs from the strictly constitutional argument that any Nigerian who meets the constitutional requirements is entitled to seek the presidency regardless of region.

He said, however, that constitutional eligibility should not be the only consideration in determining the timing of political contests.

His comments come amid growing positioning by major political figures ahead of the 2027 election, with Messrs Tinubu, Atiku, Obi, Makinde and other candidates already on INEC’s final list.

World.title: Rainbow Coalition doesn’t exist in Ebonyi – Umahi
World.content:
Minister of Works, David Umahi

Minister of Works and former governor of Ebonyi, David Umahi, has ruled out the existence of the Rainbow Coalition in Ebonyi, declaring that the state remains firmly aligned with the All Progressives Congress (APC) and its candidates ahead of the 2027 elections.

The Rainbow Coalition is a multi-party platform promoted by FCT Minister Nyesom Wike to mobilise support for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election bid while allowing politicians from different parties to retain their affiliations and support candidates in other elections.

Umahi also warned politicians planning to campaign in the state against hate speech and actions capable of triggering unrest, insisting that no political actor would be allowed to foment crisis in Ebonyi.

“Nobody can foment crisis in Ebonyi State,” the minister said.

He made the remarks on Friday, September 25, 2026, while inspecting Section Two of the Calabar-Abuja Superhighway project in Ado, Benue State.

According to a statement issued on Saturday by Francis Nwaze, Senior Special Assistant to Umahi on Media, the minister said, “If Wike has candidates here, he has not told me. And his candidate cannot break our relationship, but his candidate is not part of our relationship. There is no rainbow coalition in Ebonyi State.”

Umahi’s comments come amid disagreements between Wike and some APC governors over the political arrangements being considered ahead of the 2027 general elections.

Umahi maintained that political actors were free to campaign in Ebonyi but cautioned against inflammatory rhetoric and attempts to destabilise the state.

“Anybody that wants to campaign, come and campaign. But don’t dish out hate speeches and you want to take those speeches, and you want that we should lay a red carpet for you. We will not do that,” he said.

The former governor also revisited his decision to leave the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), accusing the party of failing to recognise the interests of the South-East despite the region’s support for its presidential candidates.

“We supported PDP. We voted for presidents in PDP. And when it was our time for them to honour us, they did not honour us. They maltreated us,” Umahi said.

World.title: Obi not godfather to any of Soludo’s children – First Lady’s aide
World.content:
Nonye Soludo

Daniel Ezeigwe, media aide to Anambra State First Lady Nonye Soludo, has clarified the godparent relationship between the families of former governor Peter Obi and incumbent Governor Chukwuma Soludo, saying Obi is not a godfather to any of the governor’s children.

Ezeigwe said the clarification became necessary following widespread circulation of a video in which Obi claimed that he and his wife were godparents to Soludo’s children.

In a statement issued on Saturday, the aide disclosed that the actual relationship was that Nonye Soludo is the confirmation godmother to Obi’s daughter, while Margaret Obi is the baptismal godmother to one of Soludo’s daughters.

“Mr Peter Obi is not a godfather to any of the children of Professor Chukwuma and Dr Nonye Soludo,” the statement read.

It added that neither Obi nor Soludo had served as a godparent to the other’s children.

The statement said the relationship between the two families remained cordial, while suggesting that Obi might have misspoken during his remarks.

“It is possible that Mr Peter Obi simply misspoke in the course of making his remarks. However, given the widespread circulation of the video and the enquiries it has generated, it is important that the record be set straight,” Ezeigwe stated.

The clarification followed Obi’s remarks at the 22nd Conference of the Nigerian Guild of Editors in Enugu on Friday, where he described his relationship with Soludo as close despite their political differences.

The presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress said he and his wife shared a godparent relationship with the governor’s family, insisting that there was no personal disagreement between them.

“People might not know, my wife and I are godparents to Soludo’s children. Yes, we are that close. So we are not quarrelling, and we will never quarrel. If I see him any day, me and him will hug and everything. If they say anything, I’ll answer them,” Obi said.

The First Lady’s aide added that “the relationship between the two families is cordial and there is no need to misrepresent it in any manner.”

World.title: NIS releases appointment link for UK special passport intervention
World.content:
The Nigeria Immigration Service (NIS) has released an updated appointment link for the United Kingdom (UK) Special Passport Intervention Exercise.

The NIS released the link for Nigerians interested in the exercise via the service’s official X (formerly Twitter) handle on Saturday.

The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the NIS had earlier extended the exercise to run from Oct. 6 to 30, following high turnout and sustained demand by Nigerians.

The NIS released the appointment link for Nigerians in the United Kingdom seeking to access the 2026 Special Passport Intervention Exercise – Phase 2.

The service said interested Nigerians should use the link https://form.jotform.com/passportlondon/2026-passport-intervention-phase2 to take advantage of the extension. (NAN)

World.title: ‘Support people to vote’ – Obidient group seeks diaspora Nigerians’ help
World.content:
Justice Crack

Obidient Connect, a support group backing Peter Obi’s 2027 presidential bid, has urged Nigerians living abroad to help mobilise voters at home, asking each diaspora member to support at least 10 people to participate in the election.

The group acknowledged that Nigerians in the diaspora may not be able to vote directly but said they could contribute to the electoral process by encouraging eligible voters in the country to exercise their civic responsibility.

In a social media post shared by Justice Crack, an Obi supporter, Obidient Connect appealed to Nigerians abroad to assist people back home in casting their ballots.

“To all Nigerians in the diaspora, even though you may not be able to vote directly, you can still support someone back home to participate in the election,” the group stated.

“You can support at least 10 people to exercise their civic responsibility—and you can even do more.”

The group said Nigerians living abroad had experienced governance systems outside the country and could use their knowledge to encourage democratic participation ahead of the 2027 general election.

“If you live in the diaspora, you have seen how good governance can work, and you understand the kind of Nigeria many of us want to build at home,” it added.

Obidient Connect also urged Nigerians abroad to join its platform and support efforts to increase participation in the forthcoming polls.

“Join Obidient Connect. Let’s support civic participation and work towards a better Nigeria in 2027. Nigeria must be OK,” the group said.

The appeal comes amid disagreements between the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and some support groups over the organisation and leadership of Obi’s 2027 presidential campaign.

On September 17, the Obi-Kwankwaso (OK) Movement, a group supporting Obi and Rabiu Musa Kwankwaso, announced a 59-member presidential campaign council.

The NDC has since distanced itself from the said campaign council, saying only the party is authorised to constitute such.

Also, Obi said the council was constituted without his knowledge or approval.

World.title: Man City could face ‘drastic’ sanctions after reported guilty verdict – Ex-chairman
World.content:
Manchester City’s Norwegian striker #09 Erling Haaland holds the trophy as City players celebrate after the English League Cup final football match between Arsenal and Manchester City at Wembley Stadium in London on March 22, 2026. City won the game 2-0. (Photo by Glyn KIRK / AFP) / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE. No use with unauthorized audio, video, data, fixture lists, club/league logos or ‘live’ services. Online in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No video emulation. Social media in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No use in betting publications, games or single club/league/player publications. /

Former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein said the club could face potentially “drastic” sanctions after reportedly being found guilty on all but one of 115 charges for breaching Premier League financial rules.

No official announcement has been made by the Premier League over the case and there is no indication of any possible punishment.

Abu Dhabi-backed City have always strenuously denied the charges and a club spokesperson said the position had not changed.

It is understood City will appeal should the charges be upheld.

“The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence,” the spokesperson said.

City were charged by the Premier League in 2023 following an investigation into alleged breaches of rules between 2009 and 2018.

The club were accused of failing to provide accurate financial information and details of payments to players and coaches, as well as breaches of financial sustainability rules.

They were also charged with failing to cooperate with an investigation.

A hearing by an independent commission started in September 2024.

– ‘Severe penalty’ –

Bernstein, who was City chairman between 1998 and 2003, told Times Radio that “money is not sufficient” in terms of a potential punishment, urging a swift appeal process.

“The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, I think that would be a disaster,” he said. “Not just for this particular case but for English football generally. The timing is crucial.

“I can’t give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of (the) charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty.

“All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that.”

Oasis star and City fan Noel Gallagher described his “shock” at the developments.

Speaking on the Let Me Talk podcast, he said: “Surprised because only that the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges.

“So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we’ve been found guilty of all but one. But really overall just quite sad really. Sad for the fans and for the players.”

UK culture secretary Lisa Nandy described the case as “unsettling” for football fans and called for a swift resolution.

In 2020, UEFA imposed a two-year European ban on City as well as a fine for breaking financial fair-play rules, though that ban was later overturned by the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

If the reported guilty verdicts are confirmed, sanctions could include a severe points deduction and possibly even expulsion from the Premier League.

Everton and Nottingham Forest were both hit by points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of profit and sustainability rules.

Other Premier League clubs are understood to be taking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges.

Under the ownership of Sheikh Mansour, whose Abu Dhabi United Group acquired the club in 2008, City have become the dominant force in English football.

They have won eight Premier League titles, a Champions League crown and multiple other trophies over the past 15 years.

The latest developments in the case come just months after former City manager Pep Guardiola left the club following a golden decade in charge at the Etihad.
