World.title: Damaged fragment deemed 'unremarkable' turns out to be rare piece of Homer's 'Odyssey' history
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An ancient fragment of Homer's "Odyssey" was hiding in plain sight for decades in a university library in the Netherlands — until a professor took a closer look.

The discovery, announced by Utrecht University this month, was made in the university's Special Collections.

Mark de Kreij, an assistant professor of Ancient Greek and Papyrology at Radboud University, came across the unidentified parchment while studying Greek manuscripts in the university's collection.

EXPERTS STUNNED AFTER UNCOVERING HOMER'S 'ILIAD' ON EGYPTIAN MUMMY IN UNPRECEDENTED FIND

De Kreij told Fox News Digital the fragment had originally been kept with Coptic Christian manuscripts, which he said was "probably why it was missed in the early research on the collection."

By the time he examined it, however, the still-unidentified fragment had been moved to a box containing Greek manuscripts.

Utrecht University said the fragment was first considered ordinary.

"Hidden among these, first regarded as an unremarkable 7th-century fragment, was a damaged and discolored fragment with very small, neat letters," the university said.

"De Kreij soon recognized a few words typical of the Homeric epics."

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER 1,700-YEAR-OLD CHRISTIAN CITY HIDDEN BENEATH EGYPT'S DESERT

The fragment contains verses from Book 12 of the "Odyssey" — including the pivotal moment when the sun god Helios discovers that Odysseus' crew killed and ate his sacred cattle.

Helios then demands vengeance from Zeus — an episode recently depicted in the Christopher Nolan film adaptation.

Researchers believe the manuscript was owned by a reader living in Egypt's Fayum oasis, southwest of modern-day Cairo, around 300 A.D.

The fragment has been dated to the 3rd or 4th century A.D.

And its age isn't the only thing that makes it a rarity. The university says only a few fragments like it exist across the world.

ONE OF HISTORY'S MOST FAMOUS BATTLES COULD BE REWRITTEN BY LONG-LOST PAPAL LETTER

"There are only around 30 fragments like it worldwide," the statement said.

Though the university described the fragment as part of a "pocket edition" of the complete epic, one expert told Fox News Digital she was not convinced by that interpretation.

"This is something that people held in their hand. This is something they carried with them."

Anna Dolganov, a Roman historian and papyrologist at the Austrian Archaeological Institute of the Austrian Academy of Sciences in Vienna, questioned whether the fragment came from a complete copy of Homer's epic.

"The entire ‘Odyssey’ would require 480 pages," she said.

ANCIENT BOOK OF REVELATION CITY GIVES UP STUNNING SECRET BURIED FOR 1,500 YEARS

Dolganov noted that a parchment volume of that length would be extremely thick in such a small format — making it unlikely, in her view, that the codex contained the entire epic.

The expert also pointed to the handwriting, which she described as more casual and cursive than what she would expect in a complete literary work.

"What I think it's more likely to be is an anthology," she posited. "Or a private collection of excerpts from literary texts, possibly for use in schools, for education, or a private anthology that would have been much, much smaller — not the entire 'Odyssey.'"

De Kreij pointed to the text preserved on both sides of the parchment as evidence that it belonged to a complete copy of the epic.

CLICK HERE TO 

"Both sides contain passages from book 12 of the ‘Odyssey,’ which are nearly contiguous," he told Fox News Digital.

De Kreij said an anthology is theoretically possible, but he knows of no similar examples from the period. Complete copies of works such as the "Iliad" and "Odyssey," by contrast, have numerous parallels, he said.

Dolganov said the discovery also reflects Homer's widespread popularity in the ancient world, where his works played an important role in education.

The ancient poet "was very popular indeed all over the Mediterranean world where Greek was learned," Dolganov said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

"Homer was used to teach Greek," she added, explaining that his works were widely used as school texts around the Eastern Mediterranean.

Dolganov noted that dating ancient literary manuscripts can be difficult and imprecise, particularly in situations where scholars rely on handwriting as evidence.

"It would be important not to overstate how certain we are that this is indeed as early as the third or fourth century," she said.

"But it doesn't need to be, to be a very interesting and exciting discovery," she said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

De Kreij said the dating is based on several features of the fragment, including its codex format, parchment material, the appearance of the ink and its handwriting.

"The neat, small bookhand cannot be dated with absolute certainty, but there are good parallels from the late third and fourth century," he said.

"All such dating has to be approximate, but in the scientific edition, I cite a number of dated parallels to back up my estimate."

Dolganov also reflected on the human connection offered by the discovery.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"This is something that people held in their hand," she said. "This is something they carried with them and read, and it's a text that's also accessible to us."

"So it kind of connects us to the ancient reader because we are similarly excited by this timeless work of literature."

World.title: 'Primetime' Review: Robert Pattinson channels Chris Hansen in riveting dramatization of 'To Catch a Predator'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"Have a seat."

Those words were memorably said by Chris Hansen, the "Dateline NBC" correspondent who hosted the provocative reality series "To Catch a Predator" during the 2000s.

Hansen, notably, had zero involvement in the making of A24's new film, "Primetime," which was adapted from a 2007 Esquire article titled "Tonight on Dateline This Man Will Die." In fact, according to Hansen, the studio wanted him to sign a restrictive agreement before showing him the movie, which he refused to do.

After watching "Primetime," you can see why A24 was hoping for a legal cover. Because unless you're Hansen or any other key people involved, it's difficult to know where the reality ends and where the fiction begins.

‘RESIDENT EVIL’ REVIEW: DIRECTOR ZACH CREGGER DELIVERS INFECTIOUS REBOOT TO GORY VIDEO GAME FRANCHISE

Robert Pattinson steps into the role as Hansen, a self-aggrandizing and rather eccentric journalist eying to be taken seriously by his NBC colleagues — perhaps with the success of "To Catch a Predator."

If you aren't familiar, "To Catch a Predator" exposed men who believed they were meeting minors after sexually explicit online conversations. Instead, they walked into sting operations that typically ended with Hansen emerging from another room to confront them before police made arrests.

The show's producer, Andie Bender (Merritt Wever) is just as essential as its star. Her job is to keep the engine running and to make sure Hansen doesn't drift into a mental abyss. It isn't until she and Hansen are brought into the office of NBC chief Jeff Zucker (humorously played by Zucker himself), who informs them he's moving their show into primetime, giving them the daunting task of going up against ABC juggernaut "LOST" in the same time slot.

'THE DOG STARS' REVIEW: JACOB ELORDI FIGHTS FOR SURVIVAL IN RIDLEY SCOTT'S DULL POST-APOCALYPTIC WESTERN

In "Primetime," the predators are also the prey as Hansen and his team go to incredible lengths to nab a creep, but more importantly, to make great television. Some members of the team grapple with the ethics and morality of their line of work. Hansen, at least the film's version of him, views himself as a saint, carrying out a righteous mission despite his own shortcomings in his personal life. But it's far more nuanced for new hire Dan Plumb (Skyler Gisondo), a 23-year-old aspiring actor hired to play a 13-year-old decoy. You can tell how visibly shaken he is by the process, and he struggles with whether obtaining the coveted Screen Actors Guild membership card is worth ruining other people's lives for.

BOX OFFICE COMEBACK: HOW SUMMER 2026 OFFERS A GLIMMER OF HOPE FOR HOLLYWOOD IN THE POST-COVID ERA

Pattinson has had an impressive year between "The Drama" and "The Odyssey" (not to mention "Dune: Part Three" in December), proving he's come a long way from his "Twilight" days. He gives a career-best performance as a self-obsessed, borderline unhinged NBC host. While he gets top billing, the emotional crutch of the entire movie rests on Gisondo's shoulders. Best known for his stint on HBO's "The Righteous Gemstones" and more recently playing Jimmy Olsen in the new "Superman" movie, Gisondo is able to show depth from Dan's charming naivety to utter demoralization. Wever also shines as the no-nonsense producer who has to put up with a lot of nonsense.

Director Lance Oppenheim's background in documentaries shows in "Primetime" between the reliance on the hidden cameras that only fuels the intensity and the cutaways to various cultural references. The low-resolution style takes viewers back to a pre-4K era and the shadows provide a noir element.

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

The Verdict

What can be viewed as an indictment of how sleazy the television industry can be, "Primetime" isn't exactly the feel-good movie of the year, but it's a riveting thriller that showcases outstanding performances from Pattinson, Gisondo and Wever.

★★★ ½ — SEE IT NOW

"Primetime" is rated R for disturbing sexual material, graphic nudity, some violent content, and language. Running time: 1 hour, 50 minutes. In theaters now.

World.title: Hidden California desert pet cemetery holds unexpected piece of White House history
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

When members of the Secret Service swarmed Charley Stewart’s plot of land in the middle of California's Sonoran Desert, he wasn’t confused or worried — he knew what they had come for.

"They have representatives, the Secret Service, and the secretaries, and all those people come by," he told Fox News Digital. "It’s like a circus."

Stewart owns and operates Haven for Pets, a pet cemetery in Desert Hot Springs. When one of the nation’s most famous dogs — former President Gerald Ford’s golden retriever, Liberty — was set to be buried there, Secret Service agents visited the cemetery to inspect the grounds ahead of the burial, Stewart said.

DISCOVERIES THAT RESHAPED WHAT HISTORIANS KNEW ABOUT AMERICA'S FOUNDING FATHERS

"Before she got buried out there, the Secret Service had to go out and look for mines and walk around," said the cemetery owner. "I mean, Gerald Ford was the President of the United States."

The female golden retriever arrived at the White House as a puppy and became the nation’s first dog, later giving birth to nine puppies in 1975 on the third floor of the White House.

Liberty was the first dog to give birth in the White House.

The frequently photographed canine enjoyed the White House life. She posed on the North Lawn, lounged beside the commander in chief in the Oval Office, swam in the pool at Camp David and even received fan mail from Americans across the country.

The Fords kept one of Liberty’s puppies, a female named Misty, who is buried alongside her mother at Haven for Pets. Their grave sites leave an unexpected piece of presidential history tucked away in Stewart’s pet cemetery.

RONALD REAGAN'S GRANDDAUGHTER, KEVIN MCCARTHY HONOR LATE PRESIDENT'S LEGACY ON HIS 115TH BIRTHDAY

Stewart’s Haven for Pets dates back to the 1960s. It opened as an extension of a full-service Palm Springs kennel called Dogtown USA, which was known for providing grooming services to celebrity pets.

Dogtown was purchased by Stewart’s father, Charles Stewart, in 1959, and Stewart recalled the story of how the pet cemetery came to be.

"My father told me a story one time — he went over to talk to some people and their dog had died, and they threw it in a garbage can, and the head was hanging out," Stewart said. "From that horrible sight, my father said, ‘We’ve got to take care of these babies.’ And so he decided to do that."

"It took a couple years to do the paperwork, but that’s what he did … This was an input my father never got over," he added.

Haven for Pets’ celebrity canine clientele extends beyond the White House, all the way to Hollywood.

STAGECOACH FESTIVALGOERS SPLIT ON WHETHER AMERICA IS HEADED IN THE RIGHT DIRECTION AHEAD OF ITS 250TH BIRTHDAY

World-famous pianist Liberace has six of his dogs buried in the cemetery, under headstones that list their owner as "Lee," his nickname. Actor Michael Landon and Academy Award-winning composer Jimmy Van Heusen also have their pets buried there.

Stewart told Fox News Digital the VIP connections grew out of his family’s work caring for pets belonging to celebrities who lived in the Coachella Valley.

"Going back to Leonard Firestone and the Marx Brothers down here in Thunderbird Country Club, my dad would take care of their dogs," he shared. "We’d groom them and we boarded them … We did business with them."

Roughly 1,000 pets are buried in the cemetery. In its early days decades ago, the burial rate was $35. These days it costs nearly $900.

Stewart said that, at one point, the cemetery would handle five burials a week, but the figure has fallen to three or four a year because he wants to limit the frequency of burials and extend the life of the cemetery grounds.

1,000-YEAR-OLD CHURCH MYSTERY CRACKED BY STUDENTS FROM KING CHARLES' ALMA MATER

Stewart told Fox News Digital the unadvertised cemetery is not easy to find — and he intends to keep it that way.

"I don’t advertise the cemetery, it’s all word of mouth," he said. "I don’t want to speed up the process. The cemetery right now is set up in a way that it’s going to last way in excess of 200 years."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Stewart, who has been part of the cemetery for nearly his entire life, said he spends about two hours each day sitting in a lawn chair among the headstones, surrounded by the animals he believes "never die" — and keeping watch over Liberty.

World.title: Europe frets as the Kremlin pushes the limits of its hybrid warfare
World.content:
The Kremlin is testing Europe‘s limits.

After months of covert attacks and sabotage across the continent, leaders are warning that Moscow may be about to grow bolder as it seeks to sow chaos and intimidate allies of Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin could try to test NATO’s resolve to defend members on its eastern flank or respond to attacks that fall short of all-out war, these officials say, at a time when the U.S. is distracted by other conflicts and weighing reducing its military presence in Europe.

An assessment by the Danish Defence Intelligence Service released Thursday warned that in the coming months Moscow will further intensify its campaign of so-called hybrid warfare, “with greater consequences for the targeted countries than in the past.” It also assessed “a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia.”

While Moscow has for years embraced tactics that straddle the threshold of war, a string of increasingly brazen incidents in recent months has alarmed U.S. allies.

‘A bit freaked out’

A key moment was the discovery of a Russian drone carrying explosives at an airport in eastern Germany near a Ukrainian aircraft last month. Berlin formally blamed Russia for what it said was a thwarted attack and imposed a diplomatic freeze, though Moscow denied involvement.

That incident appears to have changed the mindset about Russia’s growing threat in Europe, said Ed Arnold, a senior associate fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It just showed that Putin’s risk calculations are getting more liberal,” Arnold said. “Everyone just got a bit freaked out by that, quite frankly.”

It was followed by the unexpected visit of CIA Director John Ratcliffe to Moscow, during which NATO was discussed.

Incidents have continued to pile up — at defense facilities in Estonia, rail networks in Poland and the power grid in Germany. Many have passed without clear attribution, only intensifying speculation.

All this against the backdrop of near-daily drone incursions into European airspace, fueling anxiety in eastern border towns.

A locomotive damaged in a Russian drone attack at Yahodyn railway station near Ukraine's border with Poland on Sept. 13. Ukrzaliznytsia Railway via AP

In Ukraine, a passenger train was hit less than 2 miles from the Polish border earlier this month, a close call on NATO’s doorstep that came as European diplomats returned from Kyiv on the same rail line. Another train, with former CIA Director David Petraeus on board, was still at the station when the drone struck.

Just days later, NATO fighter jets shot down a drone that entered the airspace of Lithuania, one of the Baltic member states whose proximity to Russia, analysts say, could make it a prime target for the Kremlin’s next move.

What could this look like? As unease increasingly swirled last week, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the Kremlin plans to launch drone and missile attacks against European countries that it would argue were accidental to try to weaken any response.

Russia has not claimed involvement in any of the incidents and has repeatedly denied conducting hybrid warfare or sabotage operations in NATO territory. Putin himself accused European leaders earlier this month of seeking out “a war against Russia” and “frightening their populations with an imaginary threat.”

On Friday, Russian state news agency RIA published and quickly deleted an op-ed laying out a potential scenario for a “lightning fast” war that Russia might wage against a NATO state, specifically focusing on the Baltic nations. The article was deleted because it did not “align” with editorial policy or Russia’s state policy, RIA said.

Lithuanian soldiers securing the area where NATO fighter jets shot down a drone on Sept. 15 near Pratkunai village AP

U.S. allies have little doubt that the broad pattern reflects the Kremlin increasingly pushing the boundaries.

“With these incidents now so frequent and so brazen, it is increasingly difficult to distinguish them from actual acts of war,” said Katja Bego, a senior research fellow with the Europe program at London-based think tank Chatham House. “The Kremlin is playing with fire here: The risk of more serious escalation — even if unintended — is very real.”

Baltic states urge caution

There is a mounting sense that something must be done, but what?

Lithuania has made plans for the evacuation of older adults and is lifting its ban on hosting nuclear weapons. Finland has warned citizens to be “mentally prepared” for new sabotage attacks. France is putting a plan in place to protect the country’s critical infrastructure.

Hanging over all of this is Article 5, NATO’s collective defense clause.

For Moscow, escalating hybrid attacks could highlight Western divisions over how best to respond and undermine the alliance at a time when the U.S. commitment to this mutual defense has been in question.

“I think they are trying to show Europe they can act without consequences, and more recently, to show Europe that the U.S. will not come to their rescue. It’s worrisome,” said William Alberque, a former senior NATO official based in Berlin.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov on Wednesday and told a media briefing that the U.S. was concerned that the Ukraine war could “metastasize and spread into other places ... be it through a hybrid attack, be it through a sabotage attack, be it through a misunderstanding.”

He added: “We watch reports carefully, and we raise them with the right people at the right levels.”

A State Department spokesperson told NBC News: “We continue to monitor Russia’s hybrid activities in Europe and are working closely with our allies and partners to strengthen resilience against the hybrid threat.”

Despite the spreading sense of alarm, some in Europe are urging against getting carried away.

NATO’s Baltic member states have not changed their security assessments, saying there is no imminent risk of a Russian invasion while much of Moscow’s military resources are tied up in Ukraine — and struggling to make progress there.

World.title: Some lawmakers doubt a Congress that’s ‘barely capable of email’ can regulate AI
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Amid warnings that artificial intelligence could soon wipe out humanity, some lawmakers are not confident that Congress has the expertise or ability to regulate AI.

“A lot of them can’t spell it,” quipped Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C. “They just don’t have the experience.”

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., was equally skeptical. “They still don’t know how to get on the internet,” let alone understand AI, he said.

Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., who represents parts of Silicon Valley, argued that many members of Congress are just not up to speed on AI, and some seem uninterested.

“The problem in Congress is not that we don’t have enough computer scientists. It’s that we don’t have enough people who have a basic understanding of how the technology works or are using it,” Khanna said in an interview with NBC News.

“It’s like talking about making the rules for driving the road. You don’t have to be an auto mechanic, but it would be nice if you at least were a passenger in a car or had driven a car,” he continued. “And we’ve had a lot of members of Congress who’ve not been passengers in a car when it comes to AI, or certainly haven’t driven it.”

One thing that everyone seems to agree on: Congress is not close to regulating AI. Capitol Hill has been notoriously slow to regulate new technology. It hasn’t passed any sweeping, comprehensive legislation regulating the internet, invented more than 40 years ago, instead taking a more piecemeal approach and relying on existing laws. And exactly 20 years after Facebook became available to the public, lawmakers are still struggling to figure out how to regulate social media.

New rules aimed at protecting kids online are popular in theory, but actual legislation remains stalled, with House and Senate negotiators deadlocked on the issue.

“This is the United States Congress you’re talking about. I mean, nothing moves very quickly,” said Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a former astronaut and Navy combat pilot who backs AI regulation.

It’s “much easier” to fly a fighter jet than to pass AI legislation, he added.

But while there are plenty of skeptics who believe Congress doesn’t have the capability to tackle AI regulations, there are optimists who think it does.

One is Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., who is pursuing a master’s degree in machine learning at George Mason University to keep pace with new technology. Beyer served on the bipartisan House Task Force on Artificial Intelligence and now serves on a Democratic commission on AI.

“Oh, I very much think there’s a capacity here. Yeah, you don’t need to be a Ph.D. or a master’s in computer science to know what to do next,” said Beyer, who is 76. “I think the parallel is we don’t have to be biologists or chemists to set up the FDA, or lawyers or stockbrokers to set up the SEC. There are 12 to 20 members of Congress already, just in the House, that have AI bills.”

What’s blocking any significant legislative movement on AI is political will from Republicans, he argued.

“I think we definitely have the capacity. What we need is a speaker who will let us put the bills on the floor,” said Beyer, who has been advocating for Democratic leaders to create a select committee on artificial intelligence if the party wins control of the House this fall.

Democrats, a handful of Republicans and key tech leaders believe that Congress needs to step in now and regulate the AI industry following high-profile AI breaches.

“AI is certainly powerful enough to drive events that … cause a billion deaths,” Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates said in an interview with Kristen Welker that will air Sunday on NBC News’ “Meet the Press.”

“No one thinks self-regulation is enough,” he added.

President Donald Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., will host an AI summit with tech leaders in Washington on Tuesday, according to a White House official and a source familiar with the plans. But, given their past comments, it’s likely to focus more on tech innovation and competition than on reining in the companies.

Trump has repeatedly said that he does not want to “stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution,” as he put it in a speech to world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly this week.

“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in,” Trump said.

He has also dismissed the recent apocalyptic warnings as a “hoax” and said regulations will impede America in its race with China for AI dominance. Johnson has said some safety guardrails are needed but has argued Congress should not get in the way of American innovation.

At a recent campaign rally, Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., who is running in one of the most competitive Senate races in November and is mentioned as a potential 2028 presidential candidate, blamed Trump and the “weakness of our politics” for congressional inaction on AI.

“Tech titans dig bunkers while warning us the new intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction. Congress debates youth sports, and the president builds a ballroom,” Ossoff said. “An ancient establishment, barely capable of email, sleepwalks into a technological revolution, while the president dismantles precautions and calls us fools for worrying.”

The House made a big push on AI in 2024, with a bipartisan task force that held two dozen hearings and produced a 273-page report on a framework for potential AI legislation, with nearly 90 recommendations.

Many of those recommendations have been translated into bills that are now being considered by committees and subcommittees, said Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., who chaired the task force and holds a master’s degree in AI from UCLA. One of these measures is the Frontier Act, his bipartisan bill with Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., that would create national safety rules for building and using advanced AI models.

“Would I prefer that the process had moved faster? Yes, absolutely,” Obernolte said. “Has it been moving as fast as it could, given the constraints that everyone was under? Yes, I believe it has.”

Obernolte said the bipartisan AI task force was not renewed this Congress because it had issued its report and fulfilled its mission. But he said it has created a group of AI experts on Capitol Hill whom other lawmakers can rely on and ask questions of.

The task force, he said, began with members who knew nothing about AI and are now “deeply educated” on the issue.

Asked if he’s confident Congress can rise to the occasion and pass something on AI, Obernolte replied: “Confident is too strong, but hopeful.”

Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, was more pessimistic, pointing out that the Senate this month failed to pass a landmark cryptocurrency bill despite years of bipartisan work, and that AI developments seem to be moving at warp speed.

“This process of legislating takes so long that by the time we even got to that step — I mean, crypto, we’re four years in. We haven’t passed it,” Moreno said. “So imagine AI four years in. We’re dealing with stuff that’s not even relevant in four years.”

Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., who serves on the Judiciary and Homeland Security committees, said he doesn’t believe most members of Congress have the expertise to understand all of the complexities of AI, but nor should they focus on trying to regulate every aspect of the technology.

Instead, he said, lawmakers should focus on passing legislation, like his AI LEAD Act, that would hold tech companies legally liable for any harm caused by AI.

“Expertise? No, but we … don’t need to set minute regulations. What we should do is, for example, we should open the courthouse doors so that citizens who are harmed by AI, who when AI agents go out and crash the banking system or commit cyberattacks or hack data, the companies should be liable for that,” Hawley said.

World.title: White House blocks CNN from covering Trump’s Tennessee trip
World.content:
The White House on Friday night removed CNN from joining President Donald Trump on his trip to Tennessee on Saturday, where it was supposed to cover the president on behalf of major TV networks.

According to media guidance sent out by the White House on Friday night, CNN was removed from the list of outlets designated for pool coverage of Trump’s trip, in which he is set to attend a college football game in Knoxville.

The pool is a rotating group of networks that share duties of filming the president both in Washington and on official trips. Other member networks — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — briefly boycotted participating in the pool this week after Trump banned CNN from serving as a member.

CNN on Friday reported that it had been scheduled to fly with Trump on Air Force One on Saturday as part of its pool duties covering the president’s trip to the game between the University of Texas and the University of Tennessee. However in the president’s schedule released Friday night, CNN was not listed as a member of the pool and no other network was listed as replacing it.

The move is the latest development in the White House’s attempt to restrict access by CNN and other outlets to cover the White House. The president last week had banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House before a judge temporarily blocked that move Thursday and ordered the administration to restore their reporters’ credentials for 14 days.

But while the order restored the outlets’ access to the White House, it didn’t explicitly require the administration to restore CNN’s participation in the television pool.

The White House did not immediately return a request for comment.

World.title: Supreme Court rejects Republicans’ Missouri redistricting push for third time
World.content:
WASHINGTON — For the third time, the Supreme Court on Friday shut down efforts by Missouri Republicans to use a new congressional map in the midterm elections that are already underway.

The court blocked an appeals court ruling that sought to revive the 2025 map despite two previous Supreme Court decisions and a ruling by the Missouri Supreme Court that ruled against Republicans on the same issue. There were no dissents.

“At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos,” the ruling said.

In doing so, the justices granted an emergency application filed by People Not Politicians, the group challenging the new map.

“We are done with corrupt politicians trying to force their map into effect outside the process outlined in the Missouri constitution,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, said in a statement. “We have said from the beginning, people, not politicians will be the final deciders on this DC power grab.”

The election will proceed using a 2022 map that includes six seats held by Republicans and two held by Democrats. The state has already started sending out ballots to military and overseas voters, and some absentee voting began Tuesday.

The high court cited the fact that Missouri has already begun its voting processes.

“This Court has repeatedly cautioned that ‘lower federal courts should not ‘alter the election rules’’ of a state ‘on the eve of an election,’” the ruling said. “The election is not merely upcoming; it has already started.”

The proposed 2025 map would have eliminated one of the Democratic seats, held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.

The Missouri map was part of a nationwide push by Republicans at the urging of President Donald Trump to draw new congressional districts that would favor their candidates. Democrats in other states, including California, responded by drawing new maps, too.

Cleaver told NBC News in a brief phone call Friday that he was “very happy” with the ruling and relieved the issue is settled for November.

“It lasted much too long, but it’s over now,” Cleaver said. “The manufactured chaos, you know, has at long last ended, been brought to a final state, and we can move on.”

Cleaver said his campaign will now work to get the word out to voters ahead of the midterm elections in order to address their confusion after the status of their congressional districts has bounced between courts this year.

The St. Louis-based 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday ruled that the Republican-drawn Missouri map could be used, but it never went into effect. The Supreme Court’s ruling Tuesday overturns that decision.

The appeals court had ruled the state had to use the 2025 map in part because the primary election had already taken place using it. But in a conflicting ruling, the Missouri Supreme Court said the 2022 map had to be used, while making it clear that Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, was to blame for the confusion.

The state high court ultimately held Hoskins in contempt for his actions.

In its ruling on Friday, the Supreme Court wrote that Hoskins “was well aware that conducting the August primary election with the 2025 map carried significant risks,” citing a May opinion from the state high court that made clear the new map would not go into effect ahead of the 2026 elections.

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe, a Republican, said in a post on X on Friday that it was “disappointing” that the Supreme Court’s ruling meant the general election will use a different map than the one used in the primary elections.

“Voters deserved consistency and certainty, and not for the rules to be changed between elections,” Kehoe wrote. “Nevertheless, Missouri will follow the Court’s order.”

The court battle started after opponents of the new map gained enough signatures to trigger a state referendum on whether it should be used. Under state law, whenever a state law is subject to a referendum, it is suspended until after the vote takes place.

But Hoskins delayed a decision on whether the referendum push was legitimate until the eve of the primary. He rejected the proposal and ordered the new map to be used.

The Missouri Supreme Court then quickly ruled that there were no grounds to reject the referendum proposal and that, with the issue being put to voters in November, the map should be put on hold and the 2022 districts used instead.

The litigation seemed to be over until a new lawsuit was filed on Sept. 4 by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo., and two voters.

That moved the fight into federal court, where Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark ruled that the new map should be used. That decision ultimately led to the appeals court ruling and Supreme Court intervention.

World.title: Iran says choice on reopening Hormuz ‘rests with the United States’ after deal offer
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, after Iranian officials indicated that shipping through the critical waterway could resume within days if a deal was sealed.

“I rejected the Iranian proposal,” Trump told reporters as he boarded Marine One on the White House lawn, after indirect talks between the two countries were held on the sidelines of this week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York.

The Wall Street Journal first reported that Trump had rejected Iran’s offer to revive a ceasefire and reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had said Friday that the choice “rests with the United States.”

“If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi told reporters.

He said a “concrete seven-day plan” that includes reopening the Strait had been conveyed to the U.S. through mediator Qatar and was ready to start “as soon as the United States accepts this plan.”

00:48 Iran offers new proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz 00:00 00:00

Araghchi said the actions required of the U.S. in Iran’s proposal were commitments already agreed to in the June memorandum of understanding between the two countries that laid out plans for a temporary ceasefire. That agreement, signed in June, collapsed within days after fresh strikes were exchanged.

One of the conditions of the plan is for the U.S. to accept a maritime transit route through the Strait of Hormuz that has been agreed upon by Iran and Oman, Araghchi had said Thursday.

A U.S. official said on Friday that the Trump administration was having positive and constructive discussions through the mediators but that it was not in any hurry to reach an agreement.

“The United States is in a very strong position with control of the Strait of Hormuz, so we are not in a rush,” the U.S. official said. “Over the last 48 hours, nearly 40 million barrels of oil have transited the strait.”

Earlier this week, Trump said he was still considering whether to “annihilate” Iran or make a deal. Early Saturday, he posted an image to Truth Social of the Strait of Hormuz labeled the “Trump Strait.”

In an interview with Al Jazeera on Saturday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said that resolving the Hormuz issue “is possible through negotiations, not the use of force,” but warned that his country does not “trust” talks with Washington.

Trump has repeatedly said that the goal of attacking Iran was to prevent the development of a nuclear weapon. Soon after the war started, Iran blocked the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway through which some 20% of the world’s oil flowed before the conflict, sending shock waves through the world economy.

Polls show Democrats with an advantage heading into the November midterms. The latest NBC News Decision Desk Poll found 31% of respondents approved of Trump’s handling of the Iran war, while 69% disapproved.

Pezeshkian on Thursday suggested his government was willing to make a deal with the U.S. to end the war before Americans head to the polls this November.

“We don’t want it to get to the midterm elections,” Pezeshkian said in a brief meeting with NBC News and other news organizations, two days after Trump said he believed the Iranian regime would not make a deal to settle the conflict until after the elections.

“I believe we’ll make a deal right after the election because it doesn’t make sense for them not to,” Trump said. “They’re waiting to see how I do in the midterm election.”

The U.S. this week announced it would impose sanctions on any global companies doing business ​with Iranian airlines, with the aim of grounding Iran’s entire civil fleet worldwide.

Iraq said Saturday that it was engaging with the U.S. in an effort to restore humanitarian flights to and from Iran, after Iranian airlines were barred from neighboring countries in response to the sanctions.

Efforts were ongoing to “secure exemptions for certain Iraqi airports from these measures” in order to enable “the resumption of flights for humanitarian reasons, such as medical treatment, education, religious pilgrimages, and the interests of civilians,” the Iraqi prime minister’s office said.

Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that flights had also been shut down to Oman, Georgia and Azerbaijan.

World.title: Should you bring iced coffee to a job interview? Question brews generational debate
World.content:
What started as a conversation about job interview tips online escalated into a generational debate over whether it’s taboo to show up with an iced coffee to talk to a potential employer.

The discourse over the caffeinated beverage gained momentum on TikTok this week after a creator, who goes by @caitlinrecruiter on the platform, shared a video in which she said she believes “when you show up with an iced coffee or an iced latte that this interview is just a stop on your list of errands for the day.”

“It looks a little too casual to me,” she said in the video, which she posted Sept. 16.

Caitlin Wehniainen, whose profile states she has 16 years of recruiting experience, has just over 1,000 followers on TikTok. But in the last week, her video has been clipped and recirculated by dozens of creators online, who engaged in a heated back-and-forth about whether she’s right.

The divide seemed to primarily be between younger and older users — with the former group suggesting Wehniainen’s tip “makes no sense at all” and that such a perspective is archaic.

Others, many who identified as Gen Xers in comments, agreed with Wehniainen, writing that “arguing against this is insane” and telling applicants that they should “save the iced coffee for when you actually get hired.”

By Monday, even the coffee giant Starbucks had taken a side, alluding to the debate in an Instagram post that featured an image of someone holding an iced coffee in one hand and sunglasses and their handbag in the other. “Pulling up to the interview like,” the caption read. Meanwhile, The Coffee Bean and Tea Leaf, another coffee chain, commented on Wehniainen’s video: “We’d hire them on spot...”

Outside Off-White, during New York Fashion Week, on September 12, 2025 in New York, New York Edward Berthelot / Getty Images file

When reached for comment on Friday, Wehniainen said in an email to NBC News that she was “shocked at how polarizing the topic is.”

“But I realize that the original message was taken out of context as the virality of the post grew,” she wrote. “As the topic spread, many decided to weigh in with their own general opinion on whether or not bringing an iced coffee into an interview is appropriate ... I also saw people reading into it too much, asking if coffee or water matters and what is appropriate. I will say, I think a bottled water is great to bring with you.”

The timing of the conversation coincides with a tough job market: Recent college graduates are facing higher unemployment rates than other age groups as it’s becoming more difficult to obtain entry-level jobs, NBC News reported last month. Employers are not looking to add talent, and employed people are not moving to new positions, as a rise in AI continues to threaten jobs.

For Los Angeles-based TikTok creator Esha, who preferred to be identified by only her first name, citing privacy concerns, Wehniainen’s words couldn’t be further from the truth. She was among the many weighing in online, telling her 81,000-plus TikTok followers that “the iced coffee controversy completely misunderstands interviews.”

“Thinking of a job interview as a stop in your day is very normal,” Esha, 22, added in an interview with NBC News, noting that she’s brought iced coffees to several interviews and hasn’t thought twice about it.

“Gen Z had this shift in recent years, where we can still have a life outside of work,” Esha said. “So, like, why am I changing who I am? Why am I missing my coffee for the day for this interview?”

In her video, she elaborated further on her take, saying that “the most easily relatable thing in corporate America is a coffee addiction.”

“Unless you’re like over the age of 30 and you can relate on having kids, and doing stuff with your kids, coffee is the main thing. Everyone’s like, ‘Gotta get that coffee’ ... and finding something personable about a person is so important,” she said. “Like, who is not starting their workday off with a coffee?”

Catherine Fisher, vice president of communications at LinkedIn, said she’s not surprised by the generational divisions when it comes to job etiquette.

“Gen Z is entering this workforce at such a challenging time, it’s such a competitive job market, and to then get judged by bringing an iced coffee just seems like, ‘Have we lost the plot here?’” she said.

That said, Fisher is among the cohort who believes it’s best to skip the iced coffee when headed to an interview.

“Even though I don’t like the answer, I think because everyone is so divided on it, I would be cautious and not bring one,” she said. “You just don’t know who’s on the other side of the interview, so why risk it over something so silly?”

Etiquette expert Thomas Farley, who is known as Mister Manners to his followers online, agreed with the more traditional point of view.

“I think it sends the wrong message in so many respects,” he said. “I think it shows you to be someone who didn’t plan your time accordingly, and you’re multitasking, and that’s not what you should be doing during the interview.”

Farley also warned of the physical pratfalls a coffee could bring.

“There are real practical considerations when you bring a liquid into someone’s office,” he said. “Where does it go? What happens if you spill it?”

While he doesn’t think it should be the deciding factor for any hiring manager, Farley argued candidates should be doing everything in their power to leave a positive impression.

“If it’s between you and three other people, and everyone’s qualifications are more or less equal, and that’s the one thing that potentially sinks your chance to get the job, I think that would be really unfortunate,” he said. “That would be a very expensive $7 cup of iced coffee.”

Still, Gen Zers like Esha are not convinced that bringing the beverage would make or break their job opportunity.

As another TikTok creator put it in their video: “It’s really, really not that serious most of the time.”

As for Wehniainen? Even after the online uproar, she said her “opinion still stands that you shouldn’t bring an iced coffee to your interview.”

“You want to leave outlying distractions like iced coffee behind,” she said, “and connect with your interviewer with full attention.”

World.title: New data shows most women in the Marines passing toughened fitness tests for combat roles
World.content: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said he wanted women in combat roles to be held to the same physical standards as men. One year later, new numbers from the Marine Corps show most women in combat roles are meeting, or exceeding those standards. NBC News’ Yasmin Vossoughian reports.Sept. 24, 2026

World.title: Nor'easter brings powerful winds, severe flooding to the East Coast
World.content:
The powerful nor'easter making its way up the coast of New England led to tens of thousands of power outages and severe flooding on Saturday morning.

Tens of millions of people are in the path of the storm, which has canceled flights, concerts and sporting events. Dangerous flooding is expected along the Mid-Atlantic coast, particularly near New Jersey and Delaware, according to the National Weather Service.

More than 70,000 customers were without electricity Saturday, and forecasters were warning of gale-force winds that could down trees. Heavy rain could lead to flooding that could put roads underwater, the NWS said.

In the beachfront borough of Manasquan, New Jersey, where some roads were also flooding, Mayor Mike Mangan said he expected "a lot of water in the streets for a long time." A voluntary evacuation had been issued earlier in some low-lying areas of the community.

Further north, the residents of islands near Cape Cod, Massachusetts headed to the mainland to wait out the storm. Peak wind gusts could approach 60 to 65 mph on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50 to 55 mph farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with NWS in Norton, Massachusetts.

"It's definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you're likely to see," Belk said.



The East Coast is under several weather alerts from this weekend's nor'easter. Sept. 25, 2026. CBS News

Residents of some communities urged to evacuate

Some towns along the New Jersey shore were already getting battered by coastal flooding on Saturday morning. In Ship Bottom, roads were submerged. Some drivers attempted to push through the rising floodwaters, while some residents were grabbing what little they could and fleeing to higher ground on foot.

In Sea Bright, homeowners and businesses were preparing for the worst. However, Michael Cardelfe, owner of Donovan's Reef Beach Bar, said his doors would stay open.

"We are like the local watering hub and Donovan's Reef is the kind of place, when we have a storm, we get busier," Cardelfe told CBS News.

In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, rippling water was already flooding streets and inundating homes on Saturday morning.

Kelly, the mayor of Sea Bright, said the borough is bracing for winds up to 50 mph and flooding that could reach up to 6 feet on some streets. Officials expect the flooding to start Saturday and worsen by midday.

Forecast rainfall totals from this weekend's nor'easter. Sept. 25, 2026. CBS News

"It's going to be worse than average. We do have probably one or two flooding events a year, sometimes more, sometimes less, but I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event," Kelly said, referencing the 2011 storm that caused major flooding in the Northeast. "I hope I'm wrong, but that's my gut feeling."

Kelly hopes hundreds of residents living in low-lying areas will consider evacuating. He said the town will open its recreation center for evacuees. "A lot of the homes are elevated, but obviously, you know, people can get trapped in their house temporarily," he added.

In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, rippling water was already flooding streets and inundating homes on Saturday morning.

The system was already kicking up high surf and causing beach erosion in Ocean City, New Jersey, where block after block was underwater.

On New York's Long Island, a state of emergency was declared. Crews built a wall of sand along the beach to keep the rising tide away from homes.

"If the tide goes out, we don't expect to have such bad flooding," Robert Kennedy, mayor of the Long Island village of Freeport, told CBS News. "If the tide stays in, it could increase the flooding in the village."

In Plymouth, Massachusetts, south of Boston, boaters were clearing out the harbor. "I just want people to take some extra precaution, plan ahead a little bit," Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said in a Friday news conference.

On Massachusetts' South Shore, the towns of Cohasset and Scituate sit right in the bullseye of the storm. While parts of the coastline are protected by seawalls, some of those seawalls are in the middle of repair projects or have seen those projects stall due to federal funding cuts.

A wave crashes over an unfinished seawall near Oceanside Drive in Scituate, Massachusetts, on Sept. 24, 2026. David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images

Strong winds could push the ocean water over the seawalls, creating flooding.

"So the waves hit the seawall and they go straight up about 60, 70, 80 feet, and the wind hits it from the northeast and every wave ends up hitting the house," Kevin Gill, owner of an oceanfront Scituate home, told CBS News Boston on Thursday.

Peak wind gusts could approach 60 to 65 mph on Cape Cod, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket on Friday night and Saturday, compared with about 50 to 55 mph around Boston and 35 to 40 mph farther inland, according to Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with NWS in Norton, Massachusetts.

"It's definitely going to be a case of the closer to the coast you are, the more impacts from the storm you're likely to see," Belk said.

Belk said nor'easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but one concern this early in the season is that leaves remain on the trees, creating more wind resistance. That could increase the risk of downed limbs, which in turn can cause power outages and leave debris in roads, he said.

Nor'easter cancels sporting events, concerts

Air travel was also being disrupted, with Boston particularly hard hit. Flight-tracking service FlightAware reported 39 cancellations at Boston Logan International Airport between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. Saturday, compared with 22 at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport. Another 12 flights were delayed at Logan.

The Boston Red Sox announced their weekend series against the Chicago Cubs would be adjusted. The team moved the Sunday afternoon game to Friday to create a split doubleheader. Separately, Ed Sheeran announced that his high-profile Friday and Saturday shows at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, would be canceled due to the storm.

In New York City, the Global Citizens Festival and All Things Go NYC were canceled ahead of the storm.

Meanwhile, the public ferry service connecting Cape Cod with the islands of Nantucket and Martha's Vineyard was experiencing widespread cancellations Friday due to strong winds and choppy water. Several flights to the islands were also canceled.

A car is seen submerged in water on a flooded road during a nor'easter storm on September 26, 2026 in Point Pleasant, New Jersey. Ryan Murphy / Getty Images

Over in Rhode Island, ferries were also canceled for Block Island. The disrupted ferry service was also expected to spill into Saturday.

For people who regularly travel to and from the islands, the possibility of getting stuck on one side or the other is "part of life," said Sean Driscoll, a spokesperson for the Woods Hole, Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket Steamship Authority. Most people have backup plans in place for when boats are canceled.

"It's a nuisance, but you know, we know what to do with this kind of stuff at this point," he said. "This is not out of the realm of ordinary. Part of living in this region is just kind of knowing how to deal with this stuff."

World.title: 4 American tourists dead after building explosion in Greece
World.content:
Four Americans were among the six people who died after an explosion and building collapse in Athens' tourist district of Plaka near the Acropolis on Friday, officials said.

The blast, which occurred at dawn on Friday, was likely caused by a gas leak, according to Athens Mayor Haris Doukas.

The two other people killed were an elderly British man and his Greek wife who lived on the second floor of the three-story building, Greece's state broadcaster ERT reported.

Rescuers search for survivors after a blast in the Plaka district of Athens, Greece, on September 26, 2026. Costas Baltas/Anadolu via Getty Images

The American family of four had been renting an apartment on the first floor and were preparing to go to the airport hours later Friday for their return to the United States when the blast occurred, according to the Kathimerini newspaper.

The explosion brought down the residential building and damaged properties and vehicles along the street. Two other women were injured from an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, fire brigades said, according to the Associated Press.

The New York Times reported that the U.S. family was composed of a couple, their son and his girlfriend. Greek authorities did not immediately give their identities, ages or where in the U.S. they came from.

The explosion happened near the Acropolis, one of Greece's best-known landmarks. Costas Baltas/Anadolu via Getty Images

On Saturday, AFP reporters saw mechanical diggers moving debris at the site and thermal-imaging cameras deployed.

"We are talking about an incredible disaster," Doukas said.

Two nearby buildings were left in a dangerous state, he added, with inspections underway "to determine if they can remain standing or if they also have to be demolished."

The owner of the ground-floor apartment, Mathaios Artavanis, told the Kathimerini daily he was absent at the time of the blast. He said he had tried afterward to contact the U.K.-Greek couple who lived there, without success.

Video footage from the scene showed rubble strewn across the street, with parked cars smashed by falling debris. The people rescued by the fire department from the adjacent building were all tourists, resident Andreas Martzaklis said.

The pastor of a nearby church said this Sunday's service would be held outdoors because of damage to the church.

A year ago, locals in the Plaka neighborhood had warned the city and utility companies about the risk of gas leaks or short circuits, according to a letter by the residents' association published by Kathimerini.

The residents had urged a fire drill to identify possible weaknesses in the emergency response plans for the district.

A citizens' group said on social media that one resident in the street where the explosion happened had alerted authorities after smelling a possible gas leak.

The neighborhood is one of Athens' most popular tourist areas. The nearby Acropolis, one of Greece's best-known landmarks, welcomed 4.6 million visitors last year.

World.title: Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History celebrates 10th anniversary
World.content: Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History celebrates 10th anniversary The Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture is marking a major milestone this week - celebrating its 10-year anniversary. Photojournalist Parrish Smith looks back at when the doors opened, takes us inside to see some current exhibitions, and makes a stop at the museum's Sweet Home Cafe.

World.title: The story behind the first CIA officers in Afghanistan after 9/11
World.content:
Twenty-five years ago, a Soviet-designed helicopter crossed the mountains of Afghanistan carrying the first CIA officers sent into the country after the attacks on Sept. 11, 2001, marking the opening move in the U.S. response that would soon become America's longest war.

The seven-man CIA team, code-named JAWBREAKER, landed in the Panjshir Valley on Sept. 26, 2001, just 15 days after the attacks, carrying millions of dollars in cash intended to help enlist and equip Afghan allies. Their mission was to gather intelligence and prepare the ground for the looming U.S. campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban — including by shoring up ties with the Northern Alliance, whose military leader, Ahmad Shah Massoud, had been assassinated by al-Qaeda operatives just two days before 9/11.

The Mi-17 that carried them there is now on display at CIA headquarters in Langley, Virginia, where it has undergone an extensive restoration ahead of the anniversary.

Former CIA officer David Tyson followed JAWBREAKER into Afghanistan weeks later as a member of Team Alpha, and remembers flying aboard the same aircraft before the war.

"It was shaking a lot, fuel was leaking, very noisy, and I didn't know if it was airworthy," Tyson told CBS News in an interview, "but I was assured by the pilots it was a good bird."

A helicopter built to blend in

The CIA acquired the Mi-17 in the 1990s, calculating that its Soviet origins would be an advantage in the region.

"The Northern Alliance and the Taliban both used Mi-17s," CIA historian Rob Byer told CBS News. "They're Russian helicopters and kind of the pickup truck of helicopters in that region."

"The big reason we got an Mi-17 rather than flying in a Blackhawk is because it blends in," Byer said. "And when you're going behind enemy lines, you'd like to blend in as much as you can."

It could also handle the punishing altitude. To reach the Panjshir Valley, JAWBREAKER had to cross the Anjuman Pass, which rises roughly 14,500 feet above sea level.

"The Mi-17 is one of the few helicopters that can actually make it over that pass," Byer said.

Central Intelligence Agency

The aircraft had no transponder to identify it to American warplanes, leaving its crew to improvise. They painted "USA" and an American flag across the tops of its stabilizers, visible to friendly pilots overhead but concealed from enemy eyes on the ground. With no blue paint available, the crew left the flag unfinished. And in a reminder of the attacks that had brought them there, they gave the helicopter the call sign "9-11-01."

The Mi-17 would go on to fly more than 300 missions in Afghanistan, remaining in service until 2012.

Team Alpha goes to war

Tyson was a CIA case officer based in Central Asia who was steeped in local languages, including Uzbek, Turkmen and Russian. On Sept. 11, 2001, he was on a flight to the United Kingdom for a meeting related to the CIA's efforts to recover Stinger missiles that had remained in Afghanistan, many of which were sent there in a U.S.-backed initiative during the Soviet war.

Central Intelligence Agency

Soon after he landed, he began planning his return, realizing his expertise would likely take him to Afghanistan.

"I knew that I would be involved given my languages and experience and so forth and where I was based in Central Asia," Tyson recalled.

On Oct. 17, less than three weeks after JAWBREAKER arrived in the Panjshir Valley, Tyson and the rest of Team Alpha were inserted into a different part of northern Afghanistan, becoming the first Americans sent behind Taliban lines. Their mission was to work with forces commanded by Uzbek leader Abdul Rashid Dostum as part of the campaign against the Taliban and al-Qaeda.

"This was something we hadn't done before," Tyson said, describing a mission that involved working with local forces to "basically prosecute a war."

David Tyson

His principal role was intelligence and liaison work. He worked closely with Dostum's Uzbek-speaking forces, helping his team understand the people and environment around them. The Americans traveled with Afghan fighters on horseback through the mountains, sometimes riding as long as 14 hours a day.

"The horses were not friendly," Tyson recalled. "They were stallions, they fought between each other, they bit us, they kicked us, they tried to knock us off. And the gear, the kit, the saddles were basically wooden frames with carpets thrown on them."

By late November, Taliban forces had collapsed across much of northern Afghanistan. Hundreds of foreign fighters had surrendered and were taken to Qala-i-Jangi, a sprawling 19th-century fortress near Mazar-e-Sharif.

On Nov. 25, Tyson and fellow CIA officer Johnny Micheal "Mike" Spann entered Qala-i-Jangi, where their initial task was to determine who the prisoners were and where they came from.

"For the most part, they were responding and identifying themselves as al-Qaeda members, people who had given oath of allegiance to bin Laden," Tyson said. Among the prisoners was John Walker Lindh, a California native who moved to the region in 2000 and joined the Taliban.

Central Intelligence Agency

Hours into their mission, the prisoners rose up.

"There were explosions, gunfire, and a lot of yelling," Tyson recalled. "I started seeing things in what I would call slow motion," he said. "Things were moving slowly, but almost automatically."

At a certain point he heard Spann call his name, and began moving toward his partner through the fighting.

"I remember seeing his … silhouette or body on the ground," Tyson said. "I believe Mike was already dead when I got to him and I was able to shoot the men on top of him and took Mike's rifle from him."

Spann, 32, became the first American killed in combat in Afghanistan. His was the 79th star carved into the CIA's Memorial Wall.

Tyson fought his way to safety with Spann's rifle, which he continued using for the rest of his deployment. It is now displayed in the CIA Museum, alongside the pair of boots Tyson wore throughout his deployment. Tyson's then-8-year-old son later dubbed them "Dad's lucky boots."

"That rifle saved my life, I think, among other things," Tyson said. "It's very fitting, I think, that that rifle's in the museum. Again, it reminds us of Mike and who he was."

David Tyson

Restoring a piece of CIA history

After its final operational mission in 2012, the Mi-17 was brought to CIA headquarters in 2018. Its fuel lines and other components were removed and it was installed outside amid rocks meant to resemble the Afghan landscape.

Years of exposure to the elements took a toll. "The paint had faded greatly due to the sun and a few critters were getting inside as well," Byer said.

Over the past year, the CIA sealed openings in the aircraft and repainted it to more closely resemble how it looked in 2001. The green was deliberately made slightly more vivid, Byer said, so exposure to the sun will eventually fade it to the intended shade.

The restoration also brought back "607," the call sign of the Afghan pilot who flew the first mission. Painted on both sides of the Mi-17 in 2001, the number helped it pass as a Northern Alliance aircraft while signaling to allied pilots that it was friendly.

Central Intelligence Agency

For Tyson, the artifacts preserve a much more personal history.

"As Mike would say, he wanted to be on the tip of the spear," Tyson said. "He was that, and he is today. He will be that forever. And for me to be part of that was just something that obviously I won't forget."

Tyson said he still thinks about Spann and his sacrifice on "a daily basis."

"I'd like to think he helps guide me through things," he added.

Tyson and Spann's widow, Shannon Spann DeBruyn, are now among those involved with Badger Six, a nonprofit created in 2022 and named after Spann's call sign to assist the Afghan fighters who worked alongside Team Alpha, as well as their families. The organization says it currently supports about 35 families with assistance ranging from food and medicine to relocation and resettlement support.

For Tyson, that work is part of a mission that did not end when the United States withdrew from Afghanistan in 2021 as the Taliban reclaimed power, leaving some of the Afghan partners who had fought alongside Americans behind and vulnerable to Taliban reprisals. Asked whether he feels an obligation to help where governments have not, Tyson answered simply, "Sure, yeah. That's what people do. That's what we do."

World.title: Hurricane Polo is a powerful Category 5 storm off Mexico. See its path.
World.content:
Hurricane Polo regained Category 5 status as its intensity fluctuated off Mexico's southwestern coast. It had maximum sustained winds of 180 mph on Friday, well above the 157 mph needed to reach Category 5 status.

More fluctuations are possible, but the storm is expected to make landfall in California's Big Sur as a powerful hurricane, the National Hurricane Center said.

The storm was moving west-northwest on Saturday morning.

Elsewhere in the Pacific, Nolo strengthened into a hurricane as it headed for Hawaii's Big Island this weekend.

Maps show Hurricane Polo's projected path

As of Saturday, Polo's core was about 425 miles west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes, in Mexico's state of Jalisco. It was heading west-northwest at 10 mph.

It is expected to approach Baja California Sur, Mexico, on Monday. The State Department, citing forecast models, said the storm is expected to weaken to a Category 1 storm before making landfall in northern Baja California Sur on Monday, and then will continue northeast into southern Sonora.

The National Hurricane Center said the storm will remain a "powerful hurricane" as it approaches land.

CBS News/Nikki Nolan

Polo could produce 4 to 8 inches of rain, and up to a possible 10 inches, across parts of Baja California Sur, the hurricane center said, cautioning that the rain "may produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain."

CBS News/Nikki Nolan

Polo-generated swells will affect the southwestern Mexican coast over the next couple of days, spreading north along the west-central coast and the Baja California peninsula through the weekend, the hurricane center said, warning that swells are "likely to cause life-threatening surf, rip currents, and coastal flooding."

Mexican leaders ordered evacuations, opened shelters and deployed military troops to areas that could be affected by the storm.

Classes were suspended at schools across the city of Acapulco, along the coast of Guerrero, its municipal government announced. Shelters across the state remained open, and officials said they were coordinating with local and national authorities to prepare for additional impacts of the hurricane.

Michoacán authorities also canceled classes through Friday in municipalities along the coast, urging residents of those areas not to leave their homes unless it was essential.

Polo's extreme rapid intensification

Polo underwent what's called extreme rapid intensification, in which a storm's wind speeds increase by 58 mph or more over the course of 24 hours, between Monday and Tuesday.

Its intensification was dramatic even by those standards, with winds that skyrocketed from 45 mph early Monday morning to 150 mph at around the same time the following day. The hurricane center described the storm's transformation as "truly remarkable."

Its maximum sustained winds climbed as high as 180 mph at one point, far exceeding the 157 mph threshold for Category 5, the strongest on the hurricane scale. By Saturday morning, the maximum sustained winds had lowered to near 160 miles per hour, with some higher gusts.

Polo's central pressure — an indicator of its strength and potential destructiveness — made it the second-strongest hurricane on record in the Eastern Pacific, behind 2015's Hurricane Patricia. The storm's wind speeds tied 2009's Hurricane Rick as the third-strongest on record for the region.

Unusually strong El Niño conditions this year have been amping up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific, with warmer waters, moist air and less wind shear enabling storm formation.

World.title: The story of the first CIA officers in Afghanistan after 9/11
World.content: The story of the first CIA officers in Afghanistan after 9/11 Saturday marks exactly 25 years since the first CIA officers entered Afghanistan in the aftermath of 9/11. Olivia Gazis got a rare look inside the mission to shore up the Northern Alliance as America prepared to go to war.

World.title: Hurricane Nolo could cause "catastrophic" flooding in Hawaii, forecasters warn
World.content:
Hurricane Nolo strengthened into a Category 2 storm as it approaches Hawaii as a potential "catastrophic" rainmaker, the National Hurricane Center said, and is expected to grow stronger throughout the weekend.

The storm was nearly stationary on Saturday morning, the NHC said. It is forecast to move westward with increasing speed later Saturday and Sunday. It is expected to strengthen later Saturday before weakening on Monday.

A hurricane watch is in effect for Hawaii County due to the storm, which could dump up to 3 feet of rain on Hawaii's Big Island. Catastrophic and life-threatening flash flooding is possible on the Big Island into this weekend, forecasters warn.

President Trump on Friday approved an emergency declaration for Hawaii that will provide federal resources and assistance to the state in its recovery from Nolo, Hawaiian Gov. Josh Green said.

Map shows Hurricane Nolo's expected path

The center of the storm was hundreds of miles from Hawaii as of Saturday morning and is expected to stay "well south" of the main Hawaiian Islands. But hurricane-force winds were extending outward up to 45 miles from Nolo's core and tropical storm-force winds extended outward up to 140 miles.

Nolo had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, making it a Category 2 hurricane. The Miami-based hurricane center said it is expected to keep strengthening and become a major hurricane this weekend, which is defined as a Category 3 hurricane or stronger.

The trajectory of Hurricane Nolo as it moves toward Hawaii. Nikki Nolan/CBS News

A tropical storm warning is in effect for Hawaii County (in addition to the hurricane watch there), and a tropical storm watch is in effect for Maui County.

The Big Island was beginning to experience tropical storm conditions Friday night, forecasters said, with hurricane conditions possible for the island early Saturday, especially in areas with steep terrain.

A satellite image of Hurricane Nolo in the Pacific Ocean as it approaches Hawaii. NOAA/NESDIS/STAR

Nolo could bring up to 25 inches of rain to the eastern and southern portions of the Big Island. That much rain could trigger "catastrophic life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in areas of steep terrain," the hurricane center warned.

The Big Island's western areas could see 2 to 4 inches of rain and 8 at most. For Maui, 4 to 6 inches is possible with as much as 10 inches in some spots. The rest of Hawaii is likely to get 1 to 3 inches and 5 at most, enough to set off isolated flooding, forecasters said.

The rain forecast for Hawaii from Hurricane Nolo. Sept. 25, 2026. Nikki Nolan/CBS News

All state parks on the Big Island and on Maui will be closed because of the storm, the state's Department of Land and Natural Resources said.

The forecast wind speeds for Hurricane Nolo as it approaches Hawaii. Sept. 25, 2026. Nikki Nolan/CBS News

Nolo formed as another storm, Hurricane Polo, continued to swirl in the Pacific, off Mexico's southwestern coast.

The Eastern Pacific tropical outlook as of Sept. 25, 2026. CBS News/Nikki Nolan

The latest storms add to an unusually active season in the Pacific. Earlier this month, Hurricane Lowell brought damaging winds and heavy rain to the western Hawaiian islands of Kauai and Niihau, bringing down trees, damaging roads and knocking out power for thousands.

Last month, Hurricane Lala washed away about 100 homes, triggered landslides and caused widespread power outages as it brushed past Hawaii.

World.title: Teen's headache reveals family health risk: "Saving people's lives"
World.content:
Caroline McCaffrey usually ran in the morning, but on Father's Day 2025, she was feeling tired and decided to exercise in the evening instead. She invited her mother Kim to bike alongside her.

Just a few minutes into the run, Caroline, then 18, was struck by a "really bad headache." She had experienced and received treatment for migraines before, but this was a new sensation.

"It felt like I got punched in the face," Caroline said. Within minutes, she was vomiting. She couldn't walk, so Kim called her husband to come pick them up. When the symptoms didn't immediately recede, Kim started to panic.

"I literally Googled, as she was throwing up, the signs of (ruptured) brain aneurysms. My husband was like, 'Do you think this is what it is?' And I was like, 'I don't know. This isn't normal,'" Kim recalled.

Caroline and Kim McCaffrey. The McCaffrey family

At an area hospital, Kim quickly raised her concerns, but Caroline's physician was skeptical.

"I was like, 'I'm pretty sure she's having a brain aneurysm or a ruptured brain aneurysm,' and he's like, 'I don't think we should go there yet,'" Kim recalled. Caroline was given another dose of migraine medication, but it had no effect.

A few hours later, a second doctor ordered a CT scan. That test found bleeding in Caroline's brain. Caroline said she was relieved to be on the path to treatment.

"I think I was in so much pain that I couldn't really even be scared at that point," Caroline said.

Treating a deadly diagnosis

Caroline was transferred to the University of Maryland Medical Center. The next day, she woke up in the intensive care unit with a bald spot. Her parents filled her in: Tests had shown two brain aneurysms. One had ruptured and caused an aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, which led to her symptoms, said neurointerventionist Dr. Gunjan Parikh.

The condition typically affects people in their mid-50s. It's a dangerous diagnosis, Parikh said: About 1 in 4 patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhages die before making it to the hospital. Another 13% of patients die at the hospital. But Caroline had been lucky: Neurosurgeon Dr. Jacob Cherian had treated the ruptured aneurysm and repaired the damaged brain tissue. Despite the delays in care, she had been treated "really quickly," Kim said.

Caroline McCaffrey in the hospital. The McCaffrey family

Caroline said she was "really shocked" by the news. It took her a few days to "comprehend what happened."

"Once I did that, I was ready to get things going, get treatment going," Caroline said. "Once I processed it, I kind of just wanted to get things on the road."

It would be a long road. The drain was still removing fluid from her brain. She needed regular ultrasounds and monitoring to ensure that she wasn't having any strokes or seizures, as well as occupational and physical therapy. Then she underwent another surgery to remove the second aneurysm. It was over three weeks before she was finally released from the hospital.

Caroline McCaffrey in the hospital with her parents and brother. The McCaffrey family

Finding a family connection

In the meantime, Caroline's parents were trying to figure out how their 18-year-old daughter could have had such a dangerous condition. While poring over the family's medical history with Caroline's care team, they realized Caroline's paternal great-grandmother had an aneurysm in the 1960s.

That suggested a genetic cause for Caroline's condition. The McCaffreys were encouraged to undergo testing for other potential aneurysms. Usually, aneurysms occur in about 1 in 50 people, Cherian said, but having a first-degree relative with one brings those odds to more like 1 in 5.

"Caroline's very young, at 18, to have something like this. So that was already a clue that maybe there could be something in the family," Cherian said.

Kim was the first family member to be tested. A CT scan found two small aneurysms, which Cherian surgically removed in November 2025.

Kim McCaffrey in the hospital after her surgery, with Caroline on the far left. The McCaffrey family

Kim's husband and son did not have an aneurysm, but her sister-in-law had two. Other family members are continuing to undergo testing, Kim said.

It's not clear why the family is prone to aneurysms on both sides, but Parikh said there is likely a genetic component. Cherian said that neurologists aren't sure why aneurysms form, but they can run in families.

"Caroline was like, 'Okay, I'm tired of saving people's lives,'" Kim joked.

"Now I have a reason"

Both McCaffreys are now fully recovered from their aneurysm experiences, though they will undergo regular monitoring for the rest of their lives. Caroline, now 20, is at Bucknell University for her junior year and is back to running competitively.

She is also taking part in a National Institutes of Health study. The study has enrolled thousands of patients to look at the impact of aneurysms and strokes on the brain over the course of years. Because Caroline is young and had a hemorrhage typically seen in older patients, the data she can offer is unique, Parikh said.

From left: Kim McCaffrey, Dr. Jacob Cherian and Caroline McCaffrey. University of Maryland Medical Center

"It really gives scientists a real-time way to observe what the human brain's maximum potential for self-repair is. It allows us to, in a way, reverse engineer for everybody else," Parikh said. "You're searching for the biological blueprint, and the ultimate goal of this research is to figure out how to use medications or pharmacology or physiologically trigger those exact same youthful healing pathways in a 60- or 70-year-old patient."
