USA & Canada Intelligence Dossier — Saturday, 26 September 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web and updated through the day. Read the web dossier → · Every edition on the dossier page →

The national mood — Gloomy about its own economy, and agreed at least on the direction. The voter rolls — Distrustful, and in court while the voting has already begun. The Atlantic coast — Braced, sandbagged and told to keep away from the water. British Columbia — Angry at Washington, and asked to say so at the ballot box.

The American mood this weekend is gloom that crosses party lines. The country’s oldest survey of how households feel found every political group lower than it was a month ago.

Washington spent Friday watching its own courts decide who may vote, and on which map. The Supreme Court obliged the administration on the first question and refused Missouri’s Republicans on the second.

The figure that carries the week measures temperament rather than money. The University of Michigan’s final September reading of consumer sentiment came in at 48.1, against 51.7 in August.

The Atlantic coast has a weekend of its own. A coastal storm flooded streets in New Jersey overnight and cut power to nearly 55,000 customers by Saturday morning, CNN reports.

Canada’s temperament is combative, and it is being tested on Canadians rather than on Washington. British Columbia is fighting an election it did not need to hold, and Quebec opens its advance polls tomorrow.

What steadies the picture is how ordinary the machinery looks. Two courts published their reasons, two governors declared states of emergency, and an electoral agency printed its opening hours.

Key Facts — The national mood, measured. American consumer sentiment came in at 48.1 on 25 September, against 51.7 in August and 12.7 per cent below a year earlier. — Gloom across party lines. Breitbart, a conservative American site, put Republicans at 77.2 this month, Democrats at 35.6 and independents at 47.7, all lower than in August. — The citizenship database revived. The Supreme Court ruled by six votes to three on 25 September that states may check voter rolls against a federal citizenship database, Townhall reports. — Missouri’s map sent back. The same court, the same day, ordered Missouri to hold its 3 November election on the 2022 map, not the Republican-drawn 2025 one. — Emergencies on the Atlantic coast. New York declared a state of emergency for eight counties on 25 September and New Jersey for eight more, against a forecast of gusts to 60 miles an hour. — British Columbia votes early. David Eby called a snap election on 22 September for 24 October, and the pollster Angus Reid then put his New Democrats on 35 per cent against 43 for the Conservatives. — Quebec opens its advance polls. Advance voting runs on 27 and 28 September before the 5 October election, with the polling firm Léger putting the Parti Québécois on 29 per cent. — The tariff bill in border states. Stateline, a non-profit American news service, reports nearly US$28 billion of American exports to Canada now carry duties of up to 50 per cent.

A Country That Agrees Only About The Direction

The clearest statement about America on Friday came from Americans themselves. The University of Michigan has asked households the same questions about their finances since the 1940s.

Its final reading for September, published on 25 September, put consumer sentiment at 48.1. August’s reading was 51.7, so the month cost 3.6 points.

That is 12.7 per cent below September 2025. On the survey’s own arithmetic it is a fall of 7 per cent in a single month.

The two halves of the survey are moving at different speeds. Americans rated their present situation at 50.9 and what they expect next at 46.3.

Over the month expectations fell 10.1 per cent against 1.9 per cent for conditions. Over the year the order reverses, with conditions down 15.7 per cent against 10.4 per cent for expectations.

The survey’s director put the size of it plainly. Joanne Hsu said sentiment had reached “the lowest reading in four months and down 15% from January 2026.”

Advisor Perspectives, an American investment research site, sets that level against the past rather than against last month. It places September below the first percentile of the whole series.

The comparison it draws is starker still. The reading sits below the level at which each of the six American recessions since 1978 began.

What makes this a psychological fact rather than an economic one is who is gloomy. Breitbart, a conservative American news site, put Republicans at 77.2, Democrats at 35.6 and independents at 47.7.

Those three figures portray a country that agrees only about the direction. The University of Michigan’s own release says that “Overall, interviews reveal broad agreement across the political spectrum that the outlook for the economy has weakened since the beginning of the year.”

Both sides have lost ground from their own starting points this year. Advisor Perspectives records Republican sentiment down 20 per cent since January and Democratic sentiment down 13 per cent.

Households named two culprits, and the release named both. It says that “The short-run outlook for business conditions plunged amid renewed worries that elevated fuel prices and re-escalating trade disputes could pass through to the economy as a whole.”

Expectations of inflation moved with them. Americans now expect prices to rise 4.6 per cent over the coming year, against 4.0 per cent in August.

The survey calls that the highest such reading since June. Over the longer run households expect 3.4 per cent a year.

A second account set the inflation worry against the war. Quartz, an American business news site, reported that the year-ahead expectation stood at 3.4 per cent before the fighting with Iran began.

The fuel worry is not irrational, although it is not simple either. November Brent crude settled at US$104.32 a barrel on Friday, down 2.14 per cent on Thursday.

Over the week the two big crude grades went opposite ways. That same November Brent contract finished 0.43 per cent higher, while the American grade on its own November contract fell 3.82 per cent.

The sharpest energy move of the week was in the fuel that heats American homes. The November natural gas contract closed the week at US$3.196 per million British thermal units, 9.75 per cent higher.

The price of American borrowing rose all week. Two-year Treasury debt closed at 4.81 per cent against 4.76 per cent on 18 September, and the ten-year at 5.17 against 5.01.

The longest debt moved the most. The thirty-year ended the week at 5.49 per cent against 5.34 per cent, and on Friday it was still rising while the two-year had turned down.

Investors spent the week doing the opposite of worrying. The S&P 500 closed on Friday at 7,743.41, up 0.51 per cent on the day and 1.21 per cent on the week.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average did better still, ending Friday at 51,828.62, up 0.93 per cent. The distance between the market and the household is the psychogram of this week.

Traders are paying very little to insure themselves against turbulence. The Cboe volatility index, the standard measure of it, ended Friday at 14.87, down 5.11 per cent on the day.

Across the week, however, that gauge barely moved. It began the week at 14.81, so the calm arrived on Friday rather than lasting all week.

None of this was set by the central bank, which has already moved. The Federal Reserve raised its target range for overnight lending between banks to 3.75 to 4.00 per cent on 16 September.

That was its first increase since 2023. No central bank anywhere took a decision on Friday.

Distrust Written Into The Voter Rolls

The most consequential American decision of the week was about a filing system. On 25 September the Supreme Court allowed the Department of Homeland Security to keep offering states a rebuilt federal database.

Its purpose is to let election officials test whether people on their voter lists are citizens. The department is the federal ministry that runs immigration enforcement and border control.

The system has a name that explains nothing and a history that explains a good deal. It is called the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system, and it was built in 1986 to check eligibility for welfare benefits.

In May 2025 the department rebuilt it for a different job. The new version carries Social Security records and can answer questions about many people at once.

Townhall, a conservative American site, puts the vote at six to three. The order was unsigned, and all three of the court’s liberal justices joined a dissent by Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, Hot Air reports.

The majority gave a reason of duty rather than of policy. It wrote that “The Federal Government has an obligation to respond to requests from state and local election officials seeking to verify the citizenship of voters,” Townhall and Hot Air both report.

It also pointed at the calendar, which is the part a foreign reader should notice. The blocked ruling, the court said, “inhibits the Federal Government’s efforts to assist state and local agencies in the proper administration of the midterm elections,” NPR reports.

The judge whose ruling was lifted had been blunter. Sparkle Sooknanan, a federal district judge, struck the rebuilt system down in June for breaking the Social Security Act, the Privacy Act and the Administrative Procedure Act.

Her reasoning went to privacy rather than to elections. Sooknanan wrote that “The federal government has knowingly trampled on the privacy rights of American citizens in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote,” NPR reports.

The dissent argued about which harm is the larger. Jackson wrote that “The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the government experiences…”, Hot Air reports.

She named the people she had in mind. Jackson warned of the “risk that States might cancel the voter registrations of at least some recently naturalized citizens”, NPR reports.

The checking is already large, and the two outlets count different things. NPR reports 65 million voters run through the system across 26 states since May 2025, while the Boston Globe counts 67 million registrations scanned.

What the checking has produced is a short list and a real error rate. NPR reports 28,635 people flagged as possible non-citizens, of whom 2,724 were in Texas.

Of the 2,724 Texans flagged, about a fifth turned out to be citizens. And 117 cases — 4.2 per cent of the Texas total — were referred for investigation, NPR reports.

A county-sized version of the same figure is also on the record. The Boston Globe reports that Travis County in Texas had 97 voters flagged, of whom between 10 and 21 per cent were confirmed as citizens.

What changed on Friday is a matter of volume. States may now search the database in batches, where before they could ask only about “one person at a time”, Jessica Huseman of Votebeat told PBS News.

Votebeat is a non-profit news service that covers election administration. The challengers are two civic organisations rather than a political party.

The League of Women Voters and the Electronic Privacy Information Center brought the case. They argued that the government had built “an error-laden master citizenship database that endangers millions of Americans’ privacy and voting rights”, NPR reports.

There is a brake on the ruling, written into American election law. The National Voter Registration Act forbids large removals from the rolls in the 90 days before a federal election.

That limits what Friday’s order can do this autumn, PBS News and Hot Air both report. The last check on a bad match is a local official, which is what reassures the people who run elections.

Huseman told PBS News that county clerks “tend to be much more careful with these matches than the federal government or even many state governments are”. The urgency comes from the fact that Americans are already voting.

Virginia opened in-person early voting on 18 September. Voters in Idaho, Minnesota and South Dakota can now cast absentee ballots in person, the Associated Press reports, before the elections of 3 November.

One state’s chief election officer used the moment to say the obvious aloud. Minnesota’s Secretary of State, Steve Simon, said his state’s elections are “fundamentally free, fair, accurate, honest and secure”, the Associated Press reports.

Nothing about the lawfulness of the rebuilt system has been settled. The order holds only while the appeal is heard, so whether the database survives remains open.

The conservative reading of the week is worth recording, because it cuts against the obvious story. Hot Air noted that the same court had lately refused the administration’s attempt to restrict voting by post, and Townhall called Friday a win for election integrity.

A Map The Court Would Not Let Them Draw

The same nine justices spent the same Friday disappointing the other side. The Supreme Court stopped Missouri using the congressional map its Republican legislature drew in 2025.

The state must instead run its 3 November elections on the map it has used since 2022. The order was short and left no room for argument.

The court wrote that “as a matter of state law, the 2022 map — not the 2025 map — must be used in the 2026 congressional election”. The Missouri Independent, a non-profit news service covering Missouri state government, records the decision as unanimous.

It also told the lower courts to stop trying. St Louis Public Radio reports the order as instructing them not to “enjoin or otherwise prohibit the use of the 2022 map” in this election.

A conservative American site read the order the same way. Townhall reported that “There are no noted dissents,” and that the 2022 map returns six Republican seats and two Democratic ones where the blocked map drew seven and one.

Redrawing a map between censuses is the point of the fight, and it has a national purpose. The 2025 map was drawn to turn a Kansas City seat held by the Democrat Emanuel Cleaver into a Republican one, St Louis Public Radio reports.

A handful of seats decides which party runs the House of Representatives. Missouri’s voters were given a way to stop the map, and they used it.

Opponents gathered signatures to put the map to a referendum. The Missouri Supreme Court held on 3 September that the petition was constitutional and that the 2025 map had therefore never come into effect.

The federal case then ran up and down the courts for three weeks. The Supreme Court directed the use of the 2022 map on 10 September, and a federal appeals court ordered the 2025 map imposed on 21 September.

That appeal court order was held until 28 September, and Friday ended it. The practical consequence falls on a great many ordinary voters.

The 2022 map reverses the redrawing of one district. It also changes which seat 28 counties vote in across five others, the Missouri Independent reports.

Republicans in the state said they were disappointed rather than defiant. Governor Mike Kehoe said it was disappointing that Missouri would “conduct its November general election under a different congressional map than its primary election”, the St Louis television station First Alert 4 reports.

One congressman aimed his complaint at the state court instead. Bob Onder called it “Another disappointing decision by the Supreme Court” and said the state court’s “activist decision disenfranchised 1.2 million Missourians”, First Alert 4 reports.

Another Republican declined to treat the map as decisive at all. The office of Congresswoman Ann Wagner said she “has been clear, she will win this election no matter what map is implemented”, First Alert 4 reports.

The Democrats read it as a third strike. Fred Wellman, a Democratic candidate, said Republicans had gone to the court three times “to force their rigged map on voters” and had lost three times, First Alert 4 reports.

The campaign that forced the referendum was not cheap. People Not Politicians, the group behind the petition, has spent about US$800,000 on broadcast advertising, the Missouri Independent reports.

Its measure, Proposition A, goes on the same 3 November ballot. The wider American figure behind all this explains why tempers are short.

About one in ten Americans this autumn lives in a different congressional district from the one they voted in during 2024. The cause is maps redrawn in the middle of the decade, the Associated Press reports.

Vancouver. David Eby called a snap election for 24 October and is fighting it against Washington, with the first poll of the campaign putting his New Democrats eight points behind.

A Coast That Has Learned To Sandbag Early

From North Carolina to Maine the weekend was cancelled on Friday, calmly and in advance. A nor’easter is the sort of Atlantic storm that spins up off the eastern seaboard and drives the sea inland.

This one arrived on Friday afternoon and is forecast to sit over the coast until Monday. Two governors declared states of emergency before the worst of it reached them.

Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency on 25 September for the five boroughs of New York City and for Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties. She said the order was for those places “as this powerful coastal storm bears down on the region”.

New York’s own forecast explains the wording. The state expected 1.5 to 3 inches of rain, 3 to 5 on eastern Long Island, and gusts of up to 60 miles an hour.

Offshore the sea was the bigger threat. Waves of 15 to 22 feet were forecast off the eastern end of Long Island, the governor’s office said.

The state answered with equipment rather than with rhetoric. Hochul’s office listed 5,675 workers for response and restoration, 3,375 transport department staff and 1,404 dump trucks.

The authority that runs the city’s bridges and tunnels banned empty articulated lorries from Saturday 26 September. New Jersey acted the same day.

Governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency in eight counties. They are Atlantic, Burlington, Cape May, Cumberland, Middlesex, Monmouth, Ocean and Salem, ABC7 New York reports.

By Saturday morning the forecast had become a photograph. Streets in Surf City were under water and some homes flooded, the Associated Press reports.

In Manasquan the mayor expected a long day. Mike Mangan said he expected “a lot of water in the streets for a long time”, the Associated Press reports.

One mayor reached for the worst comparison his town remembers. Brian Kelly said “It’s going to be worse than average” and that “I think this one will be closer to an Irene-scale flooding event,” the Associated Press reports.

Hurricane Irene flooded the New Jersey shore in 2011, which is why the name still works as a measure. The small human details are where the mood sits.

Officials in Sea Bright told residents to move cars and themselves to higher ground. One resident observed that “They never say sandbags unless it could be bad,” ABC7 New York reports.

The fire service in Atlantic City chose the plainest possible warning. Scott Evans said “You don’t want your vehicle driving through that much water at all. This is not a puddle,” ABC7 New York reports.

New England spent Friday being told the same thing in a different accent. Governor Maura Healey of Massachusetts said “Our top priority is keeping people safe, and Massachusetts is prepared for this storm,” the Boston Globe reports.

On Cape Cod the tone was flatter. Justin Tavano, the fire rescue chief in Chatham, said “We’re prepared for the worst,” the Boston Globe reports.

His reason was the wind rather than the rain. Tavano said high gusts were a concern “both in regards to power outages [and] also pushing water into our flood-prone areas”, the Boston Globe reports.

The electricity company said the same thing in its own vocabulary. Olessa Stepanova of Eversource said it was treating the storm as “a potentially significant wind event”, the Boston Globe reports.

A town administrator south of Boston put the request more bluntly. Jim Boudreau of Scituate said “If you don’t need to go out, don’t go out. If you don’t live by the water, don’t come down just to watch,” the Boston Globe reports.

The National Weather Service offered the one rule that covers everything. Matthew Belk, a meteorologist with the service, said the closer to the coast people were, “the more impacts from the storm you’re likely to see”, WBUR, a Boston public radio station, reports.

Measured gusts on Friday night were high without being extraordinary. Fox Weather recorded 57 miles an hour at Oakland Gardens in New York, 55 at Stony Brook and 54 on Block Island in Rhode Island.

Further east the readings were similar. Nantucket recorded 52 miles an hour and Sea Bright in New Jersey 48, Fox Weather reports.

The damage so far is measured in inconvenience and in lost power. CNN reports that nearly 55,000 customers were without electricity across New York, New Jersey and Pennsylvania by early on Saturday.

The storm is very wide, which is the reason for the emergency orders. More than 40 million people lie in its path through Sunday, CNN reports.

The weekend’s cancellations read like a list of what Americans do in late September. More than 200 flights were cancelled on Friday to and from Boston, Nantucket, Martha’s Vineyard and New York.

Ferries to the Massachusetts islands stopped, and a baseball series and two stadium concerts were moved or called off, the Associated Press reports. One traveller gave the storm its regional shrug.

Marc Sarkady said it had changed his travel plans and those of many others, “but that’s fall living in New England,” the Boston Globe reports. Two things temper the picture, and both are about timing.

ABC News reports that widespread river flooding is thought unlikely, because the rain is spread over several days. But Saturday’s full moon lifts each high tide, with coastal water up to three feet above normal from the Outer Banks to Maine.

The one confirmed piece of structural damage is on a barrier island. About 500 feet of North Carolina’s Highway 12 at Rodanthe has been damaged, CNN reports, on the only road along the Outer Banks.

A Province Campaigns Against A President

Canada’s loudest political act this week was a province choosing a fight it could have avoided. David Eby, the premier of British Columbia, dissolved a legislature in which his New Democrats held a majority.

He called the vote for Saturday 24 October, two years into a four-year mandate. He named an American as his opponent in almost the same breath.

Eby said “Donald Trump is attacking our workers. He’s targeting our businesses, and he is threatening our sovereignty,” Global News, a Canadian broadcaster, reports.

His justification was consent rather than arithmetic. Eby said British Columbians “deserve a say” and that “The conditions in our country have changed,” The Tyee, an independent news site in Vancouver, reports.

He described his own government as a piece of fire-fighting equipment. Eby called his party “a fire break in a wildfire”, The Tyee reports, an image that carries weight in a province that spent the summer burning.

The timing was also a judgement about his opponents, and they know it. The British Columbia Conservatives won 44 seats at the last election and were down to 24 by the call, The Tyee reports.

Their leader had resigned days earlier. Kerry-Lynne Findlay stepped down over the weekend before the call, leaving Lorne Doerkson as interim leader with a campaign to assemble, Global News reports.

Doerkson is running on competence and on the cost of the exercise. He says his party offers “hope and real change”, The Tyee reports, and blames the government for mismanaging the budget.

He also says it has been weak against American trade threats. The bill for the vote itself is part of his case.

The election costs between C$83 million and C$84 million (about US$59 million), which Doerkson set against a record provincial debt, Global News reports. The province’s own books give him material.

British Columbia’s first-quarter update of 14 September put this year’s deficit at C$13.8 billion (about US$9.8 billion). That is C$450 million (about US$318 million) worse than the February budget, Victoria News reports.

The debt line runs further out. Provincial debt is expected to pass C$235 billion (about US$166 billion) by 2029, Victoria News reports.

The finance minister chose a diplomatic verb. Josie Osborne said the province’s economy was “navigating a period of significant global uncertainty” when she presented the update, Victoria News reports.

Underneath the politics the tariff damage is specific and one-directional. British Columbia’s exports to the United States fell 6.2 per cent while its worldwide exports rose 4.2 per cent, Victoria News reports.

The province has also cut what it expects of itself. Its growth forecast for the year came down from 1.3 per cent to 0.9 per cent, Victoria News reports.

The labour market is where voters feel it. The province has shed 16,400 jobs so far this year, unemployment has risen 0.4 points to 6.5 per cent, and housing starts are down 9.3 per cent.

There is a second bill that has nothing to do with Washington. The update added C$614 million (about US$434 million) for this year’s wildfires, Victoria News reports, which is the literal version of the premier’s metaphor.

Not everyone accepts that the American threat required a ballot. Vaughn Palmer, the veteran columnist of the Vancouver Sun, called it “as cynical and dishonest and unnecessary an election call as I have witnessed in more than 40 years”, The Tyee reports.

Vancouver’s mayor objected on grounds of simple congestion. Ken Sim protested that the provincial vote lands a week after municipal elections on 17 October, Global News reports.

What Eby is offering is protection rather than expansion. He has promised to pause a planned widening of the provincial sales tax and to have new public ferries built in Canada, Global News reports.

Canadian markets barely registered the drama. The S&P/TSX Composite closed on Friday at 35,800.90, which left the week 0.02 per cent lower.

The currency was steadier than the politics too. The Canadian dollar finished at 1.4145 to the US dollar on the Bank of Canada’s own average for 25 September.

Measured over the whole week it lost a little ground. On the European Central Bank’s Friday-to-Friday reference rates the currency was 0.94 per cent weaker.

Quebec Votes Early, In Five Directions

Quebec starts voting tomorrow, and it does not yet know what it is voting for. The province’s independent electoral authority said on 21 September that advance polls open on 27 and 28 September.

They are open from 9.30 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time, before the general election of 5 October. The mechanics have changed as well as the politics.

The province votes in 127 constituencies on a new electoral map. No changes may be made to the list of electors once advance voting has begun, Élections Québec says.

The agency was candid about one thing it cannot fix. More than 94 per cent of polling places on election day will be accessible to people with limited mobility, and it says suitable buildings are hard to find.

The campaign’s last set piece was a five-way argument. Radio-Canada, the French-language public broadcaster, hosted the final debate in Montreal on 23 September, moderated by Patrice Roy, CTV News and Narcity report.

The five on stage are a map of a fragmented province. They were Christine Fréchette of the governing Coalition Avenir Québec, Charles Milliard of the Liberals and Ruba Ghazal of the left-wing Québec solidaire.

The other two were Paul St-Pierre Plamondon of the pro-independence Parti Québécois and Éric Duhaime of the Conservative Party of Quebec, Narcity reports. The subject a foreign reader expects to dominate did not.

Independence was not seriously joined until the second hour. The argument was less about leaving Canada than about the Parti Québécois plan to postpone any referendum until after Donald Trump has left office.

What the leaders actually fought over was hospitals. Waiting times in emergency departments took the early part of the debate, Narcity reports.

The opposition made it a question of broken promises. Milliard argued that Quebecers had been betrayed by the governing party’s undertakings on delays and on access to doctors.

Housing entered the debate through one small and specific story. The discovery of a baby at an encampment in east Montreal in mid-September opened the first segment, on housing and the cost of living.

Even the clock favoured the front-runner. St-Pierre Plamondon had nearly 24 minutes of speaking time against under 18 minutes each for the Liberal and Conservative leaders, Narcity reports.

The polling explains why the others were chasing him. Léger puts the Parti Québécois on 29 per cent, the Liberals on 23 and the governing Coalition Avenir Québec on 20, Vantage Canada reports.

His support is concentrated where it counts in Quebec. The pro-independence party has 37 per cent among French-speaking voters and 32 per cent among those aged 55 and over.

Two numbers under that surface decide whether he governs alone. The Conservatives have reached 34 per cent in the Quebec City region, up five points, Vantage Canada reports.

The seat arithmetic is tighter than the party gap suggests. The projection site 338Canada has the Parti Québécois on 62 seats when 64 are needed for a majority, Vantage Canada reports.

The contest for the premier’s job is narrower still. Léger has St-Pierre Plamondon preferred as premier by 26 per cent and Fréchette by 19.

The likeliest result is a government that has to ask permission. A five-way split points at a minority, Narcity reports, which in a province whose leading party wants to leave Canada is more interesting than a landslide.

The Tariff Bill Comes Due In Thirteen States

The Canadian quarrel is no longer only Canada’s problem, and American candidates have noticed. Nearly US$28 billion of American exports to Canada now carry duties of up to 50 per cent, Stateline reports.

Stateline is a non-profit news service covering the American states. Washington put 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian goods in August, and Ottawa matched them from 9 September.

Stateline reports that Ohio is hit hardest by the Canadian countermeasures. It sends US$17.5 billion of exports to Canada, about a third of everything it sells abroad, and it has the tightest Senate election of the lot.

Its Senate contest is between the Republican Jon Husted and the former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown. The pattern repeats wherever the border is close.

Two more Senate races sit on the same fault line. Michigan has the Republican Mike Rogers against the Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, and Maine the Republican Susan Collins against the Democrat Troy Jackson, ABC News reports.

The dependence runs deeper than the duties do. Canada is the largest foreign buyer of exports from 26 American states and the largest source of imports for 22 of them, ABC News reports.

Kansas has competitive races for governor and for the Senate. It also hosts the American headquarters of Bombardier, the Canadian aircraft maker, in Wichita, Stateline reports.

Forecasters have named the most exposed places. Oxford Economics, a British forecasting firm, lists North Dakota, Montana, Michigan, Illinois and Vermont as the states most vulnerable.

A conservative Washington outlet counted the same problem and got thirteen. The Washington Examiner published a list on 11 September of the border states it judged particularly hard hit.

Its thirteen were Alaska, Idaho, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, Montana, New Hampshire, New York, North Dakota, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Vermont and Washington. The most pointed objection is coming from the President’s own party.

Susan Collins, the Republican senator for Maine, is fighting a close re-election. She said “Canada is not China. It is not an adversarial nation”, Stateline reports.

She has also put the complaint in commercial terms. Collins said the stop-start talks “lead to higher costs, risk, and uncertainty for Maine businesses”, ABC News reports.

The head of a beekeeping business on the Maine coast made the same point more warmly. Garret Denniston said “We thank Canadian tourists every time we see them,” ABC News reports.

Michigan’s car industry is watching a threat rather than a tariff. Trump has threatened to raise duties on cars from 25 per cent to 50 per cent from January, and Glenn Stevens of the industry group MichAuto called that prospect “absolutely untenable”, ABC News reports.

The President’s own framing is about who pays for what. Trump said of Canada that “They don’t pay for anything, and they want to be treated like a state, but they’re not a state,” Stateline reports.

Ottawa is explicit that the pain is the point. Canada’s industry minister, Mélanie Joly, said “We’re being wise and strategic to put political pressure,” Stateline reports.

The quietest measure of the quarrel is the one nobody legislated. Canadians made 25 per cent fewer return crossings of the border in 2025 than in 2024, PBS News reports, citing Statistics Canada.

Two big holiday states felt it unevenly. Canadian visits to Florida fell 7 per cent and to California 20 per cent, and air travel to the United States was below its year-earlier level in every month to June 2026.

American tourism boards would like that reversed, and are finding it hard work. Josh Loewen, a marketing executive in Vancouver, said of their campaigns that “It’s such a big ask right now. It’s just a wasted effort,” PBS News reports.

One economist offered the reason the anger is so local. Tyler Schipper, an economist at the University of St Thomas, said that far to the north the border is “an arbitrary line in the dirt”, ABC News reports.

The steadying fact is that the quarrel is still narrow in the customs data. Tariffs currently touch about 6 per cent of American imports from Canada and 5 per cent of Canadian imports from the United States, ABC News reports.

No new Canada-United States talks had been announced by 11.35 UTC on Saturday. The quarrel is therefore running on into an American election campaign with nothing scheduled to end it.

That is the awkward shape of the autumn for both countries. The households whose gloom the University of Michigan measured on Friday are also voters in states where the quarrel is priced into the shops.

What This Means From Latin America

The figure to carry away from this week is a mood, not a market. A North American household that has stopped expecting improvement buys fewer Brazilian aircraft parts and fewer Colombian flowers.

The cost of money in the region is moving the other way from the American one. Brazil cut its Selic rate (the benchmark the Central Bank of Brazil sets for the whole economy) to 13.75 per cent on 16 September.

American borrowing went the other way in the same month. Ten-year Treasury debt ended the week at 5.17 per cent against 5.01 per cent a week earlier.

Currencies took the harder half of the week, and not where the headlines were. Mexico held its main rate at 6.50 per cent on 24 September and still watched the peso fall 3.03 per cent over the week.

That was the sharpest move of any major currency. The real ended at 5.19910 to the dollar on Brazil’s own closing rate for 25 September, 0.81 per cent weaker on the week.

The worst-performing currency of the week is not a major at all. Colombia’s official rate for 26 to 28 September is 3,306.86 pesos to the dollar, 3.57 per cent weaker in a week.

That has happened with the benchmark rate held at 12.00 per cent since 31 July. For oil exporters the shape of the market matters more than its level.

November Brent settled at US$104.32 a barrel on Friday and stood US$6.88 above the December contract. That is the widest that gap has been all week, which means buyers are paying a premium for cargoes now.

The political lesson is a familiar one, seen from the other side. Readers who have watched their own courts referee their own elections will recognise a country where the electoral machinery, not the legislature, is doing the arguing.

What We Are Watching

The storm at its peak — Saturday 26 September. The heaviest rain and the highest tides fall on Saturday, with the full moon lifting each tide and water up to three feet above normal.

The heaviest rain and the highest tides fall on Saturday, with the full moon lifting each tide and water up to three feet above normal. Quebec’s advance polls — 27 and 28 September. Advance voting opens on Sunday 27 September and runs to 28 September, from 9.30 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time in 127 constituencies.

Advance voting opens on Sunday 27 September and runs to 28 September, from 9.30 a.m. to 8 p.m. local time in 127 constituencies. Quebec’s general election — 5 October. Léger has the Parti Québécois on 29 per cent, and 338Canada projects it 62 seats, two short of a majority.

Léger has the Parti Québécois on 29 per cent, and 338Canada projects it 62 seats, two short of a majority. American spending and growth figures — early next week. Three forecasting calendars put the personal spending and final growth figures on different days, so the week is safer than the day.

Three forecasting calendars put the personal spending and final growth figures on different days, so the week is safer than the day. American payroll figures — Friday 2 October. All three calendars agree on the date, with an expectation of 100,000 jobs, and it is the one date nobody disputes.

All three calendars agree on the date, with an expectation of 100,000 jobs, and it is the one date nobody disputes. British Columbia’s municipal elections — 17 October. Vancouver’s mayor has objected that they fall a week before the provincial vote, so the province goes to the polls twice in eight days.

Vancouver’s mayor has objected that they fall a week before the provincial vote, so the province goes to the polls twice in eight days. British Columbia’s provincial election — 24 October. David Eby is running against Washington with a one-seat majority, against a Conservative opposition down from 44 seats to 24 and led on an interim basis.

David Eby is running against Washington with a one-seat majority, against a Conservative opposition down from 44 seats to 24 and led on an interim basis. The referendum on Missouri’s map — 3 November. Proposition A asks Missouri voters to reject the 2025 congressional map outright, after the court ruled that the 2022 map governs this election.

Proposition A asks Missouri voters to reject the 2025 congressional map outright, after the court ruled that the 2022 map governs this election. The American midterm elections — 3 November. Early in-person voting opened in Virginia on 18 September, and about one in ten Americans votes in a new congressional district.

Early in-person voting opened in Virginia on 18 September, and about one in ten Americans votes in a new congressional district. The appeal over the citizenship database — no date set. Friday’s order lets the rebuilt system be used only while the case is heard, so its future is unresolved.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the SAVE system, and what did the Supreme Court actually allow?

It is a federal database run by the Department of Homeland Security. Its name is the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements system. It was built in 1986 to check whether people applying for welfare benefits were entitled to them. In May 2025 the department rebuilt it to carry Social Security records and to answer questions about many people at once. The purpose was to let states test their voter lists for non-citizens. A federal district judge, Sparkle Sooknanan, struck that rebuild down in June for breaking three federal statutes. On 25 September the Supreme Court set her ruling aside by six votes to three while the appeal is heard, Townhall reports. What changed in practice is volume, because states may now search in batches rather than one name at a time. What has not changed is the law forbidding large removals from the rolls within 90 days of a federal election, so the effect on 3 November is limited, PBS News reports.

Why did the same court block Missouri’s new map on the same day?

Because the two cases turned on different questions. The Missouri fight was about state law, not federal rights. Republican legislators drew a new congressional map in 2025 to convert a Kansas City seat held by a Democrat. Opponents collected enough signatures to force a referendum on it. The Missouri Supreme Court held on 3 September that the petition was valid and that the map had therefore never taken effect. The federal courts then disagreed with one another for three weeks. On 25 September the Supreme Court settled it, writing that the 2022 map must be used in this election. The Missouri Independent records the decision as unanimous. Governor Mike Kehoe called it disappointing, noting that the state will hold its general election on a different map from its primary. Voters still get the last word on 3 November, when Proposition A asks them to reject the 2025 map.

Why is British Columbia holding an election two years early?

Because its premier has decided that the American quarrel is a mandate question. David Eby’s New Democrats already held a majority, so nothing forced the vote. He called it on 22 September for 24 October. Donald Trump was attacking the province’s workers and threatening its sovereignty, he said, Global News reports. The timing also finds his opponents at their weakest. The British Columbia Conservatives have gone from 44 seats to 24 since the last election, and their leader resigned days before the call, The Tyee reports. The province’s books give both sides an argument. Its deficit for this year is now put at C$13.8 billion (about US$9.8 billion). Its exports to the United States are down 6.2 per cent, and it has lost 16,400 jobs this year, Victoria News reports. The opposition replies that the vote itself costs between C$83 million and C$84 million (about US$59 million).

How bad is the American consumer mood, and what does the figure measure?

The University of Michigan has asked American households the same questions about their finances since the 1940s. The result is the closest thing there is to a national thermometer. Its final reading for September, published on 25 September, was 48.1. That is against 51.7 in August and 12.7 per cent below September 2025. Advisor Perspectives notes that this sits below the first percentile of the whole series. It is also below the level at which each of the six American recessions since 1978 began. The survey’s director, Joanne Hsu, said sentiment had reached “the lowest reading in four months and down 15% from January 2026.” The striking part is the agreement. Breitbart puts Republicans at 77.2, Democrats at 35.6 and independents at 47.7, all three lower than in August. Households expect prices to rise 4.6 per cent over the next year, up from 4.0 per cent.

Asia Intelligence Dossier — Saturday, 26 September 2026 · Web edition Take it with you. The full dossier is published on the web. Read the web dossier → · Open the dossier page →

Pakistan — Worn down rather than frightened, paying for a barricaded capital and then being told the march has moved. Nepal — Unembarrassed about asking, putting its case to the world while the roads into its own capital are shut. Australia — Resigned rather than angry, waiting on a decision its own lenders have already agreed about. Bangladesh — Jumpy about a birthday, as a banned party appears on a Dhaka street for a few minutes at a time. India — Watching a deadline expire that the man it was set for has not acknowledged.

Asia spent the last days of September waiting rather than acting, and the waiting is the temperament. Islamabad was sealed against a march its organisers then put off, Dhaka policed a procession that lasted minutes, and Delhi let an ultimatum run out.

The register in these capitals is tired competence, not alarm. Officials are renting containers, clearing mud from highways, counting detainees and writing letters to opposition leaders, with the manner of people who expect to do all of it again next week.

Pakistan is the clearest case of expense without event. Its capital has been ringed with rented containers at a cost of Rs46.5 million a day in Pakistani rupees (about US$168,000), and the party whose march justified them moved the date to 4 October.

Nepal did its asking in New York. Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the United Nations on Thursday that his country contributes less than 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse-gas emissions, and asked for grants rather than loans.

Australia is the calmest and the most fatalistic. All four of its largest banks expect borrowing to be made dearer on Tuesday, and household spending grew by 0.1 per cent in August on the Commonwealth Bank’s own measure.

Dhaka’s unease is older than any of this. A party barred from political activity marched briefly on a Dhanmondi street on Saturday for the birthday of the leader it lost in 2024, and two crude bombs went off beside it.

Key Facts — Islamabad’s container bill. Rented containers sealing Pakistan’s capital cost Rs46.5 million a day (about US$168,000), or Rs325.5 million (about US$1.18 million) a week, Dawn reported on 26 September. — Pakistan’s petrol price. Petrol rose Rs2.02 to Rs391.30 a litre (about US$1.41) for 26 to 28 September, while high-speed diesel fell Rs3.59 to Rs408.53 (about US$1.47). — What Shah told the Assembly. Nepal’s prime minister said on 24 September that August’s Bhotekoshi-Trishuli floods had left at least 1,400 confirmed dead and more than 6,000 missing. — Nepal’s Gulf job permits. New labour approvals for Gulf jobs fell 52.12 per cent year on year, from 228,165 to 109,249, by mid-September, the Kathmandu Post reported on 26 September. — Australia’s expected rate rise. All four of Australia’s largest banks expect the Reserve Bank to raise its cash rate from 4.35 per cent to 4.60 per cent on 29 September. — Dhaka’s Saturday blasts. Two crude bombs went off beside a banned Awami League procession in Dhanmondi on 26 September, with three people detained on one account and four on another. — India’s election chief. A satirical youth party’s deadline for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to resign expired on 26 September with no resignation reported.

Islamabad Pays For A March That Was Called Off

Pakistan’s temperament this weekend is exhausted rather than tense. The state spent a fortnight fortifying its capital against a protest, and on Friday the protest was moved a week to the right.

The postponement came from a provincial capital, not from the party’s founder. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa’s chief minister, Sohail Afridi, said the party’s political committee had “unanimously agreed” to put the long march off, Dawn, a liberal Karachi daily, reported.

The party says the obstacles will not stop it. Mr Afridi told the same press conference “Put spikes on the roads, place containers or even fire bullets, we will come out”, The Nation, a conservative Lahore daily, reported.

He also read the barricades as a design. Mr Afridi asked whether a deliberate effort was under way to disconnect his province from the rest of the country.

Its account of the state’s preparations is more specific than the federal one. The same paper reported 35,000 police deployed against the march, routes sealed between Attock and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, metal spikes laid on provincial roads and provincial ministers and assembly members detained.

The new date is 4 October and the starting point is Peshawar. Mr Afridi described the aim as “the supremacy of the Constitution, restoration of the independent judiciary, media freedom and Haqiqi Azadi”, an Urdu phrase meaning real freedom, as the same paper reported it.

For a reader with no background, this is a party locked out of the centre. Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf governs Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, the province on the Afghan border, and its founder, the former prime minister Imran Khan, is in prison.

The scale of the preparation was published before it was needed. More than 43,000 police were assigned across the Rawalpindi division and Islamabad had 110,000 tear-gas shells ready, the Express Tribune, a centrist Karachi English-language daily, reported on 24 September.

The cost of the barricades is the figure the newspapers are now counting. Dawn reported on 26 September that 1,550 rented containers seal the capital at Rs46.5 million a day (about US$168,000), or Rs325.5 million (about US$1.18 million) over a week.

The transporters, organised as the All Pakistan Goods Alliance, are not doing it as a favour. It first asked Rs40,000 a day (about US$144) for a twelve-metre container and Rs20,000 (about US$72) for a shorter one, and now asks Rs30,000 (about US$108) for either, Dawn reported.

Feeding the police is a separate bill. The same account put three meals a day for 2,000 Sindh officers at Rs1.2 million (about US$4,300) and for 16,000 Punjab officers at Rs9.6 million (about US$34,700).

The government’s answer is that the province, not the capital, is the problem. The information minister, Attaullah Tarar, accused the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa administration of facilitating terrorism and put this year’s attacks in the province at 2,456, with 472 security personnel killed, Dawn reported.

The case against the fortification is made outside party politics. The Human Rights Commission of Pakistan, an independent watchdog, said reports indicated scores of workers, including women, had been arbitrarily detained, Dawn reported.

Its point was addressed to the state rather than to the party. The commission said it was incumbent on the state to uphold the right to peaceful assembly for all citizens.

A quieter negotiation runs underneath the barricades. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has invited the opposition leader, Mahmood Khan Achakzai, for direct talks, and a person close to him told Dawn that nothing had come back.

What the talks are formally about is an overdue appointment. Sikandar Sultan Raja remains chief election commissioner although his five-year term expired on 26 January 2025, and he holds over until a successor is confirmed, Dawn reported.

That consultation has not happened. No reply from Mr Achakzai had been reported by 11.25 UTC on 26 September.

The fuel price arrived in the middle of all this. Petrol rose Rs2.02 (about US$0.01) to Rs391.30 a litre (about US$1.41) for 26 to 28 September, while high-speed diesel, the grade used by lorries and buses, fell Rs3.59 (about US$0.01) to Rs408.53 (about US$1.47).

Two papers carried the same figures. The Pakistan Observer and The Nation, a conservative Lahore daily, both reported them.

One of the two marches on the capital was put off without a new date at all. Kissan Ittehad, a farmers’ alliance, postponed its own Islamabad march after assurances from the Balochistan government, Dawn reported on 26 September.

Nepal Asks The World For Grants, Not Loans

Nepal’s mood is unembarrassed. Its government is asking the rest of the world for money in public, without the apologetic tone smaller states often use, and doing it while the highways into its own capital are shut.

The asking was done in New York on Thursday evening. Balendra Shah spoke for about a quarter of an hour to the 81st United Nations General Assembly on 24 September, the Kathmandu Post, a Kathmandu English-language daily, reported.

The hour explains a common error about the date. It was about five in the morning in Kathmandu when he reached the rostrum, which was still Thursday evening in New York, the same paper noted.

He is new to the job. He became prime minister on 27 March, after his Rastriya Swatantra Party won this year’s general election.

He opened on a disaster rather than on a grievance. The text of the address, published by the United Nations Development Programme, reads: “The Bhotekoshi-Trishuli disaster was not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world.”

The toll he cited is the largest single figure in this brief. The same text gives “at least 1400 confirmed deaths and over 6,000 people still missing” after the August floods on the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers, which run from the Chinese border towards India.

The count has moved since he spoke. The Indian daily Business Standard reported on 26 September that the confirmed dead had risen to 1,453, with more than 5,200 still missing.

His figures were about scale rather than blame. Nepal contributes less than 0.1 per cent of global greenhouse-gas emissions, he said, and rapid assessments put physical recovery needs at about a tenth of everything the country produces in a year.

The proposal he brought was regional and awkward. He asked for a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism “led by Nepal, India and China”, to share satellite data and watch dangerous glacial lakes, the Business Standard, an Indian financial daily, reported.

For a reader in São Paulo, the awkwardness is the point. Nepal is a landlocked country of about thirty million people wedged between the two most populous states on earth, and it is asking them to cooperate over the mountains all three share.

Neither neighbour has said yes. No public response from the Indian or Chinese governments had been reported by 11.25 UTC on 26 September.

The foreign coverage was not all admiring, on the Kathmandu Post’s own survey of it. That survey records the New York Times, a liberal American daily, leading on the dark sunglasses he wears in public rather than on his argument.

The same survey splits the rest by what they chose. It has the Guardian, a left-leaning British daily, taking the climate-justice case, Deutsche Welle, Germany’s state international broadcaster, leading on grants rather than debt, and Chinese state outlets carrying no separate account at all.

His own version of the injustice was about logistics. The published text reads: “Inter-continental missiles arrive on time. Rifles and ammunition cross borders, clear every bottleneck, meet each deadline. But a peasant in Nepal cannot procure his fertilizer or fuel at market price at a time of need.”

The other half of Nepal’s story is a job market closing abroad. New labour approvals for Gulf countries fell 52.12 per cent year on year by mid-September, from 228,165 to 109,249, the Kathmandu Post reported on 26 September.

The war it is measured from began in late winter. The United States and Israel started striking Iran on 28 February, the same paper notes, and the Gulf economies that employ Nepalis have been contracting since.

The falls are steep almost everywhere at once. Recruitment is down 59.05 per cent to the United Arab Emirates, 57.02 per cent to Saudi Arabia and 42.93 per cent to Kuwait, while Oman is up 24.33 per cent.

Two more Gulf states sit in between. Recruitment of Nepali workers is down 45.49 per cent to Bahrain and 35.08 per cent to Qatar on the same comparison.

This matters because there is little else earning foreign money. Nepal took in Rs2.363 trillion in Nepali rupees (about US$15.4 billion) in remittances in the 2025-26 financial year, and 40 to 45 per cent of that came from the Gulf, the same paper reported.

Workers put it in flatter language than ministers do. Arun Rai, a hotel worker from Dharan in the east who has not been told he is dismissed and has no work either, said his employer “reduced its staff to just 20 percent”.

Another gave the shorter version. Shankar Lal Shrestha, from Pokhara in central Nepal, said: “There are simply no jobs”.

The government’s answer is domestic. Mira Acharya, a spokeswoman for the labour ministry, said: “The government has prioritised promoting employment at home”, against the roughly 500,000 young Nepalis the World Bank counts entering the labour market every year.

Organised labour does not think that is ready. Binod Shrestha, who leads the Joint Trade Union Coordination Centre, said: “Workers returning from abroad have no reliable way to have their skills assessed”.

What steadies the picture is that the money has not stopped. Guru Prasad Paudel, a spokesman for Nepal Rastra Bank, the central bank, said: “If fewer workers are leaving now, the impact will not be felt immediately”.

The weather is the problem of the hour. Three days of rain closed sections of the Prithvi and BP highways and the Nagdhunga-Mugling road into Kathmandu, the Kathmandu Post reported on 26 September.

The mountains were closed too. Manang district banned high-altitude trekking from Friday to Sunday.

One search ended well. Six shepherds reported missing in Jumla in the west were found safe on Friday.

Higher up it was snow rather than rain. The mountaineer Mingma G Sherpa put the fall around Gokyo, in the Everest region, at three to three and a half feet, about a metre.

One piece of infrastructure did open this week. Flydubai’s first Pokhara service landed on Wednesday, at an airport that cost about US$216 million and is still arguing about its debts.

The passengers were mostly Gulf returnees. Sita Gharti, home from Dubai, told the Kathmandu Post: “I am very happy that I landed in Pokhara directly on the very first flight”.

Australia Braces For A Rise And Argues About The Next One

Australia’s temperament is resignation rather than anger. Its central bank is widely expected to make borrowing dearer on Tuesday, and the argument is no longer about that but about what follows it.

The expectation is unanimous among the people who lend the money. All four of Australia’s largest banks expect the Reserve Bank to lift its cash rate from 4.35 per cent to 4.60 per cent on 29 September, the market site investinglive.com reported on 21 September.

For a foreign reader this is a reversal, not a continuation. The cash rate is the price the central bank sets for overnight money between banks, and it was being cut last year.

The turn came this year. Three rises have already been delivered in 2026, the Australian site MacroBusiness reported on 22 September.

The governor has been unusually plain about what she wants. Michele Bullock said at a Committee for Economic Development of Australia event in Sydney on Tuesday that unemployment between 4.5 and 5 per cent would probably take enough heat out of the labour market.

That is a striking thing for a central bank to say aloud. The Australian Broadcasting Corporation, the public broadcaster, reported the Sydney event on 22 September, and said she was echoing what she had told a federal parliamentary hearing the previous Friday.

The number she named has already arrived. Unemployment rose to 4.6 per cent in August on figures released on Thursday 24 September, the highest in five years, the market site investinglive.com reported.

Her argument at the Sydney event was about imported prices. She said global supply shocks must not be allowed to become embedded in Australian prices, the business site Proactive Investors reported.

Her deputy had framed the same thing as a return to normal at the parliamentary hearing on 18 September. Andrew Hauser told it: “Interest rates were never going to be zero or near zero for a long while”.

He then put the open question. He asked whether borrowers had “adjusted to that new reality”.

The disagreement is about November and beyond. Of 34 economists in a Reuters poll, 33 expected Tuesday’s rise, but 26 of 31 expected the rate to stay at 4.60 per cent to the end of December, investinglive.com reported on 24 September.

The banks are not of one mind either. Only ANZ forecasts a further rise in November, with the Commonwealth Bank and Westpac treating it as a risk rather than a call.

One outside economist puts the bank’s motive bluntly. Paul Bloxham, chief economist for Australia and New Zealand at HSBC, said the Reserve Bank “is growing impatient with above-target inflation”.

Westpac reads the governor as having cleared her own condition. Its chief economist, Luci Ellis, said “the Governor’s comments met the condition the Board had set in August for further action”.

A right-of-centre reading of the same week came to the same forecast. The Nightly, an Australian daily owned by Seven West Media, headlined its 24 September report that a rate rise was tipped despite unemployment at a five-year high.

The evidence that borrowers have not adjusted is in the spending. Household spending rose 0.1 per cent in August on the Commonwealth Bank’s own measure after 0.6 per cent in July, and annual growth slowed to 4.7 per cent from 5.2 per cent, MacroBusiness reported.

Housing is where the pressure shows, and the bank is calm about it. Its assistant governor for the financial system, Brad Jones, said house prices had run up further in Australia than in comparable economies.

He then gave the falls since. Mr Jones said “we’ve seen 5 per cent to 6 per cent declines in Sydney and Melbourne, 1 per cent to 2 per cent in the other states”.

He did not think much of them. Mr Jones said the falls had “not been overly material”.

The governor gave the reason for that calm. Ms Bullock said “housing prices are still around 50 per cent higher than they were in early 2020”, and the broadcaster summed the bank up as sanguine about the downturn.

The social picture underneath is a long grind rather than an emergency. The Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia survey has followed more than 17,000 people for the Melbourne Institute since 2001, the broadcaster reported on 24 September.

Its reading on young adults is a plateau, not a jump. The share of 18 to 21-year-olds living with their parents stands at 85 per cent, and the broadcaster notes that most of that growth happened by the mid-2010s.

Not everything in that survey points downwards. The share of working-age Australians on government benefits fell from 24 per cent in 2001 to 13 per cent in 2024.

What could unsettle the whole calculation is a word the governor will not use with confidence. Asked about the worldwide enthusiasm for artificial intelligence, Ms Bullock said “it might not be a bubble, but it might be”, and that it was a risk the bank was watching.

The next figure lands the day after the decision. Australian consumer price data are expected on 30 September, which is the sort of sequencing that makes a central bank’s life harder rather than easier.

Sydney. All four of Australia’s big banks expect the Reserve Bank to raise its rate again on Tuesday, days after unemployment reached the level the governor said would take the heat out of the labour market.

A Banned Party Marches For A Birthday In Dhaka

Bangladesh is jumpy in a very particular way. The party that governed it for fifteen years is barred from political activity, and it keeps reappearing on the street for a few minutes at a time.

Saturday’s appearance was timed to a birthday. Awami League activists held what Bangladeshi papers call a flash procession on Road 27 in Dhanmondi, a central Dhaka district.

The date was the point. The procession was held to mark the birthday of Sheikh Hasina, the prime minister ousted in 2024, which falls on 28 September.

The marchers chanted the party’s own slogan and then bombs went off. They shouted “Joy Bangla”, meaning victory to Bengal, as they moved along Road 27, bdnews24.com, a Dhaka news site, reported.

Three accounts of the same few minutes do not agree. The Business Standard, a Dhaka business daily, reported two blasts in front of a Meena Bazar store and three people detained, while bdnews24.com reported four crude bombs and three detained.

The Daily Star’s count is higher again. That paper, a Dhaka English-language daily, reported four detained in front of a Bata showroom, and it alone attributes the procession to the party’s Mohammadpur unit.

The differences have not been reconciled. All three name the same officer, Dhanmondi police station’s Muhammad Imdadul Islam, who told bdnews24.com: “A group of people gathered to hold a procession and police dispersed them”.

He gave the next step in the same words. The officer said his men were “checking the identities and backgrounds of the three detainees before taking the necessary legal action”, and the Business Standard alone reports an investigation into the blasts.

For a reader with no background, the ban is the thing to understand. Sheikh Hasina left the country in August 2024 after a student revolt, her party’s activities were later prohibited, and she has since spoken to the press from Delhi.

The country now has an elected government of the other side. Tarique Rahman of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party was sworn in as prime minister on 17 February after this year’s general election, Al Jazeera, a Qatari state-funded international broadcaster, reported at the time.

The sharpest complaint comes from the Islamist opposition, which attacks both sides at once. Mia Golam Porwar, secretary general of Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami, asked how a banned party could march in Gulshan and Dhanmondi and across the districts at all, the Daily Star reported on 25 September.

His conclusion was about complicity. Mr Porwar said “It cannot be that the government, civil administration and intelligence agencies knew nothing about it”, and spoke of “pro-fascist elements” in the administration, the same paper reported on 26 September.

He then placed the danger abroad. Mr Porwar called Indian support for Sheikh Hasina, who is in Delhi, unethical and a threat to Bangladesh.

Everything else, on his account, is calm. He said: “Apart from that, we do not see any internal security threat in the country”.

The same remarks turn on the governing party too. Mr Porwar said “Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami is not ungrateful; BNP is ungrateful”, accused it of corruption beyond all previous records, and said the opposition’s 38 written proposals on the fuel crisis had been rejected.

The governing party’s answer is in what its police do rather than in what it says. Officers broke up the procession within minutes and detained those they caught, and that action is so far the only answer given to the charge that it is permitting them.

Its words have not followed. No response from the Bangladesh Nationalist Party or the home ministry to Mr Porwar’s allegation had been reported by 11.25 UTC on 26 September.

What steadies the picture is the scale of these events. The processions last minutes and end in detentions rather than in confrontation, although an earlier one in Gulshan on 11 September produced 179 arrests, bdnews24.com reported.

A larger daily emergency runs alongside the politics. Dengue killed two more people and put 955 into hospital in twenty-four hours, the Daily Star reported on 25 September.

India’s Election Chief Lets The Clock Run Out

India’s argument about its voter lists has hardened into a test of nerve. A satirical youth party gave the chief election commissioner until Saturday to resign, and Saturday arrived without a resignation.

The party is younger than the row it has joined, and its name is an insult it kept. The Cockroach Janta Party was born on social media in May after India’s chief justice compared unemployed young Indians to “cockroaches” and “parasites”, Al Jazeera reported on 25 September.

It has already removed a minister. Its protests forced out Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s education minister in July over leaked examination papers, the same broadcaster reported.

Its founder set the terms in public. Abhijeet Dipke wrote: “If Gyanesh Kumar does not resign by tomorrow, CJP will begin its nationwide protest from Mumbai on 2 October”, and added: “This Gandhi Jayanti let’s pledge to save democracy.”

The trigger was a newspaper report rather than an official finding. The Indian Express, a centrist Delhi daily, reported that two of the three election commissioners had raised questions with Mr Kumar at least fourteen times in ten months about the revision of electoral rolls.

The commission rejects that reading of its own paperwork. It said “differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution” and that all its actions had been lawful, Al Jazeera reported.

Its fuller position is reported rather than quoted. The News Minute, a southern Indian news site, records the commission saying that differing views, operational queries and administrative suggestions are part of the normal functioning of a multi-member constitutional body.

The governing party rejects the charge outright. Its spokesman Sambit Patra said: “Neither the Election Commission of India nor any constitutional body in India is under dictatorial rule”, Al Jazeera reported.

The opposition spent Friday on the street instead of in parliament. Congress workers demonstrated in thirteen states and territories including Delhi, Bihar, Assam, Punjab, West Bengal and Odisha, the News Minute reported.

The police answer was water and gas. Water cannon was turned on marchers in Patna and Chandigarh and tear gas used in Manipur, the same site reported, and the Shillong Times adds water cannon in Delhi and Kolkata.

The party’s own language has escalated with it. Congress general secretary Jairam Ramesh said the prime minister was determined to “snatch it away through underhand means”, meaning the youth vote.

Its media head went further on the process. Pawan Khera called the roll revision “null and void”.

The detentions reached senior figures. Assam’s Congress president, Gaurav Gogoi, was detained during a protest, ANI, an Indian news agency seen as close to the governing party, reported on 25 September.

Delhi’s designated protest ground took the rest. At Jantar Mantar the activist Yogendra Yadav and Dipankar Bhattacharya, who leads the Communist Party of India (Marxist-Leninist) Liberation, were among those detained, the Shillong Times reported.

The argument has now also moved to the courts. A plea before the Supreme Court asks that decisions taken without the full commission’s concurrence be declared void and that criminal proceedings be opened, the Shillong Times reported.

The plea puts its claim in one sentence. It reads: “Divested of any statutory or constitutional immunity, the CEC remains directly accountable under the law — subject to police investigation, evidence gathering, and regular trial proceedings as an ordinary accused”.

Parliament has been asked before, and it refused. Opposition members filed removal motions against Mr Kumar in both houses in April, and the presiding officers declined to admit them, News on AIR, the state broadcaster, reported.

That route has not been abandoned. Opposition parties were drafting a further attempt in both houses as of 24 September, the New Indian Express reported, which is why the pressure has meanwhile moved to the street and the court.

Mr Kumar has not said whether he intends to stay. No statement from him had been reported by 11.25 UTC on 26 September, and the protest he was threatened with is set for 2 October, Mahatma Gandhi’s birthday.

Four Of Asia’s Trading Floors Never Opened

Asia produced no single verdict on its own week, because four of its markets never opened on Friday. Seoul, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Taipei were all shut, so there is no all-Asia reading for the last day of the week.

The holidays were not even the same holiday. The Korea Exchange closed on Thursday and Friday for Chuseok, the harvest festival, while Shanghai, Shenzhen and Taipei closed on Friday for the Mid-Autumn Festival.

Hong Kong is the exception that shows how easily this is misread. It traded a full Friday session and takes its own Mid-Autumn holiday today, Saturday.

Tokyo had the best of what did trade. The Nikkei 225 closed at 66,364.20, up 850.21 points or 1.30 per cent, and ended the week up 1,345.25 points or 2.07 per cent, the strongest weekly showing of any major index.

That winning run is shorter in days than it sounds. Tokyo was shut on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday for three separate holidays, so a five-session run of gains reaches back to 16 September rather than over five consecutive days.

Hong Kong went the other way on the same day. The Hang Seng closed at 24,510.09, down 251.04 points or 1.01 per cent, and finished the week down 0.97 per cent.

Jakarta had the poorest week in the region by a wide margin. Indonesia’s IDX Composite closed at 6,241.89, down 56.72 points or 0.90 per cent on the day and 3.09 per cent over the week.

That is the worst week of any Asian index. No European or North American index fell as far either, although Buenos Aires did, by 4.24 per cent.

That sits beside a central bank that chose not to move. Bank Indonesia held its policy rate at 5.75 per cent on 23 September for a third month, and the rupiah’s Friday reference cross was 17,913.90 to the dollar.

The rate held and the currency did the moving. Bank Indonesia has now left its rate unchanged for a third month, and the market took the strain instead.

Mumbai recovered a little of a losing week. The Sensex closed at 73,895.74, up 315.20 points or 0.43 per cent, yet finished the week down 399.22 points or 0.54 per cent, and the Nifty 50 closed at 23,140.50.

Bangkok and Manila both rose on the day and cannot be measured over the week. The SET, Thailand’s main share index, closed at 1,607.63, up 5.05 points or 0.32 per cent.

Manila did better still. The PSEi, the main index of the Manila exchange, closed at 5,825.97, up 95.95 points or 1.67 per cent, the largest one-day gain of any index named here.

The levels in circulation for Korea, the mainland and Taiwan all belong to earlier sessions. The Kospi’s last close is Wednesday 23 September at 7,080.92, the Shanghai Composite’s Thursday 24 September at 3,888.37, and the Taiwan weighted index’s Thursday 24 September at 48,024.60.

Two consequences should be said plainly. No weekly change exists for Taiwan, because there was no Friday close to measure against.

The second one arrives on Monday. Seoul’s move will be measured from Wednesday, so it may look larger than one day’s trading for that reason alone.

The mainland’s calendar is the tightest in the region. Shanghai and Shenzhen reopen on Monday and then trade only on 28, 29 and 30 September before the National Day break.

The Asian currency that moved most had no share market open behind it. On the European Central Bank’s Friday-to-Friday reference rates the South Korean won strengthened 2.38 per cent, the largest weekly gain against the dollar in these figures, while Seoul’s last share price close was Wednesday’s.

Japan is the one market here whose policy rate is rising and whose ten-year yield sits less than two points above it. Its ten-year government bond yielded 3.07 per cent on 25 September, against a policy rate of 1.25 per cent decided on 18 September.

That policy rate is the highest Japan has set in 31 years. It was lifted at the meeting of 17 and 18 September and is in force now.

India has the other extreme in this region. Its ten-year government bond yielded 7.11 per cent on 25 September, the highest of the Asian markets named here.

Elsewhere in Asian money the week was quiet. The yen stood at 157.59 to the dollar on the 25 September reference cross and the Indian rupee at 95.82, while the Bangladeshi taka’s Friday closing quote was 123.66.

What This Means From Latin America

Oil is the first line of contact and the two grades went opposite ways. November Brent, the contract that prices most of the world’s cargoes, settled on Friday at US$104.32 a barrel, up 0.43 per cent over the week.

The American grade did the opposite. November WTI settled at US$92.41, down 3.82 per cent over the week on the same contract.

The gap between the grades is what a Brazilian exporter watches. Reuters reported the divergence as hopes of a truce between Washington and Tehran pressing on the American grade while Middle Eastern supply risk held Brent above US$100.

Pakistan shows what that gap does to an importing country’s politics. Its government raised petrol by Rs2.02 to Rs391.30 a litre (about US$1.41) in the same week the American crude price fell, a combination any energy ministry that sets pump prices administratively will recognise.

Nepal’s figures read most like Central America’s. Remittances of Rs2.363 trillion in Nepali rupees (about US$15.4 billion) in a year sit against new job approvals abroad that have more than halved, the same exposure El Salvador, Honduras and Guatemala carry.

Australia’s week points the opposite way from Brazil’s. Its central bank is expected to raise the cash rate from 4.35 per cent to 4.60 per cent on Tuesday.

Brazil is going the other way. It cut the Selic (its own benchmark interest rate) by a quarter point to 13.75 per cent on 16 September.

The commodity that rose most this week was not oil. American natural gas for November finished the week up 9.75 per cent at US$3.196 per million British thermal units.

Copper also held its ground. The December contract rose 1.22 per cent over the week to US$6.6955 a pound, one of the few things to end higher.

Gold gave ground for a fourth successive fix. The London afternoon price was US$4,261.05 a troy ounce on 25 September, down 2.00 per cent over the week, which matters more to Peru and Mexico than to Brazil.
