World.title: Can this German company help end Europe's lithium dependence on China?
World.content:
Inside a production facility in Krefeld, Germany, a family-owned recycling company is recovering lithium from used batteries without relying on aggressive chemicals.

 

The process was developed by Accurec Recycling GmbH, which has specialised in battery recycling for more than three decades.

Speaking to Euronews, the company's head of development, Simon Bremer, explains how the technology works, why Europe has fallen behind in battery recycling and what needs to change in its critical raw materials policy.

From power-tool batteries to electric vehicles

Founded in 1995, Accurec has focused on battery recycling from the outset. Initially, the company specialised in nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride batteries, older rechargeable technologies that have largely been superseded by lithium-ion batteries.

Over the past 15 years, lithium-ion technology has become increasingly widespread, powering everything from smartphones and cordless power tools to electric vehicles.

Accurec has spent around a decade developing its lithium-ion battery recycling operations at its Krefeld facility, where it currently processes approximately 5,000 tonnes of batteries annually.

The company employs around 85 people and operates a second recycling plant in Mülheim an der Ruhr.

In December 2025, Accurec opened a new lithium recovery plant. © Copyright by ACCUREC-Recycling GmbH

According to Bremer, the new facility, which began operating in December 2025, can initially recover 50% of the lithium contained in the batteries it processes, meeting the recovery target set by EU legislation for 2027.

But the company is already aiming higher.

"We have been working on expanding the plant for about a month now. That means ramping up both capacity and yield so that in the first quarter of 2027 we will be able to recover 80 percent or more," Bremer said.

The expansion is already underway. Accurec is investing €5.5 million to double the operating area of its Krefeld facility, with the aim of increasing annual processing capacity to as much as 20,000 tonnes of used batteries, four times its current volume.

Europe's reliance on China for lithium

Lithium is a crucial component of rechargeable batteries, making it essential to the energy transition. It is used in electric vehicles and many energy storage systems that support wind and solar power.

However, Europe remains heavily dependent on China for processed lithium. According to Bremer, around 65% to 70% of battery-grade lithium chemicals currently come from Chinese production.

China has previously demonstrated its ability to restrict supplies of strategically important materials, including rare earths and germanium, highlighting the potential risks for European manufacturers.

Accurec hopes its new facility can help reduce that dependence. While the company does not claim its technology can solve Europe's raw materials challenges on its own, it sees domestic battery recycling as an important step towards diversifying supply and keeping valuable materials within Europe rather than exporting them.

Workers transport lithium-ion batteries in a factory in Taizhou, in the eastern Chinese province of Jiangsu. Chinatopix

The science behind water-based lithium recovery

At the heart of Accurec's recycling process, known internally as "CLIMA", is a thermal pre-treatment that makes lithium soluble in water.

First, batteries are sorted and, in the case of larger units such as electric vehicle battery packs, dismantled. They then undergo pyrolysis, a process that uses high temperatures to break down organic components.

Crucially, this treatment also changes the chemical form of the lithium, allowing it to be extracted using water rather than aggressive chemicals.

"We convert the lithium into a water-soluble form. In other words, the entire rest of the battery is insoluble in water, except for the lithium," Bremer explains.

He compares the process to making filter coffee.

"You can imagine it like making filter coffee. When you pour water over the coffee, the flavour compounds are washed out and only the grounds left in the filter remain."

A glimpse into the future of battery recycling: the new plant in Krefeld is designed to secure Europe's supply of recycled lithium. © Copyright by ACCUREC-Recycling GmbH

The process is also designed to minimise energy consumption. According to Bremer, heat generated during pyrolysis is recovered and subsequently used to recrystallise the lithium salt.

"That allows us to avoid using additional energy and thus reduce overall process costs," Bremer says.

Accurec claims its technology reduces energy consumption by almost 50% and cuts CO₂ emissions per tonne of lithium carbonate by more than 59%.

China's dominance in battery recycling

Bremer identifies a structural weakness in Europe's battery recycling industry: the lack of facilities capable of processing recovered materials into individual raw materials.

Most European recycling plants currently produce what is known as "black mass", an intermediate product containing lithium, nickel and cobalt that have yet to be separated.

With few facilities in Europe equipped to extract these materials, much of the black mass is exported to Asia for further processing.

"The actual recovery of raw materials then takes place predominantly in China, and partly in Korea," Bremer explains.

As a result, valuable materials recovered from used batteries leave Europe's recycling supply chain rather than being processed and reused within the region.

Related Germany turns on Brussels as Chinese car sales on track to exceed 1m in 2026

Another challenge, according to Bremer, is the pricing strategy of Asian buyers. He argues that they offer such high prices for European black mass that local companies struggle to establish commercially viable processing operations.

Bremer believes Asian battery manufacturers can afford to pay a premium because they generate revenue further down the supply chain, particularly from finished battery cells.

In his view, paying more for European black mass remains commercially worthwhile for these companies, while also making it harder for a competing processing industry to emerge in Europe.

Lithium is indispensable for electric vehicles because of its high energy density. Copyright Business Wire 2012.

Closing the battery recycling loop in Europe

Accurec's options for processing its recovered lithium within Europe remain limited. According to Bremer, one of the few significant potential customers is AMG Lithium in Bitterfeld, Germany, which refines lithium for battery production.

The two companies have already signed a memorandum of understanding, although technical details still need to be resolved before deliveries can begin.

"Right now it is still about ironing out the final interface issues in order to enable feed-in to that plant," Bremer says.

Until the partnership is fully operational, some of Accurec's recovered lithium is being used in other applications or marketed in Asia through partners.

The company's long-term ambition is to establish a closed European battery recycling loop, allowing lithium recovered from used batteries to be processed and reused in new batteries manufactured in Europe.

What needs to change in EU policy?

Bremer welcomes the EU's decision to classify black mass as hazardous waste from December 2025, a measure intended to tighten controls on exports.

"That is an important step and, from our point of view, absolutely the right one to say: the material has to stay in Europe," he says.

However, Bremer argues that the regulation will only be effective if customs and supervisory authorities have sufficient resources to enforce it.

He also points to the EU's mandatory recycled-content requirements for new batteries, which are due to apply from 2031.

While these rules establish minimum shares of recycled materials in battery production, they do not require manufacturers to source those materials from within Europe.

Bremer wants the EU to go a step further by introducing requirements for the use of European-sourced recycled materials.

"Alongside the recycled content, we can also talk about a European share," he says.

He points to similar requirements in other sectors, such as public procurement, where contracts can include conditions requiring a certain proportion of production to take place in Europe.

More broadly, Bremer criticises what he sees as the absence of a coordinated European strategy covering the entire battery value chain.

He cites the insolvency of battery manufacturer Northvolt as an example of the risks associated with supporting major industrial projects without developing the wider network of suppliers and customers they depend on.

In his view, Europe needs a comprehensive strategy that supports every stage of the battery supply chain rather than focusing on individual flagship projects.

World.title: Thousands of protesters take to the streets in Madrid over Ceuta migrant crisis
World.content:
Thousands of people are taking part in Madrid's second "March for Dignity" on Saturday, with protesters calling for a general election and voicing their support for Ceuta amid the autonomous city's ongoing migrant crisis.

 

The demonstration, organised by the Sociedad Civil Española with the support of the People's Party (PP) and Vox, set off shortly after 10 am from the Plaza de Cibeles and headed towards the Arco del Triunfo in Moncloa, where it is expected to end at around 13:30 pm local time.

Among those taking part was Vox leader Santiago Abascal, who insisted that migrants who arrived in Ceuta must be returned to their country of origin and launched a scathing attack on the government's handling of the crisis - which began in late July when tens of thousands of people crossed into the Spanish North African territory from Morocco.

"Ceuta remains invaded because Sánchez continues to be Morocco's servant; the migrant invasion is being encouraged," he said, referring to Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

A separate "March for Dignity," held before the mass entry of migrants at the end of July, saw tens of thousands of people come together to demand Sánchez resign and for snap elections to be held.

According to the Government Delegation, that demonstration drew around 40,000 people, while organisers put the figure as high as 120,000.

On 2 September, Ceuta's official day, thousands of people also took to the streets in cities across Spain in a demonstration organised by the Spanish Federation of Municipalities and Provinces.

The crisis continues

Almost two months after the mass influx of migrants, the situation in Ceuta remains unresolved.

Around 8,300 migrants are being housed in facilities set up in the city, with more than 4,000 people estimated to still be living on the streets.

Morocco has accused Spain of obstructing the return of migrants who remain in Ceuta.

Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares recently met with his Moroccan counterpart Nasser Bourita in New York to address the issue.

During their talks, Bourita referred to "obstacles" and "controversies" that he believes are being fuelled in part by the Spanish political class and are preventing the situation from being resolved.

In the meantime, authorities are continuing to carry out surveillance and provide assistance across the city.

On Friday, the National Police arrested three Moroccan nationals who were living in a makeshift camp on Trampolín beach for their alleged involvement in the detention of two migrant minors. The two minors were taken to Ceuta University Hospital for treatment.

That same day, 63 women who were either alone or with young children were moved to a facility set up at the Hípica, as part of an ongoing effort to relocate people still living on the streets.

Firefighters have also discovered a makeshift settlement in underground tunnels in recent days, where around 30 to 50 migrants are thought to have been staying.

On Friday, a young Moroccan man died in a camp situated on the site of a former factory near Trampolín beach. The cause of death has not yet been established.

World.title: New study reveals surprising origins of bats dating back 65 million years
World.content:
For decades, it was assumed that bats had originated in Asia, Africa or somewhere in the Americas. A new study now calls that idea into question. According to its authors, the lineage arose around 65 million years ago in Europe, from where it spread to colonise the rest of the planet. In other words, the first bat species dates back to the age of the dinosaurs.

 

The research, the most comprehensive carried out to date on this group of mammals, combines the genome sequencing of 103 species with the study of 44 fossils. The work forms part of Bat1K, an international consortium devoted to gathering genomic information on bats, and has been published in the journal "Nature" (source in Spanish). On the Spanish side, researchers from the National Museum of Natural Sciences (MNCN-CSIC) and the University of Granada have taken part.

Ismael Galván, a researcher at the MNCN, sums up the scope of the study: it is the first time that the genome of a flying mammal has been reconstructed, and this resource offers the scientific community a solid framework for investigating the genes responsible for their most distinctive traits. He explains that this line of research could eventually provide useful information for studies on ageing, immunity and resistance to disease in humans.

Professor Liliana M. Dávalos, of the University of Stony Brook, notes that the method used (jointly modelling the evolution of fossil and living species) makes it possible to do something other techniques could not: to place the oldest group of fossil bats while taking genomic data into account and thus determine when and where the group appeared. The data suggest that the first descendants of that European population dispersed into Africa, forming a Euro-African core from which bats later reached Asia, the Americas and Australia.

Bat1K project showing 21 known bat species Nature

Flight and echolocation, present from the very beginning

One of the findings highlighted by the team is that powered flight and echolocation, two features that define the biology of these animals, did not emerge at later stages of their evolution but near the very origin of the group.

The position of the fossil of the genus Vielasia, regarded as an ancestor of modern bats, on the oldest branch of the family tree reinforces that conclusion, which would help explain the evolutionary success of the lineage over 65 million years.

Michael Hiller, of the Senckenberg Institute in Frankfurt, describes the procedure followed: state-of-the-art DNA sequencing techniques combined with computational methods to generate and compare genomes, identify the genes they contain and cross-reference that information with the 44 fossils collected in different parts of the world.

Phylogenetic comparison of bat chromosomes Nature

The result, according to Professor Emma Teeling, of University College Dublin, is a robust phylogenetic tree after decades of findings that often contradicted one another.

To assemble the set of samples, the team turned to little-known species found in remote locations: the bumblebee bat from Thailand and Myanmar, one of the smallest mammals on Earth; the Madagascar sucker-footed bat, able to cling to smooth leaves thanks to small suction cups; and the lesser short-tailed bat, native to New Zealand, which uses its folded wings as if they were forelegs to move along the forest floor.

A resource with implications beyond animal biology

With more than 1,500 species distributed around the world, bats represent one fifth of all living mammals. Their role in ecosystems is significant: they pollinate plants, disperse seeds and control insect populations.

On top of that comes a feature of particular interest to biomedical research: their resistance to disease and a longevity that is striking in relation to their size.

Origins of the different bat species Nature

Professor David Ray, of Texas Tech University, stresses that the volume of data generated will allow the scientific community to track genomic variation, from changes in a single base to the absence of entire segments in one lineage that are present in another.

These differences, he notes, help to explain in part the enormous diversity of bats that exists today and the origins of their unique traits, a body of work whose relevance, he adds, goes well beyond this group of mammals.

World.title: Adieu, dear listeners!
World.content:
This week is the final Sound Kitchen program, and it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listeners Corner’s” with Paul Myers, plus a special musical choice from me to you. Just click the “Play” button above to join the feast!

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October, and today’s show is our last meal together. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 7 February: I asked you a question about the 68th annual Grammy Awards that took place on 1 February. You were to re-read our article “French DJ wins Grammy for Lady Gaga remix” and send in the answer to this question: Which six artists were given “Lifetime Achievement” awards?

The answer is, to quote our article: “On Saturday evening, Nigeria's Fela Kuti was posthumously awarded a lifetime achievement award, becoming the first African artist to receive the distinction.

The king of Afrobeat was one of several artists to receive the award, including Cher, Whitney Houston, Carlos Santana, Paul Simon and Chaka Khan.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question, suggested by RFI Listeners Club member Alan Holder from the English Isle of Wight. Alan’s question was: “What would be your ideal gift from your best friend or spouse? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Mohamed Elsayed Abd Elraheim from Elsharkya, Egypt. Mohamed Elsayed is also this week’s bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club members Hans Verner Lollike from Hedehusene, Denmark; Helmut Matt from Herbolzheim, Germany; Kashif Khalil from Faisalabad, Pakistan, and last but not least, gentle Debashis Gope from West Bengal, India.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 14 February: That week, I asked you a question about the Benin Bronzes, the trove of Nigerian sculptures and artifacts that were looted by colonial powers.

One of the most well-known organizations working for the return of these works is in Nigeria: it’s the National Commission for Museums and Monuments – the NCMM- which requested the return of bronzes from Britain that were looted from the Kingdom of Benin during the British Benin Expedition of 1897. Some of the sculptures date to the fourteenth century, but the bulk of the collection dates to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

And that week, the NCMM had a win, as my good colleague Melissa Chemam noted in her article: “Cambridge University museum set to return Benin bronzes to Nigeria”.

You were to re-read Melissa’s article and give the details of the artefacts to be returned. What did Melissa name in her article about the Benin Kingdom artworks that went home to Nigeria?

The answer is, to quote Melissa: “Among the returned bronzes that will travel in the coming months are wood and ivory sculptures, as well as commemorative heads of King Oba and Queen Mother Lyoba Idia.

The term ‘Benin bronzes’ refers to objects crafted from brass and ivory as well as bronze, which were seized during the colonial-era military expedition.”

The bonus question you answered that week was: “What do you know after all these years? What have you found are important life truths?

The winners are: Faithful RFI Listeners Club member Jayanta Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Jayanta is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club member Nasyr Muhammad from Katsina State in Nigeria, as well as RFI English listeners M. Ganesan from Goa, India, and three listeners from Bangladesh: Rafiq ul Islam from Naogaon, as well as Abdul Mannan and Mahfuza Akhter, both from Chapainawabganj.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Minor Swing” by Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grapelli, performed by the composers with Le Quintette Hot Club de France; "Water No Get Enemy" by Fela Kuti, performed by Fela Kuti and Africa ’70; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer; “L'hymne à l'amour” by Edith Piaf and Marguerite Monnot, sung by Edith Piaf, and “I Wish You Love” by Charles Trenet and Léo Chauliac, performed by Laufey with the Iceland Symphony Orchestra conducted by Hugh Brant.

With much affection from The Sound Kitchen team – Erwan Rome, Paul Myers, and yours truly, Susan Owensby - fare thee well!

World.title: Podcast: Pope in secular France, vultures and farmers, first divorce law
World.content:
With its strong commitment to secularism, France is not an obvious place for Pope Leo XIV to stage an appearance, but his visit is drawing interest from Catholics and non-Catholics alike. After nearly disappearing from France, vultures are making a comeback, but their return has created new tensions with farmers. And France's revolutionary first divorce law from 1792.

Advertising

Some 800,000 people have signed up to see Pope Leo XIV on his first official visit to France, a secular country where the Catholic faith no longer dominates. Francois Mabille, head of the Geopolitical Observatory of Religion at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs, looks at why France is of interest to the Vatican, and young people of different religions talk about what Pope Leo means to them. (Listen @0'00)

Vultures all but disappeared from France by the 1940s as people sought to eradicate the scavenger birds. A programme to reintroduce the four European vulture species to the Grands Causses plateaux in the southern Massif Central has been sucessful – so successful that some farmers say there are now too many. We visit a vulture feeding station to explore the close relationship between vultures and agriculture, and the tensions that arise with the return of wild species. (Listen @20'00)

In 1792, France introduced one of Europe’s first and most liberal divorce laws, as part of a broader revolutionary effort to enact liberté, egalité et fraternité in the family itself. (Listen @14'00)

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Pakistan: Suicide attack at police stop kills at least 11
World.content:
The blast was claimed by the Pakistani Taliban, which has stepped up attacks on Pakistani security forces in recent years.

At least 11 people were killed in a suicide bombing in northwestern Pakistan on Saturday, authorities said.

The blast happened just two days after fighting between Pakistan and Afghanistan along their southwestern border killed at least 13 members of the Afghan Taliban.

Are Pakistan and Afghanistan heading for war? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What do we know?

Police said the bomber detonated an explosives-laden vehicle at a roadside police checkpoint in Dera Ismail Khan, the country's 10th largest city.

Dera Ismail Khan sits in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, which runs along the border with Afghanistan and has been repeatedly hit by Islamist militant violence.

Around 30 others were wounded in the blast, mostly security personnel and passersby, a police official said.

Emergency teams from Rescue 1122 provided medical ​assistance to ‌the wounded and took them to the hospital, the ​service said.

Police said some of the injured were in a critical condition.

The Pakistani Taliban — Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) — an Islamist militant group that targets the Pakistani state, claimed responsibility in a statement.

Islamist attacks on the rise in Pakistan

Pakistan has experienced a surge in militant attacks in recent years.

Many of them have been claimed by the TTP and the outlawed Baloch Liberation Army, or BLA, a separatist group mainly active in neighboring Balochistan province.

The TTP is aligned with Afghanistan's Taliban, which returned to power in Afghanistan in 2021 when US and NATO troops pulled out.

How 5 years of Taliban rule have changed Afghanistan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pakistan has repeatedly accused Kabul of allowing TTP members to operate from Afghan soil and demanded firmer action to stop cross-border attacks.

The Taliban have denied allowing their territory to be used for attacks.

The rift has sparked cross-border attacks by both countries, with Pakistan carrying out deadly airstrikes it says target militants on Afghan soil.

China, Turkey, Qatar and Saudi Arabia are trying to mediate a lasting peace between the two neighbors.

World.title: China rejects 'Cold War mindset' at UN General Assembly
World.content:
Skip next section Albania's Rama tells of 'Flamingo Revolution,' warning not of a rogue AI, but one following rogue orders

Edi Rama's government was an early adopter of AI, but also had an early experience of its disruptive capabilities Image: Leonardo Munoz/AFP

Prime Minister Edi Rama told the chamber that while Albania was not a developer of "frontier models" in AI, "we are a nation that has already lived the future others are still debating," given how outside actors had tried out the technology's darker capabilites on its citizens.

Rama said he felt he owed the chamber a "simple message," if not necessarily the one most commonly discussed during the week.

"The greatest immediate danger is not that artificial intelligence will stop obeying humanity. The greatest danger is that it will obey the wrong human beings perfectly," he said.

"The public debate imagines machines that awaken, acquire ambitions and turn against their creators," Rama said. "But the systems confronting us today do not wake up with hatred in their hearts, they multiply ours. They have no ambition of their own, they serve the ambition of others. They carry no flag, but they can be deployed by a state. They tell no lie for their own benefit, but they can tell a billion lies on others' behalf."

Rama mentioned how Albania had become the first government to launch an AI minister. He said this showed his government's belief that "inside an accountable state," the technology could be used to "reduced the distance between citizens and public services."

But he said Albania had also learned how "artificial intelligence outside accountability can be used to eliminate the distance between a lie and the human mind."

He relayed the story of the so-called "Flamingo Revolution," a "fabricated narrative of an Israeli invasion of the Albanian coast."

This entirely fictional invasion "was manufactured, was personalized and delivered through voices, pages and channels citizens already trusted." Rama explained how the details of the overarching story were personalized to maximize their impact with the individuals reading them.

"Different fabriactions entered different emotional worlds, all serving the same strategic lie," he said. "The consequences were real. Citizens had their own reasons to protest — don't take me wrong. But suddenly, they started to protest also against a phantom enemy. Antisemitic tropes entered our public discourse for the first time ever."

Rama said that amid the AI disinformation drive, "fear became anger, anger became mobilization and fabrication became political reality."

"And this was not a laboratory experiment. I'm not talking to you about a science fiction movie. It was a Tuesday, in Tirana, our capital city."

Rama said it wasn't an algorithm that invented the objective, but rather a human actor. The algorithm didn't develop hatred, but "it discovered how to activate ours."

He called this particular use case "systematic fraud as a service," and warned its potential for use in scenarios like elections were just as real as in trying to amplify animosity to war in the Middle East.

World.title: German Olympic Committee names Munich as bid city choice
World.content:
Munich has been voted as the city that will bid for the Olympics in 2036, 2040 or 2044. Berlin had been in the running but withdrew on Thursday.

The German Olympic Sports Confederation (DOSB) on Saturday announced it chose Munich as Germany's entry to bid for at least the next three Olympic Summer Games.

Ahead of the vote, former Olympic champion and new Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said: "We have an international task to fulfill and must enter the race with the city or region that gives Germany the greatest chances internationally. The decision on that is made by sport, and I assume that it will make it with a great deal of responsibility."

Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier said the Olympic bid represented a huge opportunity for all of Germany to "show that we are a land of opportunity."

According to the Munich bid, all competitions would take place in Bavaria, except for the football matches which would be played in Stuttgart and the sailing competitions in the northern city of Kiel.

Berlin bowing out created two-horse race

Munich and a Cologne-led bid by the Rhine-Ruhr region were the only two in contention.

As many as 17.6 million tickets could be sold for the Games in Cologne-Rhine-Ruhr, more than ever before at a Games, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia said recently.

Munich was campaigning after two failed bids for the 2018 and 2022 Winter Games and having previously hosted the 1972 Summer Olympics.

Up until Thursday, Berlin had been among the cities in contention, but the city's mayor announced that the city would withdraw from the race.

The withdrawal comes after the socialist Left Party's victory in the German capital's elections last weekend. The party's lead candidate and potential mayor, Elif Eralp, said she did not support Berlin's bid.

Take a tour of Berlin's iconic Olympic Stadium To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sports minister has sights set on 2040

On Friday, Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said he would welcome a German Olympic bid for the 2040 Games, with it coinciding with an important historical milestone.

Sports Minister Ronald Rauhe said the city or region that gave Germany the greatest chances internationally should be voted for Image: dts-Agentur/picture alliance

"2040 will mark the 50th anniversary of reunification. Here we could send a great signal that also aligns with the values of the Olympic Games," Rauhe told German news agency dpa ahead of the deciding vote on Saturday.

"Based on my personal history, 2040 would be my favorite date. That has to do with the fact that I'm a Berlin child. As a schoolchild, I experienced what happens to people when a wall falls, when people grow together again, when two population groups that had been separated become a community again,” Rauhe said.

"Ultimately, though, one thing matters above all: bringing the Olympic and Paralympic Games back to our country. No matter when," Rauhe said.

World.title: Propaganda in Russian schools prepares students to die
World.content:
The Russian government wants children to learn about patriotism from an early age. DW spoke to students in Siberia about their views on propaganda, the war in Ukraine and their future.

Earlier this year, several schools in Novosibirsk, a city of 1.6 million in southern Siberia, received a textbook on patriotism from the authorities. According to students, with whom DW spoke to on condition of anonymity, in the book the authors urge children to prepare themselves to die for their country. Furthermore, they equate homosexuality with pedophilia and Disney cartoons with pornography, and give instructions on how women should use their "charms." Europeans are described as "thieves, murderers and liars."

The textbook, which provides "materials for spiritual, moral, and patriotic upbringing" is supposed to be used as part of "patriotism lessons" that have been on the curriculum since 2022. Though it is not included on the national list of core curriculum books, the content reflects the Kremlin's intentions to spread propaganda in educational institutions.

'Love always involves sacrifice.'

One of the main topics of the book is the war in Ukraine and the idea that dying for one's country is a blessing is repeated several times: "Love always involves sacrifice," writes one of the authors. "The sacrifice of a defender of the homeland is their life."

Elsewhere in the book, the authors make constant claims that Russia is better than Western countries. They also say that children are "mentally crippled" because of "computer games, Hollywood action films, pornography and Disney cartoons."

They argue that European nations that used to be colonial empires legitimized "murder, lies and plunder" through the conquest and subjugation of new territories. Russia, on the other hand, "never exploited its numerous peoples," they say, but merely improved their living conditions. The book makes no mention of the culture of Indigenous peoples in what is Russia today, or of any religions other than Christianity and "Slavic paganism."

This textbook is used in certain Russian schools to teach children about patriotism and other subjects Image: M. Remaevich

'More cannon fodder'

For Ilya, a 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk who has read the book and whose name has been changed, the idea of dying for his country is anathema. "It's proof that the country wants more cannon fodder," he told DW, adding that "dying for the country" actually meant dying for "the president's interests and ambitions."

He said that a few years ago, he had started watching the videos of Alexei Navalny, the Kremlin critic and opposition leader who died in jail in 2024 "more for fun than for any other reason." He said it was Navalny's 2021 investigation into Russian President Vladimir Putin's Black Sea palace that had first drawn his attention.

But it was when the authorities decided to block access to the US platforms YouTube and Discord that he began to oppose the government. He set up a VPN out of "contrariness" he said, looking for information about other opposition figures and reading the independent media. As he found out more about the cruelty and senselessness of the war, he criticized the government more strongly.

He confirmed that propaganda had become an integral part of the curriculum in the past four years. On top of the "Conversations about Important Things" that take place every Monday morning, there are now also subjects such as "Fundamentals of Homeland Security and Defense." He said that people who have taken part in the war in Ukraine are invited to lessons focusing on students' future and decisions regarding what career path to take.

Even outside of the classroom, students are encouraged to be "patriotic." Ilya said that a student had been reprimanded by the principal for wearing a sweater with a slogan written in English on it. "Young man, do you realize that your sweater has words on it in the language of unfriendly countries?" she reportedly asked him. "A call to the Federal Security Service will take care of that!"

Ilya also recalled that a school assembly held to mark May 9, which commemorates the Soviet Union's victory over Nazi Germany in 1945, the principal and her deputy had compared what is known in Russia as the "Great Patriotic War" to the current war in Ukraine. They had said that Russia would once again be steadfast and emerge victorious.

Students are taught about being a soldier and told it is an honor to die for the country Image: Konstantin Kokoshkin/Picvario/Russian Look/Global Look Press/picture alliance

'I love freedom'

Alexei (name changed), another 16-year-old student in Novosibirsk, told DW that many of his classmates avoided going to "patriotic events." He too said that the blocking of YouTube had made a difference to him. "I looked into why it was blocked," he said. "Because nothing happens by chance. And that's how my interest in politics began." That's when he realized that the authorities wanted to get rid of inconvenient citizens and suppress free speech. "I love freedom, so it was hard," he said.

Ilya thinks that most students don't take the propaganda seriously. "On the one hand, we laugh about it in class, at least my friends do," he said. "On the other, we don't care. Some simply don't listen. We're very good at being quiet and not talking much about it,"

Dima Zicer is an educator and the author of the Russian-language podcast "Love, Don't Discipline" who moved to Estonia after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. He told DW that "many students are happy to be part of a pro-Putin majority that doesn't think about things, according to the principle: 'We'll crush them all; we're stronger than everyone else. Everyone will be scared of us.'"

He said that there was no statistical data to back his argument, but he said that he had drawn his conclusions from his extensive experience working with Russian children, as well as his communication with parents. He said that these often only became aware of how serious the situation was when their children started saying things such as "We'll crush them" or "Putin is great," as well as talking about supposed Nazis and fascists in Ukraine.

Alexei and Ilya, who think differently and want the war in Ukraine to end, are worried about the unstable situation in Russia. They want to leave the country after graduating.

World.title: Paris: Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass before huge crowd
World.content:
The pope addressed around 700,000 people during a Mass at the Place de la Concorde, near the Champs-Elysees. Leo XIV is on a four-day visit to France.

Pope Leo XIV on Saturday celebrated Mass for hundreds of thousands of worshippers in central Paris.

The Vatican said some 700,000 people were in attendance for the open-air service at the Place de la Concorde, near the Champs-Elysees.

Around 600,000 people registered to attend the open-air mass with Pope Leo XIV Image: Gonzalo Fuentes/REUTERS

What do we know about the Mass?

The Mass began mid-afternoon after the pontiff traveled down the French capital's iconic avenue in his popemobile, cheered by the faithful lining the route.

News agencies described how the crowd stretched ‌2.2 kilometers(1.4 miles) across ⁠central ⁠Paris, with many waving white and yellow flags and pressing against security barriers for a glimpse of the pontiff.

At the Mass site, a huge white canopy was erected to serve as a makeshift altar for Leo to deliver his service.

Dozens of screens were installed to allow worshippers to follow the proceedings.

In his homily, Leo asked worshippers not to keep their faith to themselves

"Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied," he said. "From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France."

Crowds began queuing hours before the service began, with many parents and children among those hoping to catch a glimpse of the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.

"It's a big event; we've come to share the Christian fervour," teacher Sylvie Leclerc told the AFP news agency.

"You don't hear much from us Catholics, but now we're going to make some noise! But to proclaim love, peace, joy," she added.

Earlier on Saturday, the pope visited a social center and later met with adults who had recently been baptized.

People began gathering hours before the start of the mass in central Paris Image: Gonzalo Fuentes/REUTERS

Leo's first trip to France as pope

Pope Leo is on a four-day visit to France that will see him travel to Lourdes and Metz, as well as Paris. It's his first visit to France since becoming pope last year.

On Friday, around 300,000 people gathered to see the pontiff as he waved from his popemobile on the way to the restored Notre Dame Cathedral, which had to be restored after a devastating fire in 2019.

French President Emmanuel Macron did not appear at the Mass. However, far-right leader Marine Le Pen and centrist Edouard Philippe have confirmed their attendance.

World.title: South Korea's gender pay gap grows as women get older
World.content:
A new report shows how in South Korea, women on average earn less and have fewer employment opportunities throughout their lives.

At 27, a woman in South Korea earns 8% less than male peers. By her late 50s, she earns 50% less. This is according to government wage data published in a recent Human Rights Watch (HRW) report.

South Korea is a global technology and industrial powerhouse, but its gender pay gap has remained the highest in the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) since comparable records began in 1992.

"The gender division of labor inside the home leads directly to a gender division of labor in the labor market," Min Hee Kim, a Korean activist for women labor struggles, told DW.

The problem, she argues, is not simply that women are paid less than men. As women age, the kinds of work available to them narrows and the consequences of lower pay, career breaks and precarious jobs accumulate.

For the report , "Too Old and a Woman," HRW interviewed 41 South Korean women aged 28 to 87 about their working lives.

Structural barriers to women's careers

Discrimination has changed form rather than disappeared, Kim said. Until the 1980s, it was legal for employers to fire women simply for getting married, a practice known as "marriage-based dismissal," where employers assumed a married woman would soon leave to raise children anyway.

Today, "it is difficult to openly say, 'We won't hire you because you're a woman,'" Kim added. But caregiving responsibilities still fall on women, pushing them into lower-paid jobs when they try to return to work.

According to the HRW report, women's university attainment has passed men's since the 1980s. Higher education would suggest equal opportunity after graduation, but the job market says otherwise.

One year after graduating, women already earn 22% less than men, according to a 2024 study.

Many women told HRW that after leaving work for marriage or children, chances of returning to the workforce were limited to a handful of jobs such as call centers, cleaning or caregiving.

Women who opt to focus on their career told HRW they hit a glass ceiling at work. Women held 18% of manager jobs in 2024, and only five of 38 senior civil servants were women.

Brains, beauty and barriers: the global job market To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Wages peak and drop off

Women's wages peak in their late 30s and then steadily decline, according to Labor Ministry survey data cited by HRW.

South Korea's Gender Ministry told HRW that career interruptions, along with occupational segregation and discrimination within organizations, drive the gap.

J. Mi-sook, 53, told HRW that her three years of experience weren't recognized by her next employer, so she started at entry level on a lower salary.

The longer women spend outside the workforce, the less experience they accumulate on their resumes, which results in less pay and less work stability.

Kim pointed to structural discrimination, a concept from the report that HRW describes as discrimination so embedded in social practices and institutions that even the people harmed by it may not recognize it as a problem.

"When you are alone, it is easy to think, 'It's because I'm not capable enough,' or 'It's because I'm getting older,'" she said. It's only when women who've had similar experiences meet and talk, she added, that they realize, "this wasn't just my problem."

It gets harder as you get older

Park Jae-soon, 61, was forced to retire at 60 from a utility company and now works part-time as a care worker. Her annual income fell from 55 million won ($40,500/€35,600) to 15.6 million won, a 72% drop.

HRW argues the mandatory retirement age and the "peak wage" system, which lets employers cut older workers' pay in the years before retirement, should both be abolished.

According to data cited in the report, women received 53% of men's National Old Age Pension on average in October 2025, a 47% gap.

"I think what is important here is that this is not simply a problem of middle-aged women having difficulty finding jobs," Kim said.

"The work that women have traditionally done inside the home, like cleaning, cooking, caregiving and managing other people's emotions, is classified as 'work suitable for women' when it enters the labor market, and then low wages are assigned to it," she added.

How South Korea's cosmetic industry drives career success To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

From first paycheck to pension

HRW argues the disadvantage builds stage by stage, from a woman's first paycheck up until her pension.

"Career interruption among women in their 30s is already a pension issue," Kim said. "Part-time work among women in their 40s is a pension issue, and low wages among women in their 50s are already a pension issue," she added.

South Korea's government has said it will pursue a phased increase in the statutory retirement age from 60 to 65.

"This cannot be solved with just one policy. Equal pay for equal work needs to be actually implemented, wage structures need to be transparent, and care needs to be treated as a public responsibility rather than something that is pushed onto individual families and women," Kim said.

The rights activist said the report is an important starting point, but believes its picture is incomplete.

Most interviewees were recruited through civic organizations and largely in Seoul, she noted, while disabled women, migrant workers and others may experience a different combination of age and gender discrimination.

"The important question is not simply, 'How much discrimination do women face?'" she said. "It is which women, in what positions, become increasingly distanced from which resources and rights as they grow older."

World.title: Deadly blast rips through Athens building, near Acropolis
World.content:
Several foreign tourists remain missing after an explosion brought down a building in Athens' tourist area of Plaka, with the city's mayor calling it an "incredible disaster."

Rescuers have recovered the body of a young woman following a building collapse in Plaka, in central Athens, a Greek fire brigade official said Saturday.

Later, Greek public broadcaster ERT said a man's body was also recovered from the rubble.

The building was brought down by a large blast which injured three other people and damaged shops and cars near the site.

"The damage extends along the entire street as well as the street behind the building," said Athens Mayor Haris Doukas. "We are talking about an incredible disaster."

Several people, believed to be foreign nationals, remain missing.

On Saturday, Greek news agency ANA reported that the female victim whose body was retrieved was an American tourist, sharing the holiday rental with her husband and another couple.

Cause of the blast still uncertain

Authorities suspect a gas leak caused the Friday blast, but the sequence of events was not immediately clear.

"Something went terribly wrong," Doukas said.

Local media reported the missing people included a Briton and a Greek woman who lived on the second floor, and four American tourists staying on the first floor.

While their nationalities have not been officially confirmed, a police official said the group of tourists had been expected to check in for a flight from Athens on early Friday afternoon.

Excavators on the scene

Rescuers were using sniffer dogs and thermal cameras to search for possible survivors. According to ANA, dozens of firefighters and six vehicles have been deployed to help with the search, including two specialized rescue vehicles.

Excavators were also deployed to clear the rubble, according to photos from the scene.

Plaka is close to many Athens most visited sites, including the Acropolis and the Temple of Zeus.

World.content:
09/26/2026 September 26, 2026 Police close 2 autobahns to free giant wind-turbine

A wide-load truck carrying a nearly 100-meter-long (328-feet-long) wind turbine blade forced the closure of two motorways in western Germany after it got stuck along a narrow section of the carriageway.

The daily Bild newspaper reported that the truck was traveling along the A43 autobahn near the Recklinghausen interchange in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia when the dramatic incident unfolded on Wednesday evening.

Police said the driver ignored warning signs that the highway was unsuitable for heavy-load vehicles.

"The highway is not permitted for heavy transport vehicles in that area. They have to exit because the route crosses the Rhine-Herne Canal a little further on," a spokesperson for Münster Police's highway patrol told Bild.

An automatic barrier and weighing system is meant to prevent loads over 3.5 tons from crossing an old bridge over the canal.

After initially blocking traffic on A43, the truck was ordered onto the hard shoulder to allow traffic to restart along one remaining open lane.

The police spokesperson said "several attempts" were made to free the truck with its ultra-wide cargo over the next two days.

On Friday night, the driver agreed to reverse his truck onto the nearby A2, which forced the temporary closure of a second autobahn, before being allowed to continue his journey just after midnight on Saturday.

World.title: Vox se impone al PP en la manifestación de “ultimátum” al Gobierno, con la mitad de participación que la del pasado mayo
World.content:
El audio de esta noticia utiliza una voz sintética generada por Inteligencia Artificial y podría tener algunas inconsistencias.

El partido de Abascal capitaliza la protesta convocada por Sociedad Civil Española, a la que acudió el ‘número dos’ de los populares, pero no Feijóo

Miles de personas han participado este sábado en una manifestación en Madrid convocada como un “ultimátum al Gobierno” por la plataforma Sociedad Civil Española y apoyada por PP y Vox. En la cabecera de la protesta, que ha iniciado el recorrido en la plaza de Cibeles y ha concluido en el llamado Arco de la Victoria, compartían pancarta Marcos de Quinto, exdiputado de Ciudadanos, y Alejo Vidal-Quadras, ex presidente de los populares en Cataluña y uno de los fundadores del partido de Santiago Abascal, quien se dio un baño de selfis en la marcha mientras le gritaban “¡presidente, presidente!”. El PP no envió a su líder, sino a su secretario general, Miguel Tellado, y esa ausencia no pasó inadvertida entre el público, que a cada poco coreaba: “Feijóo, ¿dónde estás que no te veo?“.

“EL PP”, explicó Tellado al inicio de la marcha, “se suma y apoya esta manifestación para exigir al Gobierno elecciones inmediatas. España está desprotegida. Ceuta ha sido víctima de una invasión y el Gobierno de España no está actuando. Tenemos a unos señores utilizando el palacio de La Moncloa como refugio para defenderse de las causas judiciales”. El número dos del PP aseguró que “un clan de narcotraficantes tiene más honorabilidad que el Gobierno de España” y exigió la disolución de las Cámaras para convocar elecciones. Preguntado por si el PP respalda, como demanda Vox, que Pedro Sánchez sea “juzgado por traición” en aplicación del artículo 102 de la Constitución, Tellado declaró que “un sentir generalizado” opina que el Ejecutivo, “pese a que sabía lo que iba a pasar [en Ceuta] no actuó”, pero no quiso aclarar si apoya esa iniciativa de Abascal. “En estos momentos hay unas diligencias abiertas en la Audiencia Nacional y nosotros confiamos en la justicia”. “Hay que echar al Gobierno igual que hay que echar a los invasores”, concluyó.

Los manifestantes llegan al final de la marcha en el Arco de la Victoria de Moncloa, este sábado. Rodrigo Jimenez (EFE) Una manifestante muestra un cartel crítico con el Gobierno al comienzo de la protesta, este sábado. Álvaro García Un participante asiste a la marcha con una camiseta contra el presidente del Gobierno. Álvaro García Asistentes a la manifestación por la Gran Vía de Madrid, este sábado. Álvaro García Varios manifestantes se fotografían durante la protesta en Madrid. Lavandeira jr (EFE) Un joven con la camiseta de Revuelta, el grupo de extrema derecha juvenil vinculado a Vox, frente al Arco del Triunfo. Álvaro García Asistentes a la manifestación portan banderas de España y Ceuta. Álvaro García Manifestantes pasan junto a un indigente durante la protesta. Álvaro García Manifestantes antes del inicio de “marcha por la dignidad” convocada por Sociedad Civil Española. Álvaro García

Abascal, por su parte, acusó al Ejecutivo de “secuestrar” a los menores de Ceuta en lugar de enviarlos inmediatamente de vuelta con sus padres, pese a que la ley vigente impide hacerlo sin unas garantías que los protejan, y cargó contra el PP por rechazar tanto su propuesta de “un gobierno conjunto” en la ciudad autónoma, como la de que Sánchez sea juzgado “por traición”. Vox rompió en 2024 los Gobiernos de coalición autonómicos con el PP precisamente por el reparto entre autonomías de menores extranjeros no acompañados, que el PP acató, de acuerdo a la ley. Sin embargo, posteriormente, cuando los populares necesitaron sus votos para seguir ocupando la presidencia de esos ejecutivos regionales firmaron con el partido de extrema derecha acuerdos donde se especifica: “No más menas”, que es como se refieren despectivamente a los niños inmigrantes. Hace apenas tres meses tanto los diputados del PP como los de Vox aplaudieron durante siete minutos el discurso en el Congreso del Papa, quien criticó a quienes discriminan a otros “por su origen nacional” y pidió que las fronteras dejasen de ser “lugares de abandono” y pudieran convertirse en “espacios de protección responsable de la dignidad humana”.

El PP no quería quedarse fuera de la foto y que fuera Vox el que capitalice el descontento en la calle, pero fue la formación que preside Abascal la que se llevó la imagen, ya que muchas de las pancartas que enarbolaban los manifestantes incluían el logo del partido de extrema derecha, que las repartía al inicio del recorrido.

El líder de Vox, Santiago Abascal, llega a la marcha este sábado en Madrid. Álvaro García

La Delegación del Gobierno cifró en 20.000 el número de asistentes, lo que supone la mitad que en la anterior protesta convocada por Sociedad Civil Española, el pasado mayo, cuando elevaron ese cálculo a 40.000. De hecho, durante el recorrido, algunos de los manifestantes, que habían participado en la anterior, se quejaban de que la de este sábado estuviera teniendo menos público. “Es que no ha habido publicidad y la gente no se ha enterado”, lamentaba Carmen, de 66 años. Otros echaban la culpa de la falta de afluencia a “los medios del régimen”. Preguntado al respecto, Vidal-Quadras aseguró que había que “esperar a ver las fotografías aéreas”, pero aseguró que “centenares de miles de personas” se habían manifestado contra un Gobierno “que está en manos de los enemigos de la nación”. Marcos de Quinto insistió en que en la protesta habían participado “centeneares de miles de personas”. Preguntado por si creía que entre ellos había gente en paro o que recibía el ingreso mínimo vital, colectivos a los que recientemente, en un tuit, pidió que se retirara el derecho de voto, contestó: “Muy probablemente, porque aquí ha venido gente de todo tipo”.

Al término de la protesta, no se ha procedido a la habitual lectura de manifiesto y más de un centenar de personas ha pretendido continuar la marcha hasta el palacio de La Moncloa “para echar al okupa”, en alusión al presidente del Gobierno. Cuando una barrera de policías se lo ha impedido, los manifestantes se han enfrentado verbalmente a los agentes, a los que llamaban “vendidos” y animaban a “unirse al pueblo y detener a Sánchez”. En este grupo abundaban las camisetas de Revuelta, la organización juvenil vinculada a Vox. Finalmente, la policía ha disuelto a los últimos concentrados y ha reabierto la vía al tráfico.

Aunque con menos participación que la del pasado mayo, la manifestación evidencia el descontento de una parte de la población con el Gobierno de Sánchez y el intento de las fuerzas de la oposición por intentar capitalizarlo en un ambiente de precampaña electoral. Muchas pancartas aludían a la crisis en Ceuta provocada por la entrada a finales del pasado julio de 80.000 inmigrantes, pero entre los cánticos y los lemas predominaban los insultos al presidente y a los miembros de su ejecutivo, y en especial, al ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska. El himno oficioso de la protesta fue “Pedro Sánchez, hijo de puta”, que algunos padres, acompañados por sus hijos, cambiaban por “Sánchez hijo de fruta”, en alusión a la excusa que dio Isabel Díaz Ayuso cuando las cámaras la captaron en el Congreso insultando al jefe del Ejecutivo. Junto a mensajes xenófobos, que vinculaban inmigración a delincuencia y advertían de un supuesto plan de reemplazo de “la España blanca y cristiana” por otra “musulmana” —una de las ideas de las que Vox y la extrema derecha europea hace bandera—, se coreaban otros que tachaban a Ejecutivo de “mafia” y a Sánchez de “traidor”.

La plataforma convocante, Sociedad Civil Española, se presenta como “plural e independiente”, pero su “decálogo” coincide, en buena medida, con el programa del PP y, especialmente, el de Vox. Así, propone derogar la ley trans, la de memoria democrática y la de amnistía, recientemente avalada por el Tribunal de Justicia de la Unión Europea, y sostienen, como el expresidente popular José María Aznar, que el Gobierno avanza en un “proceso de liquidación de la nación española y quiebre del orden constitucional”. Según esta plataforma, España se rompe “desde 2004″, año del primer Gobierno socialista de José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, y lo peor que pueden hacer los ciudadanos es confiar en el sistema, incluida Europa.

Un puesto en el recorrido de la manifestación vende bufandas con el rostro de Franco y calcetines con la bandera preconstitucional. Natalia Junquera

Un puesto en el recorrido de la marcha vendía bufandas con el rostro de Franco y calcetines con la bandera preconstitucional. En la manifestación se exhibieron pancartas “en defensa del Valle de los Caídos”, es decir, en contra de que el mausoleo ideado por el dictador para inmortalizar su victoria se convierta en un centro de interpretación que sirva para explicar la Guerra Civil y la dictadura a las nuevas generaciones.

World.title: La estafa del falso empleado de banca
World.content:
Recibir un SMS que alerta sobre un movimiento sospechoso en nuestra cuenta bancaria puede evitar que seamos víctima de un robo, excepto si no ha sido el banco quien realmente lo ha emitido

En la estafa del falso empleado de banca el delincuente primero envía un mensaje con una alerta sobre un movimiento sospechoso en la cuenta y facilita un enlace o un número de teléfono al que llamar. Ya en la conversación, intenta convencer a la víctima de que su dinero está en peligro para que autorice operaciones que resultarán fraudulentas

En 2025, Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE) registró 25.133 casos de phishing. Durante los dos últimos años, tanto la Policía Nacional como la Guardia Civil y el Banco de España han emitido alertas sobre el aumento de las llamadas de falsos empleados bancarios.

TÉCNICAS DE MANIPULACIÓN

Autoridad Suplantan a profesionales pertenecientes a bancos a los que la víctima concede poder y confianza Urgencia Crean la sensación de que hay poco tiempo para actuar, lo que evita que la víctima reflexione o consulte con alguien Sobrecarga de información técnica Emplean jerga bancaria para intimidar y hacer creer que dominan una situación compleja Aumento gradual de las peticiones Incluye a la víctima en grupos de aplicaciones de mensajería para hacerle creer que mucha gente ya está ganando dinero

CIBEREXPERTO NOMBRE Jordi Sánchez CARGO Experto en fraude de CaixaBank “Durante la llamada, el estafador te hace creer que te está guiando para solucionar tu problema, pero en realidad, está intentando que tu hagas exactamente lo que necesita, emitir operaciones bancarias, descargar aplicaciones o facilitar información, como códigos o datos de tarjetas” Play / Pause CÓMO EVITAR LA ESTAFA DEL FALSO EMPLEADO DE BANCA 1 Sospechar de mensajes inesperados. No clicar en ningún enlace que aparezca en el mensaje ni llamar al número que ofrecen. Ante la duda, siempre se debe llamar a los números oficiales del banco 2 Desconfiar de la urgencia y de las amenazas.Mensajes como “Su cuenta será bloqueada” buscan que se actúe sin pensar 3 No compartir claves ni códigos de verificación. El banco nunca solicitará contraseñas u otros códigos de seguridad 4 No descargar archivos ni instalar aplicaciones. Los estafadores pueden pedir que se descarguen programas que en realidad les están dando acceso al teléfono de la víctima

Una estafa que ha evolucionado. Este fraude comenzó como un SMS y una llamada, pero hoy se dan variantes como la que busca robar información de las tarjetas bancarias mediante el uso de la tecnología NFC del teléfono móvil. Este sistema de comunicación inalámbrica permite compartir información entre otros, tarjetas y móviles, y realizar pagos sin contacto. Los estafadores solicitan a la víctima que se descargue una aplicación maliciosa y que acerque la tarjeta al smartphone. Así, sus datos son enviados a otro teléfono de los atacantes, donde crearán una tarjeta de forma virtual con la que intentar sacar dinero o comprar en comercios.

El teléfono puede parecer auténtico. Los estafadores pueden hacer que en la pantalla del móvil de la víctima figure el mismo número que utiliza el banco para atender a sus clientes o que el SMS aparezca en el mismo hilo que las comunicaciones legítimas mediante una técnica que se conoce como spoofing (que significa suplantación).

Conocen datos personales de su víctima. En muchos casos, disponen de información de su objetivo, como el banco del que es cliente, parte del DNI o la dirección de correo electrónico.

Si ya se ha caído en la estafa. Se debe poner en conocimiento del banco de inmediato para que se puedan adoptar las medidas operativas oportunas. También es muy importante guardar las evidencias, como capturas de pantalla, SMS, correos y registro de llamadas. Presentar una denuncia ante la Policía Nacional o la Guardia Civil.

OTROS CASOS DEL FALSO EMPLEADO DE BANCA

Cada semana aparecen noticias con nuevas maneras de embaucar a ciudadanos con una estafa de este tipo:

World.title: El curioso caso de los barrios con nombres inventados por las inmobiliarias en México
World.content:
Mientras las torres de lujo avanzan sobre zonas tradicionales y las familias enfrentan una presión creciente para vender sus casas y marcharse, las inmobiliarias rebautizan las colonias populares

Una imponente escultura metálica circular recibe a los visitantes del Cuadrante Polanco, un conjunto residencial de imponentes torres de departamentos en una zona de rápida transformación de Ciudad de México. En la acera de enfrente se construyen dos edificios más. Las torres del otro costado también aparecieron en los últimos cinco años. La grama (césped) está bien cuidada, los locales comerciales son prístinos y los guaruras (personal de seguridad privada) hacen sus rondas. Lo único que parece fuera de lugar es que, en realidad, no estamos en Polanco: las inmobiliarias que han levantado este nuevo barrio ostentoso han tomado prestado el nombre de la colonia de lujo por excelencia de la ciudad, con la que colindan.

La megalópolis de Ciudad de México, dividida en sus variopintas colonias —o urbanizaciones—, atraviesa una transformación acelerada y nada discreta. New Polanco, como se le dice con sorna, se asienta sobre manzanas que hasta hace pocas décadas constituían un parque industrial. En las inmediaciones conviven sedes de multinacionales, museos y concesionarios de Ferrari con fábricas de harina, estaciones eléctricas y hasta una planta cervecera que llena el aire con olor a cebada. El barrio, como otros similares en la ciudad, también es una expresión de los factores que están cambiando la cara a las zonas tradicionales y desplazando a las comunidades en las principales ciudades del país.

Un hombre camina en la cerrada Andrómaco, en Ciudad de México. Rodrigo Oropeza

Los expertos lo han definido como una doble crisis en el mercado: de oferta y de asequibilidad, traducida en el alza sostenida de los precios de compra y renta y en la inclinación del portafolio hacia unidades de mayor valor. La gentrificación se come los barrios populares y obliga a los habitantes que han convivido durante generaciones a buscar nuevos rumbos, muchas veces en las periferias. También produce barrios que no existen en los mapas o demarcaciones oficiales: “Condesa Sur”, “Roma Oriente” y “Reforma Norte” se apropian de los nombres de las urbanizaciones de mayor plusvalía con las que limitan, en un intento por justificar los altos precios.

“Pero esto no es Polanco. Lo quieren hacer para atraer más gente para vender sus departamentos”, corrige Alfredo Sánchez, funcionario público retirado que ha vivido toda su vida, 68 años, en la “Cerrada de Andrómaco”, un pasillo angosto que recorre la distancia de una cuadra y alberga coloridas casas de dos o tres pisos a ambos lados. El contraste es tangible. El vecindario popular, un vestigio de lo que fue la zona, se ha quedado atrapado entre un centro comercial y un parque infantil que, detrás de altas murallas, forma parte de las áreas comunes de un conjunto de torres residenciales.

Algunos habitantes de las casi 60 familias que viven ahí dicen que sienten la presión de las inmobiliarias para vender sus casas y ceder el espacio a nuevos complejos. Y aunque pueda parecer una oferta tentadora, aceptarla no les permitiría seguir viviendo en su zona: las propuestas rondan los 2 millones de pesos (unos 115.000 dólares), mientras que un departamento en el área cuesta más del doble, cerca de 350.000 dólares.

Vista aérea de la cerrada Andrómaco, en Ciudad de México. Emiliano Molina

En las principales ciudades —Ciudad de México, Guadalajara y Monterrey—, cerca del 78% del inventario digital de vivienda corresponde a propiedades de alto valor, según una radiografía del sector elaborada por Propiedades.com, un sitio web inmobiliario. “Esta configuración refleja una brecha importante entre la oferta digitalizada y las necesidades de vivienda asequible para una gran parte de la población”, agrega el estudio del segundo semestre del 2025.

La empresa, que rastrea aumentos de hasta 180% en las rentas en zonas de la capital, detalla que el encarecimiento ha desplazado a residentes hacia áreas aledañas con precios más accesibles, aunque estas “zonas de contención” comienzan a registrar un aumento en la demanda e indicios de revalorización. La Condesa y la Roma, donde palpita el corazón de la gentrificación de la capital, han empezado a desbordarse hacia otras comunidades, donde las fachadas art déco, que florecieron desde 1925, dan paso a edificios con gimnasio, terrazas y áreas infantiles.

En agosto de 2026, el precio promedio por metro cuadrado de vivienda en Ciudad de México se elevó un 4,4% y alcanzó cerca de 3.500 dólares, consolidándola como el precio más alto del país, de acuerdo con el seguimiento del banco Banorte. Según estudios académicos, es también la segunda ciudad más costosa de Latinoamérica, solo por detrás de Montevideo, en Uruguay, según el Relevamiento Inmobiliario de América Latina (RIAL) de la Universidad Torcuato Di Tella, en Argentina.

Fachada de la cerrada Andrómaco, en Polanco, el 10 de septiembre. Rodrigo Oropeza

La Administración de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum ha reconocido el problema estructural, que también golpea el desempeño de la economía, y anunció el año pasado la meta de edificar y financiar 1,8 millones de viviendas populares, para beneficio de 12 millones de familias. En paralelo, el partido gobernante Morena promueve iniciativas legislativas en Ciudad de México para evitar que las desarrolladoras se asimilen a colonias de mayor plusvalía, en un intento que han denominado de publicidad engañosa y voracidad inmobiliaria. “Cuando cambia el nombre de un barrio, cambia quién puede vivir en ese barrio”, ha dicho la diputada local de Morena Cecilia Vadillo, quien promueve la propuesta.

Sin embargo, en la Cerrada de Andrómaco, que se ha hecho viral en redes sociales como reflejo de la disparidad, se quejan del abandono mientras temen por lo que pasará en los próximos años, mientras los servicios de electricidad y agua se han encarecido y han empezado a presentar fallas, dicen, ante el alto consumo de los vecinos. “Los políticos vienen, toman nota y se van. Nos preocupa que llegue un presidente al que se le bote la canica y nos diga que nos vamos porque nos vamos, con una indemnización que no nos alcance para vivir en la ciudad”, se queja José Mendoza, de 63 años. Su familia ha vivido en este pequeño vecindario durante tres generaciones. “Los de allá”, dice señalando los edificios en la otra acera, “quisieran que desapareciéramos”.
