World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: 11-year-old esports prodigy claims gold at Asian Games
World.content:
Japan’s 11-year-old esports prodigy Yuki Kurihara said he was “embarrassed” after winning Asian Games gold on Saturday by thrashing a series of opponents up to three times his age.

The bespectacled elementary school student, believed to be the youngest competitor at the Aichi Nagoya Games, won the Puyo Puyo Champions final 10-2.

He is the youngest athlete in Japan’s Asian Games history.

Puyo Puyo Champions is a puzzle game where players try to clear their screen of colored blobs by lining them up and popping them.

Looking unruffled throughout, Kurihara waltzed into the gold medal match with a string of dazzling displays.

He crushed Thailand’s Tanarak Wongkitkun — a relative veteran at 28 — 10-1 in the semifinals to ensure at least a silver medal.

He did not even smile after beating South Korea’s 24-year-old Kang Dongshin in the final, having gone down 1-0 early in the match.

“To be completely honest, I felt a bit embarrassed, so I couldn’t really show my expressions or change my face much,” he explained.

Standing on the podium, he bowed slightly as he received his gold medal and gave a small wave to the arena.

“I’m really happy,” he said. “The gold medal is really beautiful, shiny and heavy.

“Also, the plush toy is super cute, and it’s cool that it is gold-colored too.”

Kurihara started playing Puyo Puyo in his first year of elementary school and soon started competing and winning in tournaments.

He obtained his pro license in April and regularly beats adults.

“It’s hard having to balance it with school and cram school, but it’s really fun,” he said ahead of the Games.

There are no publicly available records of the youngest medalists in the history of the Asian Games, which were first contested in 1951.

But Indonesia’s Bunga Nyimas won bronze in women’s skateboarding at age 12 in Jakarta in 2018.

Cui Chenxi, 13, won Games gold when she triumphed in the women’s street skateboarding event three years ago in Hangzhou.

World.title: Organizers ‘not satisfied’ by rows of empty seats at Asian Games
World.content:
Asian Games organizers admitted on Saturday they were “not satisfied” with ticket sales after swathes of empty seats were seen at the main stadium and other venues in Japan.

The 100-meter sprints are one of the highlights of any Games, but the 30,000-capacity Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium appeared to be only about one-quarter full on Friday night for the blue-ribbon events.

Even the prospect of a women’s pole vault gold for Misaki Morota could not pull in local fans in big numbers at the start of the weekend.

The Aichi-Nagoya Games said that less than 60% of tickets had been snapped up for eight sports, including soccer, with a similar amount unsold for the closing ceremony.

“We are not satisfied,” Satoshi Murate, secretary general of the Games organizing committee said.

“We will keep aiming for full stadiums, keep selling tickets and work to make sure people who have secured seats actually come.”

He said more than 90% of tickets were sold for the opening ceremony a week ago, but blamed no-shows for large sections of empty seats greeting the parading athletes and the lighting of the Games torch.

“Overall I think sales are strong,” he said.

“But it has been pointed out that there are noticeable empty seats at some competitions.

“There are several reasons. First, some sessions include several matches in one day. Everyone focuses on the headline match.”

He said tickets that had been given away to Games stakeholders, such as sponsors, were not always used.

“Seats have been allocated, but some people can’t come.

“As a result, some competitions do have noticeable empty seats, and we find that regrettable.”

Murate also apologized for mixups with accommodation and transport.

Several teams have rounded on the organizers, with Thailand likening it to a “chaotic” game of “musical chairs” and South Korea saying “they deserve a failing grade.”

The biggest issue has been a shortage of rooms for the 17,000 participants, a problem compounded by delays at airports and hourslong waits to board a cruise ship acting as a floating hotel.

No traditional athletes’ village has been built, as a cost-cutting measure.

Teams have instead been staying in temporary container-style huts, hotels and the Costa Serena cruise ship.

Erratic transport services have seen competitors’ buses to training and venues turning up late or, in some cases, not at all.

“There have been mistakes in accommodation and transport, for various reasons,” admitted Murate.

“Whatever the cause, AINAGOC (the organizing committee) is responsible for providing the service and I sincerely apologise for the mistakes.

“Our staff work every day to identify the causes of each mistake and make sure they don’t happen again.”

World.title: Junglia theme park in Okinawa logs ¥17 billion loss in first year
World.content:
The Junglia theme park in Okinawa Prefecture suffered a net loss of ¥17.3 billion in its first year of business due to sluggish ticket sales.

The ¥70 billion park was built in a 60-hectare site in northern Okinawa last July, and there were high expectations that it would help extend tourist stays in the region and stimulate local economic growth.

Japan Entertainment Holdings, the parent company of the park’s operator, ran into severe financial difficulties in the year that ended in June 2026, making it necessary to take drastic measures to improve the business.

In a general meeting of shareholders in Naha, the capital of Okinawa, on Friday, the company explained its financial situation and future business plans.

The loss “will not affect our services provided to customers or various contracts and transactions with other companies,” CEO Takeshi Kato said in a statement. “We will continue to operate as usual.”

Junglia, straddling the village of Nakijin and the city of Nago, was planned by Katana, a marketing company based in Osaka. Katana President and CEO Tsuyoshi Morioka is known for his role in revitalizing the Universal Studios Japan theme park in Osaka.

Junglia had attracted about 1 million visitors by July this year, apparently far below their estimates.

World.title: China and U.S. to open AI ‘communication channel’ after summit
World.content:
China and the United States agreed to set up a “communication channel” for artificial intelligence incidents, the White House said Friday, after a Washington summit short on breakthroughs.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping discussed matters ranging from AI and trade to the stalled war in Iran, and confirmed that they would meet for a third and fourth time this year at international summits in China and the United States.

Xi’s visit to Washington was marked more by pomp than substance, but the White House said the nations agreed to establish a “bilateral communication channel” for AI incidents.

World.title: Japan wary China could use Trump-Xi summit to bolster narrative against Tokyo
World.content:
Thursday’s U.S.-China leaders summit has left Tokyo concerned that Beijing could seek to use the meeting to bolster its narrative against Japan as ties remain chilly over Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s comments on Taiwan last year.

During the meeting in Washington, U.S. President Donald Trump hailed the two superpowers’ “common interests” that he said had “even made us allies in World War II” — remarks likely to have raised eyebrows in Tokyo, a U.S. ally currently embroiled in a festering dispute with Beijing and facing pressure from Trump on both trade and defense issues.

Speaking after Trump, Xi noted that Chinese and Americans had “fought shoulder to shoulder against fascist aggression.”

World.title: When infinity becomes finite: How will Yayoi Kusama’s death influence the art market?
World.content:
In 1966, Yayoi Kusama appeared at the Venice Biennale with 1,500 mirrored plastic spheres and spread them across the lawn outside the Italian Pavilion.

She had not been formally invited to exhibit.

The work was “Narcissus Garden,” and Kusama began offering individual spheres to visitors for 1,200 lire, about $2 at the time, until Biennale officials stopped the sales. The gesture turned repetition into spectacle and spectacle into commerce. An apparently endless field of identical objects could, one by one, be bought and carried away.

World.title: Japan’s finance chief says Takaichi isn’t ‘reflationist’
World.content:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi is not a reflationist, her finance minister said, seeking to allay investor concerns her government would spend excessively and pressure the Bank of Japan to keep interest rates low.

“Prime Minister Takaichi always asks me to explain to people from overseas that she is not a reflationist, so we want to make sure there is no misunderstanding on that point,” Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said in an interview Friday.

Some market participants see Takaichi in the mold of former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, her mentor who favored monetary easing by the central bank and flexible fiscal policy to help reflate the economy after decades of stagnation.

World.title: Trump rejects Iranian peace proposal, report says
World.content:
Iran on Saturday awaited an official U.S. response to its proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end fighting in the wider Middle East war after the Wall Street Journal reported that U.S. President Donald Trump had rejected the deal.

Iran raised the diplomatic initiative at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, saying it had been transmitted to the Americans via Qatari mediators and could reopen the strategic waterway and put an end to hostilities in the region within seven ​days.

The Iranians also engaged their Saudi rivals regarding the strait, underscoring the stakes of a 7-month-old conflict that has disrupted oil flows through one of the ‌world’s most critical ‌shipping lanes and taken a toll on the global economy.

World.title: District councillor Peggy Wong resigns amid proxy-vote claims after Tai Po blaze
World.content:
Hong Kong district councillor Peggy Wong Pik-kiu has resigned from office and several other community roles citing health reasons, following mounting controversy over her team’s alleged proxy-vote collection before last year’s fatal Wang Fuk Court inferno.

Wong, a directly elected district councillor for the Tai Po South constituency, also stepped down from her duties as a member of the Tai Po South Area Committee and captain of the Tai Po Kwong Fuk and Plover Cove subdistrict care teams.

The Home Affairs Department announced the resignations on Saturday, issuing a statement in which Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak Mei-kuen said she respected Wong’s decision.

World.title: Woman arrested over child abuse in Hong Kong after dashcam video shows boy shoved
World.content:
A 44-year-old woman in Hong Kong has been arrested on suspicion of child abuse after dashcam footage appeared to show her shoving a boy into a roadside railing.

A police force spokesman said on Saturday that the woman was arrested on Friday afternoon in Western district after a widely circulated dashcam video drew the force’s attention.

In the video seen by the South China Morning Post, the woman gets out of a private car at a section of Wan Chai Road near Burrows Street, with a boy following suit.

The woman then turns around to hold onto the boy by his waist, before the two walk towards the pavement next to the road.

World.title: Mid-Autumn light show in Yuen Long panned online over stench and execution
World.content:
A government-hosted Mid-Autumn Festival light show at a nullah in Hong Kong has sparked widespread online criticism, with revellers complaining of foul smells and poor execution.

Attendees posted their reviews on social media on Saturday after the opening night of the two-day “Yuen Long Flood Barrier and Nullah Improvement Scheme – Mid-Autumn Light Show” organised by the Drainage Services Department.

The event was billed as an inaugural initiative to transform the Yuen Long nullah into a large-scale art exhibition space, but many visitors took to platforms such as Threads to express their disappointment.

“A foul smell was coming out while I was watching the show,” an attendee posted on Threads, sharing videos showing light projections against a wide, open-air concrete storm drainage channel.

World.title: Hikers urge live updates on free quota spots to fix Po Pin Chau booking confusion
World.content:
Hikers flocking to a popular geological attraction in Hong Kong’s Sai Kung over the Mid-Autumn Festival weekend have called for real-time displays showing when time slots are available under a trial registration system.

The High Island Geo Trail’s Po Pin Chau section continued to draw lines of visitors on Saturday morning – the second day of an extended weekend in mainland China.

While hikers who booked a slot under a newly introduced trial registration system were seen queuing at the entrance in the hot sun, others hoped to try their luck on site for walk-in openings.

Taxi drivers wait to take visitors from the High Island Reservoir East Dam during the Mid-Autumn Festival weekend. Photo: Edmond So

Among them was Maria Chen, a mainland postgraduate student studying in Hong Kong, who said she had checked for reservations four days in advance, only to find the slots fully booked.

“The staff asked us to wait 10 minutes or more to see if any on-site slots would open up, but we do not know how long we have to wait, so we are going to head to Long Ke to continue our hike,” she said.

World.title: Hong Kong police investigate suspected pinhole cameras in gym changing rooms
World.content:
Hong Kong police are investigating a case of voyeurism after three suspected pinhole cameras were found in the changing rooms of a 24/7 Fitness branch in Sha Tin.

The force said on Saturday that officers were alerted at 5.11pm on Friday to a suspected pinhole camera attached with black tape to the false ceiling of a changing room at the gym on Lek Yuen Street.

Upon searching, officers discovered three suspected pinhole cameras across three of the gym’s changing rooms, according to police.

The case had been classified as voyeurism, police said.

World.title: Hong Kong minister vows to give public account of Queen Mary Hospital lift saga
World.content:
Hong Kong’s development minister has promised a public account of her bureau’s oversight of the Queen Mary Hospital lift saga, while stopping short of saying whether a new accountability system for department heads would be invoked.

Nearly two weeks after Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu tasked the Development Bureau with submitting a report within a month, Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said she would get to the bottom of the defective works at the hospital, which left 24 of the 28 lifts at its new 34-storey clinical block deemed unfit for use.

“Why did those issues occur with the lifts? When were those problems identified, or why have they not been identified yet? All of this will be detailed in the coming report we will submit to the chief executive, which will subsequently be disclosed to the public as well,” she told a television programme on Saturday.

But Linn stopped short of saying whether she would invoke the Heads of Departments Accountability System, unveiled in last year’s policy address, stressing the first phase of the follow-up investigation had already begun.

World.title: Xi-Trump summit: Hong Kong’s Paul Chan predicts positive market response
World.content:
Hong Kong’s finance chief has predicted a positive market response to the Xi-Trump summit , saying that mitigating geopolitical uncertainties would bolster investor confidence, while local business representatives expect that greater stability in bilateral ties may reinforce the city’s role as a connector.

“I believe the market will have a positive interpretation … Previously, geopolitics caused concerns over economic prospects, leading to uncertainty and capital flow volatility,” Chan said.

“If this factor can be mitigated, investors will feel more secure when positioning their portfolios.”

World.title: Hong Kong is fast-tracking Northern Metropolis links. Will they be ready in time?
World.content:
Hong Kong will fast-track key Northern Metropolis roads, bringing forward the San Tin highway section to 2034 and targeting 2033 for the Tsing Lung Bridge, but a transport expert and lawmaker have cautioned that the first arrivals could still end up stranded.

Infrastructure projects could lag behind developments such as the Hung Shui Kiu University Town, they said, suggesting the government launch express bus routes and build the Central Rail Link as soon as possible to ensure connectivity.

A source told the South China Morning Post that authorities were pushing ahead with the Tsing Lung Bridge project, bringing forward its launch by two years to 2033.

The acceleration of the San Tin section of the planned Northern Metropolis Highway, meanwhile, would mainly be achieved through techniques such as slope stabilisation, the source said.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019073/Beijing Court Lets Widow Use Embryos Created With Late Husband
World.title: Beijing Court Lets Widow Use Embryos Created With Late Husband
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019073/Beijing Court Lets Widow Use Embryos Created With Late Husband
World.content:
A Beijing court ordered a hospital to resume embryo-transfer treatment for a widow seeking to use two frozen embryos she and her husband created before his death.

On Sept. 22, Beijing’s Chaoyang District People’s Court disclosed details of the case while releasing its annual white paper on medical disputes. The court said it had ruled in favor of the woman, surnamed Zhang, who would be responsible for the related costs. It found that her request did not violate any law, the couple’s agreement, or ethical principles.

Zhang and her husband, Li, married in 2016 and later sought fertility treatment after she experienced repeated miscarriages and Li was diagnosed with secondary infertility. In 2019, the couple underwent treatment at a Beijing hospital’s reproductive center, where three embryos were frozen.

Li died of a brainstem hemorrhage in July of that year. Zhang later used one of the embryos and gave birth to a daughter, leaving two embryos remaining.

Years later, Zhang asked to use the two remaining embryos, but the hospital refused. It cited the difficulty of obtaining consent from her late husband, concerns that the request was linked to an inheritance dispute, a contract provision allowing the embryos to be destroyed if either spouse died, and the lack of approval from the hospital’s ethics committee.

Zhang said she was willing to assume all legal, ethical and moral responsibilities arising from the embryo transfer and any resulting childbirth. Zhang’s mother-in-law supported her decision, and Zhang later filed a lawsuit.

China’s regulations on human assisted reproductive technology, issued in the early 2000s, restrict access to such procedures to married couples and exclude single women.

The hospital argued that Zhang no longer met that requirement after her husband’s death, while Zhang argued that the embryos had been created during their marriage and that she should be allowed to proceed.

The Chaoyang court found that Zhang’s request did not violate the law, the couple’s agreement or ethical principles. It said there was no unresolved inheritance dispute, as Li’s estate had already been settled through notarization and a settlement agreement. The court also found that Zhang and Li had formed a clear, shared intention to have children before his death.

The judges said Zhang’s case differed from that of unmarried women seeking assisted reproductive treatment because the embryos had been created during her marriage. Having already helped Zhang complete one successful embryo transfer, the hospital could not later rely on restrictions on treatment for “single women” to deny access to the remaining embryos, the court said.

The court ordered the hospital to resume treatment, with Zhang responsible for related costs. It said Zhang was an independent rights holder under the embryo-transfer service contract. The judges said disputes involving assisted reproductive technology should balance legal limits, ethical considerations, family consensus and contractual obligations.

The court included the case in its annual white paper on medical disputes, describing it as an example of new legal questions arising from advances in assisted reproductive technology.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: E+/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019063/Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.title: Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019063/Spleen May Affect Cognitive Decline in Women, Says Chinese Study
World.content:
Chinese scientists have identified a pathway connecting the spleen to the brain that may in part explain why women are more susceptible than men to cognitive decline as they age.

The study, published Sept. 18 in the peer-reviewed journal Neuron, was led by Ma Huan, vice dean of the School of Brain Science and Brain Medicine at Zhejiang University, in eastern China.

Existing literature shows that although women live on average longer than men, they are more susceptible to cognitive impairment from midlife onwards. Scientists have lacked a clear biological explanation for this phenomenon, attributing it until now primarily to estrogen.

The new research, however, has found that the spleen may influence brain aging through a pathway involving a gene on the X chromosome, which becomes more active in women as they age.

Using gene-expression data from 11 major organs in a preexisting database, the team found that beginning around age 40, signs of cellular senescence — when cells stop dividing and begin to malfunction — rose sharply in women’s brains and spleens, exceeding levels observed in men of the same age. A similar pattern was confirmed in naturally aging mice and in donor human brain tissue.

The researchers’ findings raise a key question: Is cognitive decline in part the result of the body sending a signal to the brain telling it to age?

In searching for that signal, the researchers identified miR-10a-5p, a microRNA — a type of gene expression regulator — whose levels rose in the spleens and brains of middle-aged female mice but not in their male counterparts.

The team then looked for proteins that regulate miR-10a-5p and discovered that RBMX, a protein encoded by a gene on the X chromosome, binds to, stabilizes, and allows the microRNA to accumulate. This process only occurred in female mice, as females carry two X chromosomes.

Next, the researchers injected mice with a compound to block miR-10a-5p, finding this lowered its levels in their brains, as did removing their spleens — indicating that the organ is a major source of the microRNA. Because the compound used does not efficiently cross the blood-brain barrier, the results imply that muting it elsewhere in the body may be enough to alter levels in the brain.

Once inside neurons in the brain, miR-10a-5p suppresses a protein called γCaMKII linked to calcium regulation within mitochondria — structures within the cell that generate its energy. When levels of this protein fall — which occurs during middle age in females — calcium signaling weakens and energy output declines, pushing neurons toward senescence. Restoring the protein in mice with reduced γCaMKII reversed these changes.

“We’ve tended to treat cognitive aging as something confined to the brain,” Qu Jing, the first author of the study, told Sixth Tone. “This work suggests the brain isn’t an isolated organ, and age-related changes in peripheral tissue may start shaping its condition much earlier than we assumed.”

The findings also suggest that because some of the brain’s miR-10a-5p originates elsewhere in the body, testing for it in patients’ blood could help assess brain-aging risk long before cognitive symptoms appear. Second, because reducing miR-10a-5p levels in the body affects the brain, it may be possible to protect against cognitive decline without developing a drug that crosses the blood-brain barrier.

“One important message from this work is that midlife isn’t just a stage where you wait for aging to happen, but a possible critical window for maintaining long-term brain health,” Qu said, adding that because the study points to a connection between the immune system and the brain, sustaining a well-functioning immune system may matter for cognitive health too.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Amana/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019060/In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
World.title: In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019060/In the Rubber Forests, ‘Shanghai Daughter’ Traces a Father’s Past
World.content:
SHANGHAI – At the Sept. 19 Shanghai premiere of her feature debut, “Shanghai Daughter,” Shen Zhongmin carried a rubber seed from the forests of the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture, nearly 3,000 kilometers away in southwestern China’s Yunnan province, where her late father had worked.

“The seed fell from the canopy and struck me as I retraced his life there,” Shen, 41, tells Sixth Tone.

Her father was among the millions of urban Chinese youths “sent down” to work in rural areas under the Down to the Countryside Movement, a campaign that ran from the mid-1950s through the late 1970s. He spent a decade on a state-run rubber farm near China’s border with Myanmar but rarely spoke to his daughter about those years.

Shen, who works professionally as Agnis Shen, first traveled to Xishuangbanna in 2011, the year after her father died. A former culture editor at the Shanghai-based magazine The Bund and the author of “The Traveler’s Desire,” a collection of short fiction. She returned to the region repeatedly, retracing her father’s life and meeting people from his generation.

Nearly a decade after her first trip, those encounters and widespread coverage of a herd of wild Asian elephants wandering north from Xishuangbanna helped inspire the idea for a film. The herd’s journey drew attention to the rubber plantations that had transformed parts of the region’s rainforest habitat.

Blending fiction with documentary methods, “Shanghai Daughter” follows Ming, a fictional Shanghai woman played by Liang Cuishan, as she seeks out her father’s former acquaintances in Xishuangbanna.

She encounters workers’ dormitories facing demolition and a landscape where mining and modern agriculture are replacing former rubber plantations. She also meets rubber tappers, village doctors, ethnic Dai villagers, and ecological researchers, all of whom appear as themselves and recount their own experiences.

“The film asks how we deal with memory,” Shen says. “When you want to understand something from the past but cannot find reliable firsthand records, how do you search for the answers?”

“Shanghai Daughter” had its world premiere in the Panorama section of the Berlin International Film Festival in February and was later selected for the Hong Kong International Film Festival and the Malaysia International Film Festival.

Seven months later, the film’s Shanghai premiere drew at least a dozen former sent-down youths from the city, all now in their 70s. They traveled about an hour by subway to attend.

At the theater, they shared old photographs from their years in Xishuangbanna, including images taken with Shen’s father, Shen Wanxiong, and posed for a group photo with the director.

Among them was Shen Weilong, 73, a former rubber tapper who had worked alongside Shen Wanxiong and describes him as his best friend. Looking at one of the photographs, he jokes, “This one doesn’t show just how handsome he was. If you want to know what he looked like, just look at his daughter.”

As he speaks about his generation, tears well in his eyes. “Our generation is rarely talked about, and now our time is running out,” he says.

Sixth Tone spoke with Shen Zhongmin the following day as she continued a multi-city promotional tour. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Not a single scene in “Shanghai Daughter” was shot in Shanghai. Why did you choose the title, and what does it mean to you?

Shen: “Shanghai daughters” was originally a local term. Villagers near the farms used it for daughters left behind by sent-down youths. Over time, the label seemed to replace each woman’s real name.

Because of my father’s history, I am also, in a sense, a “Shanghai daughter,” and so I went there too. In Xishuangbanna, the phrase took on a double meaning for me. It suggested a kind of twin existence, like looking in a mirror. We seemed to have completely different yet intersecting destinies, one born in Shanghai and the other 3,000 kilometers away in Xishuangbanna.

To me, “daughter” carries something different from either “woman” or “boy.” One of the first Dai expressions my father taught me was “long yin,” meaning “girl.” The image of a girl carries a particular gentleness that can help heal or ease the deep wounds and heaviness behind this subject. The emotional connection extends beyond father and daughter to one girl and another, and one daughter and another.

I did not want to remain trapped within a particular historical wound or view that period only through criticism. I hoped to create something relevant to the present and oriented toward the future, an expression of repair, renewed empathy, and hope.

Sixth Tone: By telling the story from a daughter’s perspective, the film approaches the sent-down youth movement through one family. How does that perspective differ from other portrayals of the movement?

Shen: This is a deeply personal and highly artistic undertaking. It emphasizes experiencing and observing our surroundings and sensory world anew.

While writing the screenplay, I did extensive research. I gathered oral histories, consulted historical archives, and reconnected with researchers at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who study rainforest restoration. But I wanted to hold back those “concrete” materials for as long as possible and put perception first. Thoughts and opinions can easily create divisions, and once expressed, they have their limits. Perception, however, can be shared and remains more open.

Later, an academically minded journalist asked whether this might be related to ecofeminism. I thought the observation was perceptive. It points toward a perspective that moves beyond anthropocentrism and rejects a structure in which “I am the center, and everyone else is the other.”

Sixth Tone: Rubber trees, dragon fruit, and other elements of the landscape recur throughout the film. How did you use them to connect personal memory with the region’s history?

Shen: During my fieldwork in Xishuangbanna, I often walked around whenever I had time. I gradually came to see the landscape itself as a theater. All the legends and stories I had heard, with their intense dramatic and emotional tension, lay silently buried in a small hill in the village.

Generations have cultivated different crops there, from rice and corn to bananas and, more recently, dragon fruit. A small patch of primary forest protected by the Dai people remains on the hillside. Beneath the present landscape lie my father’s old dormitory and the former rubber plantation.

People disappear faster than memories, but stories spanning more than half a century survive in the land’s subtle traces. When you look at the plants and the land and listen to their voices, it feels as if they are telling you stories, though not in a language humans can hear.

I brought the rubber seed to the screening because, to me, it represents a transformation of cause and effect. More than half a century ago, people had little choice but to clear primary rainforest and plant rubber trees to meet the needs of national development. We now understand that this harmed local biodiversity.

A Chinese Academy of Sciences team is rehabilitating degraded rubber groves. Its goal is not to return them to primary rainforest, which would be scientifically unsound, but to rebalance relationships among species. The researchers are restoring poor-quality groves left by haphazard planting and tapping and introducing species that can bridge rubber plantations and native tropical rainforest. By giving the rubber trees a range of “good neighbors,” they can gradually restore the ecosystem’s layers.

To me, they are taking the “effect” of an earlier decision and planting within it a new, positive “cause,” one that may bear better fruit in the future. The relationship between seed and fruit becomes a metaphor for the transformation of cause and effect. I find that deeply inspiring.

Making the film also took me to Malaysia, where I saw some of the country’s earliest rubber trees. Without that initial transplantation, rubber would not have been planted on such a large scale in Xishuangbanna, and many of these stories would not exist.

Sixth Tone: Why did you blend fiction and documentary methods rather than make a conventional documentary centered on your own search?

Shen: I have always felt that the boundary between reality and fiction is unclear, much like the line between dreams and waking life. Historical narratives also have a dreamlike quality for me, something I have explored in my fiction.

If I had relied on documentary methods alone to examine the sent-down youth movement or my relationship with my father, the film would have felt too narrow.

I drew on my own experience to present subjects I have long cared about in a more contemporary, open form. If I had appeared as myself and made a pure documentary, the film would have become too narrow, confined by the standards of historical fact and leaving viewers less room to project themselves into it and experience it openly.

Sixth Tone: How did you approach your father’s past and his former co-workers while making the film? How did they respond after the premiere?

Shen: My father rarely spoke about the decade he spent in Xishuangbanna. People of his generation generally do not talk about those experiences.

You could sense a deep wound behind the way an older audience member spoke yesterday. At times, his questions seemed to judge other people, but they ultimately revealed his own views and emotions.

I didn’t even know my father had tapped rubber. He had never told me what work he did there. Only when I first walked into the plantation did I understand that these were rubber trees and that his generation had planted and tapped them.

At first, I avoided contacting my father’s former co-workers. I knew they would be eager to help and provide a great deal of firsthand material. But the film began with the particular relationship between my father and me. He had told me very little and died before I could learn more, so I went there to search for and reconstruct that missing part of his life.

I also did not want to disturb them for what was, after all, a small personal project. Revisiting those experiences can be extremely painful, especially for some of them.

Since yesterday’s premiere, I have spent all morning replying to their messages. Today, they are gathering for a reunion lunch to discuss the film.

One of my father’s former co-workers wrote: “Thank you to the screenwriter, creative team, and director for bringing a fitting close to our 50 years as sent-down youths.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A still from “Shanghai Daughter.” Courtesy of Shen)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019062/Report Links Alibaba’s Resale App to Sex Trade Involving Minors
World.title: Report Links Alibaba’s Resale App to Sex Trade Involving Minors
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019062/Report Links Alibaba’s Resale App to Sex Trade Involving Minors
World.content:
A domestic media investigation has found vendors using Alibaba’s secondhand platform Xianyu to solicit illicit sexual services, including some allegedly involving minors.

State owned Hebei Television reported that vendors used fake listings for massages, modeling shoots, at-home personal training, and swimming lessons to direct users to private messaging platforms, where the transactions were allegedly arranged.

Xianyu said on Sept. 18, when the investigation was published, that it has been working with police since January to dismantle 15 prostitution-related groups and had frozen nearly 100,000 accounts suspected of directing users to pornographic content.

In its latest statement on Wednesday, Xianyu called for a “cross-platform alliance” to combat illicit sexual content and the exploitation of minors, stressing that the conversations cited in the investigation took place on other messaging platforms after initial contact on Xianyu.

The investigation triggered widespread debate on Chinese social media, with several related hashtags topping microblogging platform Weibo’s trending list. The most-viewed has garnered 490 million views as of Wednesday.

One listing cited in the report advertising swimming lessons directed buyers to a private chat group on Tencent’s business messaging app WeCom, where a 99-yuan ($15) deposit provided access to a price list for sexual services for additional fees. The reporter placed an order and provided an address. Shortly after, a woman arrived at the location saying she offered flirting, kissing, and bathing services.

The report also found a vendor allegedly offering girls as young as 14 for prostitution, charging 20,000 to 30,000 yuan. Another vendor sent reporters photos of a 16-year-old’s ID card as evidence of her age, offered to arrange video calls, and said the girls could fly to meet buyers if they covered the airfare.

Xianyu’s customer service told Hebei Television that automated systems are largely used to review its product listings, with human reviewers involved only in appeals.

Following the investigation, Xianyu said that it would strengthen automated detection by improving its keyword filters and image-detection algorithms, and step up manual reviews of suspicious listings and accounts.

A Wednesday check by Sixth Tone found that listings for “at-home modeling shoots” no longer yielded results, but “at-home shoots,” as well as “fitness” and “swimming” services, remained available.

With more than 600 million users, Xianyu is China’s largest secondhand trading app. In recent years, it has evolved into an informal services marketplace, offering everything from résumé writing to odd jobs like finding an owner’s lost pet or smuggling someone into a sold-out concert, with prices often negotiated through private chats.

The platform has repeatedly come under scrutiny for users selling illicit products and services. A 2019 report by Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper found Xianyu vendors were listing ads for 1-yuan items of clothing as a way to lure young women into chatting with them, with the eventual aim of providing sexual services. In 2021, consumer protection authorities ordered Xianyu and 11 other resale platforms to crack down on listings directing users to illicit sexual transactions.

Chang Dongyue, a partner at Shanghai Droit&Elite Law Firm, told Sixth Tone that Xianyu’s low barriers to entry and reliance on user traffic and transaction volume, combined with pressure to minimize moderation costs, create conditions for illicit listings to resurface repeatedly.

Under China’s Cybersecurity Law, platforms must remove illegal content, while the Law on the Protection of Minors requires them to delete illegal content directed at minors, retain evidence of the content, and report it to authorities.

In response to Xianyu’s comments on cross-platform collaboration, Chang noted that cooperation on illegal activity is necessary. “Banning accounts on individual platforms only removes one link in the chain,” he said. “Without genuine cross-platform cooperation, enforcement will be less effective.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019056/Runaway to Record Breaker: Zhao Jiaju on Willpower, Pain, and the Tor des Géants
World.title: Runaway to Record Breaker: Zhao Jiaju on Willpower, Pain, and the Tor des Géants
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019056/Runaway to Record Breaker: Zhao Jiaju on Willpower, Pain, and the Tor des Géants
World.content:
Editor’s note: In the early hours of Sept. 16, Zhao Jiaju crossed the finish line to win the 2026 Tor des Géants endurance trail race, covering 336.1 kilometers and cumulative elevation gain exceeding 24,000 meters through the Italian Alps in a record 65 hours, 55 minutes, and 22 seconds. Here, the 31-year-old talks with The Paper about the experience and shares how it feels to be the race’s first Asian champion.

The Paper: How’s your body holding up?

Zhao: It’s dehydrated. During the race, the sun just hammered down on us. It was so dry that my lips split open. My scalp was scorched red — in a few days the skin will start peeling off in sheets.

But still, I’m recovering, getting better day by day. My feet still hurt, but not as badly as they did. My upper body is fine, actually. It’s the legs that took the real beating.

Sometimes when I touch my body, it feels unreal. That feeling was far stronger yesterday; it’s less noticeable today. Even when I pinch myself, it doesn’t hurt as much.

The Paper: You wore the No. 1 bib, and at the start said you were going to win in record time. Were you really that confident?

Zhao: I didn’t think my physical capacity was strong enough, but I knew my willpower was. After all these years on the trail, it’s been honed to a fine degree. I knew the Tor des Géants would come down to sheer willpower, to who could hold on longest when everything inside you is screaming to stop. I knew that’s where I held an advantage.

Before the race, I truly meant that bold claim about breaking the record. I believed I could, and that’s the power of belief.

I started running 100-kilometer ultramarathons in 2017. Since then, I’ve been regularly competing in 168-kilometer events. I’ve always been able to run long distances. I didn’t train specifically for this race. I just spent about a month here (in northwestern Italy’s Aosta Valley) beforehand to adapt to the terrain, altitude, and food. After that, it was about drawing on years of accumulated endurance.

The Paper: Did you complete any 300-kilometer training runs?

Zhao: No, but I often run 168 kilometers. When I was 23, I competed in the Ultra Gobi (an ultra-endurance race through China’s northwestern Gobi Desert). I could handle 400 kilometers of hardship even then. So finishing 330 kilometers wasn’t the hard part. The challenge was setting a faster time and pushing my limits.

The Paper: When did you feel most exhausted?

Zhao: Climbing that final slope — everything hit me all at once. When I was most exhausted, my mind was still clear, but my vision began to blur. All I could make out was the hazy white glow where my torchlight hit the ground. My eyes kept trying to close.

I repeated to myself, “You’re doing something incredible right now.” When my eyes were about to shut, I’d slap myself hard across the face, bite down on my tongue, and grit my teeth. Every slap, every bite brought a moment of clarity. My vision would snap back into focus, like a camera lens adjusting from blurry to sharp.

The Paper: Footage from the race shows you running alone at night, with only a small headlamp beam cutting through the darkness. What would you think about in those moments?

Zhao: “Get to the next aid station. Get supplies.” For the first 200 kilometers, my mind would wander. But during that final 100 kilometers, I didn’t dare think about anything because the course has many dangerous sections. I focused entirely on the ground in front of me, reminding myself how many more climbs were ahead, what the next ascent would be like, and how to navigate the terrain beneath my feet. There was no mental space for anything else.

The Paper: What was it like having your wife at the aid stations, preparing food for you and helping with massages and recovery?

Zhao: She really went through it. I need to buy her some gifts to make up for it.

Many top Chinese runners now have family members provide support at aid stations. The people closest to you know you best, and they can tolerate your moods. During a race, when you’re pushed to extreme limits, your truest self comes out. Having your closest people there to help you makes it easier.

Things have gradually gotten better for athletes from China. Sponsors are now willing to support our families in traveling with us to compete, which is really helpful.

The Paper: Do you remember the moment you crossed the finish line?

Zhao: Honestly, I was thinking, “Just take me back. I need to lie down.” I was practically asleep on my feet. When I reached the summit, my vision blurred. I’d been forcing myself to hang on, pushing to the line. The moment I crossed it and all that tension was finally released — the full-body pain, that overwhelming urge to sleep — it swept over me.

My body and mind had reached breaking point. But once I recovered a bit, I was extremely excited. I looked at what I’d achieved and realized that I’d pushed past my limits. That really hit me.

The Paper: After the race, you said you felt “worse than death.” Why put yourself through this?

Zhao: Achieving the glory and fame I dreamed about as a kid — that’s part of it. But I also want to push the boundaries of my body and my will. That way, when I face even greater obstacles, I’ll be able to get through them more easily. I need these moments of suffering to become a stronger, tougher version of myself. I came out here representing China, and so many people were cheering me on. I had to show everyone how powerful human endurance and willpower can be.

When I was 15, I was inspired by that same kind of energy. Back then, I wanted to be a champion fighter. I watched Bruce Lee films, and he made me realize that human potential is limitless, that you have to learn how to command your body and unleash its full power. Now I hope I can pass that energy on to others who need it.

The Paper: Does being champion bring pressure or motivation?

Zhao: Win or lose, it’s motivation. I’ve had an optimistic attitude ever since I was a child.

My family treated me well, so I had a carefree childhood. I’ve always loved to laugh — so much so that I developed terrible forehead wrinkles very early. In elementary school, my physical education teacher said I looked like a little old man. I loved making people in my class laugh, too. That gave me the ability to transform negative energy into something positive and feed it back to myself. That’s what’s allowed me to keep going.

The Paper: Some have talked about you working as a delivery rider, but you’ve had many different jobs, right?

Zhao: I’ve been a florist, I prepared steamed dishes in a restaurant, and I worked at a hardware factory in Hangzhou (capital of the eastern Zhejiang province). Later I delivered food in Wuhan (capital of the central Hubei province), made fried chicken, and worked at a hotel front desk as well as an electronics factory in (the southwestern city of) Chongqing.

I was even a security guard at the Beijing National Stadium. I worked at karaoke bars in several cities — I think that was the most comfortable. It left me lots of time for training. I would get off work at 3 or 4 in the morning and head straight to training. I’d then wake at noon, have lunch, and train again in the afternoon.

The Paper: What first interested you in trail running?

Zhao: Before trail running, I was into marathons. In 2014, I was working at a flower shop when I saw marathon banners during a morning run around Hangzhou’s West Lake. That’s how I learned about competitive races. My dream back then was to become a champion fighter, but I had no systematic training, no club willing to take me on, and no way to compete. I was desperate for a path forward. I thought marathons suited me — they’re all about willpower, right? When I started competing, my initial results weren’t ideal. After a year or two, my performances improved, but still not enough to break into China’s top tier.

Then I discovered trail running. In 2016, I saw people taking part in 100-kilometer races. This was an even greater test of willpower. So I quit my job to compete, throwing myself wholeheartedly into trail running. The sport was still relatively new in China, and the prize money was generous. I was determined to carve out my place. I won my first championship in 2017. After that, things just kept getting better.

The Paper: You’ve repeatedly mentioned the importance of willpower.

Zhao: It goes back to when I ran away from home at 15. My parents worked in factories and were raising my younger sister. They wanted me to find a stable job, learn a trade, and live a comfortable, ordinary life. But I wanted to chase my dreams, to become like the people I saw on TV — strong, accomplished, and the best at what they did. So I left home. My parents even reported me missing to the police. More than 10 days passed before I called them to let them know I was safe. They told me that as long as I wasn’t doing anything illegal, I could do whatever I wanted, and that I should tell them if I ran into trouble. But when difficulties arose, I didn’t want them to worry. I felt I had to rely on myself. If you depend on your family, you’ll never grow strong enough to fly on your own.

Back then I lived on the streets. In Hubei province, I walked from Fang County, on the edge of Shennongjia forest area, to Shiyan City — about 100 kilometers. Those were the most painful 11 days of my life. I walked under the blazing sun. The daytime temperature rose to at least 39 degrees Celsius. I walked all day and into the next, blisters forming all over my feet. That was the first time I’d walked such a distance. I wore a tank top; my skin turned black, burned and peeling. I thought, “How can life be this painful?” But when I finally got through it, I felt incredible. I was 15 years old, and I’d endured all that suffering.

That lesson carries over into my racing. The person you have to defeat is yourself. Those hardships are what made me stronger. Racing has put me through everything — brutal weather, muscle pain, nausea, dizziness, nosebleeds. All that suffering. I’ve never felt sorry for myself or wanted others to pity me. The suffering I seek out makes me powerful. It makes me fearless for the future. That’s why I love this kind of pain.

The Paper: Is that because you’ve always had a clear direction?

Zhao: Yes. From the start, I’ve had one goal: to be one in a million, to find the path where I can shine, and keep working at it step by step. There’s no need to rush. As long as I keep at it, I’ll succeed.

The Paper: What’s your vision for the future of trail running?

Zhao: Whether it’s race organizers, participants, or local residents — everyone recognizes the balance between humans and nature. As more people venture into the mountains, the mountains should remain clean and beautiful. I’d love to see that become a reality.

The Paper: After completing the 2026 Tor des Géants, you said you wouldn’t compete in any more ultramarathons over 168 kilometers. Is that your body talking, or a shift in mindset?

Zhao: This race pushed me to my limit. I was truly exhausted. I don’t plan to race such a long distance again in the near future. To break through again would be excruciating. I don’t know what price I’d have to pay. So for now, I don’t want to try.

The Paper: So what are your plans now?

Zhao: I’ll continue racing. I love the feeling of standing on that starting line. Winning once doesn’t mean you’ll win next time. Trail running depends on your physical state. As long as I’m fit to race, I’ll be on that starting line, blood pumping, ready to give everything to my next race.

I haven’t thought about retirement. If one day I stop placing in races — perhaps when I’m in my 50s and can no longer satisfy my competitive drive — then I could work behind the scenes. Many athletes’ lives have shown us that you can win world championships in your 40s and 50s. I still have expectations for myself at that age.

Reported by Wei Jiaming.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Paper. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Chen Yue; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Zhao Jiaju crosses the finish line to win the 2026 Tor des Géants, Italy, Sept. 16, 2026. From @长腿公子 on Weibo)

World.title: Cooking to Drones: Shanghai Hosts Record WorldSkills Competition
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019055/Cooking to Drones: Shanghai Hosts Record WorldSkills Competition
World.content:
From preparing restaurant-worthy meals and repairing cars to programming robots and operating drones, young people from around the world will put their skills to the test in Shanghai this week at the largest WorldSkills Competition yet.

The event opens Tuesday with a record 1,385 competitors from 68 countries and regions, marking its first edition on the Chinese mainland. Often dubbed the “Skills Olympics,” the biennial competition will see participants vie for medals across 64 disciplines, ranging from traditional trades to advanced manufacturing and emerging technologies.

Unlike conventional sporting events, WorldSkills tests competitors on their ability to perform practical tasks drawn from the workplace. Participants generally must be under 22, although the age limit extends to 25 for some disciplines, and have between 15 and 22 hours to complete their assignments. They can compete only once in their lifetime.

In cooking, competitors must plan menus, prepare and plate dishes, and serve them on time while meeting food safety standards. Automobile technology contestants diagnose and repair vehicle faults, while robot systems integration contestants assemble and program industrial robots to perform automated tasks. This year’s debut unmanned aerial systems discipline tests skills in building, testing, and maintaining drones.

It’s one of seven disciplines added this year to reflect changing labor-market demands, with the others including dental prosthetics, digital media interactive design, intelligent security technology, rail vehicle technology, retail sales, and software testing.

Chen Yujie, deputy director and researcher at the Vocational and Skills Research Office of the Chinese Academy of Labour and Social Security, told state agency Xinhua that WorldSkills regularly adds, merges, or eliminates disciplines to keep pace with industry changes. Chen added that even established disciplines update their technical standards and competition content.

The inaugural competition, held in Madrid in 1950, featured just six disciplines — fitting, pattern making, turning, electrical installations, milling, and cabinetmaking — and 24 competitors from two countries.

This year’s opening ceremony will take place Tuesday evening at the Shanghai World Expo Cultural Center. The roughly 90-minute event centers on the mortise-and-tenon joint, a traditional Chinese woodworking technique.

Competition begins Wednesday and runs through Saturday at the National Exhibition and Convention Center, where roughly 300,000 square meters of space has been converted into workshops ranging from professional kitchens to drone-flight zones. Some 400,000 visitors are expected over the four days.

Admission is free, but visitors must reserve a time slot online. Once inside, they can watch competitors at work from just a meter away or try their hand at practical skills. Some events, including beauty therapy, hairdressing, and restaurant service, will also recruit members of the public to take part.

The event will also host the WorldSkills Conference, bringing together more than 2,000 delegates, including 50 government ministers, to discuss issues such as AI’s impact on labor and green development.

China joined WorldSkills International in 2010 and made its competitive debut the following year in London. From 2011 through 2024, Chinese competitors won 93 gold, 41 silver, and 28 bronze medals, along with 71 Medallions for Excellence. China topped both the gold-medal table and overall team rankings for four consecutive editions.

China will field competitors in all 64 disciplines this year, with vocational-school teachers and students making up more than 60% of its delegation, according to the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security.

(Header image: South Korean mechatronics competitors prepare for the 48th WorldSkills Competition in Shanghai, Sept. 21, 2026. Xinhua)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019050/China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.title: China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019050/China Misses Basketball Medal in 2nd-Worst Asian Games Finish
World.content:
China’s men’s basketball team has suffered its second-worst defeat in its history at the Asian Games, calling into question the coach’s abilities and the team’s training methods.

On Sunday, China lost 70-79 to Iran, two days after it lost 77-97 to Japan, host of this year’s Games, its second failure to reach the finals and its largest-margin loss in men’s basketball at the tournament. The country finished fourth, one place higher than at the 2014 Asian Games in Incheon — its worst result ever.

China has claimed eight Asian Games titles, with its most recent gold coming in 2018. Since then, China has failed to win the title.

Head coach Guo Shiqiang said the team fatigued toward the end of the tournament, noting that only nine players were available for rotation partway through the Games due to injuries. He also said the team’s younger players lacked major tournament experience and had struggled to play consistently, and that “the team had failed to execute its pregame tactical plans.”

China’s unusually long training and competition period this summer has been a focus of criticism. The team spent around 140 days in camp before the Games, domestic media reported. Internationally, teams typically spend only one to three weeks at training camps, widely considered to be intensive and demanding.

Criticism has also centered on Guo, 51, a former starting point guard for China’s national team who began coaching the team in 2006 and became head coach in 2009. After leaving the team to coach locally in 2010, he returned as head coach in 2024, and led China to a runner-up finish at the 2025 FIBA Asia Cup.

Critics have questioned Guo’s tactical approach. Against Iran, China’s defense focused heavily on protecting the net rather than the court’s three-point line, leaving space for their opponents to take jump shots and make three-pointers. The team also struggled to secure rebounds in both its matches against Iran and Japan.

Others criticized Guo’s offensive strategy, arguing that he relied too heavily on the backcourt, that players became isolated at crucial moments, and that his in-game player selection was overly conservative.

The defeats have prompted broader discussion about whether China’s traditional approach of requiring athletes to spend a large portion of the year in training camps can keep pace with changes in the sport, particularly the increasing emphasis on spacing, perimeter shooting, and shooting efficiency.

“Everyone on our team has worked extremely hard this summer,” Guo said in a post-game interview with domestic media. “Every member of the Chinese men’s basketball team has put in a tremendous amount of effort.” His comments sparked widespread backlash online, with many arguing that the team’s prolonged exhaustion from training camp caused the poor results.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Jiao Boqiao (left) of China blocks a shot by Mohammad Jamshidi of Iran during the men’s basketball bronze medal match between China and Iran at the 20th Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 20, 2026. Andy Cheung/Getty Images/VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019040/Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.title: Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019040/Three Sisters Cross China to See What Keeps Their Family Apart
World.content:
YUNNAN, Southwest China – Growing up in a remote mountain village in Yunnan province near China’s southwestern border with Vietnam, Zhou Lifang had only ever seen clouds from below. In late July, on her first flight, the 16-year-old saw them from above.

“I thought clouds were transparent because (my) textbook said clouds are made of water vapor,” she tells Sixth Tone. “But I didn’t expect them to be like a white wall. The clouds you see from the ground are in pieces, but from the sky they are one big mass.”

Lifang and her 14-year-old twin sisters, Zhou Lixin and Zhou Liyi, were among 145 students from Yunnan taking part in “Mountain-Sea Bond,” a four-day program in Shanghai that included reunions with parents working in the city.

The sisters are among China’s “left-behind children,” who remain in their home communities while their parents migrate for work, often placed in the care of grandparents or other relatives. China had 9 million such children in 2022, according to the 2023 Rural Education Development Report.

Born in Kunming, Yunnan’s provincial capital, the sisters have lived for more than a decade with their grandparents in a village in Malipo, a county in the Wenshan Zhuang and Miao Autonomous Prefecture roughly 400 kilometers away by road. Their parents, Zhou Yuneng and Zhang Shunfen, now work in Shanghai, where Zhou drives for a ride-hailing service and Zhang sorts groceries at a supermarket warehouse.

Smartphones have long allowed Zhou and Zhang to remain involved in their daughters’ lives from afar. They check in, offer advice, and try to mediate fights between the sisters. But they can see and hear only what the girls choose to share, and cannot always persuade them to talk.

Asked how well she knows her daughters now, the mother says they all like drawing, then pauses. “Close to zero,” she admits. “I don’t really know what they like anymore.”

After more than a decade of parenting largely by phone, Zhou and Zhang would spend two weeks sharing a 20-square-meter room in Shanghai with their daughters, their longest stretch together since the girls went to live with their grandparents.

On her own

Before the sisters left early that morning, their grandmother, Kuang Tianzhen, 64, tucked 50 yuan ($7) into each girl’s pocket, twice their usual weekly allowance. Rumors of scams in their border village had made her uneasy about the journey.

“Where will you stay in Wenshan?” she asks, the prefecture’s seat. “This is all reliable, right?”

After the neighbor’s car carrying them disappeared from view, their grandfather, Zhou Shucheng, 72, sat brooding outside the house for at least half an hour, staring down the rain-soaked road and gently petting the tabby cat his granddaughters had adopted.

Four hours later, the sisters arrived at a hotel in Wenshan for a predeparture meeting with participants from surrounding villages and counties. They would spend the night there, then continue to Kunming the next day for the flight to Shanghai.

“Are you Zhou Lifang’s parents? Have your three children arrived yet?” a trip organizer asks over the phone.

“I am Zhou Lifang,” she replies. “We’re already here in the lobby.”

Lifang was the only child in the tour’s WeChat group; everyone else was a parent. She had followed instructions about when and where to meet and confirmed the arrangements for all three sisters.

Inside the hotel’s meeting hall, grandparents sit beside children waiting to register while organizers address the crowd from the stage.

Elders are heard asking “Where should I sign?” and “Do I fill this part in?” At the line marked “guardian,” some pause, unsure whether to write their own names or those of the children’s parents in Shanghai.

One grandmother checks her granddaughter’s schoolbag, rebraids her hair, and films her on her phone. When organizers ask the adults to leave, she goes downstairs, then turns back and slips inside again.

Lifang sat quietly on one side of a wide pillar, her twin sisters on the other. Unlike many of the children around them, the sisters had arrived without a grandparent.

The sisters began attending boarding school around age 6. When home, they helped with farm work and tended the family’s wood-burning stove. Before they had smartphones of their own, they called their parents using their grandmother’s phone or a public telephone at school.

At 12, Lifang went alone to a hospital near her school for a tuberculosis screening while her mother guided her through the process over a video call.

“Sometimes I felt pretty helpless,” she says. “I would ask adults passing by for help and follow their directions.” On other visits, her mother advised her to follow a classmate who knew the hospital better.

When the village prepared to allocate plots of collectively owned farmland, Lifang took the call and passed the information to her grandmother. During school vacations, she tidied the twins’ room and called her mother when she needed money or help handling her sisters.

Her grandfather divides farm work and allowances equally among the three girls. But when they argue, he tells Lifang, “You’re the older sister. You’re the eldest. You should give way to them.”

The twins usually side with each other against Lifang, and a stray remark can set off a fierce argument. From Shanghai, Zhang tells her, “If someone hits you, whether it’s your sisters or your schoolmates, you should hit them back.”

Lifang sometimes goes into a room and locks the door instead. “Then they can’t come in,” she says. “They’ll play a game, and after that, everything will be fine.”

She has repeatedly asked her parents for a room of her own. When she wants to be alone, she sometimes sits on a swing her father built on the rooftop. On a nearby window, smiling faces the sisters traced with their fingers years ago remain visible beneath layers of dust.

“Sometimes I wish I could be the younger sister, not the older one,” Lifang says.

Close to zero

When the twins moved to the village at 3, they sometimes cried for their mother. Their grandmother would carry one of them outside and point toward Kunming, along the road winding over the mountain.

“I’d hold her for a while and tell her that her mother was there,” Kuang recalls. “Then she’d stop crying. They’re good girls, easy to coax.”

Their father had tried to leave the twins in the village a year earlier. He drove them there when they were 2, but couldn’t bear to leave them and took them back to Kunming.

By 2015, private kindergarten in Kunming cost 1,800 yuan ($250) per child per month, meaning fees for all three would have consumed 5,400 yuan of the couple’s roughly 6,000-yuan monthly income.

The family was also hundreds of thousands of yuan in debt after rebuilding the village house and paying hospital bills for the grandfather and one of the twins, who had spent several weeks in neonatal intensive care with meningitis. Because the girls lacked local household registration, or hukou, enrolling them in Kunming’s public schools was difficult.

For the next decade, their parents remained in Kunming, making the six-hour drive to the village every month or two for a weekend or holiday.

Years of installing wood floors damaged both of Zhou’s knees. The work required him to squat and sometimes kneel. “After every shift, I would get off my scooter and walk stiff-legged,” he says. In 2025, chronic arthritis forced him out of construction, and the couple moved to Shanghai, approximately 2,500 kilometers away.

When the sisters missed their parents, Lifang says, they video-called them. “Mom and Dad would always say they only had a few more days of work and would be back to see us soon.”

Over time, however, the girls stopped asking when their parents would return for good. “They used to say, ‘Mom, I miss you,’” Zhang says. “Since I moved to Shanghai, I hardly ever hear that anymore.”

In 2023, the couple installed a camera at the gate of the village house, primarily for safety. It lets them check on the grandfather and see when the girls return from school. They chose not to install one in the girls’ bedroom.

“I just feel that girls, after all, need some privacy,” Zhang says.

The mother also bought her daughters smartphones with large screens to make video calls easier and placed few restrictions on how they used them.

“Kids today are different from us back then,” she says. “Digital devices aren’t just for studying anymore. They have access to so many things on their phones. I don’t restrict them too much.”

The twins often decline their parents’ calls or hang up after a few sentences. Sometimes, one answers while playing on the computer, points the phone’s camera at the ceiling, and keeps playing.

Asked why, one of the twins says, “Just because I don’t have the patience.”

Every time this happens, Zhang just smiles and rarely lets her temper show.

“I feel that if I push too hard, I lose the right to speak,” she says. “I’m afraid they’ll think, ‘You didn’t raise me. You weren’t there when I was small, and now you want to tell me what to do.’ So sometimes I can’t be too direct. I have to be careful how I put it.”

When Lifang and the twins argue, the parents try to settle their disputes by phone, usually scolding both sides. Each girl comes away believing that she alone has been blamed.

“That’s because of the distance and what a phone call can’t do,” the mother says. “If it were face to face, a few sentences would clear it up.”

Unlike the twins, Lifang video calls Zhang almost every day and has her saved in her phone as “Dear Mom.” But she seldom calls Zhou. “Dad is quite busy driving day and night, so I rarely call him,” Lifang says. “I’m afraid of interrupting his work. I feel like I’m not close to him because he’s too strict.”

Even with Zhang, much of Lifang’s life remains outside their conversations. At school, some classmates seek her out for tarot readings, calling her “Master Zhou.” Others mock the way she speaks, comparing it to barking, and give her insulting nicknames.

Lifang spends nearly every break between classes drawing. She draws when she feels happy, angry, or embarrassed, and says it helps her relax. She keeps one sketchbook, which she rarely shows others, for times when she feels low.

One drawing shows a figure with its arms crossed and an X over its mouth. In the background, Lifang has written, “What if speaking is also a fault?”

“All I can do is draw them as ugly monsters,” Lifang says.

She closes the sketchbook.

“There are some words I cannot show,” she says. “Cannot.”

In another sketchbook, Lifang has created Yumeng, a cheerful girl from the sea who grows increasingly troubled as she tries to save a city from destruction. “Why should I, who am already living such a miserable life, have to save others?” the character asks.

Lifang also has a circle of friends her parents know little about. She met them through a nonviolent multiplayer game she describes as “healing.” Unlike the competitive games her sisters prefer, it lets players explore different settings, build homes and farms together, and talk.

“Besides my best friend at school, they are the most important friends in my life,” Lifang says.

Before boarding the flight to Shanghai, Lifang sent them an update: “I’m boarding now, so I can’t reply to your messages. I’ll send you some amazing pictures later.”

Under one roof

Two days after reuniting privately with their parents, all three sisters stepped onto a stage in matching pale green T-shirts and brand-new canvas shoes their mother had prepared before their arrival. “Mountain-Sea Bond” organizers had chosen the family for a letter reading at the Aug. 1 reunion ceremony.

Standing between the twins, Lifang began reading, with Zhang beside her daughters and Zhou watching from the audience.

“Before, I never understood why you were always away and could not be with us,” she reads. “Only on this trip, after coming to Shanghai where you live and work, did I truly understand how hard you work and how much you have given.”

When Lifang finishes, the audience applauds, and Zhou begins to sob. As the sisters come down from the stage, he pulls the twins close and continues crying until his face turns red. The twins’ eyes fill with tears.

“You don’t see your children often,” he says after regaining his composure. “And then suddenly you realize they have grown up all at once.”

After the ceremony, the family go to Jing’an Joy City, a Shanghai mall the sisters had long wanted to visit for its anime shops. Lifang taught herself to draw manga and now takes commissions through an app from clients across China, earning several dozen yuan per drawing. She hopes to attend one of China’s leading art academies, though she usually tells adults she wants to become a civil servant like her older cousin.

The program ended that day, but the sisters remained in Shanghai for the rest of their two-week stay. All five shared a one-room, 20-square-meter unit with a private bathroom and an induction cooker in one corner.

Zhou and Zhang had moved there at the beginning of the year, hoping the girls might eventually join them in Shanghai. Before the trip, Lifang had assumed the move had made her parents’ lives easier.

“Now that Mom and Dad work in Shanghai, the conditions are better, and the work is a little easier,” she says.

Zhou no longer installs floors, but his ride-hailing shifts often last at least 12 hours. “If you work less, you can’t make enough,” he says. “You drive for 11 or 12 hours, come back, charge the car, make something to eat, then sleep. The next day, you get up and repeat it. That’s the job.”

Zhang works similar hours sorting groceries at a supermarket warehouse and has no regular weekends. Sometimes they go an entire day without seeing each other awake; one leaves breakfast behind before the other gets up.

During the visit, Zhou took another week off from driving, while Zhang continued working. The parents would not allow the girls to go out alone in an unfamiliar city.

Before leaving Yunnan, Lifang says, “I want to help my mom sort groceries at the supermarket warehouse.” In Shanghai, she often accompanied Zhang to work, while the twins remained in the apartment.

One night, Zhang returned late from work and began tidying the room. One of the twins ran over and hugged her.

“Mom, I feel like you’ve worked so hard,” Zhang recalls her saying. The girl then began to cry.

“I feel like she’s really growing up,” Zhang says.

Despite all five sharing one room, the sisters argued less during the visit. Disputes that had been difficult to settle over the phone rarely became as heated in person, Zhang says.

Even before his daughters arrived, Zhou had been considering returning to Yunnan after another year in Shanghai.

“Whatever happens, I should go back and do whatever work I can, as long as we are by their side,” he says.

But Zhou has taken no steps toward moving and cannot say what work he might find near the village. Its karst terrain leaves little room to expand farmland, and 796 of its 2,172 residents work elsewhere, according to a village official.

Zhou and Zhang each earn about 8,000 yuan ($1,120) a month in Shanghai, though Zhou can make more by taking fewer days off. Returning would mean giving up the income that had drawn them farther from their daughters.

During their stay in Shanghai, the sisters called their grandmother about once a week. One day at a café, a blue parrot perched on Lifang’s shoulder. She has long wanted one like it, and blue is her favorite color. Lifang immediately called Kuang on video.

“Grandma, look what’s on my shoulder,” Lifang says. “Isn’t it impressive?”

“Behave yourself,” Kuang replies. “Where are the twins?”

“They went with Mom to work.”

“When will you come back?” Kuang asks. “How are you getting home?”

“Dad says he’ll drive us back next weekend,” Lifang says. “My school starts early.”

Editor: Apurva.
