Taranaki pig farmer goes whole hog to stay ahead Country Life Download MP3 13m

Follow Country Life on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, iHeart or wherever you get your podcasts.

Stanley, who orginally started out in viticulture and winemaking, came back to the family farm 12 years ago.

His grandfather and great uncle bought the original farm, a rehab block, and farmed both dairy cows and pigs. That was continued by Stanley's father and his brother.

Six years ago, the family decided to expand the pig operation and move into cropping "because we thought that we could make better utilisation of our fertiliser that the pigs were creating for us".

The 133-hectare farm now grows silage, hay and maize for neighbouring livestock farmers, "and we do it on 100 percent natural fertiliser".

The "farrowing to finish" operation runs 500 sows and delivers 240 to 260 grown-on pigs weekly to the domestic market, Stanley said.

Karl Stanley with one of his days-old piglets RNZ/Sally Round

Stanley Bros is among the 52 percent of New Zealand's commercial pig farms which keep pigs fully indoors.

Stanley's grandfather used to keep his sows outside but the family learnt Taranaki's volcanic soils were not suitable.

"Pigs can tend to turn the place over in the mud pretty quick."

Going indoors was also a way of staying viable "when you're competing with the foreign pork coming in".

Three years ago a $1m upgrade to the four farrowing (birthing) units saw larger pens and nesting areas alongside the farrowing crates which restrict the sow's movement.

"We've always had this mentality on the farm that we'd always be hoping to be two or three steps ahead."

The welfare code is tightening to reduce the time sows spend in the metal crates (from a maximum 33 days to seven). Moveable rails will be mandated and minimum space for grower pigs increased by 13.3 percent. These changes must happen by the end of 2035.

Debate continues over whether farrowing crates should still be allowed at all, after animal welfare advocates won a High Court case in 2020 banning them outright, as in a handful of European countries.

That ruling was superceded by an easing of regulations brought in by the Coalition government in 2025 with a 10 year transition period.

Piglets suckle on a sow in a farrowing crate RNZ/Sally Round

Stanley said his new shed will lower stocking density throughout the farm and should be up and running by Christmas.

"Our changes will be certainly towards making sure that we're well and truly ahead of the new regulations.

"Being steps ahead gives you flexibility and also better efficiencies, but also just being a few steps ahead means that you can really get yourself scope."

Stanley took Country Life on a tour of the piggery and farrowing area, where newborn piglets scurried between a nesting box under a heat lamp to suckle on their mum, who is restricted to lying - enclosed by the rails - for two and a half weeks, able to sit up but not move around.

Weaned piglets RNZ/Sally Round

"It's 100 percent protection of the piglet. A sow can be a little bit clumsy at times and lay-ons are certainly a concern.

"When the new system gets put in place with the temporary confinement, she'll be confined for the first three days after farrowing and then she will be able to hop out and rotate around and do her thing."

He hopes the current nine-percent piglet mortality rate will not climb further under the new system which will see a refit to allow the rails to be pushed back.

"It's going to find that balance between the welfare and protection of the piglets and also the welfare of the sow.

"Probably the hardest part is we're competing with imported product that's not following the same standards."

Grower pigs RNZ/Sally Round

Stanley's refit comes as the pork industry continues to warn that local producers are struggling against a flood of lower welfare imports.

He hopes to make changes to the first farrowing unit in the next year to 18 months, then acclimatise staff and fine-tune things "to make sure that the piglet welfare and the sow's welfare is at the optimum and before we make the changes to the rest of the facility".

Along from the farrowing area a nursery houses hordes of tiny piglets in 22 degree warmth "running around and being silly buggers like they want to be", Stanley said.

Welfare regulations require enrichment which Stanley said would be enhanced in the new development.

"We've gone from little ballcock balls that they can push around and play with or else going to the chains, which they quite enjoy ... because they sit there and chew it with their teeth and just something for them to do. A bit of fun.

"We'll be certainly adding more."

The foundations of the new piggery at Stanley Bros in Opunake RNZ/Sally Round

Stanley said experts from Europe - where some countries' welfare regulations are tightening too - had advised on the new development.

"They're 100 percent to increase the square meterage of the entire farm without really increasing the actual production. So this expenditure is not a gain in production, unfortunately, but it's certainly going to give us a better, how would I say, a better future knowing that we've got that scope."

The adjoining 400-panel solar farm, put in two years ago, produces 200 kilowatts, enough to power the piggery from 9am to 5pm during the summer, with lower production during the winter, Stanley said.

A solar farm was put in in 2024 to power the piggery RNZ/Sally Round

It's a saving of $75,000 annually and with power 10 percent of the farm's cost, they hope to invest further in wind turbines and batteries to create more energy.

"It's a great investment, and it's good for us, lowers our footprint."

Stanley said the overall investment had been daunting and had caused "a few headaches" and he hoped consumers would back New Zealand pork growers like him.

World.title: ACT promises noise cameras to combat boy racers in Tāmaki
World.content:
The ACT Party is pledging to crack down on noisy vehicles and hike fines for drivers causing a nuisance.

It wants to spend $2 million on buying and installing 20 relocatable noise cameras, initially rolling them out in Tāmaki.

A noise camera is used to detect particular sounds and then identify and record the vehicle they come from, information from the NZTA website said.

A noise camera mounted during a 2013 trial to detect loud engine braking. Supplied/ NZTA

ACT Tāmaki candidate James Christmas said his election campaign door-knocking missions had drawn consistent pleas to do something about noisy neighbourhoods.

"People should be able to sleep, relax and enjoy their homes, without having their street turned into someone else's racetrack," he said.

"I can see the attraction for boy racers to come to Tāmaki, but it's not fair on the families and working people who have their life disrupted, just because they live in a great location with nice streets."

Such disturbance was already illegal, but effective currently, enforcement relies on a police officer being in the right place at the right time, Christmas said.

If elected, ACT would:

Introduce a fleet of relocatable noise cameras to be deployed in communities frequented by excessively noisy vehicles

Establish an objective noise limit measured by the cameras (86 decibels on roads with speed limits of 50 km/h or less and 90 decibels on roads between 50-70 km/h)

Increase penalties for excessive vehicle noise from $50 to $300, with the maximum court fine increasing from $1000 to $3000.

Christmas said noise cameras would capture evidence of offending the moment it happened.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said everyone generally was "a bit sick of boy racers", but ACT's timing was transparent.

"I've been fighting for a local community in my own electorate for the last three years to get any government agency to take it seriously.

"There is certainly more work to be done on boy racers and on the noise and the nuisance that they're creating, but suddenly doing this in an election campaign when they've ignored the issue for the last three years looks a bit rich," he said.

World.title: Adam Scott, Min Woo Lee lead sweep of US at Presidents Cup
World.content:
Adam Scott and Min Woo Lee have helped the Internationals to a shock 7-3 Presidents Cup lead over the USA with an incredible sweep of the foursomes matches.

The Australian pair were mighty in giving the Internationals a golden opportunity to win the Cup for the first time since 1998 as Geoff Ogilvy's underdogs claimed all five points on day two in Illinois.

Scott had his long wand weaving magic in teaming with South African Christiaan Bezuidenhout for a 3 and 2 win over Justin Thomas and Cameron Young.

Lee partnered New Zealand Cup debutant Ryan Fox to a clutch 1 up win over the American pair of double major winners Collin Morikawa and Wyndham Clark.

Reigning Open champion Fox sealed victory on the 18th green after Lee's supreme driving proved a feature of the day at Medina Country Club.

Canadians Corey Conners and Nick Taylor set the tone for the Internationals with a nerve-shredding 1 up win over world number one Scottie Scheffler and Sam Burns.

Adam Scott has played every Presidents Cup since 2003. (Getty Images: Luke Hales)

Clinging to a one-hole lead heading up the last hole, Taylor's errant drive placed the duo under extreme pressure but he replied with a magical approach to two feet after Conners was forced to lay up 148 yards short of the green.

Conners duly holed the putt to leave tie the scores up at 3-3 after Team USA won three of the five day-one four-ball matches.

A 4 and 3 victory for Tom Kim and Si Woo Kim over Xander Schauffele and Patrick Cantlay and a 3 and 2 win for fellow South Korean Sung-jae Im and Japanese superstar Hideki Matsuyama over Russell Henley and Jacob Bridgeman completed only the Internationals' second-ever foursomes whitewash.

With 20 points still up for grabs, the 13th edition of the Presidents Cup is realistically only one-third through.

But the Americans will still need to collect 12.5 points from the remaining three sessions to pull off a comeback victory.

There will be eight more team matches on Saturday (Sunday AEST) before 12 last-day singles encounters.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Stunning Lions comeback breaks Freo hearts in all-time great grand final
World.content:
Brisbane has claimed its third straight premiership after erasing a 17-point deficit inside the final four minutes of the game to overrun a stunned Fremantle in the AFL grand final.

The Lions kicked four straight goals after 'Wharfie Time' was triggered to claim a 14.12 (96) to 12.17 (89) win in front of 100,023 spectators at the MCG.

Fremantle forward Patrick Voss's third goal of the match with 4:18 remaining on the clock was followed by the iconic bell toll of 'Wharfie Time', only for the season-long gimmick to backfire spectacularly on the Dockers.

Quick goals to Charlie Cameron and Zac Bailey put the Lions back within a goal with 3:31 left on the clock before a pair of Logan Morris goals delivered Brisbane the premiership.

The first of those goals came via a set shot as Morris kicked truly from 40m out to put the Lions in front with just over a minute left on the clock, before he put the final nail in the Fremantle coffin with another goal with 12 seconds remaining. All three of Morris's goals came in the final quarter.

The three-peat is the second for Brisbane in club history after the Leigh Matthews-led sides claimed flags between 2001 and 2003.

Fremantle forward Shai Bolton was the surprising choice for the Norm Smith Medal, becoming the first losing player to win the prestigious honour since Chris Judd in 2005.

There were plenty of concerns about the weather in the lead-up with this year's clash, the first heavily rain-affected decider since Geelong's slugfest with St KIlda in 2009.

Small forwards were always going to be doubly dangerous in slippery conditions and it was fitting that one of the most prolific small forwards in finals history, Cameron, got proceedings underway with a left-footed snap.

Josh Treacy nailed Fremantle's first goal of the match after drilling a set shot from beyond 50m, before Jye Amiss and Patrick Voss joined the party in the second term, with Voss the only multiple goalscorer at half-time.

Treacy was controversially denied a shot at a second goal on the quarter-time siren when umpires deemed a kick into him did not go the required 15m journey.

Brisbane's smalls in the non-Cameron division were also active early, with preliminary final hero Kai Lohmann hitting the scoreboard in the first term following a rapid-fire Morris handball that needed a replay to be believed.

The second quarter was mostly a goal-for-goal affair as Brisbane's Conor McKenna, days after winning the goal of the year, kicked another stunner from an acute angle.

Much of the pre-game focus had been on Lachie Neale and his availability, and Brisbane's star midfielder entered the ground to some hearty boos midway through the opening term.

Brisbane's big off-season recruits, Sam Draper and Oscar Allen, also settled their nerves by making early impacts.

Allen hit the scoreboard in the first quarter before Draper joined the party in the second quarter with a terrific long-range set shot.

There was little separating the two teams as the quarter drew down, with Brisbane co-captain Josh Dunkley denying Fremantle a goal with a pair of desperate smothers inside a minute, the second leaving him with blood gushing from his mouth.

Fremantle began the third quarter in dominant fashion, registering seven of the first nine inside 50s of the quarter.

Amiss kicked the first goal of the quarter after winning a heavyweight grappling match with Darcy Gardiner in the goalsquare before tragedy struck.

Fremantle's inspirational skipper and its longest-tenured player, Alex Pearce, was crumpled in a heap without any contact when chasing a ball on the wing and had his right Achilles heavily taped shortly afterwards.

Dudley's second of the afternoon shortly after Pearce's exit put the Dockers up by 15 points and put Brisbane firmly on the mat.

Just as Brisbane looked dead and buried, Lohmann, Cameron and Allen goaled in quick succession, wiping out what had seemed like a comfortable Fremantle lead in a heartbeat.

Hayden Young restored Fremantle's lead with a terrific running finish on his non-preferred right boot and then doubled up by snapping truly from the same pocket made famous by Dom Sheed in 2018 to give Fremantle a 10-point lead heading into the final change.

The final quarter was a tense affair as Brisbane began it by peppering the goals to no avail.

Michael Frederick snapped truly to put Fremantle up by nine points with 7:37 left on the clock, before Voss thought he had sealed it with 4:18 remaining, as Wharfie time rang out around the ground.

Fremantle could have been further ahead in the final quarter, but left the door ajar after Treacy missed to the right from inside the goal square under heavy pressure from Ryan Lester with 6:36 remaining.

Lions football manager Danny Daly told ABC Sport before the match that Chris Fagan had played 'Wharfie Time' to his players in the week before the game, with players revealing after the match they had been told to use it to energise their own counterattack.

It is the second unsuccessful grand final appearance in Fremantle's 31-year history after losing its only previous decider in 2013 against Hawthorn.

World.title: Aussie star reaches WTA final as opponent says she was 'pressured' to withdraw
World.content:
Australian Talia Gibson has progressed to her first singles final on the main WTA tour at the expense of Tatiana Prozorova, who says she was "pressured" into withdrawing from their semifinal after failing part of a concussion test.

Gibson reached the final of the Singapore Open, where she will face a former grand slam finalist, as this year's French Open runner-up Maya Chwalinska and 2021 US Open finalist Leylah Fernandez face off in their final-four clash.

But 22-year-old Gibson was not required to step on court for her semi after receiving a walkover past Prozorova, who was hit by a smash during a doubles match.

The Russian stayed on the ground for some time before receiving a medical timeout and ultimately retiring from the match with partner Sofya Lansere, handing Australian Ellen Perez and Miyu Kato the victory.

But it later emerged, after Gibson's upset win over seventh seed Maria Sakkari in the quarterfinals, that Prozorova would not be able to line up in the final four.

The world number 180, who stunned popular Filipino third seed Alex Eala in the second round, said her "dream week came to an end" and she was clearly upset with the process.

On Instagram, Prozorova wrote that Kato's smash had mostly hit her shoulder and only "grazed" her cheek.

As she lay on the court, the umpire jumped from their chair and appeared to call for the physio, who Prozorova said "insisted" she leave the court for a medical timeout.

Tatiana Prozorova upset popular third seed Alex Eala earlier in the tournament. (Getty Images: Then Chih Wey/Xinhua)

"Unfortunately, I didn't know I could refuse," she wrote.

"The test wasn't easy. Given that I'd spent over three hours on court each of the last three days, I was fatigued and I struggled with some of the exercises — like standing on one leg with my eyes closed.

"To be honest, even when I'm fresh and well-rested, I find that difficult anyway. I explained this to the physio, too."

Prozorova said that one-legged test was the only aspect of the assessment she did not ace, but it was enough to rule her out.

"The physio also pressured me, implying I couldn't make my own decisions and needed at least six days (!!!) rest from tennis — which sounds crazy considering I was perfectly fine," she wrote.

Prozorova said she went through her usual recovery routine and "felt great" but the wheels were already in motion on the WTA's protocols.

"My team and I had a long discussion with the organisers; throughout the process, the physio pressured everyone present and even claimed I wasn't capable of taking responsibility for my own life," she wrote.

" The organisers' decision really upset me. My dream week came to an end today. "

She called on the WTA to "reconsider" the rules because the current system "renders players absolutely helpless".

If forced to sit out for six days, the 22-year-old will miss the chance to qualify for the China Open in Beijing, which starts on September 30.

"It is completely absurd and an overreach of authority by the WTA staff member," she wrote.

The WTA has been contacted for comment.

World.title: How the Dockers went from perpetual underdogs to top of the game
World.content:
It's a Dockers dream 32 years in the making — Fremantle are just one win away from premiership glory.

To their fans, the Dockers are the perpetual underdogs, a team that — according to historian Les Everett — was started to "dilute the West Coast Eagles".

Victorian clubs feared the Eagles were "getting too powerful" following their 1991 grand final appearance and premierships in 1992 and 1994.

There were many names put forward for Western Australia's second team, all with links to the port and sea, including the Pirates, Pelicans, Sharks, Dolphins and even the Doctors after Perth's famous sea breeze, the Fremantle Doctor.

The Dockers joined the competition in 1995, with futuristic purple footy shorts that were the "roomiest shorts in the AFL" compared to the tight fits of the 1980s.

Fremantle played their first AFL game in April 1995, taking on the Richmond Tigers at the MCG. (Supplied: Fremantle Football Club )

The purple origin

Coach Gerard Neesham paraded the team on the Fremantle Cappuccino Strip, telling reporters at the time "one of our briefs was to be innovative and we have definitely been that."

It was future thinking, with a nod to the past: the purple was inspired by the woollen hats historically worn by port workers, while the red and green colours on the kit came from the maritime signals for port and starboard.

The Dockers' identity is steeped in the maritime history of Fremantle and its dock workers, nicknamed wharfies. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

On the docks of Fremantle, wharfies still wear those purple beanies but in 2026, they have club logos.

As for the spirit of Wharfie Time, "it's passion, resilience and having that fight to never give up," said wharfie Jenson Chattaway.

"There will be tears if we win, I'll be crying for sure," added Port Services Officer Mike White.

Wharfies, including Jenson Chattaway (second from left) and Mike White (second from right), show their support for the Dockers. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

Frustration forging greats

The early years were tough, with very little in the way of funding. The football club instead relied on 1000 donations of $1,000 each from their original fan group, the Harbour Masters.

Fremantle and West Coast quickly became fierce rivals. (Getty Images: Mandatory Credit: ALLSPORT/Tony McDonough)

But finally purple reigned in 1999. The club won its first game at the hallowed MCG and its first Western Derby, officially stepping out of the Eagles' shadow.

"In round 10, 1999, one of the Victorian newspapers said Melbourne only had to turn up to win the game at the MCG," historian Everett said.

"Fremantle played brilliantly, Tony Modra kicked 10 goals.

" The first derby win the same year was important, after losing the first nine to the Eagles, it was just a great relief really after being trapped as the little sibling to the Eagles. "

A year later, in 2000, Matthew Pavalich joined the Dockers. Through his career, he kicked 700 goals and as captain he took the team to its first decider in 2013.

Matthew Pavlich (centre) leads his teammates onto the MCG for the AFL grand final in 2013. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The famous all-rounder played alongside dual Brownlow Medal winner Nathan Fyfe. But it was not to be, and the Hawks shattered the Dockers' premiership dream by 15 points.

Fremantle lost to Hawthorn in the 2013 grand final. (AAP Image: David Crosling)

Daring to dream again

A new generation of players has taken the Dockers to the decider once again, and for Mr Everett, this is best team Fremantle has ever fielded.

Justin Longmuir's Dockers won the minor premiership and are now seeking their first flag. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

"There is something about the way this team operates, there is a connection that makes it better than any team before," he said.

"It's been organically grown — it doesn't have any father-son gifts in it. Forged through good drafting, good trading, good development.

" That's been the story of Fremantle right from the start, it has been left to its own devices and if it wins the premiership it has done so itself. "

Even before the game began, the town was painted purple, and the team immortalised with a massive mural.

WA artist Jerome Davenport is painting the mural on the facade of Sailing for Oranges on the Cappuccino strip. (ABC News: Lucy Murray)

But the players will achieve living legend status if they can take home the club's first ever premiership flag.

"If we do win it, I'll be watching the game again, again and again. I'll know every minute of it," Mr Everett said.

" Fremantle supporters, we've put ourselves through some misery, but I have never called myself a long-suffering Fremantle supporter, I have loved it. "

World.title: Mason Cox chases second premiership after his AFL career was all but over
World.content:
Mason Cox still remembers arriving at the MCG for his first AFL grand final back in 2018.

"I took an Uber to the grand final and it ended up being like a Toyota Prius. So I was stuffed in the back of that, which is real humbling to start off the day," he said.

It may have been a humbling experience for the 211-centimetre American, but it was also not his last on the AFL's biggest day.

He returned in 2023 as the Magpies won the flag for the first time since 2010, and he will be back there again today, in what is a remarkable turn of events for the veteran.

Cox became a cult hero after winning an AFL premiership with Collingwood in 2023. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

In October last year he was delisted by Collingwood after 139 games, and at age 34, it appeared his remarkable career, which saw him plucked out of the United States and arrive at one of the biggest clubs in the land, was over.

But a month later, a lifeline came his way.

From disaster to destiny, it's taken a decade to rebuild the Dockers Football is full of sliding doors moments. Just ask the Fremantle Dockers, who crashed and burned in 2016 and are now on the cusp of winning their first-ever premiership 10 years later.

"It wasn't like I had a huge selection of people chasing after me once it all kind of happened and transpired with Collingwood," Cox said.

"I think Fremantle have been trying to get me for [a while], this is probably the third time they tried to get me."

Door opens in Dockers line-up

Cox arrived very much as backup for the established ruck pairing of Luke Jackson and Sean Darcy, before he found himself in the mix for a game.

Luke Jackson (centre) and Cox were once opponents but now make up Fremantle's ruck duo. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

Darcy missed the round six western derby due to concussion, opening the door for the American.

He took the opportunity with both hands, going on to play 19 of the next 21 games and becoming a constant in Justin Longmuir's side.

"Being an older guy, I was probably more relying on a bit of experience and just kind of seeing where the chips fall," Cox said of his expectations going into the season.

Cox kicked the go-ahead goal in last week's win over Sydney as the Dockers grabbed a grand final berth. (AAP: Dan Himbrechts)

"At the end of the day, some things have to go your way and sometimes some things don't go your way.

"Over 12 years I think I've been playing now, I've kind of gotten used to that a bit."

Cox praises talent, 'big dogs'

While Cox admitted he was not batting away offers to play on, the culture at Fremantle still impressed him.

"Day one of getting here, just seeing how hard they work and they're a young team and they've got a lot of talent," he said.

" I thought this was the best list in the comp. "

Beyond the talented playing list, which saw the Dockers finish as minor premiers with a club-record 19 wins, including a streak of 14 straight, Cox became aware of the history of the club, which struggled in the early years and is yet to taste the ultimate glory.

For Cox, it is Fremantle's culture that made an early impression on him. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

"A lot of us are understanding of just how much we're in this situation because of the people that came before us," he said.

"You talk about the big dogs before us that have set this club up to be where it's at, and the fans and supporters have kind of supported them through thick and thin.

What keeps Fremantle's purple army going? After the club's long struggle for success and on the cusp of what might be a maiden flag, Fremantle supporters reflect on why they keep coming back for more.

"We understand that we don't exist and we don't get to this position without them, and I think that's a real kind of thought process for a lot of the guys on the team.

"I think they kind of realise just how big of a deal it is for not only us but everyone around us, and then who's been able to kind of get us to this position."

If Fremantle beats Brisbane, Cox will become part of an immortal Dockers team, and will join the small list of players to have won AFL premierships at two different clubs.

Remarkable from the most unlikely of AFL players.

World.title: Stunning free kick shows Irankunda's star is aligning for Socceroos
World.content:
With some players, there's always a moment in their career that, years into the future, you can look back on as a beacon of when they truly announced themselves.

Perhaps we will be able to point to a stunning free kick for the ages as that moment in the young career of Nestory Irankunda.

Those 25,440 people lucky enough to be in Townsville to see Socceroos 1-1 Brazil will certainly never forget it.

Neither, you suspect, will Chelsea wonder kid Estêvão.

The 19-year-old probably had the best view of anyone, lying at the base of the four-man wall looking back towards Hugo Souza.

He could see, with devastating precision, the ball fly over him and into the top corner, Souza skittishly crabbing across his line before admitting defeat.

It might be fun to wonder what was going through Estêvão's mind as he rolled onto his back to stare into the sky above the Townsville stadium.

Whatever he was thinking, Irankunda was already flipping towards the corner flag.

Nestory Irankunda celebrates in emphatic style after his magical free kick. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

"I mean, good goal, good goal," he told Channel 10, the confidence of youth oozing from his voice as he was asked about his free kick.

"I've done it before and to do it again today against a top team in Brazil, it's amazing.

"Sometimes [when I try it], the ball goes outside the training ground. Sometimes I miss completely.

"For it to go in today, it felt good. You see there, beautiful."

Estêvão already had first-hand experience of Irankunda's slipperiness: on the half hour mark the Sporting forward showed brilliant balance to turn the Chelsea man and then exploded with power to dance away up field.

That, almost as much as the goal, was a moment worth remembering, an Aussie displaying the audacity to spin a Brazilian in the middle of the pitch.

"There were some big stars out tonight," Irankunda said on Channel 10, marvelling at the crowds that had come out to support both Australia and Brazil.

"But we've got some big stars too."

That is true, but already Irankunda deserves to be considered one that could burn among the brightest.

Having made the move to Portuguese giants Sporting from Watford in the off-season, Irankunda has not quite had time to make his mark yet.

Nestory Irankunda scores a stunning free kick. (Getty Images: Albert Perez)

Only once in five games has he started in the Portuguese Primeira Liga, and he is yet to provide an assist or score a goal.

But given this moment against Brazil, a team that still carries the romance of an illustrious past despite a 24-year-and-counting absence from the World Cup final, one wonders whether the ripples through the lusophone world may just nudge those in power at the Lisbon giants to afford him greater chances to prove his worth.

It certainly caught the eye of the club's social media team, who slapped a "GOLAÇO" label on it within three minutes of the net rippling 16,844 kilometres away.

Of course there must be caveats.

Brazil were most certainly off-colour, "average" according to Bruno Guimarães's damning assessment post-match.

In the first half at least, it was the Socceroos who were bossing the game, charging forward, rampaging through a fragile Brazilian midfield that still seems bruised from its last-16 defeat at the World Cup a few months ago, crafting the chances, delivering the crosses and winning the corners.

Of course Brazil started to turn it on. With the quality up front that they had, how could they not?

Endrick of Real Madrid. Raphinha of Barcelona. Estêvão of Chelsea. Vinícius Júnior of Real Madrid. Despite an atrocious pitch, which rolled up like a cheap carpet at a shabby motel, Brazil's bevvy of stars began to knock the ball around with the playful nonchalance of men who are all too aware of their own brilliance.

But it was their lesser lights, Flamengo pair Samuel Lino and Pedro, as well as Bournemouth's Rayan who finally made the breakthrough.

And it was Irankunda who provided the stand-out moment of the game.

Hopefully, Tony Popovic is telling Nestory Irankunda that he will always play him on the left. (Getty Images: Ian Hitchcock)

It is his liveliness and confidence imbues in the Socceroos a dash of verve and belief in their own abilities.

Playing on the left, cutting back inside and posing a threat from set pieces, Irankunda has the sort of aura that few Socceroos players in recent years can command.

His ability to cut back inside and unleash with that right foot, just as he did inside the opening 10 minutes to force a fine save from Hugo Souza, is explosive.

Tony Popovic only made three changes from the side that started the game against Egypt in the World Cup but playing Irankunda left was so decisive, the pain of seeing him so wasted as a target man in Dallas surely enough to forever wipe that option from Popovic's mind.

Yengi played his part centrally as a willing runner and constant menace to an inexperienced Brazilian back four, while the Seleção's pitiful midfield was readily overrun by fullbacks Jacob Italiano and Aziz Behich, with Paul Okon-Engstler's driving runs from midfield the telling factor in winning the free kick that Irankunda so magnificently placed into the net.

Brazil may prove to be better in Brisbane.

A quiet night may have those who were singing Irankunda's praises on Friday bemoaning a lack of consistency by Tuesday.

But given he is showing himself repeatedly capable of such brilliance, it seems unlikely to be long before the next career-defining moment will come along.

World.title: Heartbreak in the heart of Fremantle as thousands watch Dockers fall short
World.content:
The streets of Fremantle were flooded by a sea of purple and white as fans crammed into pubs and clubs on Saturday.

But the buzz of anticipation as their beloved team opened a 17-point lead 23 minutes into the final term quickly turned to heartbreak as the Lions kicked four unanswered goals to clinch a third consecutive flag, matching their historic 2001-2003 "three-peat".

Devastated fans are shocked and in disbelief. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

Crowds leave Fremantle heartbroken after the Dockers lost to the Lions by 7 points in the grand final. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

The street party fell silent in Fremantle, with fans in shock after the Lions' late goals let history slip for the Dockers.

Fans watched the game in the street. (ABC News: Gian De Poloni)

Fremantle decked out for Dockers' big day

Huge screens were set up at multiple locations across town for home-bound Dockers fans to cheer on their beloved team.

The sea of purple in Fremantle settled down in front of screens showing the game on the Cappuccino Strip. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

Streets were closed, public transport was free for the day, and thousands of people filled venues to capacity with lines waiting outside from early morning in anticipation of Freo's first grand final appearance since 2013.

Dockers fans were queuing for up to four hours before a Fremantle venue opened on Grand Final day. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

Flags and signs lined every wall and corner of the city centre, with purple scarves becoming the city's uniform.

Purple reigns on the streets of Fremantle. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

Earlier in the week, people walking down the famous Cappuccino Strip watched in awe as artist Jerome Davenport painted a mural in honour of the club.

"I really do hope that this inspires a few people, and the players," he said after finishing the giant work in just four days.

Jerome Davenport finished the mural, which is painted on the facade of Sailing for Oranges. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

"I sat here 13 years ago in this street and watched them the first time they were in the finals.

"What an honour to be here and be a part of it for the second time."

Businesses were decked with in purple cannolis, ice creams, beer and hot dogs.

Purple sausages are being sold at a butcher in Fremantle. (ABC News)

The local school was temporarily rebranded as the "Fremantle Dockers College" and allowed students to dress up in purple on Friday for a gold coin donation to one of the team's charities of choice, the Starlight Children's Foundation.

Principal Stan Koios said the city felt electric.

"We thought, let's get on board the euphoria that started with the Dockers and their success … let's get a bit quirky and crazy," he said.

To their fans, the Dockers are already winners. (ABC News: Cason Ho)

World.title: Neale the common thread in Fremantle and Brisbane's eerie shared history
World.content:
When Fremantle coach Ross Lyon activated his sub in the fourth quarter of the 2013 grand final against Hawthorn, he scarcely could have believed the impact that player was going to have.

On the odd occasion, the sub would come in and make a serious impact, acting as a spark plug, while on other days, their impact would be negligible.

Fremantle's sub that day came on to replace ruckman Zac Clarke and picked up seven disposals, but it was ultimately in vain as an experienced Hawthorn side held the Dockers at bay.

Fremantle's sub that day was Lachie Neale.

Lachie Neale (fourth from right) was a 20-year-old substitute when Fremantle last made a grand final appearance. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Neale, then 20, would not have believed that he would have to wait 13 years to see the Dockers in another grand final.

He also would not have believed he'd be playing against them in Brisbane colours, looking for a third straight premiership.

It is funny how time works.

Fremantle and the Brisbane Lions both entered the AFL in the mid 90s as the league was undergoing an expansion boom into states outside of Victoria.

Three-time Brisbane premiership captain Michael Voss (pictured) won a Brownlow Medal in the Bears' last season of existence. (Getty Images)

Brisbane's entry occurred as the Bears back in 1987 alongside Fremantle's WA rivals West Coast, and while the Eagles found themselves in a grand final within four years and holding the premiership cup within five, the Bears struggled.

The Lions were eventually formed in 1996 when the Bears merged with the Fitzroy Lions, another club that had been haemorrhaging money for years.

West Coast's success saw the AFL expand further into WA with Fremantle chosen as the state's second team with its inaugural season played in 1995.

It is somewhat poetic that the Dockers and Lions are playing against each other in this year's grand final when you consider how closely they are tied together right at the inception of both clubs.

Fremantle's first ever win in the AFL came against the Fitzroy Lions in round 3, 1995, while Fitzroy's last ever AFL win came against Fremantle in round 8, 1996.

Fitzroy's last ever AFL game? You guessed it, against Fremantle in Perth in round 22 of the 1996 season.

Over the three decades that have followed, both Fremantle and Brisbane have had periods of dominance, but never really at the same time until recent years.

Leigh Matthews's arrival as Brisbane's coach at the end of 1999 immediately turned the Lions into a force to be reckoned with.

Brisbane won three premierships in a row between 2001 and 2003 before losing in the 2004 grand final. (Getty Images: Hamish Blair)

Matthews masterminded Brisbane to three straight premierships and four straight grand final appearances between 2001 and 2004 before his departure and the aging of that era of Brisbane players left the club in AFL purgatory for the best part of 15 years.

Fremantle had to wait until its ninth season in the AFL to make a finals appearance, and then had to wait another three seasons before it won a final.

Since 2000, Brisbane has made the finals on 14 occasions, while Fremantle has registered 10 post-season trips, yet Brisbane has five premierships to Fremantle's zero.

And tying them together through the last 13 years has been Neale, once the best midfielder for both clubs.

Neale made his AFL debut with Fremantle in round 4, 2012, picking up seven disposals in a win over St Kilda. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Neale was drafted 58th overall by Fremantle in the 2011 draft.

He was Fremantle's fourth selection that night. The three players selected before him — Tom Sheridan, Hayden Crozier and Alex Forster — played a combined 226 games.

The grand final will be Neale's 321st appearance.

His arrival coincided with Fremantle's first real period of contention under Lyon in the early 2010s.

In Neale's first four seasons, Fremantle won the third-most home and away games in the AFL behind Hawthorn and Sydney.

In that period, the Hawks won three premierships and played in four grand finals, while the Swans played in two grand finals and won one.

Fremantle's first era of premiership contention drew to a close after losing the 2015 preliminary final to eventual premiers Hawthorn. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Fremantle came away with the one unsuccessful grand final appearance.

While Fremantle was knocking on the door of its first premiership, Brisbane was going through one of the worst periods of its existence.

By 2012, Neale's debut season, just two of Brisbane's triple premiership-winning players — Simon Black and Jonathan Brown — remained on its list.

Memories of Brisbane being one of the AFL's most feared sides were disappearing fast and players on the list originally from outside Queensland wanted to be anywhere but at the club.

The infamous 'Paddle Pop Lion' logo remains a symbol of an era of struggle for Brisbane. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Even Brisbane's logo on its jumper had changed, going from the traditional Fitzroy passant lion to a lion with a front-facing head, infamously nicknamed 'The Paddle Pop Lion'.

Fremantle won the first minor premiership in club history in 2015, with Neale becoming one of its most indispensable players, but the Dockers were again denied by Hawthorn, this time in a home preliminary final.

The Dockers cratered spectacularly the following season, dropping from first to third-last, and would not make it back to the finals for another seven seasons.

In dire need of some stability, Brisbane turned to one of the figureheads behind Hawthorn's triple premiership dynasty, Chris Fagan, to be its head coach.

Chris Fagan's arrival at Brisbane at the end of 2016 helped turn the club back into a powerhouse. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Lions struggled in Fagan's first two seasons in charge, but Neale had seen the vision and requested a trade to the then-cellar dwellers.

Had Fremantle known what he was about to become, they'd have asked for double what they received in return for him from Brisbane.

Neale's move to Brisbane put him up in lights on Broadway.

The All-Australian jackets, the Brownlow Medal wins and eventually premierships all arrived, leaving him with a resume that undoubtedly has him in the conversation as one of the best players of his generation.

His departure from Fremantle, which looked like someone getting the last life raft out of a sinking ship, proved to be a pivotal moment in the Dockers' trajectory to the grand final as well.

The following year's draft proved to be a watershed moment for Fremantle, as it supercharged its rebuild with the selections of Hayden Young and Caleb Serong.

Luke Jackson (left) and Shai Bolton's (right) arrival at Fremantle has transformed the Dockers into a premiership threat. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Having seen Brisbane supplement its young core with shrewd recruitment of seasoned players such as Neale, Charlie Cameron, Josh Dunkley and others, Fremantle has done the same, adding Luke Jackson and Shai Bolton.

For both clubs, the addition of star talent from rival clubs has resulted in an immediate uptick in on-field fortunes.

All of it leads us here, to two teams inextricably linked from their inceptions and still connected by one man.

Now that he has been freed to play, don't be surprised if that one man, Lachie Neale, has a big say in who holds the premiership cup.

Tech.title: Can Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince save the web from AI?
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Matthew Prince, who is CEO of Cloudflare. This episode is part of a two-part series on the future of business.

Matthew last joined us on the show about two and a half years ago, at what we thought then was a wild pivot point for the internet — and now it turns out things are even wilder because of AI, and Matthew and Cloudflare are right at the center of it.

Cloudflare found in June that bots made up more than half of internet traffic. That number just keeps going up as more and more AI companies scrape more and more of the web, and now as more and more AI agents try and do things for people on the web. Cloudflare sits between websites and all those agents, and allows website owners some level of control: Owners can block all those AI tools, allow them, or, as you’ll hear, only allow those that might pay money for access.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

So Matthew and I talked about how to control all these bots, what kind of mess they’re making of the web, and what kinds of information might be valuable in the future as some of the payment schemes come into focus. You’ll hear me ask pretty directly if some of the outcomes he’s describing are actually good — Matthew is a thoughtful guy, and his answer is something I’m still thinking about well after we had this conversation.

AI is also upending everything inside of Cloudflare. Earlier this year, the company laid off more than a thousand people — 20 percent of the company — and then Matthew wrote an op-ed about that decision that ran in the Wall Street Journal under the headline, “How I choose which Cloudflare employees to replace with AI.” That’s pure Decoder bait in every single dimension: AI, big controversial decisions, and org charts, all in one.

And one last thing, before we get going: You can subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Matthew Prince, CEO of Cloudflare. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Matthew Prince, you’re the cofounder and CEO of Cloudflare. Welcome back to Decoder.

Thanks for having me.

I’m really excited to talk to you again. It’s been about two years since you were on the show. I was just looking back over that episode and I said something to you like, “it’s a momentous time for the internet.” And I was not even close. It’s now an even more momentous time for the internet.

You are at the forefront of rebooting how companies work with AI. That is the most Decoder bait of all time. I want to talk about bots and the internet and publishers and Google and all the things that you are in the middle of. But let’s start at the very beginning.

Cloudflare is a complicated, important company. The last time you were on the show, you said, “Cloudflare is a service that makes the internet faster and protects it from bad guys.” Is that still how you would describe what Cloudflare does?

That’s usually what I say when I’m trying to answer a question at a cocktail party and I don’t want to talk to the person any more. What I say if I’m interested in talking to the person more is that Cloudflare is trying to rebuild the internet the way it should have been built from the beginning if we knew how important it was going to be.

We run a giant network. We’re in over 350 cities worldwide, literally thousands of data centers. We have equipment running in all those places, and then we do a handful of things. If you’re trying to put an application or content online, we make sure that it’s safe. If you’re a person or an employee online, we make sure that wherever you go online is safe. We help give people the ability to write applications that can scale to an entire internet audience and run on the infrastructure that we have. That’s the fastest-growing part of our business.

We’ve recently started to think about how the business model of the internet is changing dramatically and we’re trying to help shape what that future business model of the internet looks like and make it as healthy as possible.

Can I connect the dots between the business model of the internet, how the internet should have worked, and Cloudflare trying to build the internet as it should have been?

That is different than, “Cloudflare protects from bad guys.” I will note that’s what you said to me last time, which now makes me feel like you don’t want to talk to me at the cocktail party, but that’s fine. That’s a shift. It’s just a notable shift.

The business model of the internet has dramatically changed because of AI, because of bot traffic, because of AI scrapers, the whole thing. Describe what you think the business model of the internet is right now and what it should be.

For at least the last at least 30 years, the business model of the internet has been advertising. It’s not the entire business model of the internet, but it’s really driven all of the growth of the web and built what we all enjoy today, which really is a miracle.

The company that is responsible for that more than any other is Google, which for the last 28 years has really defined that. We all think about it for search, but they really built out all of the ecosystem around advertising online. They bought DoubleClick, they built things like Google Analytics that let you actually see who was coming to your property. It really is the hero of what I call the first generation of the internet and the first generation of the web.

What’s changing though, very quickly, is who is actually using the web, or what is using the web. Last November I was at Web Summit, the big European tech event, and I was asked, “When do you think that non-human traffic — agents and all of those things — are going to pass human traffic online?” We have a lot of data because we see a huge percentage of the internet, so we pulled all of that data and looked at it and said that in the second half of 2027, automated traffic would become larger than human traffic. It felt like a big deal that we could see that for the first time in the internet’s history.

I was asked again at South by Southwest in March of this year, 2026, and we pulled the data again and it had moved up, where it was going to then be the first half of 2027. We’re like, “Wow, this is growing. This AI thing is a big deal and people are using it like crazy and it’s driving a huge amount of traffic.”

I was stunned when just a few months later in May, the team came to me and said, “You won’t believe it, but automated traffic has now passed human traffic online.” And that’s just expanding like crazy. If you extrapolate that out, with the giant caveat that I’ve gone wrong so far in every prediction that I’ve made on this, five years from now, we think that automated traffic will be 1,000 times human traffic online. Not because human traffic is going to decline, we think it’ll stay around the same, but because we’re just seeing such an explosion in all of the rest of the traffic.

The challenge of that is, if you have 1,000 times more traffic, someone’s got to pay for the infrastructure to power that. That’s going to require bandwidth, that’s going to require servers, that’s going to require a lot of things in order to make that happen.

And, the traditional model of how to pay for that, which was advertising, doesn’t work for bots. Bots don’t click on ads. They don’t respond to pretty swirls of paint and what we traditionally think of as a brand. We’ve got to come up with something else that’s going to power that incredible insatiable demand that’s going to be put on the internet going forward. I’m spending a lot of my time trying to think about what that’s going to look like.

When you describe that as a business model, that implies that there’s going to be customers and revenue and profits. And I don’t know if any of that’s true.

There’s certainly a lot of revenue.

Well, maybe for the CloudFlares and the Googles of the world, but for the —

Or for the Anthropics of the world! Anthropic added $10 billion of revenue in a single month. There is enormous demand for these AI services. And if you’re an AI company, what you really need are three things.

You need great talent and researchers. And right now, that’s scarce. Right now we have a scarcity of people who really understand how to build these systems, but that’s going to change. Every single university in the world is standing back up their AI department. We’re training people like crazy. Labor markets are pretty efficient. We’re going to have more and more people coming into the space.

The second thing that you need is chips. You need the silicon to run these things. Today, Nvidia is the best in the world at that, but you’ve got a whole bunch of others, whether that’s AMD or Qualcomm or all the hyperscalers, that are building their own chips in order to power these things. While we have a massive shortage in the availability of silicon and the ability to actually power it up and turn it on, that’s going to change as well.

The third thing that you’ve always needed is the data to feed into all of these different models. And that’s been the one thing that I think is going to go the other direction. Historically we’ve just made the internet completely open and given bots access to all of the stuff that’s being created.

I think that’s starting to change. We’re seeing a shift where more and more of the people who are creating content, really creating information, are saying, “Maybe we’ll give that away for free to humans, but if a bot is coming for it, then bots have to pay for it because they don’t have that traditional give-to-get. We can’t put an ad in front of them and have that be something that allows me to help pay for the content creation that’s there.”

What we’re seeing actually goes back to some of the original protocols of the internet. The 403 protocol, which was written in the very first version of Netscape, was actually payment required, and you actually have to pay for the content that you’re receiving. Oh, excuse me, I said 403, it’s actually 402.

We are working with other leading companies like Coinbase and Stripe in order to say, “How do we make sure that we can allow people who are creating content, people who are doing things online, anyone who’s putting a website up, to say that in exchange for that thousands and thousands and thousands of times more traffic that’s going to come to you, you’re not going to maybe get the advertising revenue that comes from it, but maybe you can get a fraction of a penny every time somebody actually accesses that information.”

Where does that fraction of a penny come from? It comes from the fee that people are going to be paying for their AI agents and other systems that are out there, similar to how a Spotify or an Apple Music works today.

I like that we’re less than 10 minutes in and we’re already at the 1996 dream of micropayments on the web. We’re going to stick with that for one more turn here.

When I said business model, what I was really pushing at was the idea of incentives. So maybe there is some business model for information. You’re going to publish some new information and bots will come and find it and yep, the 402 protocol will come back to life and we’re going to do, I don’t know, crypto micropayments using Stripe powered by Cloudflare. That’s a version of the future that many people have talked about for a long time.

The incentives to stand all that up on the web is the thing that I’m worried about, when I say there’s a business model and customers and revenue. If I stand up a website, and I think most of my customers are going to be bots and not people, I might not do that. I might just start a TikTok channel instead, and then monetize my TikTok audience in whatever way I might want to monetize a TikTok audience. That seems like a really big inflection point right now at this second.

You mentioned Google, and I’ve asked you about this many times. The incentives to put new information on the web just seem to be in permanent decline. It just doesn’t seem like a good idea any more. On the flip side, the web as an application program, it’s like the absolute apex. Every new app that comes out is a web app, or if it’s a desktop app, it’s just Electron. There’s something happening with the web as an application platform that is incredible, and something happening to the web as an information platform that is devastating. And you’re trying to connect those dots, right? You’re trying to say we can change the incentives over here.

What’s a version of the future — maybe it’s microtransactions, maybe it’s not — where the incentives to make the web an information platform are as good as YouTube?

You’ve illustrated a tough to reconcile dichotomy that’s happening right now. If you look at things like the publicly accessible data on Wikipedia contributions, it’s down significantly, because people are like, “What’s the incentive to put information on Wikipedia?” Something that, again, people are doing for a lot of different reasons.

Back in the day, if you were contributing things to Wikipedia, you knew people were at least reading Wikipedia. Now, the interface through which people consume that information isn’t Wikipedia itself. It’s just reading the answer through whatever answer engine you’re using, whether that’s OpenAI, ChatGPT, or Anthropic Claude, or Grok on X or whatever it is. And that means that the people who are the editors of Wikipedia are saying, “Maybe it doesn’t make as much sense for me to do that.”

The flip side of that is, the web as a whole actually had been declining since about 2012. The web grew like crazy in the late ‘90s and through the 2000s. Starting around 2012, you really saw it plateauing and actually decreasing, up until about 2025, where something flipped. Starting in about October of 2025, the various vibe-coding platforms made it easy for anyone to create a website, and so more and more people were creating those applications. And as you said, even your desktop application, your mobile application, increasingly is just a wrapper around what is fundamentally a web application.

The growth of the web itself — with really high-quality stuff and a lot more people contributing to it — is faster today than it has been at any time since the early 2000s. That’s the tension between those various things.

What’s unique about Cloudflare is that because we sit in front of more than 20 percent of the web, we have the ability to overcome some of the incentives problems. We can very quickly turn something on and say, “Okay, you have to pay a fraction of a penny in order to get access to this information.” And that can kickstart the beginning of what we need.

If you don’t have something like that, we face a massive tragedy of the commons problem. Let’s say today I ask my favorite AI agent where I should go to lunch.If I were doing research, I might go look at a couple of different menus as an individual. My AI agent today goes and scans every single menu in the local area in order to figure out what’s going on. Only one of those places is going to actually get my lunch dollars. If that just expands infinitely, if there’s no cost to doing that, at some point my agent’s just going to look at literally every resource that’s available everywhere on the internet, and then come back and say, “You know, you should go to Wendy’s.”

That’s an enormous waste. We’ve got to have something saying that there’s a cost every time you load a webpage. There’s bandwidth, there are servers, there are things that are behind that, and someone has to pay for that. If it’s not going to be advertising and it’s not going to be direct commerce, then there has to be something that actually puts some constraints there. We are in a good place to say, yeah, it can be a tiny amount of money, a thousandth of a penny or something like that. But that’s enough that we can actually start to say, okay, that will help pay for the infrastructure.

If you have incredibly valuable content, if you’re a news publisher or you’re an academic, then maybe there’s a premium on top of that that you charge and say, “Hey, I’m not going to give you this content unless you pay even more for it, but I believe that it’s valuable and we can create a market for it.”

In order for that to happen, you’ve got to have a player like us that’s in the market that can kickstart that. But once you kickstart it, we’ve seen from the side of the buyers, the big AI companies, that they’re all willing to do this. We’ve seen from the side of the sellers, the big content creators, that they’re all really excited about this. What’s really been lacking is the technology that links those things together, and that’s what we’re spending a lot of time building.

It feels like the theoretical underpinning of this conversation is the very notion of scarcity itself. I’m an old copyright lawyer, and copyright law for years and years and years had a built-in mechanism to be important, which was that one copy of a CD was one copy of a CD. And if you wanted another one, it was pretty hard to make another copy of a CD. Even when it got easy, you still needed another physical CD-R, and that imposed some cost on how many copies you could make, and then it was hard to distribute them.

All of that went away with the internet. We moved everything to digital files and the burden of making another copy fell to zero. And I think a bunch of consumers expected everything would be free. There’s that famous quote, “Information wants to be free.” There’s a second half of that quote everyone forgets, which is, “Information also wants to be expensive because it’s hard to generate.” And the internet just turned that upside down.

The gating mechanism of physical media, which provided some scarcity, and thus some economic value that you could measure, went away and we decided information should be zero and maybe supported by advertising. There was actually a tension that became valuable, because that was scarce in its way. You’re talking about imposing scarcity with your technology.

We always talk about markets needing supply and demand. That’s not exactly right. You need demand for sure, and you want infinite demand ideally, or as much demand as you can get. Infinite would probably be bad, because then it would be hard to discover price, but you want demand.

And then, you actually want constrained supply. There’s no market for air where either of us are sitting right now, because there’s plenty of air. But if we go scuba diving, then all of a sudden there’s a market for air, because air is constrained underwater, and so you have to buy it in order to be able to do it.

Music is the example that I look to when I think about what this could look like in the future. I flew up to Stockholm to meet with Daniel Ek, who started Spotify, and it was just a fascinating conversation. If you think about the history of music, once upon a time, the majority of music sales were from CDs or albums or whatever it was. And then, along came the internet and along with it, Napster and Grokster and Kazaa, and all of the things that essentially commodified music and made it available for free for everyone. Even if you’re an incredibly law-abiding human, the majority of people were just downloading music because they wanted access to music.

If you go back 23 years, the music industry in total was valued at about $8 billion, which is a lot of money, but it’s not a lot of money for the entire music industry. That’s The Beatles and The Rolling Stones and everything else. But people were like, “We can’t make any money off of this.”

And then, Steve Jobs steps on stage, and announces iTunes and that it’s going to be 99 cents a song, but they include cover art and they’re going to make sure it’s high-quality and all these things.

But mostly it appealed to this emotion of, “you should be paying for music.” Now, that’s not the business model that won, but it was a flag in the ground that said that this information is actually worth paying for, and it’s really valuable. And it was the iTunes that then eventually begat the Spotifys of the world. And the incredible thing is, just last year, Spotify sent something like $12 billion back into the music creator ecosystem. We can debate whether the right people are getting it and whether it’s fairly allocated.

This is my favorite thing to argue about because I think whatever happens to the music industry happens to everybody else five years later. So I spend a lot of time thinking about it.

And the turn there, which I think is fascinating and is either good or bad, is that the amount paid or the music files themselves became very small. You can get a million streams on Spotify and you’re not making any money, but the amount generated by touring, commercial sponsorships, sync licensing, and advertising all skyrocketed.

That’s just simply not true.

Why is private equity buying all of the music catalogs for hundreds of millions of dollars? The answer is because actually making money off the streaming of the music is extremely lucrative. Spotify alone is sending $12 billion back to the music industry, back to the actual rights holders behind these various things.

There’s way more money coming from Spotify into this than there is from touring or any of the other things that are there. Those are other ways to make money, but it’s the streaming that is really driving all of the real growth.

I just want to draw a distinction here. You’re not here to argue with me about music, which is my favorite thing to do, so I apologize for just doing it. But private equity is going to make that money, not the musicians. They’re paying some of the catalog holders for some of the things, but that money flooding in —

If The Beatles or The Rolling Stones or whoever’s the latest ones to sell their music catalogs had held onto the music catalogs, then the musicians would’ve made that. They are making the determination. And when they sell the rights, they get the check.

They do get the check, but the comparison I’m making here —

If you win the lottery, is it better for you to take the annuity of payments over the course of the next 50 years or to take the lump sum up front? That’s the trade-off that they’re making, but there’s more money going into music creation at this point in time than there ever has been in human history. Technology is not inherently a destroyer of value of information. In this case, it has been a massive enabler of value and allowed people to find audiences, and yes, sell more tickets to their concerts as well.

That’s actually the model that we need to think about. How do we take what Spotify has done, which is to say we pool together the resources of a bunch of people that are paying for access to the entire catalog of music, and then give that back to musicians based on some sort of algorithm that hopefully rewards real value creation.

What if you had the same thing where with a portion of what is being paid for for the various AI companies, you had to pay for the researchers that built the AI systems and you had to pay for the chips, but also to pay for the content, which is actually the real knowledge that is training these things? That’s exactly the type of model that you need to actually unlock what could be a real golden age of information creation.

The comparison I’m making is not whether a bunch of aging rock stars are going to sell their catalogs and cash out because they’re old. That’s fine. They can do that. It’s more that the shift you’re describing, into gaining access, into wide open access on Spotify to every song ever made, and then we’re going to move some pennies around and some people get rich, and we’ll create some winners and losers, fundamentally change the entire business model of music.

The conversation with Dan was fascinating, but one of the things he said was he said, “Okay, listen, if you go onto Spotify and you search for Taylor Swift, ‘Shake It Off,’” they return a result and they’re pretty sure that they have given you what you are looking for.”

On the other hand, if you go to Spotify and you search for, “I want a song to a disco beat about how much fun it is to dance with my cat,” there aren’t a lot of songs like that out there. They know that whatever they return is a pretty bad result. But the interesting thing is what happens next. They then take those searches for things that they don’t have good results for, and they publish that back to music creators.

There’s something that’s pretty amazing about that. They’re saying, “Here’s an emotion that someone is searching for, which we don’t have a good answer for, which we’re then going to go and publish back to music creators.

This is one of those moments where everyone’s going to be like, “I’m in the wrong profession.” There’s a guy in Denmark, who makes 40 million euros a year writing songs for unfulfilled Spotify queries, and he’s not alone. He’s the most successful, but there’s a whole bunch of people that are making literally millions of euros or millions of dollars a year doing this thing, writing songs for what people are searching for that isn’t out there.

Now extrapolate that to the next level. For the first time in human history, we’ve built a mathematical model of human knowledge. That’s what the LLMs are. We know where they know things, but we also know where they’re missing things. I picture it like a giant block of Swiss cheese, and there’s a lot of cheese, but there’s a lot of holes in the cheese.

The really interesting thing is, when you talk to the leaders at the big AI companies and you say, “What do you want to pay for?” They don’t want yet another story about what’s happening at 1500 Pennsylvania Avenue [sic], which is what the current media environment is feeding us like crazy. What they want is to fill in the holes in the cheese. They want new knowledge that no one ever knew about before.

I have an example where this is actually working: My wife and I own a small local newspaper in our hometown of Park City, Utah. I think we will make more money off AI licensing deals this year than we do off digital advertising. Local media is exactly the sort of thing that is much more valuable in the media world that we’re going into, but was completely decimated in the media world that we are coming out of, where what mattered was volume and scale and dividing things. Whereas local media is all about, let’s tell you about the cool new restaurant that just opened down the street.

If you’re an AI company, and you want to be able to be the best travel planner that’s out there, you want to have artificial general intelligence, you need to know what the hot new restaurant is in Park City, Utah. And if you don’t have access to the Park Record, our newspaper, you don’t know that.

We’re not going to protect all media. In the same way that with the move to Spotify, there are a whole bunch of losers in the musician space, but there are going to be new winners, like that person in Denmark who’s creating things off unfulfilled Spotify queries.

The winners in this new space might actually be the kind of things that people really want to come back to media: more local news, more unique things, more Reddits of the world, more of what the internet used to be when I was first on it in the ‘90s. I think that’s actually what most internet users are craving. And I think if we get the incentives right, we actually have a way of incentivizing more of that unique original content as opposed to what we have today, which is a media ecosystem that is largely just rage-baiting people into clicking on things so that they can serve them an ad.

One of the things you would need to build in order to make that work is a way to stop the AI crawlers, to stop the model companies from showing up. Just today, there’s yet another lawsuit. The music companies are going to sue Anthropic. The White House came out in support of OpenAI in its case against The New York Times today, saying that training should be fair use.

I think I need to disclose that in some series of corporate mergers, The Verge’s parent company is now suing Google in some way. I have literally nothing to do with it. It’s just all that. It’s all the swirl, right? And that is a legal swirl.

We’re going to use the law to say, “This is illegal and we’ll punish you if you do the bad thing.” That’s just up for grabs. Those are 50/50 and maybe existential problems.

Maybe not. The law right now in the US is different than everywhere else, and so you’ve got this patchwork around it. But the best case on this is part of the Anthropic case, where the judge basically said that training is fair use against all the books. And by the way, you shouldn’t have stolen the books. So when you’re building technology, you’re keeping that in the back of your mind, right? The market is coming to some sort of understanding of what’s valuable and what’s not, and you need to stop them from showing up —

Different regulations are going to be passed in different places around the world. Again, as an also recovering intellectual property attorney, I very quickly go to like, “Oh, let’s just use intellectual property.” But that’s such a kluge versus the much easier thing, which is, let’s just use technology.

I remember sitting with a bunch of media execs and they’re like, “Oh, how are we going to stop these nerds in Palo Alto from scraping our stuff?”

And I was like, “I go to war every day with North Korean and Iranian and Chinese hackers.” They’re really good at it and they hide. Whereas the nerds in Palo Alto have a Delaware-based C-corporation. What we’re seeing is actually much more of them being willing to say, “Listen, we will specifically identify when we are coming to a site that it is us, that you can rely on us, and we’ll tell you exactly what we’re doing, so that you can have the right to control how that information is being taken.”

I think that was an interesting question, like, two years ago. But even the Googles of the world, who have been at times challenging through this — Google is sort of like a Marvel character, like the hero of yesterday becomes the villain of tomorrow. The challenge has been that they’re like, “We struck all these deals to get access to all the internet and now we can use it for whatever we want.”

We were like, “Eh, in the past you were sending people traffic. Now you’re training on things and sending them no traffic. That’s a different give-to-get.” And what I’ve been really actually impressed by with the Google team is that they are much more willing to engage here. They understand the value of the ecosystem. There are people at Google who really do believe in making sure that there is a healthy, sustainable ecosystem going forward.

Some of the things that they’ve already committed to around transparency of their crawler, and some of the things that I expect that they will do over the next little bit, I think that’s a good sign and it’s going to make it so that if even Google is doing it and is willing to say, “I’ll announce what I’m doing, and in many cases I’ll even be willing to pay for content,” that actually makes it even easier to convince all of the other AI companies to do the same.

Do you think you need to turn the screws all the way and actually block the Google crawlers to get them to pay?

As of September 15th, we’re going to set the defaults across all of our free customers for it to be that Google is going to be blocked for AI training, but if they won’t differentiate between AI training and search engine training, we’re just going to block them across the board.

If you’re a site owner, you’re like, “I don’t want that to be for me,” we’ll make it easy for you to turn it off. It’s just about what we set the defaults to.

But I’m really encouraged that the good forces at Google are realizing that this has to be a healthy ecosystem, and that they have to play by somewhat the same rules for this new AI market that everyone else is playing by, and that they can’t leverage the monopoly that they had in search yesterday to create a monopoly in AI tomorrow.

I’ve talked to Sundar [Pichai, Google CEO] about this many times. I don’t think he loves the fact that I am the person who keeps calling it Google Zero, but so be it. Sundar is very thoughtful. He’s very kind. Every time I talk to him, I get the sense that what he wants to say is, “Well, you didn’t do anything about it. All you publishers are complaining. This feels like the something. We’re going to block the Google search traffic. We’re going to block the crawler. I think the CEO of People Inc. is talking about literally blocking Google.

Steve [Huffman, CEO] at Reddit has really become more aggressive in this line. Google doesn’t work if it can’t search these things. And it’s actually more existential for them.

The very nature of how Google’s search ranking works is it builds a tree. That’s what page rank was. It sort of says, “Okay, here’s a super reputable thing and then let’s see how it’s connected to everything else that’s online.”

The problem is, with Cloudflare being 20-plus percent of the internet, if that just disappears, that’s in a giant hole in the middle of the tree. It doesn’t just break it for this, it breaks it for everything. That’s what we realized, that on behalf of and in conjunction with a lot of our customers, we could say, “Listen, this isn’t fair anymore. You are creating costs, you are taking content, you are getting value from that content, either in terms of the subscriptions that you’re selling to your AI tools, or to the ads that you’re running against that.
